a.etymology: The preposition a continues Latin ad ('to, toward, at'). It marks motion toward a destination, clock schedules (a las ocho), indirect objects, and specific human direct objects.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: a

a.notes: Before masculine singular article el, a + el contracts obligatorily into the single word al (al patio, al mediodía).

aakif.etymology: Romanization of the Arabic male given name ʿĀkif (عَاكِف, 'devoted, assiduous, cleaving to worship'), active participle of the root verb ʿakafa ('to devote oneself, remain secluded in a mosque'). In Paquita Salas, it appears as the given name of actor Aakif Ndel, which Paquita comically misreads as 'Aquí Fandel'.

sources.title: Wiktionary — عاكف (Arabic)

aakif.notes: In Spanish casting dialogue, unfamiliar double vowels and pharyngeal consonants in foreign stage names are often nativized to the nearest Spanish word—here turning Aakif into aquí ('here').

abajo.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the preposition a ('to, toward') and bajo ('low, underneath'), descending from Late Latin bassus ('thick, low in stature').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abajo
Wiktionary — abajo

abandonar.etymology: Borrowed from Old French abandoner ('to surrender to someone's control, let go, forsake'), built on the phrase a bandon ('at one's disposal, without restraint'), from Frankish *bann ('proclamation, jurisdiction').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abandonar
Wiktionary — abandonar

abandonar.notes: Covers everything from dramatically deserting someone to simply stepping out of a room or theater hall (abandonar la sala).

ablandar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Spanish from a- + blando ('soft, gentle') + -ar, ultimately from Latin blandus ('flattering, smooth, soft to the touch').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ablandar
Wiktionary — ablandar

abogado.etymology: Inherited from Latin advocātus ('one called to aid, legal counsel'), the substantivized past participle of advocāre (ad- + vocāre 'to call, summon'), with regular voicing of -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abogado
Wiktionary — abogado

abouk.etymology: Stage surname of Madrid-born Spanish actress Hiba Abouk (born Hiba Aboukhris Benslimane), shortened from the Maghrebi Arabic family name Abū Khrīs, formed with the Arabic patronymic element abū ('father of').

morphemes.meaning: father of (< Arabic abū, French-influenced Maghrebi spelling)

history.meaning: clipped professional surname of Hiba Abouk

sources.title: Wiktionary — أبو (Arabic)

abouk.notes: Hiba Abouk rose to fame across Spain in the hit Telecinco crime series El Príncipe (2014–2016) and is referenced in Paquita Salas as an A-list Spanish TV star.

abrigado.etymology: Participial adjective of abrigar ('sheltered, warm, bundled up'), which descends from Late Latin aprīcāre ('to warm in the sun, protect from cold'), derived from Classical Latin aprīcus ('exposed to the sun').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abrigado
Wiktionary — abrigado

abrigo.etymology: Deverbal noun from abrigar ('to shelter from the cold, wrap up warm'), descending from Late Latin aprīcāre ('to warm in the sun'), from Classical Latin aprīcus ('sunny').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abrigo
Wiktionary — abrigo

abril.etymology: Inherited from Latin aprīlis (mēnsis Aprīlis, 'the month of April'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -p- to -b- and apocope of the final vowel.

history.meaning: April, fourth month of the Roman calendar

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abril
Wiktionary — abril

abrir.etymology: Abrir continues Latin aperīre ('to uncover, open'), with regular syncope of the unstressed internal vowel and voicing of -p- to -b- between vowels.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abrir

abrir.notes: Conjugates regularly in the present and preterite (abro, abrió), while preserving the irregular Latin-derived past participle abierto.

absoluto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin absolūtus ('complete, unrestricted, unconditional'), past participle of absolvere (ab- + solvere 'to loosen, set free').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: absoluto
Wiktionary — absoluto

abuela.etymology: Feminine form of abuelo, descending from Vulgar Latin *aviŏla (diminutive of Classical Latin avia 'grandmother', alongside masculine *aviŏlus from avus 'grandfather').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abuelo
Wiktionary — abuela

abuelo.etymology: The DLE traces abuelo to Vulgar Latin *aviŏlus, a diminutive built on Classical Latin avus ('grandfather, ancestor').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abuelo

abuelo.notes: Feminine la abuela means grandmother, while plural los abuelos can refer collectively to both grandparents.

aburrido.etymology: Participial adjective of aburrir ('bored; boring'), which evolved from Latin abhorrēre ('to shrink back from, detest'), shifting semantically in Spanish from causing aversion or weariness to boring.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aburrido
Wiktionary — aburrido

aburrir.etymology: Inherited from Latin abhorrēre ('to shrink back from, shudder at, detest'), compounded from ab- ('away from') + horrēre ('to bristle, tremble'). In Castilian its sense softened from 'to loathe or drive to despair' into 'to weary, bore'.

cognates.meaning: to regard with disgust (learned Latin borrowing)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aburrir
Wiktionary — aburrir

aburrir.notes: Used reflexively as aburrirse ('to get bored': aburrirme hasta morir, 'to bore myself to death'), while transitive aburrir means 'to bore someone'.

acabado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from acabar ('finished, completed; final surface finish'), formed from a- + cabo ('end, extremity'), from Vulgar Latin *capum (Classical Latin caput 'head').

history.meaning: to bring to an end, finish

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acabado
Wiktionary — acabado

acabar.etymology: Formed in Romance from a- + cabo ('end, extremity'), literally 'to bring to the end or head', from Vulgar Latin *capum for Classical Latin caput ('head').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acabar
Wiktionary — acabar

acabo.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of acabar ('to finish, complete'), formed in Romance as a parasynthetic verb from a- ('to') + cabo ('end, extremity', from Vulgar Latin *capum for Classical Latin caput 'head') + -ar.

history.meaning: to bring to an end, finish
I finish; (with de) I have just

cognates.meaning: to complete, finish off (from chef < caput)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acabar
Wiktionary — acabo

acabo.notes: Most frequent in the verbal periphrasis acabo de + infinitive ('I have just done something': acabo de llegar de Los Ángeles).

accidente.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin accidēns, accidentis ('chance occurrence, mishap'), substantivized present participle of accidere (ad- + cadere 'to fall upon, happen').

history.meaning: to fall upon, happen by chance

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: accidente
Wiktionary — accidente

acción.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āctiōnem (nominative āctiō, 'a putting in motion, doing, dramatic performance, legal action'), action noun from agere ('to drive, do, act on stage').

history.meaning: action; film/stage cue; share of stock

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acción
Wiktionary — acción

acción.notes: On film sets ¡Acción! is the director's cue to start rolling, while de acción labels the action genre.

aceite.etymology: The DLE traces aceite to Hispanic Arabic azzáyt, from Classical Arabic zayt ('olive juice, olive oil'), with the Arabic definite article al- assimilated to z-, ultimately from Aramaic zaytā ('olive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aceite

aceite.notes: Replaced Latin oleum in everyday Spanish, while oliva survived alongside aceituna (< azzaytúna).

acento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin accentus ('song added to speech, vocal pitch, intonation'), a morphological calque of Ancient Greek prosōidía built from ad- ('to') + cantus ('song, chant', from canere 'to sing').

history.meaning: song sung to music, pitch accent (calqued into Latin)
spoken accent, stress, written accent mark

rootFamily.gloss: to accentuate, place an accent mark on

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acento
Wiktionary — acento

acento.notes: Spanish distinguishes acento prosódico (spoken syllable stress), tilde or acento ortográfico (the written mark ´), and regional/foreign pronunciation (poner acento argentino).

aceptar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin acceptāre ('to receive willingly, welcome'), the frequentative of accipere (ad- + capere 'to take, receive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aceptar
Wiktionary — aceptar

acera.etymology: Evolved from older Spanish facera ('row of house fronts along a street, sidewalk edge'), derived from faz ('face, facade', from Latin faciēs) + -era.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acera
Wiktionary — acera

acercar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from a- + cerca ('near, close by') + -ar, ultimately from Latin circā ('around, near').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acercar
Wiktionary — acercar

acercarla.etymology: Infinitive acercar ('to bring closer') with the enclitic feminine singular direct-object pronoun -la ('her/it'). Acercar is a parasynthetic verb built from a- + cerca ('near', from Late Latin circa 'around', related to circus 'ring') + -ar, while -la continues Latin illam.

morphemes.meaning: her / it (feminine direct object < Latin illam)

cognates.meaning: to bring near / to seek (shared circa root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acercar
Wiktionary — acercar

acercarla.notes: In Spanish, unstressed object pronouns attach directly to the end of infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative imperatives as one orthographic word (acercarla, acercándola, acércala).

acero.etymology: Acero descends from Late Latin aciārium ('steeled weapon edge'), a derivative of Classical Latin aciēs ('sharp edge, point').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acero

acero.notes: Used for tempered metal in blades, tools, and high-tension piano strings.

acoger.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accolligere ('to gather in, receive, shelter'), formed from Latin ad- + colligere ('to collect, gather together').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acoger
Wiktionary — acoger

acordar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accordāre ('to bring hearts or minds together, reconcile, recall to heart'), formed from ad- ('to') + cor, cordis ('heart', the seat of memory and judgment in Roman thought).

history.meaning: to bring into agreement, recall to heart
to agree upon; (acordarse de) to remember

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acordar
Wiktionary — acordar

acordar.notes: Stem-changing (o -> ue: me acuerdo). Non-reflexive acordar means 'to agree on', whereas pronominal acordarse de means 'to remember' (¿Te acuerdas de mi prima?).

acordarse.etymology: Pronominal form of acordar ('to remember, call to mind'), from Vulgar Latin *accordāre ('to bring into harmony or back to one's heart/mind'), built on Latin cor, cordis ('heart, seat of memory').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acordar
Wiktionary — acordarse

acorde.etymology: Deverbal noun from acordar ('to tune, harmonize', influenced by French accord and Italian accordo), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *accordāre (< Latin cor, cordis 'heart', or influenced by chorda 'musical string').

history.meaning: to bring into agreement or harmony

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acorde
Wiktionary — acorde

action.etymology: Unadapted English film-directing command ('Action!'), borrowed in English via Anglo-Norman and Old French action from Latin āctiōnem ('doing, dramatic performance', from agere 'to act, set in motion').

history.meaning: director's cue to begin a take

sources.title: Wiktionary — action (English)

action.notes: Used playfully in English during self-tape auditions for international castings in Paquita Salas alongside native ¡Acción!

actor.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āctor, āctōrem ('driver, doer, stage performer, pleader'), agent noun formed with -tor from agere ('to drive, perform, act').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actor
Wiktionary — actor

actor.notes: Unlike English, where 'actor' increasingly covers all genders, Spanish consistently pairs masculine actor with feminine actriz in everyday usage.

actrices.etymology: Regular plural of actriz ('actress'), formed with -es (orthographically changing final -z to -c- before -e to preserve the /θ/ or /s/ sound). Actriz descends as a learned borrowing from Latin āctrīcem (nominative āctrīx), feminine agent noun of agere ('to perform').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actriz
Wiktionary — actrices

actrices.notes: Every Spanish singular ending in -z rewrites z as c in the plural before -es: actriz -> actrices, voz -> voces, vez -> veces.

actriz.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āctrīcem (nominative āctrīx, 'female agent or stage performer'), the feminine counterpart of āctor built with the Latin female agent suffix -trīx on the supine stem of agere ('to act, perform').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actriz
Wiktionary — actriz

actriz.notes: Standard, neutral occupational term in Spanish for a woman who acts in theater, film, or television; plural las actrices.

actual.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin āctuālis ('active, practical, belonging to present reality'), derived from Latin āctus ('act, activity', from agere 'to do'). Under French actuel influence, the temporal sense 'present-day, current' became primary.

morphemes.meaning: act, reality in motion (< Latin āctus)

cognates.meaning: real, existing in fact (semantic false friend)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actual
Wiktionary — actual

actual.notes: Classic false friend for English speakers: Spanish actual means 'current, topical, up-to-date' (muy actual), whereas English 'actual' translates as real, verdadero, or efectivo.

actuar.etymology: The DLE traces actuar to Medieval Latin actuare, from Latin actus. Spanish uses it both for taking action or behaving in a certain way and for performing on stage or screen.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actuar

actuar.notes: Present-tense singular and third-person plural forms carry a written accent on ú to mark hiatus (actúo, actúa, actúan).

acústico.etymology: Learned borrowing via scientific French or New Latin from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós, 'of or for hearing'), derived from ἀκούειν (akoúein, 'to hear').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: acústico
Wiktionary — acústico

adaptar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin adaptāre ('to fit or adjust to something'), compounded from ad- ('to') + aptāre ('to fit, join', from aptus 'fitted, suitable').

history.meaning: to adapt (a script, work, or oneself)

cognates.meaning: to adjust or rework for a new medium

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adaptar

adaptar.notes: Notice the remarkable doublet: inherited Latin aptāre eroded phonetically into Spanish atar ('to tie'), while learned adaptar entered later intact for reworking novels or plays for stage and screen.

adelante.etymology: Formed from a- + delante ('in front, ahead'), which evolved by dissimilation from Old Spanish denante, a compound of Late Latin dē + in + ante ('from before, forward').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adelante
Wiktionary — adelante

adelgazar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Spanish from a- + delgado ('thin, slender') + -ar (with -d- + -izar/-iar palatalized to -zar via Vulgar Latin *addelicātiāre or romance derivation on delgado), ultimately from Latin dēlicātus ('delicate, fine, slender').

history.meaning: to lose weight; to make thinner

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adelgazar
Wiktionary — adelgazar

adelgazar.notes: Works intransitively without a reflexive pronoun to mean 'to lose weight' (he adelgazado tres kilos), paired with its antonym engordar ('to gain weight').

además.etymology: Formed by compounding a + demás ('the rest, besides'), itself from de + más, descending from Latin dē + magis ('more, in addition').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: además
Wiktionary — además

adivinar.etymology: Inherited from Latin dīvīnāre ('to foresee, prophesy, guess by inspiration'), prefixed with a- in Romance, from dīvīnus ('divine, prophetic').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adivinar
Wiktionary — adivinar

adiós.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase a Dios ('to God', elliptic for a Dios seas encomendado 'may you be commended to God'), from Latin ad Deum.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adiós
Wiktionary — adiós

adoquín.etymology: Borrowed from Hispanic Arabic addukkán ('stone bench, squared paving block'), from Classical Arabic dukkān ('bench, platform'), of Aramaic and ultimately Sumerian origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adoquín
Wiktionary — adoquín

adorar.etymology: The DLE derives adorar from Latin adorāre. Spanish retains the religious sense of worship and also uses the verb colloquially for liking something or someone very much.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adorar

adorar.notes: Unlike gustar and encantar, adorar takes the person who feels affection as its grammatical subject (adoro el pan recién hecho).

adónde.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the directional preposition a ('to', < Latin ad) and the interrogative adverb dónde ('where', itself from de + onde < Latin dē + unde 'from where').

morphemes.meaning: where (< de + onde < Latin dē unde)

cognates.meaning: whence, from where (shared dē unde base)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adónde
Wiktionary — adónde

adónde.notes: Carries a written accent in direct and indirect questions of motion (¿Adónde vas?); the RAE also accepts two-word ¿a dónde?, while unaccented adonde serves as a relative adverb.

aeropuerto.etymology: Twentieth-century compound modeled on French aéroport and English airport, combining the Greco-Latin combining form aero- ('air, aviation', from Ancient Greek āḗr 'air') with Spanish puerto ('port, harbor', inherited from Latin portus with regular diphthongization o > ue).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aeropuerto

aeropuerto.notes: Keep all four vowels distinct in the initial hiatus a-e-ro-puer-to (/aeɾoˈpweɾto/), avoiding the English-style 'airo-' reduction.

afinar.etymology: Formed within Spanish from a- + fino ('fine, pure, exact') + -ar, literally 'to make fine or exact in pitch'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: afinar

afinar.notes: Applies both to bringing musical strings to exact pitch and to refining a craft or detail.

aflojar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + flojo ('loose, slack') + -ar, descending from Latin fluxus ('flowing, slack, loose').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aflojar
Wiktionary — aflojar

agarrar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from a- + garra ('claw, clutching hand') + -ar, literally 'to seize with the claws or hand'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agarrar
Wiktionary — agarrar

agarro.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of agarrar ('to grab, seize, catch hold of'), a parasynthetic verb formed from a- + garra ('claw, talon') + -ar. Spanish garra is probably an alteration of earlier garfa ('hook, claw'), of debated pre-Roman Celtic or Andalusi Arabic origin.

history.meaning: to seize with claws, grab firmly

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agarrar
Wiktionary — agarro

agarro.notes: In Spain, everyday 'take/catch' (a bus, a role) is coger, while agarrar specifically emphasizes grabbing firmly so someone or something doesn't slip away (Si no la agarro, se nos escapa); in much of Latin America, agarrar replaces coger generally.

agencia.etymology: The DLE traces agencia to Medieval Latin agentia, built on the Latin present participle agens ('one who acts or does'). Spanish uses it for a branch office or a service business such as a travel agency.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agencia

agencia.notes: Agencia is feminine (la agencia de viajes) despite containing the masculine-looking root agente.

agenda.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin agenda ('things to be done'), neuter plural gerundive of agere ('to do, carry out'). In Spanish and French it specialized first into a personal appointment book or diary, and later also a meeting schedule.

morphemes.meaning: Latin neuter plural reanalyzed as feminine singular

cognates.meaning: list of meeting items; underlying plan

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agenda
Wiktionary — agenda

agenda.notes: Partial false friend: in Spain, la agenda most often means a physical or digital daily planner/calendar and address book (míralo en la agenda), whereas a formal meeting 'agenda' is el orden del día.

agobiado.etymology: Participial adjective of agobiar ('to weigh down, overwhelm, stifle'), probably descending from Vulgar Latin *aggobbāre ('to bend double, hunch under a load'), built on Late Latin gobbus ('humpbacked'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek kýphos ('hump, bent').

morphemes.meaning: bend down, hunch under weight (< Late Latin gobbus)

history.meaning: humpbacked -> to bow down under a burden

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agobiar
Wiktionary — agobiado

agobiado.notes: One of the most quintessential Peninsular Spanish emotional adjectives: estar agobiado/a captures feeling claustrophobic, swamped with work, or emotionally pressured all at once.

agobió.etymology: Third-person singular preterite indicative of agobiar ('to overwhelm, bow down under pressure'; pronominally agobiarse 'to panic or feel overwhelmed'), traced to Vulgar Latin *aggobbāre ('to bend double') from Late Latin gobbus ('humpbacked').

morphemes.meaning: bend under a load (< Late Latin gobbus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agobiar
Wiktionary — agobió

agobió.notes: With se, preterite se agobió pinpoints a sudden moment of panic or claustrophobic overload ('she got overwhelmed and bolted').

agradable.etymology: Derived from agradar ('to please') + -ble, built on grado ('will, pleasure, liking') from Latin grātum ('pleasing, welcome').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agradable
Wiktionary — agradable

agua.etymology: Agua descends directly from Latin aqua ('water'), showing regular Western Romance voicing of intervocalic -qu- to -gu-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agua

agua.notes: Agua is feminine, taking el in the singular solely to avoid two adjacent stressed /a/ vowels (el agua fría, las aguas claras).

aguantar.etymology: Borrowed from Italian agguantare ('to seize firmly, grasp with a glove, hold fast'), formed from a- + guanto ('glove', from Frankish *want 'mitten, gauntlet'). In Spanish the image of gripping tightly broadened into 'bearing weight, holding back, putting up with'.

morphemes.meaning: glove, firm grip (< Italian guanto < Frankish *want)

history.meaning: glove -> to seize firmly, hold fast
to endure, hold in, put up with

cognates.meaning: armored glove (via French gant from Frankish *want)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aguantar
Wiktionary — aguantar

aguantar.notes: Extremely versatile everyday verb: no lo puedo aguantar means either 'I can't stand him/it' or 'I can't hold the secret/urge in any longer'.

ah.etymology: Natural expressive interjection continuing Latin ah, used to voice sudden realization, surprise, relief, or admiration.

history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, realization, or emotion

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ah
Wiktionary — ah

ahora.etymology: Ahora developed from older agora. The DLE traces agora to the Latin phrase hac hora, meaning at this hour, so a phrase about the current hour became the everyday word for now.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ahora
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agora

ahora.notes: Ahora mismo emphasises the present moment or current situation.

ahí.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish aí, from Vulgar Latin *ad ibī ('there, at that place'), combining Latin ad ('to, at') and ibī ('there').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ahí
Wiktionary — ahí

aire.etymology: Inherited through Old Spanish from Latin āēr, accusative āerem ('air, atmosphere'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, 'lower air, mist, atmosphere').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aire
Wiktionary — aire

aislante.etymology: Active participial adjective and noun derived from aislar ('to isolate, insulate') + -nte, built on isla ('island', < Latin īnsula) with reinforcement from Italian isolare.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aislante
Wiktionary — aislante

ajo.etymology: Inherited from Latin āllium (variant alium, 'garlic'), showing the regular Castilian palatalization and velarization of Latin -li- + vowel: āllium > Old Spanish allo / ajo (/ʒ/ > Modern Spanish /x/).

rootFamily.gloss: garlic-and-oil emulsion (via Catalan all i oli)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ajo
Wiktionary — ajo

ajo.notes: Pan de ajo ('garlic bread') and gambas al ajillo are staples, and un diente de ajo ('a tooth of garlic') is the Spanish idiom for 'a clove of garlic'.

ajá.etymology: Expressive reduplicated vocalic interjection (related to ah) used to signal approval, agreement, or sudden understanding.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ajá
Wiktionary — ajá

al.etymology: Al is the obligatory Spanish contraction of preposition a ('to, at') + masculine singular definite article el ('the'), formed in medieval Castilian.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: al
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: a
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

al.notes: Also introduces an infinitive to express 'upon doing' (al salir de la puerta = upon stepping out the door).

ala.etymology: First half of the Spanish TVE sitcom title ¡Ala... Dina! (2000–2002), a playful wordplay splitting Aladina (feminine of Aladino, from Arabic ʿAlāʾ ad-Dīn 'nobility of the faith') into the Peninsular Spanish expressive interjection ¡hala! / ¡ala! ('wow!, come on!') and the name Dina.

history.meaning: expressive exclamation blended with female genie name
2000–2002 TVE comedy series starring Paz Padilla and Lidia San José

rootFamily.gloss: come on!, wow! (standard spelling of the interjection)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hala
Wiktionary — hala

ala.notes: In Paquita Salas, Lidia San José (playing a satirical version of herself) is constantly recognized solely as 'la niña de ¡Ala... Dina!' from her real teenage role on that early-2000s show.

alambre.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin aerāmen ('copper, bronze work, metal wire', derived from Classical Latin aes, aeris 'copper, bronze'), via older Spanish arambre with dissimilation of r...r to l...r.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alambre
Wiktionary — alambre

alba.etymology: Substantivized feminine of Latin albus ('dull white'), from the phrase lūx alba ('the pale white light before sunrise').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alba

alba.notes: Although feminine, singular alba takes the article el (el alba, al alba) before stressed initial a-.

alcachofa.etymology: Borrowed from Andalusi Arabic al-kharshūfa (الْخَرْشُوفَة, Classical Arabic khurshūf 'artichoke'), probably mediated or reshaped via Old Italian carciofo / Spanish alcarchofa with dissimilation of the first r.

cognates.meaning: edible thistle bud (via Northern Italian articiocco)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alcachofa
Wiktionary — alcachofa

alcachofa.notes: Celebrated vegetable of the Ebro valley (La Rioja and Navarre, Paquita's home region around Navarrete); in Spanish TV slang, la alcachofa also means a handheld reporter's mic or a shower head.

alegrar.etymology: Derived from alegre ('happy, cheerful') + -ar, descending from Vulgar Latin *alĭcer, *alĭcrem, reshaped from Classical Latin alăcer ('lively, brisk, eager').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alegrar
Wiktionary — alegrar

alegre.etymology: The DLE derives alegre from Vulgar Latin *alĭcer, *alĭcris, reshaped from Classical Latin alăcer ('brisk, lively, eager').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alegre

alegre.notes: Cognate with Portuguese alegre, French allègre, and the musical tempo marking allegro (via Italian).

alegro.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of alegrar ('to gladden'; pronominally alegrarse 'to be glad, rejoice'), derived from alegre ('happy, lively'), which descends from Vulgar Latin *alecrem for Classical Latin alacrem (accusative of alacer 'lively, brisk, cheerful').

rootFamily.gloss: to cheer up (alegrarse: to be glad)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alegrar
Wiktionary — alegro

alegro.notes: Me alegro de verte ('Nice to see you / I'm glad to see you') and ¡Cuánto me alegro! ('I'm so happy for you!') are warm, high-frequency conversational formulas.

alegría.etymology: Derived within Romance from alegre ('cheerful, joyful') + abstract-noun suffix -ía, tracing back through Vulgar Latin *alecrem to Classical Latin alacer, alacrem ('lively, brisk, spirited').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alegría
Wiktionary — alegría

alegría.notes: Used both as an exclamation (¡Qué alegría!, 'What a joy / How lovely!') and in dar una alegría a alguien ('to make someone's day'); plural alegrías also names an upbeat Andalusian flamenco palo.

alejar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from a- + lejos ('far away') + -ar, where lejos descends from Latin laxius ('more widely, farther off'), neuter comparative of laxus ('loose, wide').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alejar
Wiktionary — alejar

alfabético.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin alphabēticus, from Ancient Greek alphabētikós ('pertaining to the alphabet'), built from alphábētos—a compound of the first two Greek letter names, álpha (ἄλφα) and bē̂ta (βῆτα), themselves of Phoenician/Semitic origin ('ox' and 'house').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alfabético
Wiktionary — alfabético

alfabético.notes: While everyday Spanish often calls the ABCs el abecedario, the fixed phrase for alphabetical order is always por orden alfabético.

alfombra.etymology: From older Spanish alhombra / alfámara, borrowed from Hispanic Arabic alḥánbal, from Classical Arabic ḥanbal ('fur lining, thick rug or carpet').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alfombra
Wiktionary — alfombra

algo.etymology: Inherited from Latin aliquod ('some, something'), the neuter singular of the indefinite pronoun aliquī / aliquis, with regular syncope and voicing of -qu- to -g-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: algo
Wiktionary — algo

alguien.etymology: Inherited from Latin aliquem ('someone, somebody'), accusative singular of aliquis, with final stress remodeled in Spanish by analogy with quien (< quem).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alguien
Wiktionary — alguien

alguno.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alicūnus ('some, someone'), a compound of Classical Latin aliquis ('someone') and ūnus ('one').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alguno
Wiktionary — alguno

aliento.etymology: Deverbal noun from alentar ('to breathe, encourage, hearten'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *anhēlitāre (a blend of Classical Latin anhēlāre 'to pant, draw deep breath' and hālitus 'breath, exhalation'), with regular Spanish diphthongisation of stressed short e to ie (aliento).

history.meaning: to breathe deeply, pant / breath, exhalation

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aliento
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alentar
Wiktionary — aliento#Spanish

aliento.notes: Covers both physical breath (tomar aliento 'to catch one's breath', sin aliento 'out of breath') and moral encouragement (dar aliento).

alita.etymology: Diminutive of ala ('wing'), formed with the affective/diminutive suffix -ita. Spanish ala descends directly from Latin āla ('wing, armpit').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ala
Wiktionary — alita

alita.notes: Note the article switch: singular el ala takes el because it begins with stressed /a/, whereas diminutive la alita (stressed on -li-) takes normal la; plural alitas (de pollo) is the standard menu term for chicken wings.

aliviada.etymology: Feminine singular participial adjective of aliviar ('to relieve, lighten, ease'), semi-learned descendant of Late Latin alleviāre ('to lighten a burden, comfort'), formed from ad- ('to') + levis ('light in weight').

cognates.meaning: to make suffering less severe (learned borrowing)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aliviar
Wiktionary — aliviada

aliviada.notes: Often used predicatively with verbs of breathing or posture—such as suspirar aliviada ('she sighs in relief')—agreeing in gender and number with the subject.

alivio.etymology: Deverbal noun from aliviar ('to lighten, relieve, soothe'), inherited from Late Latin alleviāre (ad- + levis 'light in weight').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alivio
Wiktionary — alivio

allá.etymology: Inherited from Latin illāc ('that way, over there'), prefixed with a- by analogy with the directional preposition a.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: allá
Wiktionary — allá

allí.etymology: Inherited from Latin illīc ('in that place, there'), with initial a- added by analogy with the preposition a and spatial adverbs such as aquí.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: allí
Wiktionary — allí

alma.etymology: Alma continues Latin anĭma ('breath, life, soul'), with syncope of unstressed -i- producing Old Spanish alma through dissimilation of -nm- to -lm-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alma

alma.notes: Like agua, feminine alma takes el in the singular before stressed initial /a/ (el alma, las almas).

almacén.etymology: Borrowed from Hispanic Arabic almaḫzán, from Classical Arabic al-maḫzan ('storehouse, treasury, depot'), a noun of place built on the verbal root ḫazana ('to store up, guard').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: almacén
Wiktionary — almacén

almendra.etymology: Almendra comes from Vulgar Latin *amyndŭla, altered from Classical Latin amygdăla, itself borrowed from Greek amygdálē ('almond'). Influence from the Arabic article al- helped reshape the initial syllable.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: almendra

almendra.notes: The tree is el almendro, whose early spring blossom is famous across eastern Spain.

almohada.etymology: The DLE traces almohada to Hispanic Arabic almuẖádda, from Classical Arabic miẖaddah ('pillow, cushion'), an instrument noun derived from ẖadd ('cheek').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: almohada

almohada.notes: Literally 'the place where one rests one's cheek'; cognate with Portuguese almofada.

alojar.etymology: Borrowed via French loger or Italian alloggiare ('to quarter, lodge, host'), ultimately from Frankish *laubja ('arbor, covered shelter, lodge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alojar
Wiktionary — alojar

alquilar.etymology: Derived from older Spanish alquile ('rent, lease'), borrowed from Hispanic Arabic alkirá, from Classical Arabic al-kirāʾ ('rent, hiring, lease').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alquilar
Wiktionary — alquilar

alquiler.etymology: From older Spanish alquile, borrowed from Hispanic Arabic alkirá (< Classical Arabic al-kirāʾ 'rent, hire'), with final -r added by analogy with the verb alquilar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alquiler
Wiktionary — alquiler

alto.etymology: Inherited from Latin altus ('high, tall, deep; loud'), originally the old participial adjective of alere ('to nourish, make grow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alto
Wiktionary — alto

altura.etymology: Derived from alto ('high, tall', < Latin altus, originally past participle of alere 'to nourish, make grow') + abstract-noun suffix -ura (or continuing Late Latin altūra 'height, elevation').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: altura
Wiktionary — altura

altura.notes: Covers human stature on casting sheets (¿Cuál es tu altura? alongside estatura) as well as idioms like estar a la altura ('to live up to expectations') and a estas alturas ('at this late stage').

am.etymology: English first-person singular present indicative of be, quoted in Mariona Terés's English audition slate ('I am 25 years old'). Inherited from Old English eom, from Proto-Germanic *immi and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European copula *h₁ésmi ('I am'), the exact Indo-European cognate of Latin sum (> Spanish soy).

cognates.word: soy (< Old Spanish so < Latin sum)

rootFamily.gloss: to have (used in Spanish age expressions: tengo 25 años)

sources.title: Wiktionary — am (English)

am.notes: Notice the classic Spanish–English contrast highlighted in audition slates: English uses 'I am 25 years old', whereas Spanish expresses age with tener (tengo veinticinco años).

amable.etymology: Borrowed from Latin amābilis ('lovable, worthy of love, kind, pleasant'), derived from amāre ('to love').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amable
Wiktionary — amable

amaia.etymology: Basque female given name Amaia (traditionally spelled Amaya in Castilian), literally meaning 'the end, culmination, fulfillment', formed from Basque amai ('end') + the suffixed definite article -a.

sources.title: Euskaltzaindia (Royal Academy of the Basque Language) — Euskal Onomastikaren Datutegia: Amaia
Wiktionary — Amaia

amaia.notes: Popularized across Spain by Francisco Navarro Villoslada's historical novel Amaya o los vascos en el siglo VIII (1879); in Paquita Salas, it refers to Madrid actress Amaia Salamanca (Sin tetas no hay paraíso, Gran Hotel).

amarillo.etymology: Inherited from Medieval/Low Latin amarellus ('pale, yellowish'), a diminutive of Classical Latin amārus ('bitter'), originally referring to the sallow complexion associated with bitter bile.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amarillo
Wiktionary — amarillo

amasar.etymology: Formed within Spanish from a- + masa ('dough') + -ar; masa continues Latin massa ('kneaded lump, dough'), borrowed from Greek mâza ('barley cake, kneaded dough').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amasar

amasar.notes: Used for working flour, water, and yeast by hand until smooth.

americano.etymology: Derived from América + gentilic suffix -ano (< Latin -ānus). The continent's name was coined in Neo-Latin as America in 1507 by German cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann in honor of Florentine navigator Amerigo Vespucci (Italian Amerigo < Medieval Latin Emericus < Germanic *Haimirīks).

history.meaning: of the Americas; (by narrowing) United States / American

cognates.meaning: of the Americas or the United States

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: americano
Wiktionary — americano

americano.notes: While estadounidense is the precise Spanish adjective for 'U.S.', inglés americano ('American English') is completely standard when contrasting US and British accents, and una americana is Peninsular Spanish for a blazer.

amiga.etymology: Inherited from Latin amīca ('female friend, companion, sweetheart'), feminine of amīcus, derived from amāre ('to love') with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amigo
Wiktionary — amiga

amiga.notes: Spanish allows grading nouns of relationship directly with muy as if they were adjectives: es muy amiga suya ('she is a very close friend of hers').

amigas.etymology: Regular feminine plural of amiga ('female friend'), descending from Latin amīcās (accusative plural of amīca, from amāre 'to love') with regular lenition of -c- to -g-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amigo
Wiktionary — amigas

amigas.notes: Specifically denotes an all-female group of friends (somos muy amigas); a mixed-gender group takes masculine plural amigos.

amigo.etymology: Inherited from Latin amīcus ('friend, ally'), derived from the verb amāre ('to love'), with regular Western Romance voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amigo
Wiktionary — amigo

amistoso.etymology: Derived within Spanish from amistad ('friendship') + adjectival suffix -oso ('full of, characterized by'). Amistad descends from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem (for Classical Latin amīcitia, from amīcus 'friend').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amistoso
Wiktionary — amistoso

amistoso.notes: Describes cordial relations, non-competitive exhibition games (un partido amistoso, often used metaphorically in flirting or truce-making), whereas warm personal friendliness is usually simpático or amable.

amistosos.etymology: Masculine plural of amistoso ('friendly, exhibition'), derived from amistad ('friendship', < Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem) + -oso + plural -s.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amistoso
Wiktionary — amistosos

amistosos.notes: In Spanish sports and everyday banter, partidos amistosos (or simply amistosos) means non-league exhibition games played without official stakes.

amor.etymology: Inherited from Latin amor, amōrem ('love, affection, longing'), abstract noun built on the root of amāre ('to love').

cognates.meaning: loving (via Old French from Late Latin amōrōsus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amor
Wiktionary — amor

amor.notes: Used constantly in Peninsular Spanish as an affectionate vocative (mi amor, oye amor) among partners, close friends, and theatrical colleagues.

amplio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin amplius (comparative of amplus 'spacious, wide, large') or a learned reshaping of amplus alongside the inherited popular doublet ancho.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: amplio
Wiktionary — amplio

ana.etymology: Spanish female given name Ana, from Late Latin Anna, via Ancient Greek Ánna (Ἄννα) from Biblical Hebrew Ḥannāh (חַנָּה, 'grace, favor', from the root ḥ-n-n 'to show favor').

cognates.meaning: female given names from the same Hebrew source

sources.title: Wiktionary — Ana (Spanish)

ana.notes: In Paquita Salas, 'Ana y los siete' refers to the smash-hit TVE family sitcom (2002–2005) created by and starring Ana Obregón.

ancho.etymology: Inherited through regular phonetic evolution from Latin amplus ('wide, broad, spacious'), where the post-nasal cluster -mpl- palatalized to Castilian -nch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ancho
Wiktionary — ancho

anchura.etymology: Derived within Spanish from ancho ('wide, broad', < Latin amplus) + the abstract measurement suffix -ura.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anchura
Wiktionary — anchura

and.etymology: Unadapted English coordinating conjunction ('and'), spoken in Mariona Terés's English audition self-tape. Inherited from Old English and / ond, from Proto-Germanic *andi and ultimately Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti ('facing, in addition'; related to Greek antí 'opposite').

rootFamily.gloss: and (native Spanish equivalent, becoming e before i-/hi-)

sources.title: Wiktionary — and (English)

and.notes: Appears inside quoted English audition lines in Paquita Salas ('Hello, my name is Mariona Terés, and I am 25 years old').

anda.etymology: Conversational Peninsular Spanish interjection ('come on!, oh really!, get out of here!'), grammaticalized from the second-person singular imperative (or third-person present) of andar ('to walk, go'), probably descending from Vulgar Latin *amlāre, a syncopated colloquial variant of Classical Latin ambulāre ('to walk around').

history.meaning: walk! -> come on!, well I never!

rootFamily.gloss: past habit or escapade (volver a las andadas)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anda
Wiktionary — anda

anda.notes: Intonation decides everything in Spain: drawn-out ¡Anda! expresses pleasant surprise ('Oh wow!'), while brisk Anda, qué tonterías brushes off nonsense ('Oh, come off it, what rubbish').

andando.etymology: Gerund of andar ('walking, on foot; get moving!'), formed with the -ando gerundial suffix (< Latin ablative gerund -andō) on the stem of andar (likely from Vulgar Latin *amlāre < Classical Latin ambulāre 'to walk').

history.meaning: walking, on foot; off we go!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: andar
Wiktionary — andando

andando.notes: In Spain ir andando is the everyday way to say 'to walk / go on foot' (rather than a pie), and standalone ¡Andando! means 'Let's get moving!'

andar.etymology: Inherited from Romance *andāre, most widely explained since Corominas as a phonetic reduction of Vulgar Latin *amlāre (with dissimilatory -ml- > -nd-), a rapid-speech syncope of Classical Latin ambulāre ('to walk, travel'), perhaps crossed with ambitāre ('to go round').

morphemes.meaning: walk, move along (< Vulgar Latin *aml- < ambul-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: andar
Wiktionary — andar

andar.notes: Regular in the present (ando, andas), but keeps an archaic strong preterite stem modeled on estar/haber: anduve, anduviste, anduvo (never *andé in standard Spanish). Can also be nominalized as el andar ('one's gait').

andén.etymology: According to the DLE, inherited from Vulgar Latin *ambitāgo, *ambitāginem (from Classical Latin ambitus 'walkway around, border'), phonetically crossed with andar ('to walk').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: andén
Wiktionary — andén

anillo.etymology: Inherited from Latin anellus ('little ring, finger ring'), diminutive of ānus ('ring, circle'), with regular palatalization of -ll-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anillo
Wiktionary — anillo

animado.etymology: Participial adjective of animar ('lively, bustling, cheerful'), from Latin animātus, past participle of animāre ('to give breath or life to, encourage'), from anima ('breath, soul').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: animado
Wiktionary — animado

animales.etymology: Plural of animal, a learned borrowing from Latin animal, animālis ('living breathing creature'), substantivized neuter of animālis ('endowed with breath or life'), derived from anima ('breath, vital spirit, soul').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: animal
Wiktionary — animales

animales.notes: Notice the doublet pair from Latin anima: inherited alma ('soul') vs. learned animal ('living breathing creature').

anoche.etymology: Evolved from the Latin/Romance temporal phrase ad noctem or Old Spanish en a noche ('last night'), built on Latin nox, noctis ('night').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anoche
Wiktionary — anoche

anotar.etymology: Anotar comes from Latin annotāre ('to jot down, add a note to'), built from ad- + notāre (from nota, 'written mark').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anotar

anotar.notes: Anote (formal usted command) and anota (informal tú command) are standard for jotting down a phone number or address.

ante.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin ante ('in front of, before, in the presence of').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ante
Wiktionary — ante

antes.etymology: Inherited from Latin ante ('before, earlier in time'), expanded in Romance with the characteristic adverbial -s.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: antes
Wiktionary — antes

antiguo.etymology: Inherited from Latin antīquus ('ancient, old, former'), a derivative of ante ('before'), showing regular voicing of -qu- to -gu- before the back vowel.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: antiguo
Wiktionary — antiguo

anual.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin annuālis ('yearly, recurring every year'), derived from Classical Latin annus ('year').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anual
Wiktionary — anual

anuncio.etymology: Deverbal noun from anunciar ('to announce, advertise'), borrowed from Latin annūntiāre ('to make known, proclaim'), compounded from ad- ('to') + nūntiāre ('to report', from nūntius 'messenger').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anuncio
Wiktionary — anuncio

anuncio.notes: In Spain, un anuncio is the everyday word for a TV commercial or print advertisement (hice un anuncio en televisión), where parts of Latin America also say un comercial.

anécdota.etymology: Borrowed via French anecdote from Medieval/Neo-Latin anecdota, from Ancient Greek anékdota (ἀνέκδοτα, 'things unpublished'), neuter plural of anékdotos (an- 'not' + ek- 'out' + dotós 'given'), popularized by Procopius's 6th-century Secret History (Anecdota) of private court stories.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anécdota
Wiktionary — anécdota

anécdota.notes: Antepenultimate stress (esdrújula: a-NÉC-do-ta); contar una anécdota is a staple of Spanish talk-show interviews and actor auditions.

apagado.etymology: Participial adjective from apagar ('extinguished, switched off, dull'), which descends from Latin appācāre (ad- + pācāre 'to pacify, calm, quench', from pāx 'peace').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apagado
Wiktionary — apagado

aparato.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin apparātus ('preparation, equipment, instruments, pomp'), action/result noun from apparāre ('to make ready, equip', from ad- + parāre 'to prepare').

rootFamily.gloss: spectacularly messy, dramatic-looking (e.g., una caída aparatosa)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aparato
Wiktionary — aparato

aparato.notes: Much more everyday than English 'apparatus': Spanish uses aparato for any household gadget, appliance, braces (llevar aparato), or phone handset.

aparcar.etymology: Formed from a- + parque ('enclosed park or yard', < French parc) + -ar, originally a military term for stationing artillery or wagons and later reinforced by English to park for motor vehicles.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aparcar
Wiktionary — aparcar

aparecer.etymology: Inherited from Late/Vulgar Latin *apparēscere, inchoative derivative built with -ēscere on Classical Latin appārēre ('to come into view, become visible', from ad- + pārēre 'to be visible, appear').

history.meaning: to begin to appear, show up
to appear, show up, turn up

cognates.meaning: to come into sight (via Old French aparoir)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aparecer
Wiktionary — aparecer

aparecer.notes: Conjugates with -zc- before -o/-a (aparezco, aparezca). Never confuse aparecer ('to show up/become visible') with parecer ('to seem/look like').

apartar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Spanish from a- + parte ('part, side', from Latin pars, partis; cf. the adverb aparte 'aside') + -ar, literally 'to put to one side'.

cognates.meaning: to one side (via Old French a part)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apartar
Wiktionary — apartar

apartar.notes: Apártalo means 'set this one aside / move it out of the way', while reflexive ¡Apártate! means 'Step back / get out of the way!'

apetecer.etymology: Formed in Spanish with the inchoative ending -ecer (< Latin -ēscere) on Latin appetere ('to strive after, desire eagerly, have an appetite for'), from ad- ('toward') + petere ('to seek, aim at').

history.meaning: to appeal to, make one feel like

cognates.meaning: desire for food (via Old French apetit < Latin appetītus)

rootFamily.gloss: to ask for (inherited verb from Latin petere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apetecer
Wiktionary — apetecer

apetecer.notes: Signature Peninsular Spanish verb working grammatically like gustar: ¿Te apetece un café? ('Do you fancy / feel like a coffee?'), Me apetece desayunar ('I feel like having breakfast').

aplauso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin applausus ('a clapping of hands, striking wings together, approbation'), action noun from applaudere (ad- 'to' + plaudere 'to clap, strike, beat').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aplauso
Wiktionary — aplauso

aplauso.notes: Countable in Spanish: hosts ask the audience for un fuerte aplauso ('a big round of applause'), while sustained clapping is los aplausos.

aplicación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin applicātiōnem ('a joining or attaching to, devotion'), from applicāre ('to fold toward, attach, apply', from ad- + plicāre 'to fold'). In the digital era it calqued the semantic extension of English application ('software app').

cognates.meaning: putting to use; software app; job form

rootFamily.gloss: to arrive (inherited doublet of Latin applicāre 'to put ashore')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aplicación
Wiktionary — aplicación

aplicación.notes: Means a software/phone app or practical implementation, but Watch Out: a 'job application' in Spain is una solicitud (not una aplicación).

apostaba.etymology: First- or third-person singular imperfect indicative of apostar ('to bet, wager, back someone'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *appositāre ('to place beside, put down a stake'), frequentative of Classical Latin appōnere (ad- + pōnere 'to put, place').

morphemes.meaning: place a stake, wager (< Vulgar Latin *apposit-)

history.meaning: to place -> to set down a stake
to bet -> used to bet / was betting

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apostar
Wiktionary — apostaba

apostaba.notes: Apostar por alguien ('to bet on / believe in someone': por mí no apostaba mucha gente, 'not many people believed in me') is central to talent-agency talk.

apostado.etymology: Past participle of apostar ('to bet, wager; to station'), continuing Vulgar Latin *appositātus from *appositāre ('to set in place, lay down a wager'), built on the supine stem apposit- of Classical Latin appōnere ('to place near').

morphemes.meaning: lay a stake, place (< Vulgar Latin *apposit-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apostar
Wiktionary — apostado

apostado.notes: Notice how infinitive/participle apostar / apostado keep unstressed -o-, whereas stressed present forms diphthongize to -ue- (apuesto, apuestas, la apuesta).

apoyar.etymology: Borrowed from Italian appoggiare ('to lean, rest, support'), from Vulgar Latin *appodiāre, built on Latin podium ('pedestal, elevated base, foothold', from Greek πόδιον).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apoyar
Wiktionary — apoyar

aprender.etymology: The DLE traces aprender to Vulgar Latin *apprehendĕre, reduced from Classical Latin apprehendĕre ('to seize, grasp physically or mentally'). Grasping an idea with the mind became the everyday verb for learning.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aprender

aprender.notes: Followed by the preposition a before an infinitive (aprender a tocar el piano).

apretar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin appectorāre ('to press tightly against the chest'), formed from ad- + pectus, pectoris ('chest, breast'), via Old Spanish apretar by metathesis of r.

history.meaning: to press to the chest, squeeze

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apretar
Wiktionary — apretar

aprovechar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + provecho ('benefit, profit, advantage') + -ar. Provecho descends regularly from Latin profectus ('progress, profit, success', from proficere 'to advance, do good'), with Latin -ct- palatalizing to Castilian -ch-.

history.meaning: profit -> to put to good use
to make the most of, seize an opportunity

cognates.meaning: to make the most of, enjoy
gain, benefit (via Old French from Latin profectus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aprovechar
Wiktionary — aprovechar

aprovechar.notes: Positive aprovechar algo means 'to make the most of / seize' (aprovecha esa oportunidad), whereas reflexive aprovecharse de alguien carries the negative sense 'to take unfair advantage of someone'. At mealtimes in Spain, ¡Que aproveche! means 'Bon appétit!'

apuntado.etymology: Past participle and participial adjective of apuntar ('to jot down, note, aim, sign up'), formed from a- + punto / punta ('point, tip', from Latin pūnctum / pūncta, from pungere 'to prick').

history.meaning: to write down, aim -> written down, signed up

cognates.meaning: designated (via Old French apointier from the same root)

rootFamily.gloss: to jot down, aim (apuntarse: to sign up)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apuntar
Wiktionary — apuntado

apuntado.notes: In Spain tener algo apuntado is the everyday way to say 'to have something written down' (in a notebook or planner), and estar apuntado means 'to be signed up / enrolled'.

apuntar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + punto ('point, dot') / punta ('sharp tip') + -ar, ultimately from Latin punctum ('point, prick', from pungere 'to prick').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apuntar
Wiktionary — apuntar

apunte.etymology: Deverbal noun from apuntar ('written note, sketch, jotting'), built on punto ('point', < Latin punctum).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: apunte
Wiktionary — apunte

aquel.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille ('behold that one yonder'), combining the demonstrative presenter eccum ('here is, look at') with the Latin distal pronoun ille ('that').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aquel
Wiktionary — aquel

aquí.etymology: The DLE derives aquí from Vulgar Latin *eccum hic ('behold here'), combining demonstrative particle eccum with Classical Latin hic ('here').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aquí

aquí.notes: Aquí points to the immediate spot right beside the speaker (aquí tiene = here you go).

arco.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin arcus ('hunting bow, curved vault, rainbow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arco

arco.notes: Names both an architectural stone arch over a courtyard gallery and a stringed-instrument bow.

argentino.etymology: Gentilic and relational adjective of Argentina, borrowed as a learned formation from Latin argentīnus ('of silver, silvery'), derived from argentum ('silver'). Early Spanish explorers named the Río de la Plata ('River of Silver') after rumored inland silver wealth, and Neo-Latin Argentina ('land of silver', popularized in Martín del Barco Centenera's 1602 poem La Argentina) became the nation's name.

history.meaning: relating to the Río de la Plata ('Silver River') region

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: argentino
Wiktionary — argentino

argentino.notes: Spanish nationalities are never capitalized (acento argentino); Rioplatense Argentine accents—famous for voseo (vos tenés) and pronounced 'sh'/'zh' yeísmo—are a classic audition skill in Madrid.

armario.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin armārium ('closet, chest, cupboard, originally a storage place for weapons or tools'), derived from arma ('implements, gear, weapons').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: armario
Wiktionary — armario

aromático.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin arōmaticus ('fragrant, spicy'), from Ancient Greek ἀρωματικός (arōmatikós), derived from ἄρωμα (árōma, 'sweet spice, fragrant herb').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aromático
Wiktionary — aromático

arquitecto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin architectus ('master builder'), from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn), a compound of ἀρχι- (arkhi-, 'chief') and τέκτων (téktōn, 'builder, carpenter').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arquitecto
Wiktionary — arquitecto

arreglar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + regla ('rule, straightedge, order') + -ar, ultimately from Latin rēgula ('straight stick, rule, pattern').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arreglar
Wiktionary — arreglar

arriba.etymology: Univerbation of Old Spanish a riba ('up toward the high bank or slope'), from the Latin prepositional phrase ad rīpam ('to the riverbank or steep shore').

history.meaning: to the bank or steep shore

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arriba
Wiktionary — arriba

arriesgada.etymology: Feminine singular participial adjective of arriesgar ('to risk, venture'), formed from a- + riesgo ('risk, hazard') + -ar. Spanish riesgo (earlier riezgo / risco 'jagged cliff, peril to ships') is of debated origin—traced by Corominas to a postverbal derivative of Vulgar Latin *resecāre ('to cut sheer', > risco 'crag') or via Mediterranean maritime Romance.

cognates.meaning: hazard / daring (ultimately from the same Romance word)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arriesgar
Wiktionary — arriesgada

arriesgada.notes: Una estrategia arriesgada or una apuesta arriesgada describes a bold, high-stakes move that could either pay off big or backfire.

arruga.etymology: Deverbal noun from arrugar ('to wrinkle, crease'), inherited from Latin irrūgāre or formed with prosthetic a- from Latin rūga ('wrinkle, crease in the face or garment'), with regular geminate-like reinforcement of initial r- after the prefix.

cognates.meaning: street (from Latin rūga in the sense 'furrow, wheel-rut, lane')
ridged, wrinkled (learned borrowing from Latin corrūgātus)

rootFamily.gloss: to wrinkle, crumple (arrugarse: to shrivel or chicken out)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arruga
Wiktionary — arruga

arruga.notes: Covers both skin lines (ni una arruga) and clothing creases; amazingly, French rue ('street') comes from the very same Latin rūga ('furrow').

arruinar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + ruina ('ruin, collapse') + -ar. Ruina descends from Latin ruīna ('tumbling down, downfall, disaster'), derived from ruere ('to rush down, collapse').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arruinar
Wiktionary — arruinar

arruinar.notes: Notice the spelling rule: single r- of ruina doubles to -rr- between vowels after prefix a- (arruinar) to keep the strong trilled /r/. Reflexive arruinarse specifically means 'to go broke'.

artista.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin artista or Italian artista ('practitioner of the liberal or fine arts, craftsman, performer'), formed from Latin ars, artis ('skill, craft, art') + the Greek-derived agent suffix -ista (< -istḗs).

history.meaning: master of the arts, creator, performer

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: artista
Wiktionary — artista

artista.notes: Gender-invariable noun (el artista / la artista). Unlike English 'artist' (mostly visual arts or music), Spanish artista routinely includes actors, singers, and variety performers (representante de artistas).

arturo.etymology: Spanish male given name Arturo, from Late Latin Artūrus (variants Artōrius), of Celtic/Brittonic origin—most often derived from Common Brittonic *Artorījos ('bear-king', from *artos 'bear', cognate with Greek árktos, + *rīxs 'king'), spread across medieval Europe by Arthurian romance.

sources.title: Wiktionary — Arturo (Spanish)

arturo.notes: In Paquita Salas, 'Hombre, Arturo' greets beloved Valencia-born Spanish actor, comedian, and ¡Ahora caigo! TV host Arturo Valls in a cameo appearance.

asa.etymology: Inherited from Latin ansa ('handle of a vessel, loop, grip'), showing the regular Vulgar Latin reduction of the cluster -ns- to -s-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asa
Wiktionary — asa

asado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from asar ('roasted; roast meat'), which descends from Latin assāre ('to roast, broil'), derived from assus ('dry, roasted').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asado
Wiktionary — asado

asegurar.etymology: Formed from a- + seguro ('safe, sure, firm') + -ar (or Late Latin assēcūrāre), from Classical Latin sēcūrus ('free from care, safe', from sē- + cūra 'care').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asegurar
Wiktionary — asegurar

asentir.etymology: Borrowed or inherited from Latin assentīre (Classical deponent assentīrī, 'to agree with, approve, give assent'), a compound of ad- + sentīre ('to feel, perceive, judge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asentir
Wiktionary — asentir

asesinado.etymology: Past participle of asesinar ('to murder, assassinate'), borrowed via Italian assassinare / French assassiner from asesino ('murderer'), which comes from Arabic ḥashshāshīn (حَشَّاشِين, 'hashish-users'), the medieval sobriquet applied by Crusaders and chroniclers to the Nizari Ismaili fedayeen of Alamut.

cognates.meaning: killed (narrowed in English to political/targeted killings)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asesinar
Wiktionary — asesinado

asesinado.notes: Subtle scope difference: English 'assassinate' is restricted to public figures, whereas Spanish asesinar / asesinado is the standard word for any intentional murder (alongside colloquial matar 'to kill').

asiento.etymology: Deverbal noun from asentar ('to seat, set down, settle'), descending from Vulgar Latin *assedentāre, built on the present participle stem sedēns, sedentis of Latin sedēre ('to sit').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asiento
Wiktionary — asiento

asomar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + Old Spanish somo ('summit, top, ridge') + -ar, originally meaning 'to come into view over the top of a hill', from Latin summum ('highest point').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asomar
Wiktionary — asomar

asombrado.etymology: Participial adjective of asombrar ('astonished, amazed'), formed from a- + sombra ('shadow, shade', < Vulgar Latin *subumbrāre / umbra), having shifted from 'frightened by a shadow' to 'amazed'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asombrado
Wiktionary — asombrado

aspira.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative of aspirar ('to inhale, breathe in deeply; to aspire to'), a learned borrowing from Latin aspīrāre ('to breathe upon, blow toward, strive to reach'), compounded from ad- ('toward') + spīrāre ('to breathe').

history.meaning: to breathe -> to breathe upon, long for

cognates.meaning: to strive for / draw in by suction

rootFamily.gloss: to inhale; to vacuum; (aspirar a) to aspire to

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aspirar
Wiktionary — aspira

aspira.notes: In Spanish subtitle stage directions, (ASPIRA) marks a character taking a deep, savoring breath through the nose (such as breathing in fresh country air).

asuntos.etymology: Plural of asunto ('matter, affair, business, subject'), semi-learned borrowing from Latin assūmptus ('taken up, adopted'), past participle of assūmere (ad- + sūmere 'to take up'), referring originally to the topic or proposition 'taken up' for discussion.

history.meaning: to take up -> proposition or matter taken up

cognates.meaning: to take upon oneself, suppose (from Latin assūmere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asunto
Wiktionary — asuntos

asuntos.notes: Singular Asunto: is the label on every Spanish email 'Subject:' field, while plural asuntos covers personal business (asuntos propios) or professional engagements.

asustes.etymology: Second-person singular present subjunctive (used in negative commands: no me asustes) of asustar ('to frighten, startle'), formed as a parasynthetic verb from a- + susto ('fright, sudden scare') + -ar. Susto is a deverbal noun from Old Spanish asostar / sustar, traced to Latin suscitāre ('to rouse suddenly, startle awake').

morphemes.meaning: sudden startle, fright (< susto < Latin suscitāre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asustar
Wiktionary — asustes

asustes.notes: Negative tú commands always switch to the present subjunctive (-ar -> -es): ¡No me asustes! ('Don't scare me!'), the instant Spanish reply when someone opens with ominous news.

asusté.etymology: First-person singular preterite indicative of asustar ('to scare, startle'), formed from a- + susto ('sudden fright', probably via Old Spanish sustar from Latin suscitāre 'to rouse abruptly') + -ar.

history.meaning: to scare -> I scared / (me asusté) I got scared

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asustar
Wiktionary — asusté

asusté.notes: Watch the written accent: asusté (/asusˈte/, 'I scared') vs. subjunctive asuste (/aˈsuste/, 'that I/he/she scare'). Transitive te asusté means 'I scared you'; reflexive me asusté means 'I got scared'.

así.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish assí, formed by compounding the preposition a (< Latin ad) with sí (< Latin sīc 'thus, in this way').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: así
Wiktionary — así

atado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from atar ('tied, bound; bundle'), inherited from Latin aptāre ('to fit together, join, fasten').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atado
Wiktionary — atado

atascado.etymology: Participial adjective of atascar ('stuck, clogged, jammed'), formed from a- + tasco ('bundle of coarse flax tow used to plug gaps') + -ar, of pre-Roman (likely Celtic) origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atascado
Wiktionary — atascado

atascar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + tasco ('bundle of coarse flax tow used for plugging or caulking') + -ar, of pre-Roman (likely Celtic) origin, meaning 'to plug up, obstruct, jam'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atascar
Wiktionary — atascar

atender.etymology: Inherited from Latin attendere ('to stretch toward, direct the mind to, pay attention, wait upon'), formed from ad- + tendere ('to stretch').

history.meaning: to direct one's attention to, heed

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atender
Wiktionary — atender

atornillar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from a- + tornillo ('screw', diminutive of torno 'lathe, turn', from Latin tornus < Greek τόρνος) + -ar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atornillar
Wiktionary — atornillar

atractivo.etymology: Learned formation from Medieval/Late Latin attractīvus ('drawing toward itself, alluring'), built on attract-, supine stem of Classical Latin attrahere ('to draw toward, attract', from ad- 'to' + trahere 'to pull, draw').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atractivo
Wiktionary — atractivo

atractivo.notes: Peninsular speakers regularly distinguish ser guapo ('having classic facial beauty') from ser atractivo ('having magnetism, style, or sex appeal', even without classic features).

atril.etymology: The DLE derives atril from Old Spanish letril, which came from Late Latin lectorīle ('reading stand', built on lector, 'reader'). Speakers reanalysed initial l- as part of the article, turning el letril into el atril.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atril

atril.notes: Used both for a standing lectern and for the hinged wooden music rest on a piano.

atrás.etymology: Formed by compounding the directional preposition a (< Latin ad) with tras ('behind, after', < Latin trans 'across, beyond').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atrás
Wiktionary — atrás

aun.etymology: Unstressed proclitic form of aún ('even, including'), inherited from Latin adhūc ('until now, still, even so'), with Romance nasalization of the final syllable.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aun
Wiktionary — aun

aunque.etymology: Compound concessive conjunction formed within Spanish from aun ('even', < Latin adhūc) + que ('that', < Latin quid / quod).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aunque
Wiktionary — aunque

autoral.etymology: Modern relational adjective formed from autor ('author, creator, auteur', borrowed from Latin auctor, auctōrem 'originator, builder, writer', from augēre 'to increase, originate') + suffix -al (< Latin -ālis).

cognates.meaning: pertaining to an author or arthouse director

rootFamily.gloss: author, creator (cine de autor: arthouse cinema)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: autoral
Wiktionary — autoral

autoral.notes: In Spanish film and theater circles, muy autoral is pretentious-chic industry shorthand for 'very arthouse / auteur-driven' (synonymous with cine de autor).

avenida.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of avenir (< Latin advenīre 'to arrive, come together'), originally denoting a sudden flood or confluence of ways leading to a town, and later a wide tree-lined avenue (reinforced by French avenue).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: avenida
Wiktionary — avenida

avisado.etymology: Past participle and adjective of avisar ('to let know, warn, notify'), borrowed from Old French aviser ('to look at, consider, inform', from the phrase ce m'est a vis 'it seems to me'), ultimately from Latin ad + vīsum ('to the sight/opinion', from vidēre 'to see').

morphemes.meaning: notice, warning (< Old French avis < Latin ad vīsum)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: avisar
Wiktionary — avisado

avisado.notes: False-friend trap: avisar / avisado means 'to let someone know / give a heads-up' (no me has avisado, 'you didn't tell me you were coming'), whereas 'to give advice' is aconsejar.

avisar.etymology: Borrowed from Old French aviser ('to inform, put on notice, consider'), formed on avis ('opinion, notice', from Old French ce m'est a vis < Late Latin mihi est ad vīsum 'it seems to my sight'), from Latin vidēre ('to see').

cognates.meaning: to counsel or formally notify (with restored Latin d-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: avisar
Wiktionary — avisar

avisar.notes: Essential daily Spanish verb: Te aviso cuando llegue ('I'll text/tell you when I get there') or ¡Avísame! ('Let me know!'). Use aconsejar, not avisar, for 'to give advice'.

aviso.etymology: Deverbal noun from avisar (or borrowed via Old French avis / Provençal avís), from the Medieval Latin phrase mihi est ad vīsum ('it seems to me'), built on Latin vīsus ('sight, view', from vidēre 'to see').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aviso
Wiktionary — aviso

avión.etymology: Borrowed from French avion ('airplane'), a neologism coined in 1890 by aviation pioneer Clément Ader from Classical Latin avis ('bird') + augmentative/instrument suffix -on (< -ōnem) to name his bat-winged flying machine.

cognates.meaning: flying (coined in French 1863 from the same avis root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: avión
Wiktionary — avión

avión.notes: Drops its written accent in the plural because stress stays on -o-: el avión -> los aviones. Means of transport take en without an article: ir en avión ('to go by plane').

ay.etymology: Natural expressive interjection of pain, lament, startle, or sighing, corresponding to Latin ai and Ancient Greek αἰ (ai).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ay
Wiktionary — ay

ayer.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish er prefixed with a-, from Vulgar Latin *ad herī, built on Classical Latin herī ('yesterday').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayer
Wiktionary — ayer

ayudar.etymology: Ayudar continues Latin adiūtāre ('to help, assist'), the frequentative verb built on adiuvāre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayudar

ayudar.notes: Before an infinitive, ayudar links with preposition a (ayudar a llevar la maleta).

ayuntamiento.etymology: Derived from ayuntar ('to join, gather, assemble') + -miento, where ayuntar descends from Late Latin adiunctāre, frequentative of Classical Latin adiungere ('to join to, unite').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayuntamiento
Wiktionary — ayuntamiento

ayúdala.etymology: Affirmative tú imperative ayuda ('help!') + enclitic feminine direct-object pronoun -la ('her'). Ayudar descends regularly from Latin adiūtāre ('to give aid to'), frequentative of adiuvāre (ad- + iuvāre 'to help, support').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayudar
Wiktionary — ayudar

ayúdala.notes: Attaching -la shifts ayúdala into proparoxytone (esdrújula) stress on -yu-, requiring a written accent mark to preserve the imperative's original stress.

azul.etymology: Azul entered Spanish through Hispanic Arabic lazawárd, from Arabic lāzaward and Persian lāžward ('lapis lazuli'), with rebracketing of initial l- as part of the article.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: azul

azul.notes: Plural is azules; when modified by a shade word like azul oscuro ('dark blue'), the compound shade phrase stays invariable.

azúcar.etymology: Azúcar comes from Hispanic Arabic assúkkar, continuing Classical Arabic sukkar, Persian šakar, and ultimately Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, candied sugar crystals').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: azúcar

azúcar.notes: Commonly masculine in everyday Spain (el azúcar blanco/moreno), though the DLE accepts both masculine and feminine agreement.

año.etymology: Año descends from Latin annus. The Latin double n and the Spanish ñ give a useful visible connection between the older and modern forms of the word for a year.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: año
