año.notes: Keep ñ in both año and años. The word names a period of twelve months and also occurs in the Spanish way of giving someone’s age.

aún.etymology: Stressed temporal adverb ('still, yet'), inherited from Latin adhūc ('until now, hitherto, still'), with loss of final -c and nasalization in Ibero-Romance.

history.meaning: up to this time, still, yet

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aún
Wiktionary — aún

b&b.etymology: Title initialism of the Spanish Telecinco television dramedy B&b, de boca en boca (2014–2015), named after the fictional glossy magazine B&b at the center of the series and styled with the commercial typographic ampersand (&, originally a ligature of Latin et 'and').

morphemes.meaning: boca ('mouth', in de boca en boca 'by word of mouth')

history.meaning: Telecinco magazine dramedy starring Belén Rueda and Macarena García

sources.title: Wiktionary — & (Translingual)

b&b.notes: In Paquita Salas, Macarena García plays herself, so characters recognize her from her real-life breakthrough TV role as Sonia on Telecinco's B&b, de boca en boca.

bailar.etymology: Probably borrowed via Old Occitan bailar ('to dance, sway; originally to carry, rock, handle') from Late Latin bāiulāre ('to bear a load, carry a child in one's arms, rock to and fro'), derived from Classical Latin bāiulus ('porter, carrier'), or blended with Late Latin ballāre ('to dance', < Greek ballízō).

history.meaning: to rock in the arms / to dance

cognates.meaning: formal dance / classical dance (via French/Italian ballare)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bailar
Wiktionary — bailar

bailar.notes: Replaced medieval Spanish danzar as the everyday verb for dancing; saber cantar y bailar ('knowing how to sing and dance') is the classic triple-threat requirement in musical castings.

bailas.etymology: Second-person singular present indicative of bailar ('to dance'), via Old Occitan bailar from Late Latin bāiulāre ('to rock, sway') blended with ballāre ('to dance').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bailar
Wiktionary — bailas

bailas.notes: In auditions, A ver, ¿cómo bailas? ('Let's see how you dance') asks an actor to demonstrate rhythm on the spot.

bajado.etymology: Past participle and adjective of bajar ('to lower, go down, download'), derived from bajo ('low, short'), which continues Late Latin bassus ('thickset, low in stature'), with Vulgar Latin *bassiāre palatalizing -ssi- to Old Spanish -x- (/ʃ/) and Modern Castilian /x/ (j).

cognates.meaning: low (via Old French bas < Late Latin bassus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bajar
Wiktionary — bajado

bajado.notes: Used with llevar or tener for clothing mishaps: llevar la cremallera bajada is the natural Peninsular idiom for 'your fly/zipper is down'.

bajar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre ('to lower, go down'), derived from Late Latin bassus ('low, short in stature').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bajar
Wiktionary — bajar

bajo.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bassus ('thick, short, low'), with the palatal consonant of Old Spanish baxo influenced by the verb baxar (< *bassiāre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bajo
Wiktionary — bajo

balda.etymology: Originally a northern Spanish term for a wall or cupboard shelf, adopted into general Peninsular Spanish; of uncertain origin, linked by the DLE and Corominas to Basque balda ('shelf').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: balda
Wiktionary — balda

banda.etymology: Borrowed (partly via Italian banda and Middle French bande) from Gothic bandwō / Frankish *bandwa ('banner, standard around which a troop gathers, company of soldiers'), later extended to a troupe of musicians and modern rock/pop bands.

history.meaning: sign, banner -> troop rallying under one banner
musical band; gang; sash or strip (homophonous Germanic loan)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: banda
Wiktionary — banda

banda.notes: Covers a rock/pop group (montar una banda alongside un grupo), a brass marching band, a criminal gang, and film music in la banda sonora ('soundtrack').

bandeja.etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese bandeja ('tray, winnowing fan'), derived from bandejar ('to rock from side to side, sift grain'), built on banda ('side').

history.meaning: to sway from side to side, winnow

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bandeja
Wiktionary — bandeja

banquito.etymology: Formed within Spanish from banco ('bench, stool') + the diminutive suffix -ito; banco was borrowed from Germanic *bankiz ('bench, raised shelf').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: banco
Wiktionary — banquito

barbaridad.etymology: Derived from bárbaro ('uncivilized, outlandish, tremendous') + abstract suffix -idad (< Latin -itātem). Bárbaro comes via Latin barbarus from Ancient Greek bárbaros (βάρβαρος, 'non-Greek-speaking, foreign'), originally onomatopoeic for unintelligible 'bar-bar' speech.

morphemes.meaning: foreign, wild, extreme (< Latin barbarus < Greek bárbaros)

cognates.meaning: savage cruelty (much harsher than colloquial Spanish)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: barbaridad
Wiktionary — barbaridad

barbaridad.notes: In everyday Spain, ¡Qué barbaridad! rarely means literal savagery—it means 'How outrageous!', 'That's insane!', or 'Good grief!', and una barbaridad means 'a huge amount' (cuesta una barbaridad).

barrer.etymology: Inherited from Latin verrere ('to sweep, brush clean, drag across the floor'), with shift to the -er conjugation and regular opening of initial ve- to ba- before the trill -rr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: barrer
Wiktionary — barrer

barrio.etymology: The DLE derives barrio from Hispanic Arabic *bárri ('outer, suburban quarter'), from Classical Arabic barrī ('belonging to the open countryside outside town walls').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: barrio

barrio.notes: Names a distinct town neighbourhood with its own local shops, squares and daily life.

base.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin basis ('pedestal, foundation, base'), from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, 'stepping, foot, base'), derived from βαίνειν (baínein, 'to step, go').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: base
Wiktionary — base

basura.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *versūra ('floor-sweepings, refuse'), derived from versus, past participle of Classical Latin verrere ('to sweep'), with assimilation of -rs- to -s-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: basura
Wiktionary — basura

batería.etymology: Borrowed from French batterie ('beating, artillery battery; later an interconnected bank of Leyden jars or electrical cells, and a drum kit'), derived from Old French batre ('to beat, strike', < Vulgar Latin *battere for Classical Latin battuere).

morphemes.meaning: set of instruments or action (< French -erie)

history.meaning: artillery unit -> electrical cell bank (Benjamin Franklin, 1749) / drum set
rechargeable phone/car battery; drum kit; drummer

rootFamily.gloss: to beat, whisk, break a record

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: batería
Wiktionary — batería

batería.notes: Spanish splits English 'battery' into two words: batería for rechargeable batteries (phones, laptops, cars: no tengo batería) and pila for disposable AA/AAA batteries. La batería is also a drum kit (and el/la batería the drummer).

batir.etymology: Descends from Vulgar Latin *battĕre, reduced from Classical Latin battuĕre ('to beat, strike, pound').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: batir

batir.notes: In cooking, batir means 'to whisk or beat' eggs, cream, or lemon curd.

baño.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *banneum for Classical Latin balneum ('bath, bathhouse'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon, 'bathing room').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: baño
Wiktionary — baño

baúl.etymology: Via older Spanish bahúl, borrowed from Old French bahur / bahut (or Italian baule), a medieval European term for a domed traveling trunk of uncertain ultimate origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: baúl
Wiktionary — baúl

beber.etymology: Inherited from Latin bibere ('to drink'), showing regular Western Romance lowering of short i to e and spirantization of intervocalic -b-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: beber
Wiktionary — beber

belinda.etymology: Female given name Belinda, popularized in European literature since the 17th–18th centuries (notably Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock, 1712), likely stemming from Continental Germanic name elements such as *berō ('bear') or Old High German beti + *lind ('soft, gentle, flexible; linden shield; serpent'), later re-associated by folk etymology with Italian bella ('beautiful').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Belinda

belinda.notes: In Paquita Salas, British-born Spanish actress and 1990s Telecinco TV presenter Belinda Washington plays a hilarious fictionalized version of herself.

benéfico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin beneficus ('generous, obliging, doing good'), a compound of bene ('well', adverb of bonus 'good') + -ficus ('making, doing', unstressed combining form of facere 'to make, do').

history.meaning: well + to do -> doing good, generous

cognates.meaning: charitable / fundraising event (shared bene + facere base)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: benéfico
Wiktionary — benéfico

benéfico.notes: In modern Spain, benéfico primarily means 'charity / fundraising' (concierto benéfico, gala benéfica), whereas 'beneficial for you' is usually beneficioso.

besito.etymology: Affective diminutive of beso ('kiss'), formed with -ito (< Vulgar Latin *-īttus). Beso descends regularly from Latin bāsium ('kiss', originally an affectionate word of Celtic/Cisalpine Gaulish provenance adopted by Catullus), with attraction of the yod turning -āsi- > -aiso > Old Spanish beso.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: beso
Wiktionary — besito

besito.notes: Un besito is one of Spain's most ubiquitous warm phone, WhatsApp, and doorstep farewells among friends, colleagues, and family—platonic rather than romantic.

besitos.etymology: Plural of besito ('little kiss'), affective diminutive of beso ('kiss', inherited from Latin bāsium) + -ito + plural -s.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: beso
Wiktionary — besitos

besitos.notes: The breezy Peninsular equivalent of French Bisous! when hanging up the phone or ending a voice note (Besitos, chao).

beso.etymology: Inherited from Latin bāsium ('affectionate kiss', distinct in Classical Latin from formal ōsculum and passionate suāvium), a Cisalpine word popularized in Rome by the poet Catullus; regular yod-metathesis evolved bāsium > *baisu > beso.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: beso
Wiktionary — beso

beso.notes: In Spain, social greetings typically involve dos besos (one light cheek touch on the right, then the left), and mandar un beso / un beso closes phone calls and emails.

biblioteca.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca ('library, book room'), from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē), a compound of βιβλίον (biblíon, 'book') and θήκη (thḗkē, 'receptacle, storage case').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: biblioteca
Wiktionary — biblioteca

bien.etymology: Bien descends regularly from Latin bene ('well'), with stressed short Latin ĕ diphthongizing to Castilian ie and final -e dropping after -n.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bien

bien.notes: Adverbial counterpart to adjective bueno: dormir bien ('sleep well') vs un buen día ('a good day').

bienvenido.etymology: Compound formed in Spanish from bien ('well', < Latin bene) + venido ('come, arrived', past participle of venir < Latin venīre), parallel to French bienvenu and Italian benvenuto.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bienvenido
Wiktionary — bienvenido

bienvenidos.etymology: Masculine plural of bienvenido ('welcome'), formed by univerbation of bien ('well', < Latin bene) + venido ('come, arrived', past participle of venir < Latin venīre), modeled on medieval Romance greeting formulas (compare Old French bien venu).

rootFamily.gloss: welcome (f. sg., and noun dar la bienvenida)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bienvenido
Wiktionary — bienvenidos

bienvenidos.notes: Unlike invariable English 'Welcome!', Spanish inflects bienvenido (-a, -os, -as) to match the person or group addressed (Bienvenidos a Navarrete). Never use bienvenido for 'You're welcome' after 'thank you'—that is de nada.

billete.etymology: Borrowed from French billet ('short note, ticket, banknote'), diminutive of Old French bille ('written note'), an alteration of Medieval Latin bulla ('sealed document, papal bull').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: billete
Wiktionary — billete

bisagra.etymology: Probably formed from Latin bis- ('twofold, double') + Old Spanish sagra (denoting a two-leaved metal hinge), though the exact second element remains debated.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bisagra
Wiktionary — bisagra

bizcocho.etymology: Bizcocho continues Latin bis coctus ('twice baked'), originally naming crisp ship's biscuit dried twice in the oven before shifting in Spain to light sponge cake.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bizcocho

bizcocho.notes: In Peninsula Spanish un bizcocho casero is a fluffy homemade sponge cake, often baked with lemon or cinnamon for breakfast.

blanca.etymology: Feminine singular of blanco ('white'), borrowed in Late Antiquity / Early Romance from Germanic *blank ('shining, bright, dazzling white', compare Old High German blanch), which displaced Classical Latin albus across most of Western Romance.

history.meaning: white (f.); old small coin (estar sin blanca: to be penniless)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: blanco
Wiktionary — blanca

blanca.notes: Besides describing color (una pared blanca), estar sin blanca ('to be flat broke') preserves the memory of a medieval Castilian low-value silver-alloy coin called la blanca.

blanco.etymology: Blanco entered Romance from Germanic *blank ('shining, gleaming white'), displacing Classical Latin albus as the everyday Spanish word for white.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: blanco

blanco.notes: Inflects regularly across four forms: blanco, blanca, blancos, blancas.

blando.etymology: Inherited from Latin blandus ('caressing, smooth, flattering, gentle'), which shifted in Ibero-Romance from pleasantness of manner to physical softness and pliability.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: blando
Wiktionary — blando

boca.etymology: Inherited from Latin bucca ('puffed-out cheek'), which in colloquial and Vulgar Latin displaced Classical Latin ōs, ōris as the standard word for 'mouth'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: boca
Wiktionary — boca

bocado.etymology: Inherited from Latin buccātus or formed within Spanish from boca ('mouth', < Latin bucca) + -ado, denoting a mouthful, bite of food, or horse's bit.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bocado
Wiktionary — bocado

boda.etymology: Inherited from Latin vōta ('solemn vows, marriage vows'), neuter plural of vōtum ('vow, promise to the gods', from vovēre 'to vow'), reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a feminine singular noun because of its -a ending, with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

rootFamily.gloss: vote; religious vow (learned doublet of boda)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: boda
Wiktionary — boda

boda.notes: Remarkable doublet: inherited boda ('wedding') and learned voto ('vote, vow') both trace back to Latin vōtum. Plural bodas is also used for wedding anniversaries (bodas de plata, bodas de oro).

bola.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bulla ('bubble, stud, round boss, ball', or via Occitan/Catalan bola where Latin -ll- simplified to -l- rather than Castilian -ll-), alongside native Spanish bulla and learned bula.

cognates.meaning: borrowings from French boule / Medieval Latin bulla

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bola
Wiktionary — bola

bola.notes: Sports games usually use pelota or balón, whereas bola appears in billiards/lottery spheres and vivid Peninsular idioms like no dar pie con bola ('to get everything wrong / fumble hopelessly') and ir a su bola ('to do one's own thing').

bollo.etymology: The DLE traces bollo ('soft bun, small roll') to Latin bulla ('bubble, rounded knob, boss'), referring to the puffed round shape of risen dough.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bollo

bollo.notes: Un bollo recién hecho in Spain is a soft sweet roll or breakfast pastry fresh from the oven.

bolsa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bursa ('leather bag, purse'), borrowed from Ancient Greek βύρσα (býrsa, 'dressed hide, wineskin'), with dissimilation of -rs- to -ls-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bolsa
Wiktionary — bolsa

bolsillo.etymology: Diminutive formed in Spanish from bolso / bolsa ('bag, purse', < Late Latin bursa < Greek βύρσα) + -illo, specialized for a garment pocket.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bolsillo
Wiktionary — bolsillo

bolígrafo.etymology: Twentieth-century compound coined from bola ('ball', referring to the tiny rolling metal ball at the nib, < Latin bulla) + the Greek-derived combining form -grafo (-γράφος, 'writer').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bolígrafo
Wiktionary — bolígrafo

bombilla.etymology: Diminutive of bomba ('hollow sphere, glass globe, pump', ultimately from Latin bombus < Greek βόμβος 'booming sound'), applied first to spherical glass lamp globes and later to electric lightbulbs.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bombilla
Wiktionary — bombilla

bonito.etymology: Diminutive of bueno ('good', < Latin bonus), formed on the unstressed stem bon- + -ito, shifting from 'good little, nice' to 'pretty, attractive'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bonito
Wiktionary — bonito

borde.etymology: Borrowed from French bord ('edge, rim, ship's side'), which comes from Frankish *bord ('plank, board, border').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: borde
Wiktionary — borde

bordillo.etymology: Diminutive formed in Spanish from borde ('edge, rim', < French bord < Frankish *bord) + -illo, designating the raised stone curb bordering a sidewalk.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bordillo
Wiktionary — bordillo

borgia.etymology: Italianized spelling of the noble Valencian-Aragonese surname Borja, originating from the Aragonese town of Borja (Zaragoza), whose name derives from Andalusi Arabic Búrja (from Arabic burj بُرْج 'tower, fortress', itself borrowed via Late Latin burgus / Greek pýrgos).

history.meaning: town in Aragon; noble House of Borja
Italian spelling of Pope Alexander VI's family

sources.title: Wiktionary — Borgia

borgia.notes: Although native Spanish historians call the Renaissance dynasty los Borja, international historical drama series (such as Showtime's The Borgias and European co-production Borgia) popularized 'Los Borgia' in TV-production talk.

borrar.etymology: Derived in Spanish from borra ('coarse shearings of wool, sediment, dregs', from Late Latin burra 'shaggy cloth'), originally meaning 'to smear or blot out writing'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: borrar
Wiktionary — borrar

bosque.etymology: Borrowed via Catalan or Occitan bosc from Medieval Latin boscus ('woodland, thicket'), of pre-Roman or Germanic (*busk-) origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bosque
Wiktionary — bosque

bote.etymology: Conflates three homonyms: 'canister, jar' from Old Spanish bote (related to Late Latin buttis 'cask, vessel'); 'bounce, leap' from botar (< Frankish *bōtan 'to thrust, strike'); and 'small boat' from Middle English boot or Old French bot.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bote
Wiktionary — bote

botella.etymology: Borrowed from French bouteille ('bottle'), which evolved from Late Latin butticula ('small flask or cask'), diminutive of buttis ('cask, wineskin').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: botella
Wiktionary — botella

botón.etymology: Borrowed from Old French boton (modern bouton, 'flower bud, knob, button'), derived from boter ('to push out, sprout'), from Frankish *bōtan ('to push, strike').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: botón
Wiktionary — botón

bravo.etymology: Used as an interjection of acclaim via Italian ¡bravo! ('well done!, magnificent!'), sharing the origin of the adjective bravo ('fierce, untamed, brave'). Most Romanists trace bravo to Late/Vulgar Latin *brabus from Classical Latin barbarus ('wild, untamed') crossed with prāvus ('crooked, fierce').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bravo
Wiktionary — bravo

bravo.notes: As an interjection ¡Bravo! is invariable in Spanish; as an adjective, bravo means 'fierce' (toro bravo, mar bravo, patatas bravas), while 'brave' for people is usually valiente.

brazo.etymology: Brazo continues Latin bracchium ('forearm, arm'), itself borrowed from Greek brakhíōn.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brazo

brazo.notes: Llevar algo en brazos means 'to carry something in one's arms'.

brillante.etymology: Active participial adjective of brillar ('shining, bright, brilliant'), borrowed via Italian brillante / brillare.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brillante
Wiktionary — brillante

brillar.etymology: Borrowed from Italian brillare ('to shine, sparkle, glitter'), likely derived from Latin bēryllus ('beryl, sparkling crystal', from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brillar
Wiktionary — brillar

brillo.etymology: Deverbal noun from brillar ('to shine, sparkle, gleam'), borrowed from Italian brillare.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brillo
Wiktionary — brillo

brindar.etymology: Derived from brindis ('a toast'), borrowed via Italian brindisi from the 16th-century German soldiers' phrase bring dir's ('(I) bring it to you', said when raising a glass).

history.meaning: I bring it to you (as a toast)
a toast / to drink a toast

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brindar
Wiktionary — brindar

británico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin Britannicus ('British, pertaining to Britannia'), derived via Ancient Greek Prettanikḗ / Bretannía from Common Brittonic *Pritanī ('the Britons', perhaps 'the painted/figured ones' from *pritu- 'form, figure').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: británico
Wiktionary — británico

británico.notes: In casual Spain Spanish, speakers often playfully contrast 'UK English' vs. 'American English' by saying inglés inglés or inglés británico vs. inglés americano.

brocha.etymology: Borrowed from French broche ('spit, pointed peg, bristle brush'), descending from Vulgar Latin *brocca ('spike, pointed projection'), feminine of Latin broccus ('having projecting teeth').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brocha
Wiktionary — brocha

brochazo.etymology: Formed within Spanish from brocha ('paintbrush') + the suffix -azo denoting a stroke or blow ('brushstroke').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brochazo
Wiktionary — brochazo

bruja.etymology: Feminine of brujo ('witch, sorcerer'), a characteristically Iberian word (compare Catalan bruixa, Galician-Portuguese bruxa, Aragonese bruixa) of pre-Roman Paleohispanic (possibly Celtic *brixtā 'magical spell', cognate with Old Irish bricht 'incantation') origin.

history.meaning: witch; (colloq.) spiteful person or uncanny mind-reader

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brujo
Wiktionary — bruja

bruja.notes: One of Iberia's most famous pre-Roman survivals! Used dramatically as a fairy-tale insult (¡Bruja!), or affectionately when someone guesses a secret (¡Qué bruja eres!, 'Are you psychic?!').

bueno.etymology: Bueno continues Latin bonus ('good'), with stressed short Latin ŏ diphthongizing regularly to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bueno

bueno.notes: Shortens to buen directly before a masculine singular noun (buen viaje, buen sitio), and gives the plural greeting ¡Buenos días!.

buenísima.etymology: Feminine singular absolute superlative of bueno ('good', < Latin bonus), formed with the learned superlative suffix -ísima (< Latin -issima). Unlike inherited diphthongized buena, this everyday form keeps the diphthong buen- (alongside literary/elevated bonísima).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: bueno
Wiktionary — buenísima

buenísima.notes: With ser, es buenísima means 'it's/she's brilliant, top-notch' (una oportunidad buenísima); with estar about a person, estar buenísima is colloquial for 'to be super hot/attractive'.

buenísimo.etymology: Absolute superlative of bueno ('good', < Latin bonus) + superlative suffix -ísimo (< Latin -issimus), retaining the spoken diphthong buen- of the base adjective rather than the Latinate stem bon- (bonísimo).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: bueno
Wiktionary — buenísimo

buenísimo.notes: Fully endorsed by the RAE for standard speech and writing (aquel corto era buenísimo, 'that short film was brilliant'; está buenísimo for delicious food).

buhardilla.etymology: Diminutive of buharda ('skylight, garret window, attic'), originally a roof vent for smoke, likely related to Old French bouffarde / bouffer ('to puff, blow out smoke').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: buhardilla
Wiktionary — buhardilla

burbuja.etymology: Expressive onomatopoeic creation built on the imitative root *burb- (evoking the sound of bubbling or boiling water, akin to Latin bullīre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: burbuja
Wiktionary — burbuja

buscan.etymology: Third-person plural present indicative of buscar ('to look for, search, seek'), an emblematic Ibero-Romance verb (compare Portuguese buscar) of pre-Roman—most likely Hispano-Celtic—origin (Corominas compares Celto-Latin *buscus 'wood, thicket', from 'beating the bush for game', or Celtic *bhudh-sk-).

morphemes.meaning: look for, seek (< buscar, of pre-Roman Iberian origin)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: buscar
Wiktionary — buscan

buscan.notes: Crucial syntax point: buscar already builds 'for' into its meaning—never add por (*buscar por algo); say buscan actores or te buscan (with personal a for people: buscan a una actriz).

buscar.etymology: The DLE marks buscar as of uncertain pre-Roman (likely Indo-European or Celto-Romance) origin, attested early across Castilian and Portuguese.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: buscar

buscar.notes: Buscar already includes the English 'for' inside the verb: busco mis llaves (never *busco por mis llaves).

but.etymology: Unadapted English adversative conjunction ('but'), heard in a rehearsed English audition line in Paquita Salas ('But it's very important...'). Inherited from Old English būtan ('outside, except, but'), compounded from be- ('by') + ūtan ('from outside', related to out).

rootFamily.gloss: but (standard Spanish equivalent < Latin per hoc)

sources.title: Wiktionary — but (English)

but.notes: Appears verbatim inside English script-rehearsal lines in Paquita Salas, where Spanish actors struggle heroically with English phonetics.

buzón.etymology: Borrowed from Old French buisson / bozon ('thick crossbow quarrel or bolt with a blunt head; later stopper, plug, spout, and mail slot'), of Frankish origin (*bultjō 'bolt'), semantically transferred in Spanish from a conduit/slot to a letterbox and later voicemail.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: buzón
Wiktionary — buzón

buzón.notes: Covers physical postboxes, email inboxes (buzón de entrada), and mobile voicemail: salta el buzón de voz means 'it's going straight to voicemail'.

caballero.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin caballārius ('horseman, rider, groom'), derived from caballus ('workhorse, riding horse'); in the Middle Ages it came to denote a mounted knight and later a gentleman.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caballero
Wiktionary — caballero

caballo.etymology: Inherited from Latin caballus ('pack-horse, workhorse, nag', probably an ancient Balkan or Celtic loanword into Latin), which completely replaced Classical aristocratic equus for 'stallion/horse' across all of Romance (while equa survived as Spanish yegua 'mare').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caballo
Wiktionary — caballo

caballo.notes: Montar a caballo ('riding a horse') is a classic skill actors claim on their CV whether or not they have ever been near a stable!

cabaret.etymology: Borrowed from French cabaret ('intimate nightclub with satirical songs, burlesque, or variety acts; originally a tavern'), entering French from Picard/Walloon cabaret ('tavern, small room') via Middle Dutch cabret / cambret, ultimately from Old Picard cambrete ('little room', diminutive of Latin camera).

history.meaning: tavern; 19th-century Montmartre artistic music-hall (Le Chat Noir)

cognates.meaning: stage floor-show or intimate music venue

rootFamily.gloss: Hispanicized spelling recognized by the RAE

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cabaret
Wiktionary — cabaret

cabaret.notes: Spaniards pronounce either /kabaˈɾet/ (keeping final -t) or /kabaˈɾe/ (matching the RAE-accepted spelling cabaré).

caber.etymology: Inherited from Latin capere ('to take, hold, have room for'), which shifted to the second conjugation (*capēre) in Vulgar Latin with regular voicing of -p- to -b-.

history.meaning: to hold, contain, have room for

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caber
Wiktionary — caber

cabeza.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitia ('head', originally plural of *capitium 'neck-opening of a tunic'), derived from Classical Latin caput, capitis ('head').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cabeza
Wiktionary — cabeza

cabezota.etymology: Formed within Spanish from cabeza ('head', < Vulgar Latin *capitia) + the augmentative suffix -ota ('big-headed; stubborn, strong-willed').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cabezota
Wiktionary — cabezota

cable.etymology: Borrowed via French câble (or Catalan/Occitan cable) from Late/Medieval Latin capulum ('halter, lasso, heavy mooring rope'), derived from capere ('to seize, hold').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cable
Wiktionary — cable

cada.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cata ('each, every'), borrowed from the Ancient Greek distributive preposition κατά (katá, 'down, by, apiece', as in κατὰ ἕνα 'one by one').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cada
Wiktionary — cada

cadena.etymology: Inherited from Latin catēna ('chain, fetter, connected series'), showing regular Western Romance voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d- (catēna > cadena). In the 20th century it calqued English broadcasting 'network/chain' (cadena de radio / televisión).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cadena
Wiktionary — cadena

cadena.notes: In Spanish media, una cadena (de televisión) is a broadcasting network or channel (like TVE, Antena 3, or Telecinco)—just like French une chaîne.

caer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadēre, a conjugation-shifted form of Classical Latin cadere ('to fall, drop'), with regular loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caer
Wiktionary — caer

caes.etymology: Second-person singular present indicative of caer ('to fall'), inherited from Latin cadere ('to fall, drop'), which shifted in Vulgar Latin from 3rd conjugation cadere to 2nd conjugation *cadēre, followed by regular loss of intervocalic -d- (cadēs > caes).

rootFamily.gloss: to fall (caer bien/mal: to make a good/bad impression)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caer
Wiktionary — caes

caes.notes: Warning someone mid-stumble uses pronominal caerse plus warning que: ¡Que te caes! ('Watch out, you're gonna fall!'). And me caes muy bien means 'I really like you (as a person)'.

cafecito.etymology: Diminutive of café ('coffee'), formed with the interfixed diminutive -cito (used on oxytones ending in a stressed vowel). Café entered Spanish via French café and Italian caffè from Ottoman Turkish kahve, ultimately from Arabic qahwa (قَهْوَة, 'coffee, dark brew').

morphemes.meaning: coffee (< French café < Turkish kahve < Arabic qahwa)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: café
Wiktionary — cafecito

cafecito.notes: In Spanish bar culture, ordering un cafecito solo ('a quick straight espresso, no milk') softens the request and signals an unhurried chat; colloquial Spain also uses cafelito or cafetito.

cafetera.etymology: Derived from café ('coffee') + -tera (modeled on tetera / chocolatera and French cafetière), where café ultimately comes via French, Italian, and Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwah.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cafetera
Wiktionary — cafetera

cafetería.etymology: Formed in Spanish from cafetero ('coffee maker/seller', from café) + the place suffix -ería ('coffee shop, café').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cafetería
Wiktionary — cafetería

café.etymology: Café entered Spanish via French café and Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish kahve and Classical Arabic qahwah.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: café

café.notes: Names both the drink (un café con leche) and the café establishment; plural is los cafés.

caja.etymology: From Old Spanish caxa (reinforced by Catalan or Occitan caixa), descending from Latin capsa ('cylindrical box or case for scrolls').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caja
Wiktionary — caja

cajón.etymology: Augmentative formed in Spanish from caja ('box', < Latin capsa) + -ón, specialized to denote a sliding furniture drawer or large wooden crate.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cajón
Wiktionary — cajón

caldera.etymology: Caldera continues Late Latin caldāria ('cauldron, hot-water bath'), derived from Latin calĭdus ('warm, hot').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caldera

caldera.notes: In modern buildings la caldera is the central-heating and hot-water boiler.

calefacción.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin calefactiō, calefactiōnis ('a warming, heating'), derived from calefacere ('to make warm', from calēre 'to be warm' + facere 'to make').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: calefacción
Wiktionary — calefacción

calentar.etymology: Formed on the stem of caliente ('warm, hot', < Latin calēns, calentis, present participle of calēre 'to be warm') + -ar (Vulgar Latin *calentāre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: calentar
Wiktionary — calentar

calentito.etymology: Affective diminutive of caliente ('nice and warm, freshly heated'), formed from caliente (< Latin calēns, calentis) + -ito.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caliente
Wiktionary — calentito

caliente.etymology: Caliente descends from Latin calens, calentis ('being warm or hot'), the active present participle of calēre ('to be warm').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caliente

caliente.notes: Same singular form for masculine and feminine (té caliente, sopa caliente); diminutive calentito sounds warm and cosy.

callado.etymology: Participial adjective of callar ('quiet, silent'), which descends from Late/Vulgar Latin *callāre ('to lower sails, let down, stop speaking'), from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō, 'to slacken, lower').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: callado
Wiktionary — callado

callar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *callāre ('to lower, slacken sail, drop one's voice'), borrowed from Ancient Greek khalân (χαλᾶν, 'to slacken, loosen, let down', originally a Mediterranean nautical command to lower sails and fall quiet).

morphemes.meaning: lower voice, keep silent (< Vulgar Latin *callāre < Greek khalân)

history.meaning: to lower -> to drop one's voice, fall silent

cognates.meaning: to lower, drop, subside (preserving the physical sense)

rootFamily.gloss: to soak through; lower (non-palatalized maritime doublet)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: callar
Wiktionary — callar

callar.notes: Blunt ¡Cállate! means 'Shut up!', whereas repeated ¡Calla, calla! in Peninsular conversation is friendly and expressive ('Don't even get me started!' or 'Never mind, forget it!').

calle.etymology: Calle continues Latin callis ('footpath, narrow track'), which broadened in Castilian to become the standard word for a paved town street.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: calle

calle.notes: Feminine noun (la calle, nuestra calle), despite ending in -e.

callejón.etymology: Augmentative of calleja ('narrow lane, alley', itself a diminutive of calle < Latin callis 'narrow track, footpath') + -ón.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: callejón
Wiktionary — callejón

calma.etymology: Inherited via Late Latin cauma ('burning heat of the sun, windless midday stillness') from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, 'burning heat', from καίειν 'to burn'), with vocalic change of au to al.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: calma
Wiktionary — calma

calor.etymology: Inherited from Latin calor, calōris ('warmth, heat, glow'), an abstract noun derived from the verb calēre ('to be warm or hot').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: calor
Wiktionary — calor

cama.etymology: The DLE traces cama to Late Latin cama ('low bed on the floor'), recorded by Isidore of Seville and likely of pre-Roman Hispanic origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cama

cama.notes: Hacer la cama means 'to make the bed'.

cambiado.etymology: Participial adjective of cambiar ('changed, altered'), descending from Late Latin cambiāre ('to exchange, barter').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cambiado
Wiktionary — cambiado

cambian.etymology: Third-person plural present indicative of cambiar ('to change, exchange'), inherited from Late Latin cambiāre ('to barter, exchange'), a Gaulish/Celtic loanword in Roman commerce (*kambjāre 'to bend back, exchange', from PIE *kemb- 'to turn').

rootFamily.gloss: change, exchange (en cambio: on the other hand)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cambiar
Wiktionary — cambian

cambian.notes: Los tiempos cambian ('Times change') uses non-reflexive cambiar; reflexive cambiarse (de ropa) means 'to get changed (clothes)' or 'to switch places'.

cambiar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cambiāre ('to exchange, barter'), a Latin borrowing from Gaulish (Celtic) *kambjā- ('to exchange, turn back and forth').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cambiar
Wiktionary — cambiar

cambio.etymology: Deverbal noun from cambiar or inherited directly from Late Latin cambium ('exchange, barter'), of Gaulish (Celtic) origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cambio
Wiktionary — cambio

camilla.etymology: Italian female given name Camilla (Spanish Camila), continuing Classical Latin Camilla (feminine of camillus, a freeborn youth attending priests at Roman sacrifices, probably of Etruscan origin; immortalized by Virgil in the Aeneid as the Volscian warrior maiden Camilla).

history.meaning: ritual attendant; Volscian warrior heroine in Virgil's Aeneid

sources.title: Wiktionary — Camilla

camilla.notes: In Paquita Salas, Camilla Isola is the Italian-named international casting director coordinating a major European historical series; don't confuse the Italian name Camilla with the common Spanish noun una camilla ('stretcher / massage table', diminutive of cama).

caminar.etymology: Formed in Romance from camino ('road, path, way', < Vulgar Latin camīnus of Celtic origin) + -ar ('to travel along a path, walk').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caminar
Wiktionary — caminar

camino.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin camīnus ('way, road, path'), borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic) *kanmīnos ('step, path'; compare Welsh cam and Old Irish céimm 'step').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: camino
Wiktionary — camino

camisa.etymology: Continues Late Latin camisia ('linen undershirt, nightshirt'), recorded by St Jerome and borrowed into Latin from Gaulish (Celtic).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: camisa

camisa.notes: Shared across Romance languages (Portuguese camisa, French chemise, Italian camicia).

camiseta.etymology: Diminutive of camisa ('shirt'), formed with the suffix -eta (reinforced by French camisette / Catalan samarreta). Camisa descends from Late Latin camīsia ('linen undergarment, soldier's tunic'), recorded by St. Jerome as a military loanword from Gaulish or Proto-Germanic *hamiþją ('shirt').

history.meaning: button-up shirt -> undershirt, T-shirt, sports jersey

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: camiseta
Wiktionary — camiseta

camiseta.notes: In Spain, camiseta is the universal word for a T-shirt or team jersey (where Mexico says playera, Argentina remera, and Colombia/Peru polo).

camión.etymology: Borrowed from French camion ('heavy freight cart, motor truck'), originally a northern French (Norman/Picard) word for a low dray wagon.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: camión
Wiktionary — camión

campana.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin campāna ('bell'), originally vāsa Campāna ('Campanian bronze vessels'), named after Campania in southern Italy, renowned in antiquity for bronze casting.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: campana
Wiktionary — campana

campanada.etymology: Derived within Spanish from campana ('bell', < Late Latin campāna) + the suffix -ada ('stroke or toll of a bell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: campanada
Wiktionary — campanada

campanadas.etymology: Plural of campanada ('stroke or toll of a bell'), formed from campana ('bell') + blow/stroke suffix -ada. Campana descends from Late Latin campāna (short for vāsa Campāna 'bronze vessels from Campania', the southern Italian region renowned in Late Antiquity for bell-metal founding).

rootFamily.gloss: to cause a sensation / pull off an upset

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: campanada
Wiktionary — campanadas

campanadas.notes: Culturally iconic in Spain: las Campanadas specifically evokes the televised twelve midnight chimes on New Year's Eve from Madrid's Puerta del Sol, when Spaniards eat twelve lucky grapes—hosting las Campanadas is a pinnacle TV honor.

campeón.etymology: Borrowed via Italian campione from Medieval Latin campiō, campiōnis ('combatant in a judicial duel, champion'), derived from Latin campus ('battlefield') or West Germanic *kampijō.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: campeón
Wiktionary — campeón

campo.etymology: Inherited from Latin campus ('open level ground, plain, field', famously the Campus Mārtius in Rome).

cognates.meaning: Latin and French borrowings from campus

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: campo
Wiktionary — campo

campo.notes: El campo is Spain's everyday expression for 'the countryside' (ir al campo, casa de campo), alongside sports pitches (campo de fútbol) and camera framing (fuera de campo 'off-camera').

canción.etymology: Continues Latin cantiō, cantiōnem ('song, singing'), a verbal noun from canere ('to sing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: canción

canela.etymology: Canela was borrowed from Italian cannella, diminutive of canna ('reed, small tube'), named after the rolled quill shape of dried cinnamon bark.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: canela

canela.notes: Uncountable feminine spice noun (pan con canela, una rama de canela).

canelón.etymology: Adapted via Catalan caneló from Italian cannellone (plural cannelloni, 'large reed or tube, tubular stuffed pasta'), augmentative of cannella ('little reed/tube'), from Latin canna ('reed, cane') < Ancient Greek kánna.

morphemes.meaning: small reed, tube (< Italian cannella < Latin canna)

cognates.meaning: traditional St. Stephen's Day baked cannelloni

rootFamily.gloss: reed, cane; small draft beer (inherited doublet of canna)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: canelón
Wiktionary — canelón

canelón.notes: In Paquita Salas, rival powerhouse agent Fernando Canelón bears this deliciously comic food surname ('Fernando Cannelloni'), while in Spain los canelones are a beloved Sunday and holiday dish.

cansado.etymology: Participial adjective of cansar ('to tire, exhaust'), inherited from Latin campsāre ('to round a cape or headland, turn aside from one's course'), borrowed by Roman sailors from Ancient Greek kámpsai (κάμψαι, aorist stem of kámptein 'to bend, double a turning-post'). Exhausted rowers 'turning back' shifted the sense to 'growing weary'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cansado
Wiktionary — cansado

cansado.notes: Classic ser vs. estar pair: estoy cansada ('I am tired') vs. es muy cansado ('it is very tiring/tiresome').

cantar.etymology: Inherited from Latin cantāre ('to sing, chant'), originally the frequentative of canĕre ('to sing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cantar

cantar.notes: In the idiom cantar victoria, it means 'to declare victory prematurely'.

capa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cappa ('hooded cloak, cape'), first attested in Isidore of Seville (likely connected to caput 'head' as a head-covering mantle); figuratively 'layer, coat'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: capa
Wiktionary — capa

capitulito.etymology: Diminutive of capítulo ('chapter; TV episode'), formed with -ito. Capítulo is a learned borrowing from Latin capitulum ('little head, heading, section of a law or book'), itself a diminutive of caput ('head').

history.meaning: TV episode -> one little guest episode

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: capítulo

capitulito.notes: Notice the pragmatic Peninsular diminutive: un capitulito doesn't mean a short episode—it means 'just one modest little guest spot on an episode' when padding an actor's résumé.

capítulo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin capitulum ('little head, section heading, chapter'), diminutive of caput, capitis ('head').

cognates.meaning: book division (via Old French chapitre < capitulum)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: capítulo
Wiktionary — capítulo

capítulo.notes: In Spain, TV viewers and actors say un capítulo far more often than un episodio when binge-watching or filming a series (Ponme otro capítulo, 'Put on another episode').

cara.etymology: Inherited via Vulgar Latin cara ('face, countenance', attested in the 6th-century poet Corippus) from Ancient Greek kárā (κάρα, 'head, face'), which gradually displaced Old Spanish faz (< Latin faciēs) as the everyday Castilian word for 'face'.

history.meaning: face; side of a coin/page; nerve/cheek

cognates.meaning: originally 'face, expression' via Anglo-Norman chere < Late Latin cara!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cara
Wiktionary — cara

cara.notes: Rich in Peninsular idioms: dar la cara ('to step up / take responsibility'), echar en cara ('to throw in someone's face'), and ¡Qué cara tienes! ('What nerve!'). Also homophonous with feminine cara ('expensive', < Latin cāra).

caramba.etymology: Minced oath formed in Spanish by altering the ending of the taboo exclamation ¡carajo!, used to express surprise, astonishment, or mild annoyance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caramba
Wiktionary — caramba

caras.etymology: Feminine plural of the adjective caro ('expensive, costly; originally beloved, dear'), inherited directly from Latin cārus ('dear, precious, high-priced', from PIE *keh₂-ro-, cognate with English whore and Sanskrit kāma).

cognates.meaning: borrowings from the same Latin cārus family

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caro
Wiktionary — caras

caras.notes: In modern everyday Spanish, caro/cara means 'expensive' (las medias son caras, contrasted with baratas 'cheap'), while emotional 'dear/beloved' moved to querido. Also homophonous with las caras ('faces').

cards.etymology: English plural noun in the American political-drama title House of Cards ('castillo de naipes'), borrowed into Middle English carde from Old French carte ('playing card, stiff paper'), from Latin charta < Ancient Greek khártēs ('leaf of papyrus').

history.meaning: Netflix political drama referenced as an industry benchmark

sources.title: Wiktionary — card (English)

cards.notes: Referenced in Paquita Salas when characters name-drop prestige streaming series ('House of Cards'); the native Spanish idiom for 'a house of cards' is un castillo de naipes.

cargo.etymology: Deverbal noun from cargar ('to load, charge, entrust'), inherited from Late Latin carricāre ('to load onto a wagon'), derived from Gallo-Latin carrus ('four-wheeled Celtic wagon', from Gaulish *karros).

morphemes.meaning: load, responsibility (< cargar < Late Latin carricāre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cargo
Wiktionary — cargo

cargo.notes: English borrowed cargo from Spanish for freight, but in Spain freight is la carga, while el cargo means an official post, a debit charge, or personal responsibility: queda a tu cargo ('it's your responsibility') and hacerse cargo ('to take charge').

cariño.etymology: Derived from dialectal/Aragonese cariñar ('to miss someone, feel longing for'), descending from Latin carēre ('to lack, be deprived of, miss'), later colored semantically by caro ('dear, beloved').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cariño
Wiktionary — cariño

carlos.etymology: Spanish male given name Carlos (preserving an old Medieval Latin/Old French nominative -s ending, as in Marcos and Pablos), from Medieval Latin Carolus, Latinized from Frankish *Karl / Proto-Germanic *karlaz ('free man', cognate with Old English ceorl 'churl' and German Kerl), spread throughout Europe by Charlemagne.

sources.title: Wiktionary — Carlos (Spanish)

carlos.notes: Historically one of Spain's royal dynastic names (Carlos I through Carlos IV); invariable in form, with affectionate diminutive Carlitos.

carmen.etymology: Classic Spanish female given name shortened from María del Carmen (Our Lady of Mount Carmel), blending Hebrew Karmel (כַּרְמֶל, Har ha-Karmel 'vineyard/garden-land of God', the coastal mountain range in Haifa) with homophonous Latin carmen ('song, poem, charm'), which reinforced its poetic prestige in Spain.

rootFamily.gloss: (in Granada) walled villa with garden; (poetic) verse

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carmen
Wiktionary — Carmen

carmen.notes: So common in Spanish theater and cinema—think Carmen Machi or Carmen Maura—that agents regularly have to ask '¿Qué Carmen es?' ('Which Carmen is it?').

carné.etymology: Hispanicized adaptation of French carnet ('small notebook, booklet of tickets, identity card'), diminutive of Old French quern / cahier, from Medieval Latin quaternum ('quire of four folded sheets'), from Classical Latin quaternī ('four each', from quattuor 'four').

morphemes.meaning: four-sheet booklet (< French carnet < Latin quaternī)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carné
Wiktionary — carné

carné.notes: In Spain, 'driver's license' is el carné de conducir (plural los carnés; Latin America prefers la licencia de conducir/manejar). Notice its hidden twin cuaderno, from the exact same Latin 'four-sheet' root!

carpet.etymology: English noun in the rival talent agency's name Red Carpet ('alfombra roja'), borrowed into Middle English carpet ('thick woolen cloth for tables, beds, or floors') via Old French carpite / Old Italian carpita ('shaggy wool coverlet'), from Medieval Latin carpīta, derived from Latin carpere ('to pluck, card wool').

cognates.meaning: file folder, desk mat (originally 'tablecloth'—a classic false friend!)

sources.title: Wiktionary — carpet (English)

carpet.notes: Major false friend: English carpet means Spanish alfombra (or moqueta for wall-to-wall carpeting), whereas Spanish carpeta means a 'file folder' (originally the cloth covering a writing desk)!

carpeta.etymology: Borrowed via French carpette or Italian carpetta from Medieval Latin carpita ('thick woolen cloth used as a desk cover, and later the writing folder resting on a desk'), from Latin carpere ('to pluck, card wool').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carpeta
Wiktionary — carpeta

carpintero.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin carpentārius ('wagon-maker, wheelwright, carpenter'), derived from Classical Latin carpentum ('two-wheeled carriage'), itself a Gaulish (Celtic) loanword.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carpintero
Wiktionary — carpintero

carrera.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (via) carrāria ('wagon road, carriage track, racecourse'), derived from Classical Latin carrus ('four-wheeled wagon', of Gaulish origin).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carrera
Wiktionary — carrera

carta.etymology: Carta continues Latin charta ('sheet of papyrus, written document'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek khártēs.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carta

carta.notes: Covers a mailed letter (una carta certificada), a restaurant menu (la carta), or a playing card.

cartel.etymology: Borrowed via Catalan or Occitan cartell (from Italian cartello), a diminutive of carta ('sheet of paper, placard, written notice'), ultimately from Latin charta (< Ancient Greek χάρτης 'papyrus sheet').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cartel
Wiktionary — cartel

cartero.etymology: Formed within Spanish from carta ('letter', < Latin charta) + the occupational suffix -ero (< Latin -ārius), denoting a mail carrier.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cartero
Wiktionary — cartero

cartón.etymology: Borrowed from Italian cartone (via French carton), an augmentative of carta ('paper', < Latin charta) denoting heavy pasteboard or cardboard.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cartón
Wiktionary — cartón

casa.etymology: Casa continues Latin casa ('cottage, hut'), which replaced Classical domus across spoken Romance as the everyday word for house and home.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: casa

casa.notes: Used without an article in en casa ('at home') and a casa ('homeward').

casado.etymology: Participial adjective of casar ('to marry, wed, match up'), derived within Romance from casa ('house, household', < Latin casa 'cottage, hut, home'): 'setting up house together' evolved into 'getting married'.

history.meaning: to set up house, wed -> married

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: casado
Wiktionary — casado

casado.notes: Civil status normally takes estar in Spain (estoy casada, estuvimos casados cinco años), and 'married to someone' uses con (casado con Paco), never *a.

casco.etymology: Deverbal noun from cascar ('to crack, break into pieces'), from Vulgar Latin *quassicāre (frequentative of Classical Latin quassāre 'to shatter'); shifted from 'potsherd, skullcap' to 'helmet, bottle, ship's hull'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: casco
Wiktionary — casco

casero.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin casārius ('belonging to the house or cottage, tenant') or derived in Spanish from casa ('house', < Latin casa) + -ero, meaning both 'homemade' and 'landlord'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: casero
Wiktionary — casero

casi.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin quasi ('as if, just as, almost, nearly'), which replaced older Spanish cuasi in everyday usage.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: casi
Wiktionary — casi

castellano.etymology: Inherited from Medieval Latin castellānus ('inhabitant of Castile; originally keeper of a castle'), derived from Castilla (< Latin castella, plural of castellum 'castle, fortified stronghold', diminutive of castrum 'fort'), the frontier county studded with castles against Al-Andalus.

history.meaning: fortress -> of the land of castles

cognates.meaning: Spanish language or native of Castile / castle governor

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: castellano
Wiktionary — castellano

castellano.notes: In Spain (especially alongside co-official languages like catalán, gallego, and euskera) as well as in Argentina/Uruguay/Peru, hablar castellano is completely synonymous with hablar español.

casting.etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English casting ('selection of actors for roles; audition'), verbal noun of cast ('to throw, mold in metal, assign theatrical parts as in casting a mold'), itself borrowed into Middle English from Old Norse kasta ('to throw').

morphemes.meaning: assign roles (< Old Norse kasta 'to throw')

history.meaning: to throw -> assign stage roles -> actor selection

cognates.meaning: process of choosing actors (rarely 'one audition', unlike Spanish!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: castin
Wiktionary — casting (Spanish)

casting.notes: False-friend nuance: in English, an actor goes to 'an audition', whereas in Spain every actor says tengo un casting ('I have an audition') as well as director de casting.

castings.etymology: Plural of the Anglicism casting ('audition, actor selection'), retaining English -s pluralization onto a final consonant cluster (whereas the RAE's Hispanicized adaptation castin forms cástines).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: castin
Wiktionary — castings (Spanish)

castings.notes: In Spanish showbiz, hacer castings or grabar castings ('taping self-tape auditions') is daily bread for actors and talent agencies.

castiza.etymology: Feminine singular of castizo ('pure-blooded, authentically traditional, quintessentially local—especially old-school Madrid'), derived from casta ('breed, lineage, stock') + adjectival suffix -izo (< Latin -īcius). Casta (shared with Portuguese and Italian) goes back to Gothic *kasts ('group, brood') or Latin castus ('pure, unmixed').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: castizo
Wiktionary — castiza

castiza.notes: Describes Paquita Salas to perfection: muy castiza evokes authentic, unpretentious Spanish—and especially Madrid—vernacular charm (verbenas, chotis, tapas, salty idioms).

catalán.etymology: Gentilic and glottonym from Medieval Latin Catalānus (attested along with Catalonia in the early 12th-century Liber Maiolichinus), probably reshaped by metathesis from *Lacetānia or *Gotholandia / *castellānus ('land of castle-holders' in the Carolingian Spanish March).

history.meaning: Catalan person or Gallo-Iberian Romance language

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: catalán
Wiktionary — catalán

catalán.notes: Drops its written accent in feminine and plural forms when a syllable is added: catalán, catalana, catalanes, catalanas. Distinct Romance language co-official in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, and Valencia.

catorce.etymology: Inherited from Latin quattuordecim ('fourteen'), a compound of quattuor ('four') and decem ('ten').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: catorce
Wiktionary — catorce

cazar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *captiāre ('to try to seize, chase after game'), frequentative built on captāre / capere ('to take, catch'), with regular Castilian affrication of -pti- > Old Spanish -ç- (/ts/) > Modern Castilian -z- (/θ/ or /s/).

history.meaning: to take -> try to catch -> hunt
to hunt; (colloq.) to catch on quickly, spot

cognates.meaning: doublets via Old French chacier and Old Northern French cachier, both from *captiāre!

rootFamily.gloss: to capture, pick up a signal (learned doublet)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cazar
Wiktionary — cazar

cazar.notes: English 'chase' and 'catch' are both siblings of Spanish cazar! Figuratively, cazarlas al vuelo means 'to be quick on the uptake', and un cazatalentos is a talent scout.

cedro.etymology: Inherited or borrowed from Latin cedrus ('cedar tree, cedarwood'), from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, 'cedar, juniper').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cedro
Wiktionary — cedro

celosía.etymology: Borrowed from Italian gelosia (literally 'jealousy', ultimately from Late Latin zelōsus < Greek zêlos), naming a latticework screen that lets people look out onto a courtyard or street without being seen.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: celosía

celosía.notes: In Spanish architecture and gardens, una celosía also supports climbing plants such as ivy or jasmine.

cena.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin cēna ('the main afternoon or evening meal, dinner').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cena
Wiktionary — cena

cenar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin cēnāre ('to dine, eat the main afternoon/evening meal'), denominal verb from cēna ('principal Roman meal', Old Latin cesna < PIE *kert-sneh₂ 'cut portion').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cenar
Wiktionary — cenar

cenar.notes: Spanish compresses meal phrases into single verbs: desayunar ('have breakfast'), comer / almorzar ('have lunch'), merendar ('have an afternoon snack'), and cenar ('have dinner'—often between 9:00 and 10:30 p.m. in Spain!).

central.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin centrālis ('situated in the middle, central'), derived from centrum ('center').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: central
Wiktionary — central

centro.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin centrum ('stationary point of a compass, center of a circle'), from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, 'sharp point, pivot', from κεντεῖν 'to prick').

history.meaning: sharp point, pivot of a compass

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: centro
Wiktionary — centro

centímetro.etymology: Modern metric compound borrowed via French centimètre, formed from Latin centum ('hundred', hence centi- 'hundredth') + Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: centímetro
Wiktionary — centímetro

cerca.etymology: Cerca derives from Late Latin circa ('around, near'), used adverbially in Spanish for spatial or temporal proximity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerca

cerca.notes: Takes de before a noun or pronoun (cerca de aquí, cerca de la estación), and stands alone at the end of a clause (está muy cerca).

cerdeña.etymology: Toponymic Spanish surname identical to Cerdeña ('Sardinia'), inherited from Latin Sardinia ('island of the Sardī'), showing regular Romance vowel opening i > e and palatalization of -ni- + vowel to Castilian -ñ- (/ɲ/).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: Cerdeña
Wiktionary — Cerdeña

cerdeña.notes: Historically tied to the Crown of Aragon's centuries-long rule over Sardinia; in Paquita Salas, Paco Cerdeña is Paquita's ex-husband and powerful film producer.

cero.etymology: Borrowed via Italian zero (contracted from zefiro) and Medieval Latin zephyrum from Arabic ṣifr ('empty, naught, zero'), itself a semantic calque of Sanskrit śūnya ('void, zero').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cero
Wiktionary — cero

cerquita.etymology: Colloquial diminutive of the adverb cerca ('near, close by', < Late Latin circa 'around'), formed with -ita (changing c to qu before i to preserve the /k/ sound). Spanish uniquely allows diminutive suffixes on adverbs as well as nouns and adjectives.

history.meaning: near -> very close by, just around the corner

rootFamily.gloss: outskirts; commuter rail network in Spain

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerca
Wiktionary — cerquita

cerquita.notes: Whereas diminishing a noun makes it smaller, diminishing an adverb in Spanish intensifies it warmly: muy cerquita means 'super close by / right next door' (just like ahorita, despacito, prontito).

cerrado.etymology: Cerrado is the participial adjective of cerrar, traced by the DLE to Late Latin serāre ('to bolt or bar a door', from sera, 'wooden bolt').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerrado
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerrar

cerrado.notes: Pairs with estar to describe whether a door, window or shop is currently shut (¿Está cerrada la puerta?).

cerradura.etymology: Derived from cerrar ('to close, lock') + the instrument/result suffix -dura; cerrar continues Late Latin serāre ('to bolt shut'), from Latin sera ('wooden bar, bolt').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerradura

cerradura.notes: Pairs with la llave ('key', < Latin clāvis).

cerrar.etymology: Cerrar continues Late Latin serāre ('to fasten with a bolt'), from Classical Latin sera ('door bar'), with initial s- assimilating to Castilian c-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerrar

cerrar.notes: Stem-changing verb (e -> ie when stressed: cierro, cierra, cerramos).

certificado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from certificar, borrowed from Late Latin certificātus / certificāre ('to make certain, attest formally'), from certus ('sure') + facere ('to make').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: certificado
Wiktionary — certificado

cerámica.etymology: The DLE derives cerámica from Greek keramikḗ ('potter's art'), built on kéramos ('potter's clay, earthenware').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerámica

cerámica.notes: Refers both to the craft of firing clay and collectively to ceramic vessels and tiles.

cesta.etymology: Cesta descends directly from Latin cista ('wicker box, basket'), borrowed from Greek kístē.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cesta

cesta.notes: Masculine el cesto often names a taller or deeper basket, while la cesta is the standard handled market basket.

ceño.etymology: Inherited from Latin cinnus ('nod, wink, grimace or signal with the brow'), via a Vulgar Latin derivative *cinnium denoting a furrowed brow or frown.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ceño
Wiktionary — ceño

champú.etymology: Hispanicized borrowing from English shampoo, which British colonial speakers in 18th-century India borrowed from Hindi cā̃po (चाँपो, 'press!, knead!, massage!'), imperative of cā̃pnā ('to press, knead muscles or scalp'), from Sanskrit capayati.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: champú
Wiktionary — champú

champú.notes: Adapts English sh- (/ʃ/) to Spanish ch- (/tʃ/) and takes plural champús; promotional photocalls for un evento de un champú are a running joke for minor celebrity gigs.

chao.etymology: Borrowed from Italian ciao ('hello; goodbye'), which originated in Venetian s-ciào / s-ciàvo vostro ('[I am] your humble servant/slave'), descending from Medieval Latin sclāvus ('Slav; captive slave'), parallel to South German Servus! ('at your service!').

cognates.meaning: slave (learned doublet of Medieval Latin sclāvus!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chao
Wiktionary — chao

chao.notes: Crucial difference from Italian: in Spanish chao (spelled chau in Argentina/Chile/Peru) is ONLY used for 'bye!', never for 'hello!'.

chaqueta.etymology: Borrowed from French jaquette ('short coat, jacket'), diminutive of Old French jaque ('short peasant tunic or padded jerkin', derived from the given name Jacques).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chaqueta
Wiktionary — chaqueta

charla.etymology: Deverbal noun from charlar ('to chat, converse informally'), borrowed from Italian ciarlare / ciarla.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: charla
Wiktionary — charla

charlar.etymology: Borrowed from Italian ciarlare ('to chatter, prattle, converse'), of expressive onomatopoeic origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: charlar
Wiktionary — charlar

charo.etymology: Traditional Peninsular Spanish hypocoristic (nickname) of María del Rosario ('Our Lady of the Rosary'), formed by apheresis of (Ro)sario with expressive palatalization of -s- to Castilian ch- (compare Concha < Concepción, Chema < José María, Chus < Jesús).

sources.title: Wiktionary — Charo (Spanish)

charo.notes: Spanish palatal ch- is a classic nickname maker: Rosario -> Charo, Isabel -> Chabela, Ignacio -> Nacho, Mercedes -> Merche.

chicas.etymology: Plural of chica ('girl, young woman'), substantivized feminine of chico ('small, young'), whose Expressive Romance stem *tšikk- / *cīccus comes from Latin ciccum ('trifle, thin membrane of a pomegranate seed, something tiny').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chico
Wiktionary — chicas

chicas.notes: In Spain, Hola, chicas ('Hi, girls / hey ladies') is a warm, everyday greeting among female colleagues or friends of virtually any adult age.

chico.etymology: Traced by Corominas and the RAE to expressive Vulgar Latin *cīccum (Classical Latin ciccum 'membrane of a pomegranate seed; proverbially a worthless trifle, tiny speck', as in Plautus's ciccum non interduim 'I wouldn't give a fig'), with palatalization producing Castilian ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chico
Wiktionary — chico

chico.notes: In Spain, el chico / la chica is the standard neutral word for 'boy/guy' and 'girl/young woman', while pequeño is more common than chico for the plain adjective 'small' (though chiquito/chiquita thrives affectionately).

china.etymology: Entered European languages in the 16th century via Portuguese China (recorded by Duarte Barbosa c. 1516) from Persian Čīn (چین) and Sanskrit Cīna (चीन), ultimately reflecting the imperial Qin (秦, Old Chinese *Dzin) dynasty that unified China in 221 BCE.

rootFamily.gloss: Chinese; (Spain colloq.) convenience bazaar or pebble

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: China
Wiktionary — China (Spanish)

china.notes: Country names usually omit the definite article in modern Spanish: rodé una película en China ('I shot a movie in China').

chiquito.etymology: Diminutive of chico ('small; boy'), formed with -ito (rewriting c as qu before i to maintain the /k/ sound), descending from Latin ciccum ('tiny speck, trifle').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chiquito
Wiktionary — chiquito

chiquito.notes: Very Paquita Salas: older Spaniards affectionately call twenty-something actors un chiquito / una chiquita ('a young guy / a young girl') even when they are full-grown adults.

chispa.etymology: Onomatopoeic Castilian formation imitating the crisp crackling and spitting sound (*chisp-!) of glowing embers or sparks flying from a fire (documented since Nebrija, 1495).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chispa
Wiktionary — chispa

chispa.notes: In Spanish casting and everyday praise, tener mucha chispa means 'to have tons of spark, wit, and screen presence'; achispado means 'tipsy'.

chist.etymology: Onomatopoeic Spanish interjection (also spelled ¡chit! or ¡chito!) imitating the sharp sibilant-affricate hushing or attention-getting sound [tʃst] made through the teeth to call for silence or catch someone's attention.

rootFamily.gloss: to make a peep, shush (sin chistar: without a murmur)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chist
Wiktionary — chist

chist.notes: Works both ways in Spain: ¡Chist! can shush a noisy room ('Shh!') or discreetly hail a waiter or friend across the street ('Psst!').

chista.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative of chistar ('to make a shushing or clicking sound; to utter a peep'), an onomatopoeic verb derived directly from the hushing interjection ¡chist!.

history.meaning: shh! -> to shush / make a sound -> shushes

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chistar
Wiktionary — chista

chista.notes: In Spanish closed-captioning, (CHISTA) indicates that a character shushes someone ('Shhh!'); in spoken idioms, ni chistar / sin chistar means 'without uttering a single complaint'.

chos.etymology: Peninsular Spanish hypocoristic nickname Chos (derived by expressive palatalization and clipping from María José or José; compare Chema < José María, Chus < María Jesús). In Paquita Salas, it refers to veteran real-life Spanish film/TV casting director and filmmaker Chos, who calls and emails about series castings.

history.meaning: affectionate nickname; mononym of Madrid casting director Chos

rootFamily.gloss: Joseph (also shortened to Pepe, Chema, Josechu)

sources.title: Wiktionary — José (Spanish)

chos.notes: In Episode 3 of Paquita Salas, Chos's phone call and follow-up email ('me ha llegado el mail de Chos') drive the subplot around Clara's casting alongside Jon González.

chupito.etymology: Diminutive formed with -ito on the stem of chupar ('to suck, sip, lick'), an expressive onomatopoeic Romance verb (*tsupp-) imitating the lip-pursing sound of sucking liquid.

history.meaning: small shot glass of liqueur or spirits

rootFamily.gloss: iconic Spanish lollipop brand (coined from chupar)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chupito
Wiktionary — chupito

chupito.notes: Unmistakably Peninsular Spanish: un chupito (often offered free after restaurant meals, such as chupito de hierbas or orujo) corresponds to Mexican caballito and English 'shot'.

chándal.etymology: Hispanicized borrowing from colloquial French chandail ('thick knit sweater, jersey'), clipped from marchand d'ail ('garlic seller')—the nickname given in late 19th-century Paris's Les Halles market to Breton garlic vendors and market porters for their heavy ribbed pullovers.

history.meaning: market porter's knit sweater, sports jersey

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: chándal
Wiktionary — chándal

chándal.notes: One of Europe's wildest etymologies: 'garlic merchant' -> French sweater -> Spain's everyday word for a two-piece tracksuit (ir en chándal; plural los chándales)!

cielo.etymology: Inherited from Latin caelum ('sky, vault of heaven'), with regular Romance diphthongization of open e (< ae) to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cielo
Wiktionary — cielo

cien.etymology: Apocopated proclitic form of ciento used before nouns and larger numerals, inherited from Latin centum ('one hundred').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cien
Wiktionary — cien

ciento.etymology: Inherited from Latin centum ('one hundred'), showing regular Castilian diphthongization of stressed short e to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ciento
Wiktionary — ciento

cierre.etymology: Deverbal noun from cerrar ('to close, lock, fasten'), which descends from Late Latin serāre ('to bolt, bar a door', from sera 'crossbar').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cierre
Wiktionary — cierre

cinco.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cinque (dissimilated from Classical Latin quīnque 'five'), with final -o remodeled by analogy with cuatro ('four').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cinco
Wiktionary — cinco

cincuenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cinquāginta (dissimilated from Classical Latin quīnquāgintā 'fifty'), derived from quīnque ('five').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cincuenta
Wiktionary — cincuenta

cine.etymology: Clipped form of cinematógrafo (or cinema), borrowed from French cinématographe—coined and patented in 1895 by Auguste and Louis Lumière from Ancient Greek kínēma, kinḗmatos (κίνημα, 'movement', from kīneîn 'to move') + -graphe ('writer, recorder').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cine
Wiktionary — cine

cine.notes: Covers both the physical movie theater (vamos al cine) and the art/industry of film (el cine español); idiomatically, pasarlo de cine means 'to have a fabulous time'.

cinta.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cincta ('girdle, belt, band, ribbon'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin cingere ('to gird, encircle').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cinta
Wiktionary — cinta

cita.etymology: Deverbal noun from citar ('to summon, set a meeting, quote'), borrowed from Latin citāre ('to put in rapid motion, summon officially, call forward'), frequentative of ciēre ('to set in motion, call').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cita
Wiktionary — cita

cita.notes: Covers three English nouns in one: a professional/medical appointment (pedir cita previa), a romantic date (tener una cita), and a textual quote (una cita literaria).

ciudad.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish cibdad from Latin cīvitās, cīvitātis ('citizenship, body of citizens, city'), derived from cīvis ('citizen').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ciudad
Wiktionary — ciudad

clara.etymology: Spanish female given name Clara, continuing Latin Clāra ('bright, clear, shining, illustrious'), feminine of clārus, spread across Western Europe by the veneration of Saint Clare of Assisi (Santa Clara, 1194–1253).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: claro
Wiktionary — Clara (Spanish)

clara.notes: In Paquita Salas (s01e03), Clara Valle (played by Claudia Traisac) is Paquita's sweet, insecure provincial actress client; as a common noun, la clara also means 'egg white'.

claramente.etymology: Adverb formed from clara (feminine singular of claro 'clear, bright, obvious', < Latin clārus) + adverbial suffix -mente, grammaticalized from the Latin ablative phrase clārā mente ('with a clear mind/manner').

morphemes.meaning: clear, obvious (feminine of claro < Latin clāra)
in a ... manner (< Latin ablative mente 'mind')
