sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: claramente
Wiktionary — claramente

claramente.notes: Because -mente came from feminine Latin mēns, mentis ('mind'), Spanish always attaches -mente to the feminine singular form of adjectives (clara -> claramente).

clarita.etymology: Affectionate Spanish diminutive of the female given name Clara (< Latin Clāra 'bright, clear'), formed with the suffix -ita.

rootFamily.gloss: (Spain bar noun) small shandy of beer with lemon soda

sources.title: Wiktionary — Clarita

clarita.notes: Paquita's maternal pet form ('Ay, Clarita...') expresses protective fondness; lowercase una clarita in Madrid bars is also a refreshing beer-and-lemon shandy (una clara).

claro.etymology: Claro continues Latin clārus ('bright, clear, distinct'). Spanish uses it for light shades of colour (azul claro), clear sound or meaning, and as a conversational affirmation ('of course!').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: claro

claro.notes: ¡Claro! and ¡Claro que sí! are everyday spoken ways to agree warmly ('of course!', 'naturally!').

clase.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin classis ('summoned division of citizens, fleet, rank, school class').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: clase
Wiktionary — clase

clavar.etymology: Denominal verb formed from clavo ('nail', inherited from Latin clāvus 'metal nail, peg'), or continuing Late Latin clāvāre ('to nail, fasten with nails').

history.meaning: to nail in; to nail an impression/role; (slang) to overcharge

cognates.meaning: to drive in, set a gem
so named for its nail shape (< French clou < Latin clāvus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: clavar
Wiktionary — clavar

clavar.notes: Remarkably parallel to English slang: ¡Lo has clavado! means 'You nailed it!' (an accent or audition), es clavado a su padre means 'he's the spitting image of his dad', and me clavaron 50 euros means 'they ripped me off for 50 euros'.

claxon.etymology: Genericized trademark from Klaxon, the brand name coined around 1908 by F. W. Lovell for the Lovell-McConnell Manufacturing Company's electromechanical car horn, built on Ancient Greek klázō (κλάζω, future klánxō 'to shriek, clang, honk').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: claxon
Wiktionary — claxon (Spanish)

claxon.notes: Paroxytone stress on cla- (/ˈklakson/, plural los cláxones); standard in stage/subtitle directions ((Claxon)) alongside everyday tocar el pito or tocar la bocina.

clic.etymology: Onomatopoeic noun imitating a sharp, brief mechanical snapping or clicking sound (reinforced by French clic and English click).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: clic
Wiktionary — clic

clienta.etymology: Clienta is the explicit feminine counterpart created in modern Spanish from cliente (from Latin cliens, clientis) to designate a female customer or hotel guest.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cliente

clienta.notes: Both la clienta and la cliente are accepted by the RAE; la clienta is widespread in everyday Peninsula Spanish.

cliente.etymology: Cliente comes as a learned borrowing from Latin cliens, clientis ('follower, patron's protégé'), generalized in modern commerce to any customer or guest.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cliente

cliente.notes: Plural los clientes refers to guests or customers in general.

clip.etymology: Borrowed from English clip ('bent wire paperclip, fastener'), from Middle English clippen and Old English clyppan ('to clasp, grip, embrace').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: clip
Wiktionary — clip

clásico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin classicus ('belonging to the highest property class of Roman citizens; hence first-rate, exemplary, canonical', as Aulus Gellius termed scriptor classicus), derived from classis ('citizen class, fleet').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: clásico
Wiktionary — clásico

clásico.notes: One Spanish adjective covers both English 'classic' (un vestido muy clásico, El Clásico in football) and 'classical' (música clásica, teatro clásico).

cláusula.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late and Medieval Latin clausula ('close of a rhetorical period, legal stipulation or clause'), from clausus, past participle of claudere ('to close').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cláusula
Wiktionary — cláusula

cobarde.etymology: Borrowed from Old French coart (modern couard, 'cowardly'), formed from coe ('tail', < Latin cauda) + the pejorative suffix -ard, evoking an animal turning tail or tucking its tail in fear.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cobarde
Wiktionary — cobarde

cobre.etymology: Cobre continues Late Latin cuprum, shortened from Classical Latin aes Cyprium ('metal from Cyprus'), after the island's famous ancient mines.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cobre

cobre.notes: Widely used in electrical wiring (cable de cobre) and traditional cookware.

coche.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (via French coche or German Kutsche) from Hungarian kocsi (szekér) ('carriage of Kocs'), named after the Hungarian town between Vienna and Buda where spring-suspended carriages originated.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: coche
Wiktionary — coche

cocina.etymology: Cocina continues Late Latin coquīna ('kitchen, cooking'), derived from Classical Latin coquĕre ('to cook').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cocina

cocina.notes: Means the kitchen room, a stove/cooker, or cuisine.

cocino.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of cocinar ('to cook'), inherited from Late Latin coquīnāre ('to cook'), derived from coquīna ('kitchen, cooking', from Classical Latin coquere 'to cook, ripen').

history.meaning: to cook -> kitchen -> to prepare food

cognates.meaning: early Germanic borrowings from Latin coquus and coquīna!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cocinar
Wiktionary — cocino

cocino.notes: Spanish distinguishes cocinar ('to prepare dishes/meals') from cocer ('to boil or bake a specific ingredient', e.g., cocer huevos / pasta).

codo.etymology: Inherited from Latin cubitus ('elbow; cubit, forearm-length measure', related to cubāre 'to lie down, recline on one's elbow at meals'), evolving through syncope and voicing: cubitum > *cobdo > Old Spanish cobdo > codo.

rootFamily.gloss: nudge or blow with the elbow
sharp bend in a road or river

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: codo
Wiktionary — codo

codo.notes: Famous Spanish idioms include hablar por los codos ('to talk one's ear off / talk nineteen to the dozen'), trabajar codo con codo ('work shoulder to shoulder'), and empinar el codo ('to tip back drinks').

cofre.etymology: Borrowed from Old French cofre (modern coffre, 'chest, strongbox'), descending from Latin cophinus ('basket, chest'), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, 'basket').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cofre
Wiktionary — cofre

coger.etymology: Coger descends from Latin colligĕre ('to gather, pick up, take hold of'), via regular syncope and palatalization in spoken Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: coger

coger.notes: Completely standard everyday verb in Spain for taking a street, catching a train, or picking up an object (in parts of Latin America, tomar or agarrar is preferred).

cogido.etymology: Past participle of coger ('to take, catch, pick, cast/hire'), inherited from Latin colligere ('to gather together, collect, pick up', from com- 'together' + legere 'to gather, choose'), via Vulgar Latin *colligere > Old Spanish coger.

cognates.meaning: learned and Old French borrowings from colligere

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: coger
Wiktionary — cogido

cogido.notes: Crucial regional note: in Spain, coger is completely polite and indispensable—¡Te han cogido para la serie! is every actor's dream call ('They picked/cast you for the show!'). In Argentina, Mexico, and several Latin American countries, coger is taboo sexual slang, replaced by tomar, agarrar, or elegir.

cogimos.etymology: First-person plural preterite indicative of coger ('to take, grab; colloquially, to go ahead and do something impulsively'), inherited from Latin colligere ('to gather, pick up').

history.meaning: to take -> we took / we went right ahead and...

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: coger
Wiktionary — cogimos

cogimos.notes: Notice the classic Peninsular narrative construction coger y + verb ('Cogimos y pusimos su cara en unas fotos...'): here cogimos doesn't mean grabbing an object, but 'we just up and [did it]!' (like English 'we went and put...').

coincidir.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coincidere ('to fall together, occur at the same time or place'), formed from co- + incidere (in- + cadere 'to fall').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: coincidir
Wiktionary — coincidir

cojín.etymology: Borrowed via Catalan coixí or Old French coissin, from Vulgar Latin *coxīnus ('seat cushion'), a derivative of Classical Latin coxa ('hip, thigh').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cojín

cojín.notes: Cognate with English cushion and Italian cuscino.

cola.etymology: In the sense 'glue', the DLE traces cola to Vulgar Latin colla, borrowed from Greek kólla ('glue, paste'). (Its homonym cola 'tail / queue' comes separately from Vulgar Latin cōda < Classical Latin cauda.)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cola

cola.notes: Greek kólla is also the root of technical words such as colágeno ('collagen') and protocolo.

colegio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin collēgium ('association of colleagues, guild, corporate body'), derived from collēga ('partner in office', from com- 'with' + legere 'to choose/appoint'). In Spanish its primary sense shifted to a primary/secondary school or a professional association.

history.meaning: elementary/high school; professional association (e.g., Colegio de Abogados)

rootFamily.gloss: school (universal colloquial clipping in Spain: el cole)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colegio
Wiktionary — colegio

colegio.notes: Major false friend: in Spain el colegio (or el cole) is primary/secondary school for children and teens, NEVER university ('college' = la universidad / la facultad).

colgando.etymology: Gerund of colgar ('to hang, dangle; hang up a phone'), inherited from Latin collocāre ('to place together, station, lay down', from com- + locāre 'to place', from locus 'place'), with syncope (collocāre > *colgāre) and a striking Hispanic semantic shift from 'setting in place (often suspended from rafters)' to 'hanging'.

cognates.meaning: to lay down, put to bed (from the very same Latin collocāre!)
to place, position (learned doublet of colgar!)

rootFamily.gloss: to hang; hang up the phone

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colgar
Wiktionary — colgando

colgando.notes: Llevar algo colgando means 'to have something dangling/hanging off'; idiomatically, dejar a alguien colgado in Spain means 'to leave someone hanging / stand someone up'.

colgante.etymology: Active participial adjective and noun derived from colgar ('to hang, suspend', < Latin collocāre) + -nte ('hanging; pendant').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colgante
Wiktionary — colgante

colgar.etymology: Inherited through popular evolution from Latin collocāre ('to put in place, set up'), which specialized in Ibero-Romance to mean 'to hang up, suspend' (contrast learned doublet colocar).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colgar
Wiktionary — colgar

colina.etymology: Colina enters from Italian collina or Late Latin collīna ('hilly ground'), derived from Classical Latin collis ('hill').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colina

colina.notes: Names a gentle hill smaller than una montaña.

collarín.etymology: Formed with the specialized/diminutive suffix -ín (reinforced by Italian collarino) from collar ('necklace, collar'), inherited from Latin collāre ('neckband, collar'), derived from collum ('neck').

history.meaning: necklace -> cervical neck brace; clerical collar

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: collarín
Wiktionary — collarín

collarín.notes: Quick vocabulary trio: cuello = anatomical neck or shirt collar; collar = necklace or pet collar; collarín (cervical) = medical foam neck brace worn after whiplash.

colocar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin collocāre ('to put in place, arrange, station'), formed from com- + locāre (from locus 'place'), a doublet of inherited colgar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colocar
Wiktionary — colocar

color.etymology: Inherited from Latin color, colōris ('hue, tint, complexion').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: color

color.notes: Masculine in standard Spanish (el color), whereas several sister Romance nouns became feminine.

columna.etymology: The DLE records columna as a learned borrowing/retention from Latin columna ('pillar, support').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: columna

columna.notes: Used both for architectural stone pillars and for vertical columns of figures in a notebook.

comedia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin comoedia, from Ancient Greek kōmōidía (κωμῳδία, 'comedy'), compounded from kō̂mos (κῶμος, 'festive village revel, merrymaking procession') + ōidḗ (ᾠδή, 'song, ode').

history.meaning: comedy; (Golden Age theater) any full-length verse play

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comedia
Wiktionary — comedia

comedia.notes: In Lope de Vega's Golden Age theater, una comedia meant any three-act secular play (tragic or comic); today it means humorous film/TV/stage comedy, and hacer comedia colloquially means 'to put on an act'.

comedia-thriller.etymology: Modern hyphenated film/TV genre compound pairing Spanish comedia (< Latin comoedia < Greek kōmōidía 'revel-song') with the unadapted English genre loan thriller (agentive noun from thrill, from Middle English thirlen < Old English þyrlian 'to pierce, thrill with emotion').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: thriller

comedia-thriller.notes: Spanish screenwriters and agents freely coin appositional compounds like comedia-thriller or comedia dramática, usually pronouncing thriller in Spain as /ˈθɾileɾ/ or /ˈtɾileɾ/.

comentar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin commentārī ('to think over, study, write notes or commentary upon'), frequentative/intensive built on the PIE root *men- ('to think', shared with mēns 'mind' and meminī 'to remember').

history.meaning: to mention, bring up, comment on

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comentar
Wiktionary — comentar

comentar.notes: In everyday Peninsular conversation, te lo quería comentar is the natural, polite way to say 'I wanted to mention it to you / run it by you'—notice it is transitive without sobre/en!

comer.etymology: Inherited from Latin comedere ('to eat up, consume entirely'), an intensive compound of com- + edere ('to eat') that replaced simple edere in Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comer
Wiktionary — comer

comercial.etymology: Derived from comercio ('trade, commerce') + -al (reinforced by French commercial), from Latin commercium ('trade, traffic', from com- + merx 'merchandise').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comercial
Wiktionary — comercial

comida.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of comer ('to eat'), which descends from Latin comedere ('to eat up completely, consume', compounded from intensive com- + edere 'to eat', replacing simple edere across Iberian Romance).

history.meaning: to eat -> food; meal; midday lunch

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin edere / comedere root (and inherited eat!)

rootFamily.gloss: to eat; (in Spain) to have lunch

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comida
Wiktionary — comida

comida.notes: Means three things depending on context in Spain: uncountable 'food' in general, any 'meal' (la comida más importante del día), and specifically Spain's main midday lunch around 2:00–3:30 p.m.

como.etymology: Unaccented como develops from Vulgar Latin *quōmodo (from Classical Latin quō modo, 'in what manner'), functioning in modern Spanish for comparisons ('like, as') and causal clauses ('since').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: como

como.notes: Compare unaccented como ('like, as'; also 'I eat' from comer) with accented ¿cómo? ('how? / pardon?').

compartir.etymology: Inherited or borrowed from Late Latin compartīre (Classical deponent compartīrī, 'to divide with another, share'), from com- + partīre (built on pars, partis 'part').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compartir
Wiktionary — compartir

compañera.etymology: Feminine form of compañero ('companion, partner, colleague'), derived from Old Spanish compaño (< Late Latin compāniō, -ōnis 'one who shares bread').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compañero
Wiktionary — compañera

compañero.etymology: Derived with -ero from Old Spanish compaño, from Late Latin compāniō, compāniōnis ('one who eats bread with another'), formed from com- ('with') + pānis ('bread').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compañero
Wiktionary — compañero

completamente.etymology: Adverb formed within Spanish from the feminine adjective completa ('complete, full', < Latin complētus) + the suffix -mente (< Latin mente 'with a ... mind').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: completamente
Wiktionary — completamente

completo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin complētus ('filled up, full, complete'), past participle of complēre (com- + plēre 'to fill').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: completo
Wiktionary — completo

componer.etymology: Componer continues Latin componĕre ('to put together, arrange'), formed from com- ('together') and ponĕre ('to place').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: componer

componer.notes: Shares all stem irregularities of poner (compongo, compuso, compuesto).

compositora.etymology: Feminine form of compositor, learned borrowing from Latin compositor, compositōris ('one who puts together, arranger, author'), from compōnere ('to put together, compose').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compositor
Wiktionary — compositora

comprador.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin comparātor, comparātōris ('buyer, purchaser') or derived in Spanish from comprar ('to buy') + the agent suffix -dor.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comprador
Wiktionary — comprador

comprar.etymology: Inherited from Latin comparāre ('to get ready, procure, furnish, purchase'), with regular syncope of the unstressed internal vowel.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comprar
Wiktionary — comprar

compás.etymology: Deverbal noun from compasar or borrowed via Occitan/French compas, from Vulgar Latin *compassāre ('to measure by paces'), built on com- + passus ('step, pace').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compás
Wiktionary — compás

comunicar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin commūnicāre ('to share in common, impart, make generally known'), derived from commūnis ('shared, common', from com- 'together' + mūnus 'public duty, gift').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comunicar
Wiktionary — comunicar

comunicar.notes: Formal casting sign-off: Ya os comunicamos nuestra decisión ('We'll let you know our decision'). Bonus Peninsular phone idiom: ¡Comunica! means 'The line is busy / engaged!'

con.etymology: The preposition con continues Latin cum ('with'), marking accompaniment, ingredients (café con leche, té con miel), tools, or manner (con cuidado).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: con

con.notes: With singular personal pronouns mí, ti and reflexive sí, Latin cum fused twice to produce the special forms conmigo, contigo and consigo.

concierto.etymology: Deverbal noun from concertar ('to arrange, harmonize, agree', with the musical sense reinforced by Italian concerto), from Late Latin concertāre ('to contend, act together').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: concierto
Wiktionary — concierto

concreta.etymology: Feminine singular of concreto ('specific, definite, tangible'), a learned borrowing from Latin concrētus ('grown together, condensed, solid'), past participle of concrēscere (com- 'together' + crēscere 'to grow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: concreto
Wiktionary — concreta

concreta.notes: In Spain, una cosa muy concreta is the go-to everyday way to say 'something very specific/particular' (note too that building 'concrete' in Spain is hormigón, whereas Latin America calls it concreto).

concreto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin concrētus ('condensed, solidified, grown together'), past participle of concrēscere (com- + crēscere 'to grow'), contrasted in logic and philosophy with abstractus.

rootFamily.gloss: to specify, nail down a time/deal

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: concreto
Wiktionary — concreto

concreto.notes: The adverbial phrase en concreto ('specifically, in particular') is ubiquitous in spoken Peninsular Spanish.

conducido.etymology: Regular weak past participle of conducir ('to drive, lead'), formed by analogy in Spanish (-ido) replacing the older irregular Latinate participle conducto (< Latin conductus, from condūcere 'to lead together, guide').

rootFamily.gloss: behavior, conduct (retaining the old Latinate stem)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conducir
Wiktionary — conducido

conducido.notes: Watch the conjugation contrast: the past participle is regular he conducido ('I have driven'), whereas the preterite has a strong j-stem: conduje, condujiste, condujo (never *conducí).

conducir.etymology: Semi-learned adaptation of Latin condūcere ('to bring together, lead along, hire'), compounded from com- ('together') + dūcere ('to lead').

history.meaning: to drive a vehicle, lead, host

rootFamily.gloss: to produce / translate (conjugating identically: conduzco, conduje)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conducir
Wiktionary — conducir

conducir.notes: Standard Peninsular verb for driving a car (hoy conduzco yo; Latin America mostly uses manejar). Conjugates like traducir: yo conduzco in the present, yo conduje in the preterite.

conectar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnectere / connectere ('to bind or fasten together', from com- + nectere 'to tie'), reinforced in modern technical usage by English to connect.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conectar
Wiktionary — conectar

confiar.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned descendant of Vulgar Latin *confīdāre, regularized from Classical Latin confīdere ('to trust firmly, rely upon'), compounded from intensive com- + fīdere ('to trust', related to fidēs 'faith, trust').

cognates.meaning: to trust or tell a secret

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: confiar
Wiktionary — confiar

confiar.notes: Takes the preposition en for 'to trust someone' (¿Puedes confiar en mí?, never without en!) and stresses the -i- in singular/3pl present forms: confío, confías, confía, confían.

confirmación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnfirmātiōnem ('a securing, establishing, verifying'), action noun from cōnfirmāre ('to make firm, strengthen, corroborate', from com- + firmus 'firm, steadfast').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: confirmación
Wiktionary — confirmación

confirmación.notes: On Spanish event and premiere invitations, Se ruega confirmación (S.R.C.) is the formal equivalent of 'RSVP'.

confías.etymology: Second-person singular present indicative of confiar ('to trust'), from Vulgar Latin *confīdāre (< Classical Latin confīdere 'to trust firmly', from com- + fīdere), with loss of intervocalic -d- creating the stressed hiatus -í.a-.

rootFamily.gloss: to trust (no me fío: I don't trust it)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: confiar
Wiktionary — confías

confías.notes: The accent mark on í breaks the diphthong into three syllables: con-FÍ-as (/konˈfias/).

conmigo.etymology: Conmigo continues Latin mēcum ('with me'), to which Vulgar Latin re-prefixed cum (*cum mēcum > conmigo) once the final -cum was no longer felt clearly as 'with'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conmigo

conmigo.notes: Always written as one word, replacing *con mí in Spanish alongside contigo ('with you') and consigo ('with oneself').

conocer.etymology: Conocer continues Latin cognoscĕre ('to become acquainted with, recognize, know').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conocer

conocer.notes: Used for familiarity with people and places (¿Conoce usted esta calle?), whereas saber covers facts and skills.

conocida.etymology: Feminine singular participial adjective (and noun) of conocer ('known, well-known; female acquaintance'), inherited from Latin cognōscere ('to become acquainted with, learn to know', from com- + gnōscere / nōscere 'to know').

morphemes.meaning: know, be familiar with (< Latin cognōscere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conocido
Wiktionary — conocida

conocida.notes: As an adjective, muy conocida means 'well-known / famous' (es conocida por su cerámica); as a noun, una conocida means 'an acquaintance' (less close than una amiga).

conocimiento.etymology: Derived from conocer ('to know, recognize', < Latin cognōscere) + action/state suffix -imiento (< Latin -īmentum).

morphemes.meaning: state, faculty, or body of knowledge (< Latin -īmentum)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conocimiento
Wiktionary — conocimiento

conocimiento.notes: Besides academic 'knowledge' (often plural conocimientos) and 'consciousness' (perder el conocimiento 'to faint'), traditional Peninsular speech uses tener conocimiento for 'having common sense / mature judgment'!

conocéis.etymology: Second-person plural (vosotros) present indicative of conocer ('to know, be familiar with'), inherited from Latin cognōscere ('to get to know', from com- + gnōscere), with the characteristic Peninsular -éis ending (< Old Spanish -edes < Latin -ētis).

morphemes.meaning: know, be acquainted with (< Latin cognōscere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conocer
Wiktionary — conocéis

conocéis.notes: Signature Peninsular Spanish plural address: ¿No sé si lo conocéis? ('I don't know if you guys know it?'), corresponding to Latin American ustedes conocen.

conseguir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *consequīre, a regularized active form of Classical Latin deponent consequī ('to follow closely, overtake, attain, obtain'), from com- + sequī ('to follow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conseguir
Wiktionary — conseguir

consejo.etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnsilium ('deliberation, counsel, advice, advisory council', related to cōnsulere 'to consult, take counsel'), showing regular Castilian palatalization and velarization of -li- + vowel: cōnsilium > Old Spanish conseio (/ʒ/) > Modern Spanish consejo (/x/).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: consejo
Wiktionary — consejo

consejo.notes: Unlike uncountable English 'advice', Spanish consejo is countable: un consejo means 'a piece of advice' (¿Te doy un consejo?).

consígame.etymology: Formal singular (usted) imperative consiga ('get, obtain!') + enclitic indirect-object pronoun -me ('for me'). Conseguir descends from Latin cōnsequī ('to follow up, overtake, attain, obtain', deponent verb from com- + sequī 'to follow').

morphemes.meaning: obtain, get (< conseguir < Latin cōnsequī, with e > i stem raising)

cognates.meaning: learned borrowing from the same Latin cōnsequī

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conseguir
Wiktionary — conseguir

consígame.notes: Notice the double spelling rule: gu drops its silent u before -a (conseguir -> consiga, since ga is already /ɡa/), and adding enclitic -me requires an accent mark on í (consígame).

contacto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin contāctus ('a touching, contact, contagion'), action noun from contingere (com- 'together' + tangere 'to touch', supine tāctum).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contacto
Wiktionary — contacto

contacto.notes: Tener contactos ('having industry connections') is the currency of talent agencies like PS Management; estar en contacto means 'staying in touch'.

contar.etymology: Inherited from Latin computāre ('to sum up, reckon, calculate; relate a story'), formed from com- + putāre ('to trim, reckon, consider'), with syncope and assimilation of -mp't- to -nt-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contar
Wiktionary — contar

contarte.etymology: Infinitive contar ('to tell, recount; to count') + enclitic second-person singular indirect-object pronoun -te ('to you'). Contar descends from Latin computāre ('to sum up, reckon, recount in order', from com- + putāre 'to prune, reckon, think').

cognates.meaning: to tell a story / to count
Old French and learned Latin doublets from computāre

rootFamily.gloss: to tell; to count (contar con: rely on)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contar
Wiktionary — contar

contarte.notes: Tengo que contarte una cosa ('I have to tell you something!') is Spain's classic gossip opener.

contenta.etymology: Feminine singular of contento ('happy, pleased, glad'), inherited/semi-learned from Latin contentus ('contained, satisfied with what one has'), past participle of continēre (com- 'together' + tenēre 'to hold').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contento
Wiktionary — contenta

contenta.notes: Warmth nuance: English 'content' sounds lukewarm ('merely satisfied'), whereas in Spain estar muy contenta is the natural everyday way to say 'I'm really happy / thrilled!' (more common in casual speech than solemn feliz).

contigo.etymology: Fused comitative pronoun ('with you'), descending from Latin tēcum ('with thee', ablative tē + enclitic postposition -cum), which Vulgar Latin redundantly prefixed with cum to form *cum-tēcum > Old Spanish connusco / contigo (with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contigo
Wiktionary — contigo

contigo.notes: Linguistic fossil gem: the -go at the end of conmigo, contigo, and consigo is actually Latin cum ('with') said a second time! Never say *con tú or *con ti—always contigo.

contra.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin contrā ('against, opposite, facing, in return for').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contra
Wiktionary — contra

contratar.etymology: Formed in Spanish from contrato ('contract, formal agreement', < Latin contractus) + -ar ('to engage by contract, hire').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contratar
Wiktionary — contratar

contrato.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin contractus ('a drawing together, bargain, legal agreement'), derived from contrahere (com- + trahere 'to draw together').

history.meaning: to draw together, conclude a deal

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contrato
Wiktionary — contrato

contraventana.etymology: Compound formed in Spanish from contra- ('against, protective outer layer') + ventana ('window', originally 'wind-opening', from Latin ventus 'wind').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contraventana
Wiktionary — contraventana

conversión.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin conversiō, conversiōnis ('a turning around, transformation, change'), derived from convertere ('to turn around, transform').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conversión
Wiktionary — conversión

convertir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *convertīre, reshaped from Classical Latin convertere ('to turn around, transform, alter'), from com- + vertere ('to turn').

history.meaning: to turn / to turn around, transform

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: convertir
Wiktionary — convertir

convertiré.etymology: First-person singular future indicative of convertir ('to turn into, transform, convert'), formed historically by fusing the infinitive convertir (< Latin convertere 'to turn around, transform', from com- + vertere 'to turn') with present indicative (h)e of haber (< Latin habēre): convertir + he > convertiré.

morphemes.meaning: 1st-person singular future (< Old Spanish he < Latin habeō)

history.meaning: I have to turn / will turn

rootFamily.gloss: to turn into (convertirse en: to become)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: convertir
Wiktionary — convertiré

convertiré.notes: Takes the preposition en for transformations: ¡Te convertiré en una estrella! ('I'll turn you into a star!'), the timeless talent-agent promise.

convido.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of convidar ('to invite, treat someone to food or a drink'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *convītāre, altered (replacing in- with social com- 'together') from Classical Latin invītāre ('to invite, entertain as a guest').

history.meaning: to treat / invite -> I'm treating / it's on me

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: convidar
Wiktionary — convido

convido.notes: Traditional castizo gem: while invitar (¡Te invito yo!) is more common among younger speakers today, A la copa convido yo ('This drink is on me!') has warm, old-school Spanish bar charm, and el convite still names a wedding banquet.

copa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cuppa ('drinking cup, goblet, tub', expressive geminated variant of Classical Latin cūpa 'cask, vat'), with regular simplification of -pp- > -p- and opening of short u > o.

history.meaning: stemmed glass; evening alcoholic drink; trophy cup

cognates.meaning: early Germanic/Old English borrowing from Late Latin cuppa

rootFamily.gloss: wooden barrel, cask (doublet from Classical cūpa with single -p-!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: copa
Wiktionary — copa

copa.notes: Essential Spain nightlife distinction: un vaso is a tumbler, una taza is a mug/teacup, and una copa is both a stemmed wine/cocktail glass AND a mixed alcoholic night-out drink (ir de copas 'to go out for drinks').

corazón.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corāciōne (or *corāceum + -ōne), an affective/augmentative formation built on Classical Latin cor, cordis ('heart').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corazón
Wiktionary — corazón

corbata.etymology: Borrowed via Italian corvatta / cravatta (and French cravate) from Serbo-Croatian Hrvat ('Croat'), after the linen neckscarves worn by 17th-century Croatian light cavalrymen.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corbata
Wiktionary — corbata

correcto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin correctus ('straightened, amended, accurate'), past participle of corrigere (com- + regere 'to guide, make straight').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: correcto
Wiktionary — correcto

correo.etymology: Borrowed in the late Middle Ages via Catalan correu / Old Occitan corrieu ('mounted courier, dispatch rider; later the mail service itself'), derived from córrer / Latin currere ('to run, hasten').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: correo
Wiktionary — correo

correo.notes: Un correo (short for correo electrónico) is standard Spanish for 'an email' alongside un mail; capitalized Correos is the post office.

correr.etymology: Inherited from Latin currere ('to run, hasten, flow'), showing regular lowering of short u to o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: correr
Wiktionary — correr

corta.etymology: Affirmative tú imperative ('cut!') of cortar ('to cut, stop filming'), inherited from Latin curtāre ('to shorten, clip, cut off'), denominal verb from curtus ('cut short, curtailed').

morphemes.meaning: 2nd-person singular command (or feminine of adj. corto)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cortar
Wiktionary — corta

corta.notes: When filming a one-on-one self-tape with an assistant, ¡Corta! ('Cut! / Stop rolling!') addresses one camera operator (tú), whereas a full crew hears plural ¡Corten!.

cortar.etymology: Inherited from Latin curtāre ('to shorten, clip, cut off'), derived from the adjective curtus ('short, clipped').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cortar
Wiktionary — cortar

corten.etymology: Plural (ustedes) imperative of cortar ('to cut, stop rolling camera and sound'), descending from Latin curtāre ('to shorten, cut'), addressing the whole camera and sound crew on a film set.

history.meaning: Cut! (director's command to stop a take)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cortar
Wiktionary — corten

corten.notes: Interestingly, even in Spain (where crews speak to one another with vosotros), the traditional film-set command fixed across the Spanish-speaking world is ¡Corten! (paired with ¡Acción!).

corteza.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corticea ('bark, rind, crust'), substantivized feminine of Classical Latin corticeus ('of bark'), derived from cortex, corticis ('tree bark, outer shell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corteza
Wiktionary — corteza

corto.etymology: Inherited from Latin curtus ('clipped, shortened, brief, short'), with regular lowering of short u to o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corto
Wiktionary — corto

cosa.etymology: Inherited from Latin causa ('judicial cause, lawsuit, motive, matter, affair'), which in Vulgar Latin broadened semantically to replace neuter rēs as the universal Romance noun for 'thing', with regular monophthongization of Latin au > o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cosa
Wiktionary — cosa

cosa.notes: Classic inherited vs. learned doublet: Latin causa evolved naturally in spoken mouths into cosa ('thing'), then re-entered centuries later from books as causa ('cause').

cosmo.etymology: Colloquial clipping of Cosmopolitan—in Spain referring both to Cosmopolitan magazine / Cosmopolitan TV (whose annual Premios Cosmo party is a Madrid celebrity staple) and to the Greek root kósmos (κόσμος, 'order, world, universe').

morphemes.meaning: short for Cosmopolitan (< Greek kosmopolítēs 'citizen of the world')

history.meaning: magazine, Spanish pay-TV channel, and gala awards

sources.title: Wiktionary — Cosmo

cosmo.notes: In Paquita Salas, la fiesta de los Cosmo refers to the glamorous Madrid red-carpet party for Cosmopolitan Spain, where getting clients onto the guest list is an agent's obsession.

cosmopolitan.etymology: English magazine and Spanish television channel brand name Cosmopolitan (founded in the US in 1886; launched in Spain as a magazine in 1990 and TV channel in 2000), coined from Ancient Greek kosmopolítēs (κοσμοπολίτης, 'citizen of the world', attributed to Diogenes the Cynic, from kósmos 'world' + polítēs 'citizen').

history.meaning: women's lifestyle magazine and entertainment network

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cosmopolita
Wiktionary — cosmopolitan

cosmopolitan.notes: Note that the native Spanish adjective for a worldly person or city is cosmopolita (invariable for gender: un barrio muy cosmopolita), while Cosmopolitan with final -n names the magazine/channel.

costar.etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnstāre ('to stand firm, stand at a price, cost'), formed from com- + stāre ('to stand'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of -nst- to -st-.

history.meaning: to stand at a price, cost

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: costar
Wiktionary — costar

costumbre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin cōnsuētūdinem (nominative cōnsuētūdō, 'habit, custom, usage', from cōnsuēscere 'to grow accustomed'), showing the hallmark Castilian evolution of Latin -ūdinem: cōnsuētūdinem > *costūmne > Old Spanish costumne > costumbre (parallel to hominem > hombre and lūminem > lumbre).

cognates.meaning: doublets from the same Latin cōnsuētūdinem!

rootFamily.gloss: to be in the habit of (acostumbrarse a: get used to)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: costumbre
Wiktionary — costumbre

costumbre.notes: Feminine noun despite ending in -e (la costumbre, de costumbre 'as usual', tener la costumbre de), just like la cumbre, la incertidumbre, and la muchedumbre.

course.etymology: English noun in the fixed affirmative phrase 'Of course', spoken by Lidia when asked if she speaks English. Borrowed into Middle English from Old French cours ('race, flow, customary path'), from Latin cursus ('running, course', from currere 'to run')—so 'of course' originally meant 'as a matter of the normal course of events'.

cognates.meaning: course (Spanish idiom for 'of course' is por supuesto or ¡claro!)

sources.title: Wiktionary — of course (English)

course.notes: A classic comedy trope in Spain: actors asked '¿Sabes inglés?' confidently reply 'Of course!' even when their English stops two sentences later.

crack.etymology: Borrowed from British English sporting slang crack ('top-notch racehorse, star athlete, ace player', documented from the 18th–19th centuries from dialectal English crack 'something to boast of, first-rate', related to crack 'sharp report, lively conversation'). Popularized in Spanish first via Río de la Plata and Spanish football journalism and then generalized across Spain.

history.meaning: ace, genius, superstar at what they do

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: crac
Wiktionary — crack (Spanish)

crack.notes: Super high-frequency Peninsular praise! Completely unrelated to drugs in this construction: ¡Eres un crack! / ¡Ella es una crack! means 'You're a total legend / genius / absolute pro!'

crecer.etymology: Crecer continues Latin crescĕre. The Spanish verb covers physical growth in people and plants as well as increases in size, intensity or activity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crecer

crecer.notes: In the first person singular present (crezco), -c- alternates with -zc- before -o, just like conocer (conozco) and parecer (parezco).

creer.etymology: Inherited from Latin crēdere ('to trust, entrust, believe'), with regular loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: creer
Wiktionary — creer

crema.etymology: Entered Spanish from French crème (Old French cresme), which blended Late Latin chrisma ('anointing unguent', from Greek khrîsma) with Gaulish crama ('milk cream').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crema

crema.notes: Covers dairy cream, rich pastry curds (crema de limón), and puréed vegetable soups.

cremallera.etymology: Borrowed from French crémaillère ('toothed pot-hook, rack gear, zipper'), from Old French cremail, descending via Late Latin *cremasculus from Ancient Greek κρεμαστήρ (kremastḗr, 'hanger, suspender').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cremallera
Wiktionary — cremallera

creo.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of creer ('to believe, think'), inherited from Latin crēdere ('to trust, entrust, believe', an ancient Indo-European religious compound *ḱred-dʰeh₁- literally meaning 'to place one's heart', cognate with Sanskrit śraddhā), with regular loss of intervocalic -d- (crēdō > creo).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: creer
Wiktionary — creo

creo.notes: Where English speakers say 'I think so / I don't think so', Spanish uses creer (not pensar): creo que sí / no creo (note subjunctive after negative no creo que sea así, indicative after affirmative creo que es así).

criado.etymology: Substantivized past participle of criar ('to nurse, nourish, raise from childhood within a household'), inherited from Latin creāre ('to bring forth, beget, rear'). In medieval noble houses, un criado / una criada was a retainer 'brought up in the lord's household', later narrowing to 'domestic servant, maid'.

morphemes.meaning: bring up, rear (< criar < Latin creāre)
person reared in a household -> servant (f. criada 'maid')

history.meaning: household protégé reared by a patron

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: criado
Wiktionary — criado

criado.notes: In modern Spain, real-life domestic workers are called empleada del hogar, whereas criada ('costume-drama maid': solo me pones de criada) survives vividly for stock roles in period TV series.

crisis.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin crisis from Ancient Greek krísis (κρίσις, 'separating, judgment, decisive turning point of an illness'), derived from krínein (κρίνειν, 'to separate, sift, decide, judge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crisis
Wiktionary — crisis

crisis.notes: Invariable feminine noun in singular and plural: una crisis -> las crisis. Also covers 'panic attack' (crisis de ansiedad) and Spain's post-2008 economic downturn (la crisis).

cristal.etymology: Descends from Latin crystallus, borrowed from Greek krýstallos ('clear ice, rock crystal'), derived from krýos ('icy cold, frost').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cristal

cristal.notes: In everyday Peninsular Spanish, el cristal is also the standard word for a windowpane or spectacle lens.

croquetas.etymology: Plural of croqueta, borrowed in the 19th century from French croquette ('crisp breaded fried roll'), diminutive built on French croquer ('to crunch between the teeth'), an echoic verb imitating a crisp crunch.

rootFamily.gloss: to crunch, creak (native Spanish echoic counterpart)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: croqueta
Wiktionary — croquetas

croquetas.notes: Unlike French or Dutch potato-based croquettes, Spanish croquetas (especially croquetas de jamón or de cocido) are silky, thick béchamel bound with cured ham or roast meat—an almost sacred tapas institution in Spain.

crujiente.etymology: Active participial adjective derived from crujir ('to crunch, crackle, creak') + -nte, an expressive verb of onomatopoeic origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crujiente
Wiktionary — crujiente

cruzar.etymology: Cruzar is formed within Romance from cruz ('cross', from Latin crux, crucis), originally meaning to lay across or pass from one side to the other.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cruzar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cruz

cruzar.notes: Spelling changes -z- to -c- before -e (crucé el puente).

crítica.etymology: Substantivized feminine of crítico, borrowed via Latin criticus from Ancient Greek kritikós (κριτικός, 'able to discern or judge; hē kritikḗ [tékhnē] the art of criticism'), from krínein ('to judge, separate').

morphemes.meaning: art, review, or feminine adjective (< Greek -ikḗ)

history.meaning: review, critique, criticism; female critic; critical press

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crítica
Wiktionary — crítica

crítica.notes: Notice how una crítica is neutral-to-positive in media contexts ('a film/theater review', buenas críticas 'rave reviews'), not necessarily harsh fault-finding.

cuaderno.etymology: Cuaderno continues Late Latin quaternus ('folded sheet of four leaves', from quattuor, 'four'), how medieval notebooks and quires were bound.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuaderno

cuaderno.notes: Modern Spanish standard word for a bound notebook or exercise book.

cuadro.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin quadrum ('square, four-sided figure'), neuter noun related to quattuor ('four'), later applied to a framed canvas or picture.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuadro
Wiktionary — cuadro

cualquier.etymology: Apocopated prenominal form of cualquiera ('any, whichever'), formed in medieval Castilian by fusing the relative/interrogative adjective cual ('which', < Latin quālis) + the third-person present subjunctive quiera ('may want/choose', from querer < Latin quaerere): literally 'whichever one you like'.

morphemes.meaning: one may choose (< quiera, subjunctive of querer)

history.meaning: of what kind + one may seek/wish

rootFamily.gloss: anyone, whichever (full form after nouns or standalone)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cualquier
Wiktionary — cualquier

cualquier.notes: Drops final -a before ANY singular noun, masculine OR feminine: cualquier día AND cualquier época (never *cualquiera época before the noun; after the noun it stays full: una época cualquiera).

cuando.etymology: Inherited from Latin quandō ('when, at what time, since').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuando
Wiktionary — cuando

cuarenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quarranta, contracted from Classical Latin quadrāgintā ('forty'), a derivative of quattuor ('four').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuarenta
Wiktionary — cuarenta

cuarto.etymology: Cuarto descends from Latin quartus ('fourth, quarter'), developing senses for a quarter-hour (y cuarto), a fourth floor or share, and a room.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuarto

cuarto.notes: In clock time, y cuarto means quarter past and menos cuarto means quarter to (never feminine *cuarta, because cuarto here is the masculine noun 'a quarter').

cuatro.etymology: Cuatro continues Latin quattuor ('four'), with regular metathesis of final -or > -ro.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuatro

cuatro.notes: Used bare after la habitación (la habitación cuatro = Room 4) and with las for clock time (las cuatro).

cubo.etymology: Conflates two Latin words: 'bucket, pail, wheel hub' inherited from Vulgar Latin *cūpus (masculine variant of Classical Latin cūpa 'tub, vat'); and geometric 'cube' borrowed from Latin cubus (< Greek κύβος 'die, cube').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cubo
Wiktionary — cubo

cuchara.etymology: Cuchara descends from Latin cochleāre ('spoon with a pointed handle originally used for eating snails and eggs'), derived from cochlea ('snail shell'), borrowed from Greek kokhlías.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuchara

cuchara.notes: Cognate with Portuguese colher and French cuillère.

cucharada.etymology: Formed within Spanish from cuchara ('spoon', < Latin cochleāre) + the capacity suffix -ada ('spoonful').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cucharada
Wiktionary — cucharada

cucharilla.etymology: Diminutive formed in Spanish from cuchara ('spoon') + -illa ('teaspoon'); cuchara descends from Latin cochleāre ('spoon for eating snails'), from cochlea ('snail shell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cucharilla
Wiktionary — cucharilla

cuenco.etymology: Masculine formation alongside cuenca ('deep clay or wooden bowl'), inherited from Latin concha ('shell, shell-shaped vessel'), from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē, 'mussel shell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuenco
Wiktionary — cuenco

cuenta.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun from contar ('to count, reckon, tell'), inherited from Latin computāre ('to sum up, calculate'), with regular stressed short o diphthongizing to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuenta
Wiktionary — cuenta

cuenta.notes: Essential false-friend remedy: English 'to realize' is NOT realizar ('to carry out / direct a TV show'), it is darse cuenta de (que te das cuenta de que hay una pared). La cuenta is also a restaurant check or bank account.

cuento.etymology: Both the masculine noun ('short story, tale; fib/excuse', inherited from Latin computus 'calculation, enumeration, narrative') and the first-person singular present indicative ('I tell / count') of contar (< Latin computāre), with regular diphthongization of stressed short o > ue.

morphemes.meaning: 1st-person sg. present OR masculine noun ending

history.meaning: I tell; short story, fairy tale

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuento
Wiktionary — cuento

cuento.notes: ¿Te cuento una cosa? ('Can I tell you something?') uses the verb form; as a noun, un cuento is a short story or fairy tale, and tener mucho cuento means 'to be a drama queen / full of excuses'.

cuerda.etymology: Cuerda continues Latin chorda ('catgut, musical string, cord'), borrowed from Greek khordḗ ('gut string of a lyre').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuerda

cuerda.notes: Short stressed Latin ŏ diphthongized regularly to ue (chŏrda > cuerda).

cuero.etymology: Inherited from Latin corium ('thick hide, skin, leather'), with regular diphthongization of short o to ue before yod.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuero
Wiktionary — cuero

cuestión.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin quaestiōnem (nominative quaestiō, 'seeking, inquiry, judicial investigation, topic of debate'), derived from quaerere ('to seek, ask'), adapting Latin quae- to Spanish cue-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuestión
Wiktionary — cuestión

cuestión.notes: Crucial false friend: an interrogative 'question' you ask someone is una pregunta (hacer una pregunta), whereas una cuestión means 'an issue, matter, or point' (esta cuestión, es cuestión de tiempo).

cuidado.etymology: Substantivized past participle of cuidar ('to care for, look after, pay attention'), which descends from Latin cōgitāre ('to think, ponder, reflect').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuidado
Wiktionary — cuidado

cuidar.etymology: Cuidar continues Latin cōgitāre ('to think, reflect, attend carefully to'), shifting in Old Spanish from 'ponder' to 'look after, take care of'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuidar

cuidar.notes: Can take a direct object or de (cuidar las plantas / cuidar de las plantas).

cuido.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of cuidar ('to take care of, look after'), inherited from Latin cōgitāre ('to think, ponder deeply, give anxious thought to', from com- + agitāre 'to turn over in the mind'), evolving phonetically cōgitāre > *coidāre > cuidar and shifting semantically from 'thinking carefully about' to 'caring for'.

morphemes.meaning: look after, care for (< Latin cōgitāre)

history.meaning: to think, suppose -> to tend, look after
I look after, take care of

cognates.meaning: to cogitate, ponder (learned doublet of cuidar!)

rootFamily.gloss: to take care of (cuidarse: take care of oneself)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuidar
Wiktionary — cuido

cuido.notes: Takes either de or direct object (with personal a): cuido de tu madre / cuido a tu madre ('I look after your mother').

culpa.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin culpa ('fault, blame, moral or legal responsibility').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: culpa
Wiktionary — culpa

cumpleaños.etymology: Verb–noun compound formed within Spanish from cumple ('completes, turns', 3rd-person singular present of cumplir < Latin complēre 'to fill up, complete') + años ('years', plural of año < Latin annus): literally '[the day one] completes years'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cumpleaños
Wiktionary — cumpleaños

cumpleaños.notes: Invariable in singular and plural (un cumpleaños, dos cumpleaños), casually shortened in Spain to el cumple.

curiosear.etymology: Formed within Spanish from curioso ('curious, inquisitive', < Latin cūriōsus) + the frequentative verbal suffix -ear ('to browse, pry, look around curiously').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curiosear
Wiktionary — curiosear

curiosidad.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsitās, cūriōsitātis ('eagerness for knowledge, inquisitiveness'), derived from cūriōsus ('careful, inquisitive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curiosidad
Wiktionary — curiosidad

curioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsus ('bestowing care, diligent, inquisitive'), derived from cūra ('care, attention').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curioso
Wiktionary — curioso

currar.etymology: Colloquial Peninsular Spanish verb ('to work, slog away'), borrowed from Caló (Iberian Romani) currar ('to strike, hammer, forge, work'), which traces back through Balkan/Common Romani ker- / kur- to Prakrit and Sanskrit kṛ- / karoti (करोति, 'to make, do, work', PIE *kʷer-).

morphemes.meaning: beat metal, work (< Caló currar < Sanskrit kar-/kuṭṭ-)

rootFamily.gloss: to put real effort into something

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: currar
Wiktionary — currar

currar.notes: One of the many vivid Caló words woven into everyday Spain Spanish (alongside chaval, molar, chungo, paripé): ¡A currar! means 'Time to get to work!', and ¡Te lo has currado! means 'You really put a ton of effort into it!'

curro.etymology: Deverbal noun from Peninsular colloquial currar ('to work'), borrowed from Caló currar ('to work, hammer'), ultimately of Indo-Aryan / Romani origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curro
Wiktionary — curro

curro.notes: In Spain, el curro is the universal casual word for both 'my job/workplace' (voy al curro, busco curro) and 'hard work' (enhorabuena por el curro)—equivalent to Mexican chamba or Argentine laburo. (Capitalized Curro is also the Andalusian nickname for Francisco.)

currumi.etymology: Humorous colloquial Spanish malapropism in Paquita Salas for the tile game Rummikub (promptly corrected by the other characters: 'Rummikub. Rummikub.'), reshaping the unfamiliar brand name Rummikub—coined in the 1940s by Romanian-born Israeli inventor Ephraim Hertzano from English rummy (card game) + German/Yiddish Kub ('cube, tile')—with a folk-sounding Hispanic initial cu- syllable.

sources.title: Wiktionary — Rummikub

currumi.notes: Classic Spanish comedy detail: older Spanish relatives famously domesticate foreign game and brand names (turning Rummikub into el currumi, alongside playing dominó or parchís).

cuál.etymology: Interrogative pronoun and determiner ('which?, what one?'), inherited from Latin quālis ('of what kind, which'), written with an accent mark to distinguish it from relative cual.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuál
Wiktionary — cuál

cuándo.etymology: Interrogative adverb ('when?'), inherited from Latin quandō ('at what time?'), written with an acute accent in direct and indirect questions.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuándo
Wiktionary — cuándo

cuánto.etymology: Interrogative and exclamative determiner, pronoun, and adverb ('how much?, how many?'), inherited from Latin quantus ('how great, how much'), written with an accent mark to distinguish it from relative cuanto.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuánto
Wiktionary — cuánto

cuéntame.etymology: Affirmative tú imperative cuenta ('tell!') + enclitic first-person singular indirect-object pronoun -me ('me'). Contar descends from Latin computāre ('to recount, calculate'), with stressed short o diphthongizing to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contar
Wiktionary — cuéntame

cuéntame.notes: Warm phone and catch-up prompt ('Tell me, what's up?'); also famous across Spain from TVE's longest-running family historical drama Cuéntame cómo pasó (2001–2023).

cálido.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin calidus ('warm, hot', derived from calēre 'to be warm'), forming a learned doublet alongside inherited popular caldo ('broth').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cálido
Wiktionary — cálido

cámara.etymology: Learned/semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin camara (Classical Latin camera 'vaulted roof, arched chamber'), from Ancient Greek kamára (καμάρα, 'anything with an arched cover, vaulted room'). Its photographic/video sense clips cámara oscura (Latin camera obscūra 'darkened chamber'), where light projected an image through a pinhole.

history.meaning: photo/video camera; camera operator; legislative chamber; walk-in fridge

cognates.meaning: doublets from Latin camera (learned vs. Old French)
bedroom, chamber (telecamera / macchina fotografica for camera)

rootFamily.gloss: camera operator (LatAm; Spain says el/la cámara)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cámara
Wiktionary — cámara

cámara.notes: In Spain, la cámara is the camera device (both photo and video), while el/la cámara is the camera operator on set—and actors wait backstage in el camerino ('dressing room', from the same root!).

cóctel.etymology: Hispanicized borrowing from English cocktail (first attested in American print in 1806 for a mixed spirituous drink of spirits, sugar, water, and bitters), literally 'cock's tail'—originally 18th-century British equestrian slang for a spirited non-thoroughbred horse with a docked, upright tail.

history.meaning: mixed drink; cocktail party; cocktail dress code

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: cóctel
Wiktionary — cóctel

cóctel.notes: Spain stresses the first syllable: CÓC-tel (/ˈkoktel/, plural cócteles), whereas much of Latin America says oxytone coc-TEL (cocteles). Ir de cóctel means semi-formal cocktail attire.

cómo.etymology: Interrogative and exclamative adverb ('how?'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *quōmo, a shortened form of Classical Latin quōmodo ('in what manner, how').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cómo
Wiktionary — cómo

cómodo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin commodus ('having due measure, suitable, convenient, comfortable'), formed from com- + modus ('measure, manner').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cómodo
Wiktionary — cómodo

dado.etymology: As a noun ('playing die, small cube'), traced by the DLE to Classical Arabic aʿdād ('numbers') or Late Latin datum ('that which is cast or given'); as a participle ('given'), inherited from Latin datus (past participle of dare).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dado
Wiktionary — dado

dame.etymology: Affirmative tú imperative da ('give!') + enclitic indirect-object pronoun -me ('me'). Dar descends directly from Latin dare ('to give, hand over', from PIE *deh₃- 'to give').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dar
Wiktionary — dame

dame.notes: Because dame is a paroxytone (llana) ending in a vowel (/ˈdame/), it takes NO accent mark (unlike tres-syllable dáselo!). Ven, dame un beso ('Come here, give me a kiss') is Spain's warm greeting hug-and-cheek-kiss.

dando.etymology: Gerund of dar ('to give'), inherited directly from the Latin ablative gerund dandō ('by giving', from dare).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dar
Wiktionary — dando

dando.notes: Notice the light-verb contrast with English: English 'takes' a walk or 'goes for' a stroll, whereas Spanish 'gives' one—dar un paseo / dando paseos ('going for walks').

dar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin dare ('to give, offer, hand over, grant').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dar
Wiktionary — dar

das.etymology: Second-person singular present indicative of dar ('to give'), inherited directly from Latin dās ('thou givest', from dare).

rootFamily.gloss: to read opposite lines in an audition

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dar
Wiktionary — das

das.notes: Monosyllabic das never carries an accent mark in Spanish. Appears in high-frequency idioms like te das cuenta ('you realize') and tú le das la réplica ('you feed her the scene partner's lines').

david.etymology: Male given name David, via Late Latin Dāvīd and Koine Greek Dauíd (Δαυίδ) from Biblical Hebrew Dāwīḏ (דָּוִד, traditionally 'beloved, darling', from the Semitic root d-w-d 'beloved, paternal uncle'), name of the second king of Israel.

sources.title: Wiktionary — David (Spanish)

david.notes: Pronounced in Spanish with stress on the second syllable (/daˈβið/ or in Madrid colloquial speech often [daˈβiθ] / [daˈβi]), unlike English DAY-vid!

de.etymology: The preposition de continues Latin dē ('from, down from, concerning'), absorbing most functions of the Latin genitive case across Romance languages.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: de

de.notes: De expresses possession (la llave de Clara), material (de madera, de latón), origin, contents (una taza de té), and part of the day after clock hours (de la mañana).

debajo.etymology: Formed in Old Spanish by compounding the preposition de (< Latin dē) with bajo ('low, underneath', < Late Latin bassus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: debajo
Wiktionary — debajo

deben.etymology: Third-person plural present indicative of deber ('must, should; to owe'), inherited from Latin dēbēre ('to owe, have from someone, be under obligation to', contracted from de- + habēre 'to have away from another').

cognates.meaning: via Old French dette / deu from Latin dēbēre

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: deber
Wiktionary — deben

deben.notes: Grammar distinction: deber + infinitive expresses obligation ('they should/must do that': eso lo deben hacer), whereas deber de + infinitive expresses probability ('they must be tired').

deber.etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre ('to owe, be bound to, ought'), itself a contraction of dē- + habēre ('to have from another, keep on loan').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: deber
Wiktionary — deber

debo.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of deber ('I must, ought to; I owe'), descending directly from Latin dēbeō (from dēbēre 'to owe, be bound to').

history.meaning: I must, I should; I owe

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: deber
Wiktionary — debo

debo.notes: Debo llamarla ('I really ought to / must call her') expresses personal duty; ¿Cuánto te debo? asks 'How much do I owe you?'

decibelio.etymology: Twentieth-century scientific borrowing (via English decibel / French décibel), combining Latin decimus ('tenth', deci-) + belio, named in honor of telecommunications pioneer Alexander Graham Bell (1847–1922).

history.meaning: tenth of a bel (unit of sound intensity)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decibelio
Wiktionary — decibelio

decidido.etymology: Participial adjective of decidir ('decided, resolute, determined'), borrowed from Latin dēcīdere ('to cut off, settle a matter, decide', from dē- + caedere 'to cut').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decidido
Wiktionary — decidido

decimos.etymology: First-person plural present indicative of decir ('to say, tell'), inherited from Latin dīcere (1pl. dīcimus, shifted in Hispano-Romance to the -īre conjugation *dīcīmus), with pretonic vowel dissimilation i...i > e...i.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decir
Wiktionary — decimos

decimos.notes: Unlike -ar/-er verbs, decimos is strictly PRESENT ('we say': ¿Y si decimos que...? 'What if we say that...?'); the preterite 'we said' is irregular dijimos!

decir.etymology: Decir descends from Latin dicĕre. Its central use is putting a thought into words, and it also introduces reported speech or opinions. The modern verb shows several distinct stems, including digo, dijo and the subjunctive diga.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decir

decir.notes: Querer decir means to mean, and the polite imperative dígame is standard in Spain when answering the telephone or welcoming a customer.

decirlo.etymology: Infinitive decir ('to say, tell', < Latin dīcere) + enclitic masculine/neuter direct-object pronoun -lo ('it', < Latin illum/illud).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decir

decirlo.notes: Spanish requires expressing 'it' explicitly where English might leave it implicit or use a gerund: de tanto decirlo ('from saying it so many times').

decisión.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēcīsiōnem (nominative dēcīsiō, 'a cutting off, settlement, resolution'), action noun from dēcīdere (dē- 'off' + caedere 'to cut, strike'—literally cutting off hesitation to settle a matter).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decisión
Wiktionary — decisión

decisión.notes: Collocation watch: Spanish 'takes' a decision—tomar una decisión—never *hacer una decisión.

dedicar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēdicāre ('to proclaim, consecrate, devote to a purpose'), formed from dē- + dicāre ('to proclaim, dedicate').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dedicar
Wiktionary — dedicar

dedo.etymology: Dedo descends from Latin digĭtus ('finger, toe') through regular loss of the unstressed internal vowel and voicing of -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dedo

dedo.notes: Covers both fingers (dedos de la mano) and toes (dedos del pie); learned cognate dígito means 'numerical digit'.

dejar.etymology: The DLE traces dejar to Vulgar Latin *daxāre, altered from Classical Latin laxāre ('to loosen, release, let go') under influence of dare/delinquĕre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dejar

dejar.notes: Covers leaving an object behind, letting someone do something, or stopping an action (dejar de + infinitive).

del.etymology: Del is the obligatory contraction of preposition de ('of, from') + masculine singular definite article el ('the').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: del
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: de
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

del.notes: Do not contract when Capitalized El belongs to a proper title or when accented pronoun él ('him') follows de (de él).

delante.etymology: Evolved by consonant dissimilation (n...n > l...n) from Old Spanish denante, a compound of Late Latin dē + in + ante ('from before, in front').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delante
Wiktionary — delante

delantero.etymology: Formed within Spanish from delante ('in front, ahead') + the relational suffix -ero ('situated in front, front, forward').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delantero
Wiktionary — delantero

delgado.etymology: Inherited from Latin dēlicātus ('dainty, tender, fine, slender', related to dēliciae 'delight, luxury' and lacere 'to entice'), showing regular internal syncope of unstressed -i- and voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g- (dēlicātum > delgado).

cognates.meaning: slender, nimble (inherited doublet alongside learned délicat)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delgado
Wiktionary — delgado

delgado.notes: Neutral, polite adjective for slim/thin people in Spain (contrast harsher flaco 'skinny/scrawny', and note fino for thin slices or paper). Diminutive delgadita sounds affectionate.

delicioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēliciōsus ('delightful, delicious, luxurious'), derived from Classical Latin dēliciae ('delight, pleasure, charm').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delicioso
Wiktionary — delicioso

demasiado.etymology: Originally the past participle of obsolete demasiar ('to exceed'), derived from demasía ('excess, surplus'), which was built on demás (de + más, < Latin dē + magis 'more').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: demasiado
Wiktionary — demasiado

dentro.etymology: Dentro continues Latin de intro ('from within, inside'), fusing preposition de with adverb intro.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dentro

dentro.notes: Dentro de marks both spatial interior (dentro de la maleta) and time until a future event (dentro de cuarenta minutos = in forty minutes' time).

depender.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēpendēre ('to hang down from, be dependent upon'), formed from dē- + pendēre ('to hang').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: depender
Wiktionary — depender

dependiente.etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēpendēns, dēpendentis, present participle of dēpendēre ('to hang from, depend on'); substantivized in Spanish for a subordinate employee or shop clerk.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dependiente
Wiktionary — dependiente

depilar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēpilāre ('to pluck out hair'), compounded from privative dē- ('off, away') + pilāre (from pilus 'body hair').

history.meaning: to wax, pluck, or remove body/facial hair

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: depilar
Wiktionary — depilar

depilar.notes: While English 'depilate' sounds clinical, Spanish depilarse is the everyday word for waxing, plucking eyebrows (depilarse las cejas), epilating, or laser hair removal.

derecha.etymology: Derecha continues Late Latin directa ('straight, direct, right-hand'), feminine of directus, since the right hand was viewed as the straight or guiding hand.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: derecha
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: derecho

derecha.notes: A la derecha and a mano derecha mean 'on / to the right', whereas todo recto expresses 'straight ahead'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: desear
