sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: discutir
Wiktionary — discutir

diseñar.etymology: Borrowed from Italian disegnare ('to draw, sketch, design, plan'), which descends from Latin dēsignāre ('to mark out, trace, designate', from signum 'mark, sign').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: diseñar
Wiktionary — diseñar

disfrutar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from dis- + fruto ('fruit, benefit, yield', < Latin frūctus) + -ar, originally 'to reap the fruits or benefit of' and hence 'to enjoy'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: disfrutar
Wiktionary — disfrutar

disimular.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dissimulāre ('to make unlike what it really is, disguise, conceal one's feelings'), compounded from dis- ('apart, not') + simulāre ('to make like, copy, feign', from similis 'similar').

morphemes.meaning: make seem like (< Latin simulāre / similis)

history.meaning: similar -> feign -> hide what actually is
to hide one's feelings, play it cool, act natural

cognates.meaning: literary and Old French borrowings from dissimulāre

rootFamily.gloss: discretion, stealth (con disimulo: casually, on the sly)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: disimular
Wiktionary — disimular

disimular.notes: Philosophically neat pair: simular fakes what isn't there, whereas disimular hides what IS there! In everyday Spain, ¡Disimula! means 'Act natural / play it cool!'.

dispuesto.etymology: Irregular strong past participle and adjective of disponer ('willing, ready; arranged'), inherited from Latin dispositus ('set in order, arranged'), past participle of dispōnere (dis- 'apart, in order' + pōnere 'to place'), with regular stressed short o diphthongizing to ue (like puesto < positus).

rootFamily.gloss: to arrange; (disponer de) have at one's disposal

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dispuesto
Wiktionary — dispuesto

dispuesto.notes: With estar + a + infinitive, estar dispuesto a means 'to be willing/prepared to' (estoy dispuesto a jugar); with ser, es muy dispuesta means 'she's resourceful, obliging, and quick to pitch in'.

distancia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin distantia ('standing apart, remoteness, interval in space or time'), derived from distāns, present participle of distāre ('to stand apart').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: distancia
Wiktionary — distancia

divertido.etymology: Participial adjective of divertir ('to amuse, entertain'), a learned/semi-learned borrowing from Latin dīvertere ('to turn aside, divert one's mind from cares'), compounded from dī-/dis- ('aside') + vertere ('to turn').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: divertido
Wiktionary — divertido

divertido.notes: Covers BOTH English 'fun' (una fiesta muy divertida) AND 'funny / good company' (una chica muy divertida, alongside graciosa for joke-cracking).

dividir.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dividĕre ('to part asunder, separate, distribute').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dividir

dividir.notes: Forms its abstract noun división (< divisiōnem).

divinamente.etymology: Adverb formed from divina (feminine singular of divino 'divine, heavenly, fabulous', learned borrowing from Latin dīvīnus, from dīvus / deus 'god') + adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente 'in a ... manner').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: divinamente
Wiktionary — divinamente

divinamente.notes: Classic theatrical and castizo Peninsular reply to '¿Qué tal estás?': ¡Yo divinamente, no me puedo quejar! ('Fabulously, can't complain!').

división.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dīvīsiōnem (nominative dīvīsiō, 'separating, distribution, division'), action noun from dīvidere ('to force apart, divide', supine dīvīsum).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: división
Wiktionary — división

división.notes: From Spanish football's Primera División (LaLiga), jugar en primera división is everyday Spain slang for 'playing in the big leagues / A-list'.

do.etymology: Borrowed from Italian do, introduced in the 17th century by music theorist Giovanni Battista Doni to replace Guido d'Arezzo's syllable ut as the first note of the solfège scale.

history.meaning: first note of the diatonic scale (replacing ut)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: do
Wiktionary — do

doblado.etymology: Participial adjective of doblar ('folded, bent, doubled, dubbed'), inherited from Latin duplātus, past participle of duplāre ('to double').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: doblado
Wiktionary — doblado

doblar.etymology: Inherited from Latin duplāre ('to double, fold in two'), derived from the adjective duplus ('twofold, double').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: doblar
Wiktionary — doblar

doble.etymology: Inherited (via Old Occitan or Old French doble) from Latin duplus ('twofold, double, twice as large'), built on the root of duo ('two').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: doble
Wiktionary — doble

doce.etymology: Doce continues Latin duodĕcim ('twelve', literally two + ten), reduced through Vulgar Latin *dodĕce to Old Spanish doze > doce.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: doce

doce.notes: Las doce can mean either noon or midnight; al mediodía specifies noon.

docena.etymology: Built from doce ('twelve', from Latin duodĕcim) with the collective suffix -ena, naming a set of twelve items.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: docena

docena.notes: Media docena ('half a dozen') is an everyday way to ask for six items at a market stall.

documento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin documentum ('lesson, warning, example, official proof or record'), derived from docēre ('to teach, show').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: documento
Wiktionary — documento

doler.etymology: Inherited from Latin dolēre ('to feel physical pain, ache, suffer grief'), with regular diphthongization of stressed short o to ue in stem-stressed forms (duele).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: doler
Wiktionary — doler

dolor.etymology: Inherited from Latin dolor, dolōris ('physical pain, ache, sorrow, grief'), derived from the verb dolēre ('to hurt, suffer').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dolor
Wiktionary — dolor

domingo.etymology: Continues Late Christian Latin [diēs] Dominĭcus ('the Lord's day'), from Latin dominus ('lord, master'), replacing Roman diēs Sōlis ('day of the Sun').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: domingo

domingo.notes: Paired with sábado (< Hebrew šabbāt) as the two non-planetary weekday names in Spanish.

dominó.etymology: Borrowed from French domino (18th century), naming the rectangular black-backed ivory game tiles by playful comparison with a priest's black-hooded winter cloak (French domino), which itself likely came from the ecclesiastical Latin benediction Benedīcāmus Dominō ('Let us bless the Lord', dative/ablative of dominus 'lord').

history.meaning: cleric's black winter hood -> black-and-white spotted tile game

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dominó
Wiktionary — dominó (Spanish)

dominó.notes: Oxytone stress on the final syllable (jugar al do-mi-NÓ)—be careful not to confuse the noun el dominó ('dominoes') with the homographic verb dominó ('he/she dominated', from dominar)!

don.etymology: Conflates two Latin words: the courteous title don ('sir, Mr.') evolved by proclitic reduction from Latin dominus ('lord, master'); the noun don ('natural gift, talent') descends from Latin dōnum ('gift', from dare 'to give').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: don
Wiktionary — don

donde.etymology: Formed in Old Spanish by compounding the preposition de (< Latin dē) with onde ('where, whence', < Latin unde 'from where').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: donde
Wiktionary — donde

dorado.etymology: Dorado comes from dorar ('to gild'), continuing Late Latin deaurāre ('to coat with gold', from aurum, 'gold').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dorado
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dorar

dorado.notes: Describes gold-coloured metal or paper as well as golden-brown baked pastry.

dormido.etymology: Participial adjective of dormir ('asleep, sleeping'), inherited from Latin dormītus, past participle of dormīre ('to sleep').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dormido
Wiktionary — dormido

dormir.etymology: Dormir continues Latin dormīre ('to sleep') with unchanged infinitive spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dormir

dormir.notes: Stem vowel shifts o -> ue when stressed (duermo, duerme) and o -> u in third-person preterite (durmió, durmieron).

dos.etymology: Inherited from Latin duōs ('two'), the masculine accusative plural of duo.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dos
Wiktionary — dos

drama.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin drāma from Ancient Greek drâma, drámatos (δρᾶμα, 'deed, action, stage play'), derived from drân (δρᾶν, 'to do, act, perform').

history.meaning: dramatic genre; personal tragedy or fuss

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: drama
Wiktionary — drama (Spanish)

drama.notes: Masculine noun despite ending in -a (el drama, un drama), like other Greek -ma nouns (el problema, el tema, el guion/esquema). Montar un drama means 'to make a huge scene'.

ducha.etymology: Ducha entered Spanish via French douche from Italian doccia ('water pipe, spout, shower'), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *ductia (from ducĕre, 'to lead or channel water').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ducha

dueño.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin domĭnus ('master of the house, owner'), with diphthongization of short stressed ŏ > ue and palatalization of -mn- > -ñ-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dueño

dueño.notes: Its proclitic honorific doublet without diphthongization gave Spanish title don.

dueños.etymology: Masculine plural of dueño ('owner, landlord, master'), inherited directly from Latin dominus ('master of a household, lord, owner', from domus 'house'), via syncope and regular diphthongization + palatalization: dominus > Vulgar Latin *domnus > Old Spanish dueño.

cognates.meaning: honorific Mr./Ms. before first names (unstressed twin of dueño/dueña!)

rootFamily.gloss: respectful title before given names (unstressed doublet)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dueño
Wiktionary — dueños

dueños.notes: Stunning phonetic split: when Latin dominus carried full stress as a standalone noun, o diphthongized and -mn- palatalized to dueño ('owner'); when unstressed before a first name (dominus Petrus), it stayed don (don Pedro)!

dulce.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned from Latin dulcis ('sweet in taste, pleasant, gentle, agreeable').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dulce
Wiktionary — dulce

durante.etymology: Grammaticalized from the present participle durante of durar (< Latin dūrāns, dūrantis, from dūrāre 'to last, endure'), originally used in absolute constructions ('while ... lasts' > 'during').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: durante
Wiktionary — durante

duro.etymology: Inherited from Latin dūrus ('hard, firm, solid, tough, stern').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: duro
Wiktionary — duro

día.etymology: Día descends from Vulgar Latin *dia, a first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs ('day') that kept its original masculine gender.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: día

día.notes: Important gender exception: el día is masculine despite ending in -a (este día, ¡Buenos días!).

dónde.etymology: Accented dónde combines preposition de ('from') + onde (from Latin unde, 'whence'), generalized in Spanish to mean interrogative 'where?'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dónde
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: donde

dónde.notes: Takes a written accent in direct and indirect questions (¿Dónde está?, dime dónde está); relative donde carries no accent.

dúo.etymology: Borrowed from Italian duo ('musical composition for two performers, pair'), itself a learned adoption of Latin duo ('two').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dúo
Wiktionary — dúo

easy.etymology: Unadapted English adjective ('It's easy'), spoken during English-language audition coaching in Paquita Salas. Borrowed into Middle English eisy from Anglo-Norman aisé ('comfortable, at ease, effortless'), participial adjective of aisier (from Old French aise 'elbow-room, comfort' < Vulgar Latin *adiacēns 'lying nearby', from adiacēre).

sources.title: Wiktionary — easy (English)

easy.notes: Reassuring English phrase ('It's easy!') used while coaching Spanish actors through daunting English audition sides.

echa.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative (or tú imperative) of echar ('to throw, pour, cast out, emit'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *iectāre for Classical Latin iactāre ('to toss, hurl', frequentative of iacere 'to throw'), showing regular Romance evolution of *iectāre > *ieitar > Old Spanish echar (-ct- > -ch-).

cognates.meaning: French and Latin borrowings from iactāre / ēicere

rootFamily.gloss: to throw, pour, fire; put on

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: echar
Wiktionary — echa

echa.notes: TWO vital tips: (1) Spelling trap—echa ('throws/misses', from echar) NEVER has an h-, whereas hecha ('made/done', from hacer) ALWAYS has h- ('Lo primero que se echa de echar es la hache'!). (2) In Spain, echar de menos (Te echa mucho de menos, built by folk-blend on Galician-Portuguese achar menos 'find lacking') is THE everyday way to say 'to miss someone' (where Latin America prefers extrañar).

echar.etymology: Inherited from Latin iactāre ('to throw, cast, hurl', frequentative of iacere 'to throw'), via Vulgar Latin *iectāre with palatalization of -ct- to Castilian -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: echar
Wiktionary — echar

eco.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēchō ('echo'), from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ, 'reflected sound, echo'), related to ἦχος (êkhos, 'sound, ringing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: eco
Wiktionary — eco

edad.etymology: Inherited from Latin aetātem (nominative aetās, 'time of life, age, era', contracted in Old Latin from *aevitās, derived from aevum 'lifetime, eternity'), with monophthongization ae > e, voicing of intervocalic -t- > -d-, and loss of final -e.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: edad
Wiktionary — edad

edad.notes: ¿Qué edad tienes? is a slightly more polite/formal alternative to ¿Cuántos años tienes? ('How old are you?') in interviews and castings.

edificio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin aedificium ('building, structure'), derived from aedificāre ('to build', a compound of aedēs 'dwelling, temple' + facere 'to make').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: edificio
Wiktionary — edificio

educado.etymology: Participial adjective of educar ('well-mannered, polite, educated'), borrowed from Latin ēducātus, past participle of ēducāre ('to bring up, rear, train').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: educado
Wiktionary — educado

efectivo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin effectīvus ('productive, effective, real; in commerce, cash in hand'), derived from effectus, past participle of efficere ('to accomplish, bring about').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: efectivo
Wiktionary — efectivo

eh.etymology: Universal conversational interjection and tag particle (continuing Latin ēh / ehem and natural vocalic discourse particles across Romance), written with silent h after the vowel like ah, oh, uh.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: eh
Wiktionary — eh (Spanish)

eh.notes: Replaces dozens of complex English tag questions ('aren't you?', 'will you?', 'okay?') with two effortless letters at the end of a Spanish sentence: Estás un poco tensa, ¿eh? / A currar, ¿eh?.

ejemplo.etymology: Semi-learned adaptation of Latin exemplum ('sample taken out from a group, model, precedent, warning'), derived from eximere ('to take out, select', from ex- 'out' + emere 'to take, buy'), evolving Latin -x- > Old Spanish -x- (/ʃ/) > Modern Spanish -j- (/x/).

history.meaning: to take out -> chosen sample, model

cognates.meaning: both borrowed via Old French from Latin exemplum!

rootFamily.gloss: exemplary; copy/issue of a book or magazine

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ejemplo
Wiktionary — ejemplo

ejemplo.notes: Por ejemplo ('for example') and poner un ejemplo ('to give an example'—note poner or dar!) are high-frequency essentials.

el.etymology: The definite-article family el, la and lo developed from Latin ille, illa and illud, demonstrative forms meaning that one. The old pointing forms became everyday markers of an identifiable person or thing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

el.notes: El is the article in el mundo. It is written without the accent used by the personal pronoun él.

elección.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēlēctiō, ēlēctiōnis ('a choosing, selection, choice'), derived from ēligere ('to pick out, choose').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: elección
Wiktionary — elección

elegancia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēlegantia ('tastefulness, refinement, fastidious choice'), derived from ēlegāns, ēlegantem ('choosy, tasteful, refined'), an old participial formation on ēligere ('to pick out carefully, choose', from ex- + legere).

rootFamily.gloss: to choose (sharing the Latin ēligere root!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: elegancia
Wiktionary — elegancia

elegancia.notes: Exclaiming ¡Qué elegancia! ('Such elegance / How chic!') is classic red-carpet flattery in Spain when someone dresses up.

elegir.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēligere ('to pick out, select, choose'), formed from ex- ('out') + legere ('to gather, pick, read').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: elegir
Wiktionary — elegir

ella.etymology: Inherited from Latin illa ('that woman, she'), feminine nominative singular of the distal demonstrative pronoun ille.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ella
Wiktionary — ella

ellos.etymology: Inherited from Latin illōs (masculine accusative plural of the distal demonstrative ille 'that one yonder'), which across Romance weakened into both the third-person personal pronoun ('they') and the definite article (unstressed los), with geminate -ll- palatalizing in tonic position to Spanish -ll-.

rootFamily.gloss: the; them (unstressed twin of ellos from Latin illōs!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ellos
Wiktionary — ellos

ellos.notes: Because Spanish drops ordinary subject pronouns, adding explicit ellos marks contrast or focus: ¿Y ellos cómo tienen que estar? ('And how nervous must THEY be?'). Also serves after prepositions: para ellos ('for them').

embustera.etymology: Feminine singular of embustero ('liar, fibber, trickster'), derived from embuste ('artful lie, hoax, sham') + agentive suffix -ero/-era. Embuste (attested since the 16th century alongside embustir 'to swindle, deceive') probably came via Occitan/Catalan or Italianate rogue slang ultimately connected to Late Latin *impostūra / *imbūstāre ('to stuff/pack with fakery').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: embustero
Wiktionary — embustera

embustera.notes: More colorful and castizo than plain mentirosa ('liar'): calling someone embustera evokes spinning theatrical tall tales or shameless fibs.

emociona.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative of emocionar ('to move emotionally, touch deeply, thrill'), denominal verb formed on emoción ('emotion', borrowed via French émotion from Latin ēmovēre 'to stir up, shake, move out').

morphemes.meaning: stir emotion, move (< emoción < Latin ēmovēre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: emocionar
Wiktionary — emociona

emociona.notes: In Spanish acting praise, te emociona doesn't just mean 'excites you'—it means 'moves you to tears / touches your heart' (whereas English 'emotional' in the sense 'sensitive' is sensible or emotivo).

emocionado.etymology: Participial adjective of emocionar ('deeply moved, touched; excited'), derived from emoción (via French émotion from Latin ēmovēre 'to stir up', ex- + movēre 'to move') + -ar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: emocionado
Wiktionary — emocionado

emocionado.notes: Covers two warm states English splits apart: both 'excited/thrilled' about good news AND 'deeply moved / choked up' at a wedding or awards speech (estoy emocionadísimo).

empanadillas.etymology: Plural of empanadilla ('small savory turnover'), formed with the diminutive suffix -illa on empanada ('stuffed pastry', feminine past participle of empanar 'to wrap or bake in bread dough', parasynthetic verb from en- + pan 'bread' < Latin pānis + -ar).

morphemes.meaning: in, inside (< Latin in-, assimilated to m before p)

history.meaning: bake in dough -> pie -> hand-sized fried/baked turnovers

rootFamily.gloss: large family-sized savory pie (in Spain, e.g. empanada gallega)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empanadilla
Wiktionary — empanadillas

empanadillas.notes: Key Spain vs. Latin America food distinction: in Spain, una empanada (gallega) is a big rectangular or round savory pie sliced into portions, whereas individual half-moon turnovers (typically stuffed with tuna, tomato, and egg) are called empanadillas!

empapado.etymology: Participial adjective of empapar ('soaked, drenched'), formed from en- + papa ('soft mash, pap', < Latin pappa) + -ar, originally meaning 'to soak bread into a soft mash'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empapado
Wiktionary — empapado

emperor.etymology: Unadapted English noun ('the emperor'), spoken in a rehearsed English costume-drama audition line in Paquita Salas. Borrowed into Middle English emperour from Old French empereor, from Latin imperātōrem (nominative imperātor 'commander-in-chief, Roman emperor', from imperāre 'to command').

sources.title: Wiktionary — emperor (English)

emperor.notes: Appears in the famously mangled English audition sentence 'It is very important to give this envelope to the emperor' in Episode 3 of Paquita Salas.

empezar.etymology: The DLE analyses empezar as a formation from en- and pieza. The resulting verb means to begin or start, alternating between diphthongized forms such as empiezo and unstressed-stem forms such as empezamos.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empezar

history.meaning: the components identified by the DLE for empezar

empezar.notes: Before an infinitive, empezar always requires the preposition a (empieza a llover, empezamos a trabajar).

empresa.etymology: Borrowed in the Renaissance from Italian impresa ('bold undertaking, venture, emblem; later business firm'), substantivized feminine past participle of imprendere ('to undertake', from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, Classical in- + prehendere 'to take hold of').

cognates.meaning: French and Italian cousins of the same root

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empresa
Wiktionary — empresa

empresa.notes: While English 'enterprise' sounds grand, la empresa is Spain's everyday word for any company or business of any size (llevar una empresa 'to run a company', cena de empresa 'office party').

empujar.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish empuxar from Latin impulsāre ('to push against, drive forward'), the frequentative of impellere (in- + pellere 'to drive, push').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empujar
Wiktionary — empujar

en.etymology: The preposition en continues Latin in ('in, inside, on'), expressing spatial containment, surface contact ('on the table' = en la mesa), and modes of transport (en tren).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: en

en.notes: Spanish uses en both where English says 'in' (en la cocina) and where English says 'on' (en la mesa, en la pared).

enamorado.etymology: Participial adjective (and noun) of enamorar ('in love; lover'), descended from Vulgar Latin *inamorāre or formed in Old Romance from en- ('in') + amor ('love', < Latin amor) + -ar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enamorado
Wiktionary — enamorado

enamorado.notes: Preposition watch: Spanish says estar enamorado DE alguien ('in love WITH someone'—estoy enamorada de ti), never *con!

enamorados.etymology: Masculine plural noun/adjective of enamorado ('lovers, sweethearts; people in love'), from en- + amor (< Latin amor) + -ado + plural -s.

history.meaning: person in love -> sweethearts, couple in love

rootFamily.gloss: Valentine's Day (in Spain alongside San Valentín)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enamorado
Wiktionary — enamorados

enamorados.notes: Una pareja de enamorados means 'a young couple in love / sweethearts' (sweeter and more romantic than amantes, which implies an illicit affair).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enamorado
Wiktionary — enamoradísimo

history.meaning: to win someone's heart; (enamorarse) to fall in love

cognates.meaning: to charm, make fall in love
to fill with love or fascination

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enamorar

encajar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from en- + caja ('box, socket, mortise', < Latin capsa) + -ar, meaning 'to fit snugly into a box or groove'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encajar

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encaje
Wiktionary — encaje

encantada.etymology: Feminine singular participial adjective of encantar ('to charm, delight; originally to cast a magic spell over'), inherited from Latin incantāre ('to chant a magic formula upon, bewitch', from in- 'upon' + cantāre 'to sing, chant').

charmed, delighted; nice to meet you! (spoken by a woman)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encantado

encantado.etymology: Participial adjective of encantar ('delighted, charmed; enchanted'), inherited from Latin incantātus, past participle of incantāre ('to chant a magic spell over', from in- + cantāre 'to sing, chant').

history.meaning: to enchant, cast a spell / charmed

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encantado
Wiktionary — encantado

encantar.etymology: Encantar continues Latin incantāre ('to chant a spell over, bewitch, charm', from in- + cantāre, 'to sing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encantar

encantar.notes: Works grammatically just like gustar: me encanta el patio (singular subject) vs me encantan las flores (plural subject).

encargada.etymology: Feminine participial noun from encargar ('woman in charge, female manager or supervisor'), descending from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre ('to load upon, entrust').

history.meaning: to load, entrust with a task

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encargado
Wiktionary — encargada

encargar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre ('to load upon, entrust with a commission or duty'), formed from in- + Late Latin carricāre ('to load a wagon', from carrus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encargar
Wiktionary — encargar

encender.etymology: Inherited from Latin incendere ('to set on fire, kindle, light up'), a compound of in- + candēre ('to glow white-hot, shine').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encender
Wiktionary — encender

enchufar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from en- + the expressive root chuf- (from chufar 'to blow, fit a nozzle or tube into another'), denoting the coupling of pipes or plugging in of an electrical cord.

history.meaning: to fit one tube or plug into a socket

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enchufar
Wiktionary — enchufar

enchufe.etymology: Deverbal noun from enchufar ('to fit one pipe or tube snugly inside another; later to plug into an electrical socket'), an expressive Hispanic verb (documented from the 18th–19th centuries) built from en- + chufar ('to blow/squirt through a nozzle, fit a tube', of echoic *chuf- origin).

morphemes.meaning: fit a nozzle/plug into a socket

history.meaning: electrical plug or wall socket; (Peninsular slang) political/industry pull, nepotism

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enchufe
Wiktionary — enchufe

enchufe.notes: Double star of Peninsular Spanish: literally el enchufe covers BOTH the male electrical plug (clavija) AND the female wall outlet (toma de corriente); figuratively in Spain, tener enchufe means 'having insider pull / strings pulled' to land a job or role!

encima.etymology: Univerbation of Old Spanish en cima ('on the summit, on top'), formed from en (< Latin in) + cima ('top, peak, sprout', < Latin cyma < Ancient Greek κῦμα 'swelling, young shoot').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encima
Wiktionary — encima

encimera.etymology: Formed within Spanish from encima ('on top, above') + the suffix -era, specialized for a kitchen worktop or counter surface.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encimera
Wiktionary — encimera

encontrar.etymology: Encontrar derives from Late Latin incontrāre ('to meet face to face', from in + contra, 'against, opposite').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encontrar

encontrar.notes: Stem-changing verb (o -> ue: encuentro, encuentra, encontramos).

encuentro.etymology: Deverbal noun from encontrar ('to meet, come across, find'), which descends from Late Latin incontrāre ('to meet face to face'), built on in + contrā ('against, opposite').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encuentro
Wiktionary — encuentro

enderezar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indīrēctiāre ('to make straight, set upright'), derived from in- + dīrēctus ('straight, direct').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enderezar
Wiktionary — enderezar

energía.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin energīa from Ancient Greek enérgeia (ἐνέργεια, coined by Aristotle for 'activity, actuality, force in action'), derived from energós (ἐνεργός, 'active, at work'), from en- ('in') + érgon ('work, deed', PIE *werǵ-, cognate with English work).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: energía
Wiktionary — energía

energía.notes: Helpful adjective pair: a person full of pep is enérgico, while power grids or energy drinks are energético. In tarot readings and New Age chat (as with Paquita's tarot reader!), plural las energías means 'vibes / aura'.

enfadado.etymology: Participial adjective of enfadar ('angry, annoyed, upset'), shared across Ibero-Romance and Occitan enfadar ('to weary, annoy'), from Vulgar Latin *infātāre (derived from fatuus 'insipid, foolish' or fātum 'fate').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enfadado
Wiktionary — enfadado

enfermera.etymology: Feminine occupational noun of enfermero ('nurse'), formed from enfermo ('sick, ill', inherited from Latin īnfirmus, 'weak, infirm', from in- 'not' + firmus 'firm, strong') plus the Latinate agentive suffix -era (< -āria); originally designating the attendant in charge of a monastic infirmary (enfermería).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enfermero
Wiktionary — enfermera

enfermera.notes: Unlike English 'nurse' (from Old French nourrice < Latin nūtrīcia, 'wet nurse'), Spanish enfermera/enfermero is built directly on the root for illness (enfermo).

enfriar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from en- + frío ('cold', < Latin frīgidus) + -ar ('to make or become cold, cool down').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enfriar
Wiktionary — enfriar

enganchar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Spanish from en- + gancho ('hook') + -ar ('to hook, hitch, catch onto').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enganchar
Wiktionary — enganchar

engañadora.etymology: Feminine form of engañador ('deceitful; deceiver'), derived from engañar ('to deceive, trick') + agentive suffix -dora (< Latin -tōrem + -a). Engañar continues Vulgar Latin *ingannāre ('to mock, outwit, cheat'), derived from Late Latin gannāre ('to jeer, make fun of').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: engañador
Wiktionary — engañadora

engañadora.notes: Functions both as an adjective (una sonrisa engañadora) and as a noun accusation (¡Engañadora! 'Cheater / fraud!').

engañar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingannāre ('to mock, trick, deceive'), originally an expressive verb meaning 'to jeer or laugh at'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: engañar
Wiktionary — engañar

engordar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Spanish from prefix en- + gordo ('fat, stout, plump') + verbal ending -ar. The base gordo descends from Late Latin gurdus ('dull, heavy, thick'), a word that the Roman rhetorician Quintilian explicitly noted had entered Latin from Hispania.

morphemes.meaning: into a state of (< Latin in-)

cognates.meaning: to numb, make sluggish (from the same gurdus root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: engordar
Wiktionary — engordar

engordar.notes: Used both intransitively for putting on weight (engordar diez kilos, opposite of adelgazar) and transitively for making someone gain weight (el pan no engorda tanto).

enhorabuena.etymology: Univerbation of the medieval and Golden Age Spanish prepositional phrase en hora buena ('in a good or auspicious hour', originally an astrological wish for favorable timing), descending from Latin in hōrā bonā (with hōra < Ancient Greek ὥρα 'season, hour').

cognates.meaning: away; although (< em boa hora, 'in a good hour')

rootFamily.gloss: in an ill hour, cursedly (historical antonym)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enhorabuena
Wiktionary — enhorabuena

enhorabuena.notes: The everyday Peninsular Spanish word for 'Congratulations!' (¡Enhorabuena! or dar la enhorabuena a alguien), whereas Latin American Spanish more often uses ¡Felicidades! or ¡Felicitaciones!.

ensayar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin exagiāre ('to weigh, test, try out, rehearse'), derived from Late Latin exagium ('weighing, balance, assay', from exigere), with replacement of initial ex- by en-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ensayar
Wiktionary — ensayar

enseguida.etymology: Univerbation of the adverbial phrase en seguida ('in immediate succession, right away'), built on seguida, feminine past participle of seguir (< Vulgar Latin *sequīre < Classical sequī 'to follow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enseguida
Wiktionary — enseguida

enseñar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin insignāre ('to mark out, point out by signs, show, teach'), derived from Classical Latin signum ('mark, sign').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enseñar
Wiktionary — enseñar

entender.etymology: Inherited from Latin intendere ('to stretch out toward, direct one's attention or mind to', from in- 'into, toward' + tendere 'to stretch'), which shifted semantically in Vulgar Latin and Ibero-Romance from 'directing mental focus' to 'grasping, understanding'.

history.meaning: to stretch toward, turn one's mind to

cognates.meaning: to plan, mean (via Old French entendre)

enterar.etymology: Inherited from Latin integrāre ('to make whole, restore, complete', derived from integer 'untouched, whole', which also yielded Spanish entero). From 'completing an account or payment in full', Spanish developed the sense 'to inform fully', and pronominally enterarse (de) 'to find out, realize, get what is going on'.

history.meaning: to complete, pay in full; to inform
to inform / to find out, catch on

cognates.meaning: to make whole (learned borrowing from integrātus)

entero.etymology: Inherited through popular phonetic evolution from Latin integer, integrum ('untouched, whole, complete, intact'), forming a doublet with learned íntegro.

sources.title: Wiktionary — envelope

envelup.notes: Illustrates a classic Spanish classroom coaching trick—writing foreign English words out phonetically according to Spanish spelling rules ('envelup') to memorize lines without knowing English.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enviado

enviar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin inviāre ('to send on a journey, dispatch'), a parasynthetic verb formed from in- + via ('way, road').

history.meaning: to send on the way, dispatch

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: enviar

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: envuelto

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: equivocar

error.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin error, errōris ('a wandering, straying, mistake, false belief'), derived from the verb errāre ('to wander, go astray').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: error

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escalera

escalera.notes: Either singular la escalera or plural las escaleras can refer to a staircase in Spanish.

escalón.etymology: Derived within Spanish from escala ('ladder, stair', < Latin scāla) + the suffix -ón, denoting a single stair step or rung.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escalón

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escapar

escapar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excappāre ('to slip out of one's cloak and leave it in a captor's hands in order to flee'), a vivid compound of Latin ex- ('out of') + Late Latin cappa ('hooded cape, cloak').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escapar

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escaparate

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escenario

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esconder

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escribir

escribir.notes: Regular across present and preterite tenses, with irregular Latin-derived past participle escrito.

escrito.etymology: Strong past participle and noun from escribir ('written; written document'), inherited from Latin scrīptus, past participle of scrībere ('to write'), with prosthetic e-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escrito
Wiktionary — escrito

escritorio.etymology: Escritorio comes as a learned derivative of Late Latin scriptōrium ('writing room, writing desk'), from scribĕre ('to write').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escritorio

escritorio.notes: Names a study or writing desk with drawers (distinct from mesa, a general table).

escuchar.etymology: Escuchar descends from Vulgar Latin *ascultāre (Classical Latin auscultāre, 'to listen attentively').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escuchar

escuchar.notes: Like buscar and mirar, escuchar includes 'to' inside the verb: escucha la lluvia (no preposition before things).

escuela.etymology: Inherited from Latin schola ('leisure devoted to learning, lecture, school'), borrowed from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, 'leisure, learned discussion, school'), with prosthetic e- and diphthongization of short o to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escuela
Wiktionary — escuela

ese.etymology: Medial demonstrative determiner ('that, near you'), inherited from Latin ipse ('self, that very one'), with assimilation of -ps- to -s-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ese
Wiktionary — ese

esfuerzo.etymology: Deverbal noun from esforzar ('to exert oneself, strengthen'), descending from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, built on ex- + fortis ('strong').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esfuerzo
Wiktionary — esfuerzo

esgrima.etymology: Postverbal noun from esgrimir ('to fence, brandish a weapon'), borrowed via Old Occitan esgrimir (compare Old French eskermir) from Frankish *skirmjan ('to shield, defend, fight', cognate with German schirmen 'to protect').

history.meaning: to protect with a shield, parry

cognates.meaning: brief clash (via Old French eskirmir from the same Germanic root)

rootFamily.gloss: to wield; to put forward (an argument)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esgrima
Wiktionary — esgrima

esgrima.notes: Traditional conservatory skill taught in Spanish drama schools (escuelas de arte dramático) for period stage combat.

esmerilado.etymology: Participial adjective of esmerilar ('ground or frosted with emery, as of matte glass'), derived from esmeril ('emery powder'), borrowed via Italian smeriglio / French émeri from Ancient Greek σμύρις (smýris, 'emery').

history.meaning: emery / to grind or frost with emery

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esmerilado
Wiktionary — esmerilado

eso.etymology: Neuter medial demonstrative pronoun ('that, that thing'), inherited from Latin ipsum, neuter singular of ipse ('that very thing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: eso
Wiktionary — eso

esos.etymology: Masculine plural of the medial demonstrative ese ('those [near you / just mentioned]'), inherited from Latin ipsōs, masculine accusative plural of Classical Latin ipse ('he himself, that very one'), which in Vulgar Latin reorganized into the second-person (listener-oriented) demonstrative between hic/iste (este) and ille (aquel).

morphemes.meaning: that, near the listener (< Latin ips-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ese
Wiktionary — esos

esos.notes: Since the 2010 RAE orthography reform, demonstrative pronouns like esos are written without a written accent mark (uno de esos, 'one of those').

espacio.etymology: Espacio comes from Latin spatium ('room, expanse, interval of space or time'), adding prosthetic initial e- before sp-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: espacio

españa.etymology: Inherited continuously from Latin Hispānia ('Iberian Peninsula, Roman Hispania'), with loss of Latin initial H-, regular prothetic e- (as in Vulgar Latin Ispania), and palatalization of -ni- before a vowel to -ñ-. Latin borrowed Hispānia (alongside Greek Ἱσπανία) from a pre-Roman—most widely analyzed as Phoenician-Punic—name for the peninsula (traditionally linked to Punic *ʾī-šəpānīm, 'coast/island of hyraxes', applied by Phoenician sailors to Iberian wild rabbits, or to a Semitic metallurgical root).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: España
Wiktionary — España

españa.notes: Note how España shows popular phonetic evolution (-ni- > -ñ-), whereas hispano and hispánico are later learned borrowings from the same Latin Hispānia.

español.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Castilian from Old Occitan espanhol ('Spaniard, Spanish'), continuing Late/Medieval Latin *Hispāniolus (derived from Hispānia 'Iberia, Spain'). As Ramón Menéndez Pidal demonstrated and the DLE records, the Occitan origin explains the non-diphthongized ending -ol: a purely native Castilian evolution of *Hispāniolus would have produced *españuelo, whereas Provençal merchants and pilgrims along the Camino de Santiago generalized espanhol.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: español
Wiktionary — español

español.notes: Unlike English, nationalities and language names are not capitalized in Spanish (el cine español, hablo español), and the feminine singular takes -a (la lengua española).

especial.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin speciālis ('individual, particular, special'), derived from speciēs ('appearance, kind, sort'), with prosthetic e- before initial sp-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: especial
Wiktionary — especial

espectacular.etymology: Relational and evaluative adjective formed from espectáculo ('spectacle, show', learned borrowing from Latin spectāculum 'public show, sight, grandstand', from spectāre 'to watch, gaze at', frequentative of specere 'to look') + suffix -ar (< Latin -āris).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: espectacular
Wiktionary — espectacular

espectacular.notes: Invariable for gender (un vestido espectacular / una actriz espectacular); paired with estar (¡Estás espectacular!) to compliment how someone looks on a specific occasion.

espejo.etymology: Inherited from Latin speculum ('mirror, looking-glass'), an instrument noun from specere ('to look at'), showing regular syncope (*spec'lum) and palatalization of -cl- to Castilian -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: espejo
Wiktionary — espejo

esperar.etymology: Esperar continues Latin sperāre ('to hope'), expanding in Ibero-Romance to cover both 'to hope' and 'to wait for'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esperar

esperar.notes: Single Spanish verb covering English 'hope', 'expect', and 'wait for' (espero el tren = I am waiting for the train).

espiar.etymology: Borrowed from Gothic *spaihon (or via Old Occitan/French espier), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną ('to watch closely, observe, spy').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: espiar
Wiktionary — espiar

esponja.etymology: Esponja descends from Latin spongia, borrowed from Greek spongiá ('sea sponge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esponja

esponja.notes: Developed prosthetic initial e- before Latin sp- (spongia > esponja).

espontáneo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin spontāneus ('occurring of one's own accord, voluntary, unforced'), derived from Classical Latin sponte (ablative singular of defective *spons, as in suā sponte 'of one's own free will').

history.meaning: spontaneous, natural; uninvited spectator who jumps into an arena/stage

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: espontáneo
Wiktionary — espontáneo

espontáneo.notes: Carries a written accent because it is esdrújula (stressed on the antepenultimate syllable: es-pon-TÁ-ne-o). As a noun (un espontáneo), it also names someone who bursts uninvited onto a stage, pitch, or bullring.

espérate.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative of pronominal esperarse ('hold on, wait a second'), fusing espera + enclitic reflexive pronoun te (< Latin tē), written with an accent mark to preserve stress on -pe-. Esperar continues Latin spērāre ('to hope, expect', from spēs 'hope'), which in Ibero-Romance broadened to cover both 'to hope' and 'to wait'.

rootFamily.gloss: to wait; to hope; to expect

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esperar
Wiktionary — espérate

espérate.notes: Adding te to espera (¡No, espérate!) makes the command warmer, more conversational, and more immediate in spoken Spanish ('Hold on a sec!').

esquina.etymology: Borrowed from Germanic (likely Frankish *skina via Old Occitan esquina, or Gothic *skina, 'shinbone, narrow strip, sharp projecting angle'), specialized in Spanish for an external street or wall corner.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esquina
Wiktionary — esquina

estaba.etymology: First- and third-person singular imperfect indicative of estar ('I was / he, she, it was'), inherited directly from Latin stābam / stābat ('was standing'), imperfect indicative of stāre ('to stand, remain in a state', from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-), with prothetic e- before initial st-.

morphemes.meaning: stand, be located/in a state (< Latin stā-)

history.meaning: was standing, was located/in a state
was (location, ongoing state, or cast membership)

cognates.meaning: was (< Old French estoit, reshaped on Latin stābat)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estar
Wiktionary — estaba

estaba.notes: While estar has an irregular present (estoy) and preterite (estuve), its imperfect indicative (estaba, estabas, estábamos...) is completely regular.

estación.etymology: Estación continues Latin statio, statiōnis ('standing place, post, stopping point', from stare) for both a railway station and a season of the year.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estación

estación.notes: Plural las estaciones drops the written accent because stress naturally falls on -o- before -nes.

estante.etymology: Substantivized old active participle of estar ('standing rack, shelf'), from Latin stāns, stantis, present participle of stāre ('to stand').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estante
Wiktionary — estante

estantería.etymology: Formed in Spanish from estante ('shelf, upright bookcase', originally the fossilised present participle of estar, continuing Latin stāns, stantem 'standing upright') plus the collective and locative suffix -ería ('set, array, or shop of').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estantería
Wiktionary — estantería#Spanish

estantería.notes: Un estante usually refers to a single horizontal shelf board, whereas una estantería is the whole multi-shelf bookcase or wall unit.

estar.etymology: Estar comes from Latin stare, meaning to stand. In modern Spanish it expresses physical location as well as current states, conditions and resulting situations.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estar

estar.notes: Its historical association with standing does not restrict modern estar to posture: Spanish uses estar for where buildings sit (¿Dónde está la estación?) as well as temporary states (está caliente).

este.etymology: Demonstrative este continues Latin iste ('that of yours'), which shifted in Spanish to the first-person proximal demonstrative ('this, near me').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: este

este.notes: Four noun-accompanying forms: este (m sg), esta (f sg), estos (m pl, never *estes!), estas (f pl).

estilo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin stilus ('pointed writing instrument for wax tablets, hence manner of writing or artistic expression'), adapted with prosthetic e-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estilo
Wiktionary — estilo

esto.etymology: Esto continues Latin neuter demonstrative istud ('this thing'), preserved in Spanish purely as a standalone neuter pronoun referring to an unnamed object, situation or whole idea.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esto
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: este

esto.notes: Never place neuter esto directly before a noun: masculine nouns take este (este libro) and feminine nouns take esta (esta maleta).

estrategia.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin stratēgia from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, 'office, command, or art of a general'), derived from στρατηγός (stratēgós, 'general, army commander'), a compound of στρατός (stratós, 'encamped army') + ἄγω (ágō, 'I lead').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estrategia
Wiktionary — estrategia

estrategia.notes: Ends in unstressed diphthong -gia (es-tra-TE-gia, four syllables, no written accent), unlike words in stressed -ía such as energía.

estrecho.etymology: Inherited from Latin strictus ('drawn tight, narrow, close'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight'), with prosthetic e- and regular evolution of -ct- to -ch- (popular doublet of estricto).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estrecho
Wiktionary — estrecho

estrella.etymology: Inherited from Latin stēlla ('star'), with regular prosthetic e- before initial st- and an epenthetic -r- (influenced by astro or estrellar).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estrella
Wiktionary — estrella

estreno.etymology: Deverbal noun from estrenar ('to use, wear, or perform for the first time'), derived from Old Spanish estrena ('New Year's gift, auspicious first use'), from Latin strēna ('lucky omen, New Year's gift').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estreno
Wiktionary — estreno

estricto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin strictus ('drawn tight, exact, rigorous, strict'), past participle of stringere ('to bind tight'), forming a learned doublet with inherited estrecho.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estricto
Wiktionary — estricto

estudiado.etymology: Past participle and participial adjective of estudiar ('studied; deliberate/calculated'), derived from Medieval Latin studiāre ('to study, apply oneself'), denominal verb from Classical Latin studium ('zeal, eagerness, study', from studēre 'to be diligent').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estudiado
Wiktionary — estudiado

estudiado.notes: In Peninsular Spanish, Peninsular speakers regularly use the present perfect (he estudiado la FP) for completed educational qualifications whose relevance continues into the present.

estudiar.etymology: Derived from Medieval Latin studiāre ('to apply oneself to learning, study'), formed on Classical Latin studium ('zeal, devotion, intellectual pursuit', related to studēre 'to be eager, strive'), with regular Spanish prothetic e- before initial st-.

cognates.meaning: to learn, examine (via Old French estudier)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estudiar
Wiktionary — estudiar

estudiar.notes: Estudiar una carrera in Spain specifically means 'to do a university degree' (not 'a career' in general).

estudio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin studium ('zeal, diligence, study, study room'), related to the verb studēre ('to be eager, study'), with prosthetic e-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estudio
Wiktionary — estudio

estupendo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin stupendus ('worthy of wonder, astonishing, marvelous'), gerundive of stupēre ('to be stunned or amazed').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estupendo
Wiktionary — estupendo

estáis.etymology: Second-person plural (vosotros/vosotras) present indicative of estar ('you all are'), descending from Latin stātis ('you stand') through Old Spanish estades, where loss of intervocalic -d- in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries yielded estáes > estáis.

morphemes.meaning: stand, be in a state (< Latin stā-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estar
Wiktionary — estáis

estáis.notes: Standard across Spain for addressing two or more friends or colleagues informally (veo que estáis muy nerviosas), where Latin America uses ustedes están.

estés.etymology: Second-person singular (tú) present subjunctive of estar ('that you be'), inherited directly from Classical Latin stēs, second-person singular present subjunctive of stāre ('to stand'), carrying a written accent on the oxytonic final syllable.

morphemes.meaning: stand, be in a state (< Latin stā-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estar
Wiktionary — estés

estés.notes: Triggered after future-oriented or open-ended temporal clauses such as siempre que lo estés viendo ('whenever you're watching it') and negative tú commands (no estés triste).

etiqueta.etymology: Borrowed from French étiquette ('label, tag; court ceremonial'), from Middle French estiquette ('small paper note stuck to a file'), derived from Frankish *stikkan ('to stick, pierce, affix').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: etiqueta
Wiktionary — etiqueta

euro.etymology: Adopted across European languages in the 1990s for the single European currency, formed by clipping Europa / europeo (< Latin Eurōpa < Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: euro
Wiktionary — euro

europa.etymology: Learned geographical and mythological name borrowed via Latin Eurōpa from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē), in Greek myth the Phoenician princess carried off across the sea to Crete by Zeus in the form of a bull; traditionally explained either within Greek from εὐρύς (eurús, 'wide, broad') + ὤψ (ṓps, 'eye, face, aspect') or from a Semitic directional term akin to Akkadian erēbu ('sunset, the West', contrasting with asū 'sunrise, Asia').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Europa

europa.notes: Takes no article in neutral geography (vivir en Europa), unlike a few historic country names.

europeas.etymology: Feminine plural of europeo ('European'), learned relational adjective borrowed from Latin Eurōpaeus, itself from Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos, 'of Europe').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: europeo
Wiktionary — europeas

europeas.notes: Agrees in gender and number with feminine plural nouns (producciones europeas) and is never capitalized in Spanish.

europeo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin Eurōpaeus ('of Europe, European'), from Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos), ethnic and relational derivative of Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē, 'Europe').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: europeo
Wiktionary — europeo

europeo.notes: Look out for the hiatus -eo (eu-ro-PE-o, four syllables); written in lowercase even when referring to the European Union only as an adjective, though capitalized in official proper names (la Unión Europea).

evento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēventus ('outcome, result, occurrence, event'), fourth-declension action noun from ēvenīre ('to come out, come to pass, happen', from ex- 'out' + venīre 'to come'). While Classical Spanish favored evento for an unforeseen contingency (a todo evento), modern usage expanded under English influence to mean an organized promotional, social, or cultural event.

history.meaning: to come forth, happen > occurrence, outcome
contingency; organized public or promotional event

cognates.meaning: possible, contingent (from the same Latin stem)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: evento
Wiktionary — evento

evento.notes: In showbusiness Madrid (ir a un evento de una marca), un evento often means a paid red-carpet photocall or brand launch where actors pose for press.

ex.etymology: Colloquial common-gender noun extracted by clipping compounds formed with the Latin prefix ex- ('out of; former', as in exmarido, exmujer, exnovio, from Latin ex 'out of, from'), following an international pattern shared with English and French.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ex
Wiktionary — ex

ex.notes: As a standalone noun, ex is invariable in both gender and number (mi ex, mis ex). Under the 2010 RAE spelling rules, prefix ex- attaches directly to single-word bases without a space or hyphen (exmarido, exnovio), but stays separate before multi-word bases (ex primer ministro).

exactamente.etymology: Adverb formed within Spanish from the feminine adjective exacta ('exact, precise', < Latin exactus) + the suffix -mente.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: exactamente
Wiktionary — exactamente

exacto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exactus ('driven out, weighed and measured accurately, precise'), past participle of exigere (ex- + agere 'to drive out, measure, demand').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: exacto
Wiktionary — exacto

excitante.etymology: Learned participial adjective from Latin excitantem (nominative excitāns, present participle of excitāre 'to rouse, stir up, stimulate', frequentative of exciēre 'to call forth, awaken', from ex- + ciēre 'to set in motion').

morphemes.meaning: set in motion, rouse (< Latin ciēre / citāre)

rootFamily.gloss: to summon, quote, arrange to meet

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: excitante
Wiktionary — excitante

excitante.notes: Careful with register: applied to people (estoy excitado/a), excitar in Spanish strongly implies sexual arousal or nervous agitation; for everyday English 'excited' about news or plans, Spanish uses estar ilusionado/a or emocionado/a, while excitante works well for thrilling books, adventures, or stimulants.

exfoliación.etymology: Learned technical and cosmetic noun borrowed from Late Latin exfoliātiōnem (nominative exfoliātiō, 'stripping of leaves or scales'), action noun from exfoliāre ('to strip of leaves, peel off in thin layers', formed from ex- 'off, away' + folium 'leaf').

history.meaning: to strip off leaves or thin layers

cognates.meaning: removal of dead surface skin cells; flaking in layers

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: exfoliación
Wiktionary — exfoliación

exfoliación.notes: Notice the classic Spanish doublet pair in its root: learned foli- (exfoliación, folio) versus inherited popular hoja ('leaf, sheet', with Latin f- > h- and -li- > -j-).

existir.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exsistere / existere ('to step forth, emerge, appear, exist'), compound of ex- ('out, forth') + sistere ('to cause to stand, take a stand', reduplicated present stem of stāre 'to stand').

history.meaning: to step forth, come into being, exist

rootFamily.gloss: to insist (built on the same Latin sistere root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: existir
Wiktionary — existir

existir.notes: Conjugates as a completely regular -ir verb (existe, existió).

experiencia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin experientia ('trial, proof, practical knowledge gained by testing'), abstract noun from experiēns, present participle of the deponent verb experīrī ('to try, put to the test', from ex- + *perīrī, cognate with perīculum 'trial, danger' and Greek πεῖρα 'attempt').

history.meaning: to test, try out > trial, practical knowledge

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: experiencia
Wiktionary — experiencia

experiencia.notes: Remember that Spanish has no single verb *experienciar: 'to experience something' is tener una experiencia, vivir algo, or experimentar algo.

experto.etymology: Experto comes from Latin expertus, which the DLE glosses as experienced. Its modern uses connect practical experience with specialised skill or knowledge, and the adjective can also name an expert.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: experto

experto.notes: Experto, experta, expertos and expertas follow the person or group being described.

explicar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin explicāre ('to unfold, unroll a scroll, set forth clearly, explain'), formed from ex- ('out') + plicāre ('to fold').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: explicar
Wiktionary — explicar

explotar.etymology: Convergence of two nineteenth-century Gallicisms recorded by the DLE: (1) from French exploiter ('to work a mine/estate, make profit from, exploit', ultimately from Latin explicitāre 'to unfold, settle'), and (2) for 'to explode, burst', adapted from French exploser / explosion (ultimately from Latin explōdere 'to drive an actor offstage by clapping', ex- + plaudere), remodeled onto the already familiar verb explotar.

history.meaning: to drive off with noise / to unfold, carry out

cognates.meaning: to burst violently / to make use of

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: explotar
Wiktionary — explotar

explotar.notes: In Spanish, one single verb covers both English 'explode/burst' (el vestido me explotaba, 'the dress was bursting at the seams on me') and 'exploit' (explotar el talento).

exprimido.etymology: Participial adjective of exprimir ('squeezed, freshly pressed'), borrowed or semi-learned from Latin exprimere ('to press out, squeeze out', from ex- + premere 'to press').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: exprimido
Wiktionary — exprimido

exprés.etymology: Borrowed from French exprès (and English express, 'rapid service, fast train, pressure-brewed coffee'), ultimately from Latin expressus ('pressed out, specially dispatched').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: exprés
Wiktionary — exprés

extra.etymology: Borrowed from Latin extrā ('outside, beyond, in addition'), used in modern Spanish (reinforced by French and English extra) as an adjective and noun meaning 'additional, of superior quality'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: extra
Wiktionary — extra

extranjero.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Spanish from Old/Middle French estrangier (modern French étranger, 'stranger, foreigner'), derived from estrange ('foreign, strange'), which descends from Latin extrāneus ('external, from outside, foreign', built on extrā 'outside').

morphemes.meaning: belonging to, person from (< Fr. -ier / Lat. -ārius)

rootFamily.gloss: strange, odd; stranger (inherited Castilian doublet < extrāneus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: extranjero
Wiktionary — extranjero

extranjero.notes: With the masculine singular article, el extranjero means 'abroad / foreign countries' (vivir en el extranjero, irse al extranjero). Notice the doublet with native extraño ('strange').

extraño.etymology: Inherited from Latin extrāneus ('external, foreign, strange, unfamiliar'), derived from extrā ('outside'), with regular palatalization of -ne- before a vowel to Castilian -ñ-.
