fuentecita.etymology: Diminutive formed within Spanish from fuente ('fountain, spring, serving platter') + -ecita; fuente descends from Latin fōns, fontis ('spring, fountain').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fuente
Wiktionary — fuentecita

fuera.etymology: Inherited from Latin forās ('out through the doors, outside'), originally an accusative plural of *fora ('door'), with regular Castilian diphthongization of short o to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fuera
Wiktionary — fuera

fuerte.etymology: Inherited from Latin fortis ('strong, powerful, firm, brave'), showing regular diphthongization of stressed short o to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fuerte
Wiktionary — fuerte

fuerza.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin fortia ('strength, force'), originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin fortis ('strong'), reanalyzed in Romance as a feminine singular noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fuerza
Wiktionary — fuerza

fugitiva.etymology: Feminine singular of fugitivo ('fugitive, runaway'), learned borrowing from Latin fugitīvus ('fleeing, runaway [especially of an escaped slave]'), built on fugitus, participial stem of fugere ('to flee', which yielded inherited Spanish huir).

rootFamily.gloss: escape, flight; gas/water leak; musical fugue
to break out, run away, elope
to flee (inherited popular verb < Latin fugere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fugitivo
Wiktionary — fugitiva

fugitiva.notes: Notice how Latin fugere gave popular Spanish huir (f- > h-, loss of -g-) alongside the learned family fuga, fugitivo, and refugio.

funciona.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative of funcionar ('works, operates, functions'), derived via French fonctionner or directly within Spanish from función ('function, performance'), learned borrowing from Latin fūnctiōnem (nominative fūnctiō, 'performance, execution of a duty', from fungī 'to perform, discharge').

history.meaning: to perform a duty > performance, function

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: funcionar
Wiktionary — funciona

funciona.notes: Crucial learner distinction: trabajar means 'to work' for people doing a job, whereas funcionar means 'to work' for machines, systems, plans, or relationships (¿sabes cómo funciona esto?, no funciona el wifi).

funcionar.etymology: Formed from función ('function, performance, operation', < Latin functiō, -ōnis, from fungī 'to perform') + -ar, reinforced by French fonctionner.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: funcionar
Wiktionary — funcionar

fundir.etymology: Inherited from Latin fundere ('to pour out, melt, cast molten metal'), transferred from the Latin third conjugation (-ere) to the Romance -ir class.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fundir
Wiktionary — fundir

furgoneta.etymology: Diminutive formed from furgón ('covered baggage wagon, van', borrowed from French fourgon) + -eta, modeled on French fourgonnette ('light delivery van').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: furgoneta
Wiktionary — furgoneta

fusible.etymology: Borrowed via French fusible from Medieval/New Latin fūsibilis ('capable of being melted'), built on fūsus, past participle of Latin fundere ('to melt'), and specialized as a noun for an electrical safety fuse.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fusible
Wiktionary — fusible

futuro.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin futūrus ('about to be, yet to come; future'), suppletive future active participle of esse ('to be'), built on the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- ('to become, grow, be', cognate with Latin fuī and English be).

history.meaning: about to be; things to come

cognates.meaning: time yet to come (via Old French futur)

rootFamily.gloss: was (< Latin fuit, from the same *bʰuH- root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: futuro
Wiktionary — futuro

futuro.notes: Used alongside el porvenir ('what is to come') for someone's prospects ahead (tienes aquí un futuro muy bonito).

fácil.etymology: The DLE derives fácil from Latin facĭlis ('easy to do'), built on the verb facĕre ('to make, do').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fácil

fácil.notes: Keeps the same form in masculine and feminine singular, and takes a written accent in both singular (fácil) and plural (fáciles).

fútbol.etymology: Hispanized orthographic adaptation of English football, compound of foot + ball, introduced into Spain in the late nineteenth century by British mining engineers and merchants (notably at Riotinto in Huelva, where Spain's oldest club, Recreativo, was founded in 1889).

rootFamily.gloss: purist Spanish calque (balón + pie, preserved in Real Betis Balompié)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: fútbol
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: fútbol

fútbol.notes: Stressed on the first syllable in Spain (el FÚT-bol, written with an accent because it ends in -l), whereas parts of Latin America (especially Mexico) stress the final syllable and write futbol without an accent.

gabler.etymology: Germanic/Norwegian surname borne by the title heroine of Henrik Ibsen's 1890 play Hedda Gabler; derived from High German Gabler, an occupational or topographic surname built on Gabel ('fork, pitchfork, mountain fork', < Old High German gabala) + agentive/locative suffix -er.

morphemes.meaning: maker of forks or dweller at a road/river fork

history.meaning: fork > fork-maker / dweller by a fork
title protagonist of Henrik Ibsen's drama

sources.title: Wiktionary — Gabler

gabler.notes: Ibsen deliberately titled the play Hedda Gabler (using her maiden surname rather than her married name Hedda Tesman) to underscore that she remains her father General Gabler's daughter—a classic theatre reference that Paquita Salas comically mistakes for the name of a young contemporary female adaptor.

gafas.etymology: Lexicalized plural of gafa ('metal hook or clasp'), borrowed from Catalan gafa ('hook'), originally denoting the curved metal hooks over the ears that held spectacles in place.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gafas
Wiktionary — gafas

gala.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Iberia from Old French gale ('revelry, festivity, splendid attire', compare galer 'to make merry, rejoice', probably of Frankish origin akin to *wala 'well'); Spanish and Italian subsequently re-exported gala ('court dress, ceremonial evening celebration') across Europe, including into English and modern French.

history.meaning: formal dress (traje de gala); ceremonial awards show or benefit evening

cognates.meaning: festive ceremonial performance or celebration (borrowed via French/Italian from Spanish gala)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gala
Wiktionary — gala

gala.notes: In Spanish media and entertainment, una gala names both red-carpet awards ceremonies (la gala de los Goya, la gala de los Óscar) and the weekly live prime-time broadcasts of talent shows. Hacer gala de algo means 'to display or boast of a quality'.

galería.etymology: Borrowed from Italian galleria or French galerie ('long covered portico, arcade, art gallery'), from Medieval Latin galeria.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: galería
Wiktionary — galería

galleta.etymology: Borrowed from French galette ('flat round cake, ship's biscuit'), diminutive of Old French galet ('smooth flat pebble', from Gaulish *gallos 'stone'), named for its flat, round shape.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: galleta
Wiktionary — galleta

gana.etymology: Noun of uncertain pre-Roman or Germanic origin; the DLE notes it is likely back-formed from or shared with ganar ('to gain, desire', from Gothic *ganan 'to covet, yearn for, gape after', cognate with Old Norse gana 'to gape, crane after').

rootFamily.gloss: listlessness, lack of appetite or enthusiasm

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gana
Wiktionary — gana

gana.notes: Usually plural in tener ganas de + infinitive ('to feel like doing / be eager to do'), but singular in classic idioms like de buena/mala gana ('willingly/reluctantly') and porque me da la (real) gana ('because I feel like it!').

ganadora.etymology: Feminine of ganador ('winner; winning'), agent noun and adjective formed from ganar ('to earn, acquire, win') + suffix -dora (< Latin -tōrem + -a). The verb ganar descends from early medieval Iberian Romance gaanyar, of Germanic (Visigothic *ganan 'to covet' or Frankish *waidanjan 'to forage, cultivate, earn', whence French gagner) origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ganador
Wiktionary — ganadora

ganadora.notes: Notice the awards-ceremony formula Y la ganadora al Goya a la Mejor Actriz... es..., using al (a + el) before the prize title.

ganar.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish gaañar ('to acquire, earn, win'), borrowed from Gothic *ganan ('to covet, strive for') or West Germanic *waithanjan ('to forage, pasture, earn').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ganar
Wiktionary — ganar

gancho.etymology: Traditional Ibero-Romance word for a hook or shepherd's crook, likely descending from a pre-Roman Celtic base *ganskio- ('branch, forked stick') or influenced by Greek γάμψος ('curved, hooked').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gancho
Wiktionary — gancho

garcía.etymology: Spain's most frequent surname—originally a medieval Iberian royal and noble given name (attested in Latin charters from the eighth and ninth centuries in Navarre, Castile, and León as Garsea, Garçía)—of pre-Roman Vasco-Aquitanian (Basque) origin; philologists led by Koldo Mitxelena derive it from Old Basque *(h)artz ('bear', modern Basque hartz) or gaztea ('the young one').

history.meaning: given name of kings of Pamplona/Navarre, León, and Galicia
pan-Hispanic family surname (and occasional given name)

sources.title: Wiktionary — García

garcía.notes: Because García was originally a given name that functioned directly in apposition without adding patronymic -ez, it became the single most common surname in Spain (borne in Paquita Salas by real-life Goya-winning actress Macarena García, sister of series co-creator Javier Ambrossi).

gas.etymology: Coined in the early 17th century by Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont (gas), who modeled it phonetically on the Dutch pronunciation of Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, 'chaos, primordial vapor').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gas
Wiktionary — gas

gasolinera.etymology: Derived within twentieth-century Spanish from gasolina ('petrol, gasoline') + locative/commercial suffix -era (< Latin -āria, 'establishment selling or housing'). Gasolina was borrowed from English gasoline, coined in the 1860s from gas + chemical/Latinate suffixes -ol (< oleum 'oil') + -ine.

cognates.meaning: petrol station (regional; standard posto de gasolina)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gasolinera
Wiktionary — gasolinera

gasolinera.notes: Standard in Spain and Mexico (la gasolinera or estación de servicio); compare Rioplatense estación de servicio / naftera and Chilean bencinera.

gay.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English gay ('homosexual'), which shifted in mid-twentieth-century English from 'joyful, carefree, lively' (< Old French gai, parallel to Old Occitan gai, whence literary Spanish gayo as in la gaya ciencia 'the art of poetry').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gay
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: gay

gay.notes: Pronounced /ɡei/ in Spain; following Spanish orthography for words ending in diphthong -ay (like jersey -> jerséis), the RAE recommends the plural gais when written in roman type, though gays remains widespread.

gemelo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin gemellus ('twin-born, paired, double'), diminutive of geminus ('twin'), alongside the inherited popular doublet mellizo.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gemelo
Wiktionary — gemelo

generación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin generātiōnem (nominative generātiō, 'begetting, procreation; people born in the same era'), action noun from generāre ('to beget, produce', derived from genus, generis 'birth, lineage, kind', from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- 'to give birth, beget').

history.meaning: generation (age cohort; technological stage; power generation)

rootFamily.gloss: to engender, beget (inherited popular verb < ingenerāre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: generación
Wiktionary — generación

generación.notes: De última generación ('next-generation / state-of-the-art') is the idiomatic Spanish phrase for cutting-edge electronics or technology.

general.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin generālis ('belonging to a kind or whole class, universal, general'), derived from genus, generis ('birth, kind, class').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: general
Wiktionary — general

generar.etymology: Generar comes from Latin generāre, to beget or produce. Modern Spanish uses it for bringing something into existence, producing energy, or causing an effect.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: generar

generar.notes: Generar conjugates regularly across all tenses on the stem gener-.

generoso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin generōsus ('of noble birth, high-minded, magnanimous, generous'), derived from genus, generis ('birth, lineage').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: generoso
Wiktionary — generoso

genial.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin geniālis ('pertaining to one's tutelary genius, festive, pleasant'; later via French and German, 'marked by genius, brilliant, great'), from genius.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: genial
Wiktionary — genial

gente.etymology: Gente descends from Latin gens, gentis. In modern Spanish it is commonly a collective word for people, so it can denote several individuals while remaining grammatically singular.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gente

gente.notes: La gente trabaja uses a singular verb. The DLE also records plural gentes; that does not make an English plural verb appropriate in every ordinary Spanish use of gente.

getafe.etymology: Toponym of an industrial and university municipality immediately south of Madrid (historically sited at the geographical center of the Iberian Peninsula, el Cerro de los Ángeles); derived in Hispanic toponymy from Andalusi Arabic ǧaṭáf / al-jāṭāf (explained by Arabists such as Jaime Oliver Asín as 'the long street' or roadside settlement stretched along the medieval royal highway linking Madrid and Toledo).

history.meaning: city in the Community of Madrid

sources.title: Wiktionary — Getafe

getafe.notes: Pronounced /xeˈtafe/ (old spelling Xetafe shifted its medieval palatal fricative /ʃ/ to modern velar jota /x/, spelled g before e). In Madrid pop culture, Getafe represents a proud working-class commuter city just south of the capital.

gin-tonic.etymology: Borrowed from English gin and tonic (via French-style elliptical compounding omitting and), combining gin (clipping of geneva < Dutch jenever 'juniper', from Latin iūniperus) + tonic (short for tonic water, quinine-flavored carbonated water, ultimately from Ancient Greek τονικός tonikós 'stretching, invigorating').

history.meaning: highball cocktail of gin and quinine tonic water

rootFamily.gloss: gin (standard Spanish noun for the spirit alone)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yintónic
Wiktionary — gin-tonic

gin-tonic.notes: One of Spain's iconic bar and after-work drinks—Paquita Salas famously pairs un gin-tonic de Larios with un plato de torreznos (crispy fried pork belly). While the RAE registered the phonetic adaptation yintónic, menus and subtitles almost universally write gin-tonic.

ginebra.etymology: Borrowed via French genièvre ('juniper berry; juniper-flavored spirit, gin', alongside Dutch jenever), descending from Vulgar Latin *ieniperus for Classical Latin iūniperus ('juniper tree'), assimilated in Spanish spelling and pronunciation to Ginebra, the traditional Spanish exonym for the Swiss city of Geneva (< Latin Genava).

history.meaning: gin (blended in form with the city name Ginebra 'Geneva')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ginebra
Wiktionary — ginebra

ginebra.notes: Just as English folk-etymologized Dutch jenever into 'geneva' before clipping it to 'gin', Spanish shaped French genièvre into la ginebra (matching Ginebra 'Geneva'), while the juniper plant itself is el enebro in native Castilian!

girar.etymology: Girar continues Late Latin gyrāre ('to turn in a circle, wheel around'), borrowed from Ancient Greek gỹros ('ring, circle').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: girar

girar.notes: Standard verb in Spain for street directions: gira a la izquierda / gira a la derecha.

giro.etymology: Postverbal noun from girar ('to turn, spin, revolve') or directly from Latin gȳrus ('circle, ring, circular course, turn'), borrowed from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, 'ring, circle, bend').

history.meaning: turn, spin, twirl; plot twist; money order (giro postal); idiom

cognates.meaning: to spin in a circle (from Latin gȳrātus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: giro
Wiktionary — giro

giro.notes: Versatile noun: un giro can be a physical twirl in a casting/fitting, a turn in traffic, a plot twist (un giro de guion), an idiomatic expression (un giro lingüístico), or a bank/postal transfer.

give.etymology: Unadapted English verb ('to hand over, present') quoted inside an English-language self-tape audition line in Paquita Salas; in English, inherited from Middle English given (with hard /ɡ/ influenced by Old Norse gefa alongside native Old English giefan), from Proto-Germanic *gebaną.

history.meaning: give (rehearsed in an English audition script)

rootFamily.gloss: to give (native Spanish equivalent < Latin dare)

sources.title: Wiktionary — give

give.notes: In the episode's comic audition scene, the Spanish actress drops the English infinitive marker to (saying 'very important give this' on the model of Spanish es muy importante dar/entregar esto, where Spanish uses a bare infinitive).

glas.etymology: Borrowed from French (sucre) glace ('icing sugar, powdered sugar that forms a glossy ice-like glaze'), from French glace ('ice', < Vulgar Latin *glacia < Classical Latin glaciēs 'ice').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: glas
Wiktionary — glas

glaseado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from glasear ('glazed, coated with icing; sugar glaze'), borrowed from French glacer ('to glaze, ice'), from glace ('ice', < Latin glaciēs).

history.meaning: ice / to coat with a glossy glaze

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: glaseado
Wiktionary — glaseado

golpe.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish colpe from Vulgar Latin *colpus, syncopated from Late Latin colaphus ('blow with the fist, buffet'), borrowed from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos, 'cuff, blow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: golpe
Wiktionary — golpe

golpear.etymology: Formed within Spanish from golpe ('blow, knock', < Late Latin colaphus) + the iterative verbal suffix -ear ('to strike repeatedly, knock, beat').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: golpear
Wiktionary — golpear

gonzález.etymology: One of the most common Spanish patronymic surnames, formed with the Iberian patronymic suffix -ez ('son of') on the medieval Visigothic given name Gonzalo (recorded in Medieval Hispanic Latin charters as Gundisalvus, uniting Germanic *gunþiz 'battle, combat' + an uncertain second element reshaped on Latin salvus 'safe, unharmed' or Gothic *alhs 'sanctuary').

sources.title: Wiktionary — González

gonzález.notes: Takes a written acute accent on -á- because it is paroxytonic (stressed on the next-to-last syllable, gon-ZÁ-lez) and ends in -z (the same rule governing López, Pérez, Sánchez, Fernández). Referenced in the show via Basque-Spanish TV actor Jon González.

gorda.etymology: Feminine singular of gordo ('fat, thick, big'), inherited from Late Hispano-Latin gurdus ('heavy, dull, thickset'), cited by first-century Roman rhetorician Quintilian (Institutio Oratoria 1.5.57) as a vernacular word of Hispanic provenance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gordo
Wiktionary — gorda

gorda.notes: Besides physical build (¿me hace gorda?, 'does it make me look fat?'), gordo/gorda in Spain also means 'major, serious' (una mentira muy gorda, armarse la gorda) and is even used affectionately between couples or close friends (¡Hola, gorda!).

gota.etymology: Inherited from Latin gutta ('drop of liquid'), showing regular Romance lowering of short u to o and simplification of geminate -tt-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gota
Wiktionary — gota

gotear.etymology: Formed within Spanish from gota ('drop', < Latin gutta) + the frequentative suffix -ear ('to drip, fall drop by drop').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gotear
Wiktionary — gotear

gotera.etymology: Derived from gota ('drop', < Latin gutta) + -era (or Vulgar Latin *guttāria), denoting a roof leak through which water drips.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gotera
Wiktionary — gotera

goya.etymology: Eponymous name of the Premios Goya (Spain's annual national film awards, established in 1987 by the Academia de las Artes y las Ciencias Cinematográficas de España, whose bronze bust trophy depicts painter Francisco de Goya y Lucientes, 1746–1828). The family surname Goya is of Basque origin (standard Basque Goia), formed from goi ('high place, height, upper land') + definite article -a ('the high place / upper farmstead').

history.meaning: Spain's national cinema award (plural los Goya)

rootFamily.gloss: in the style or era of Francisco de Goya

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: goyesco
Wiktionary — Goya

goya.notes: When naming the ceremony collectively, Spanish leaves the surname invariable in the plural: la gala de los Goya ('the Goyas'), whereas individual statuettes can inflect or stay invariable (ganar un Goya / dos Goyas).

grabado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from grabar ('engraved, recorded; print, engraving'), where grabar was borrowed from French graver ('to incise, carve'), from Frankish *graban ('to dig, engrave').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grabado
Wiktionary — grabado

grabando.etymology: Gerund of grabar ('recording, filming, shooting'), formed with -ndo (< Latin -ndō). Grabar was borrowed in the sixteenth century from French graver ('to incise, carve, engrave', from Frankish *graban 'to dig, carve'), extending in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries from cutting grooves onto wax/vinyl cylinders to audio and audiovisual recording.

cognates.meaning: carving into a surface / excavated burial (< PGmc *grabaną)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grabar
Wiktionary — grabando

grabando.notes: In Spanish industry usage, grabar una serie is usual for television and digital video, whereas rodar una película ('to roll/shoot a film') is traditionally preferred for cinema.

grabar.etymology: Borrowed in Golden Age Spanish from French graver ('to carve, incise, engrave'), itself from Frankish *graban ('to dig, hollow out, scratch', cognate with German graben and English grave/engrave); extended via early phonograph grooves to modern audio and video recording.

history.meaning: to engrave; to record audio or video

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grabar
Wiktionary — grabar

grabar.notes: Do not confuse in spelling with its homophone gravar with v (< Latin gravāre, 'to burden, levy a tax on').

grabase.etymology: First- or third-person singular -se imperfect subjunctive of grabar ('if I/he/she recorded'), combining the borrowed stem grab- (< French graver < Frankish *graban) with the Spanish -ase subjunctive ending inherited from the Latin syncopated pluperfect subjunctive (-āssem / -āsset).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grabar
Wiktionary — grabase

grabase.notes: Peninsular Spanish uses the -se imperfect subjunctive (grabase, fuera/fuese) much more frequently in spontaneous speech than Latin American Spanish, though -ra (grabara) remains the overall majority form.

gracia.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Latin grātia ('favor, esteem, charm, goodwill; in the plural grātiae, thanks'), derived from grātus ('pleasing, welcome, thankful', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- 'to praise, welcome').

cognates.meaning: elegance, favor, divine grace (via Old French grace)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gracia
Wiktionary — gracia

gracia.notes: In the singular, tener gracia or hacer gracia means 'to be funny/amusing' (no me hace ninguna gracia = 'I don't find it funny at all'); in the plural, (muchas) gracias is 'thank you (very much)'.

gracias.etymology: Gracias is the plural of gracia, from Latin gratia ('favour, goodwill, thankfulness'; plural gratias agĕre, 'to give thanks').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gracia

gracias.notes: Always plural when thanking someone (gracias, muchas gracias); dar las gracias means 'to thank'.

gracioso.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned from Latin grātiōsus ('enjoying favor, agreeable, obliging'), formed from grātia ('grace, charm, wit') + adjectival suffix -ōsus; in Golden Age Spanish drama el gracioso became the witty comic confidant, establishing the modern everyday sense 'funny, amusing'.

history.meaning: witty, charming; stock comic character in theatre

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gracioso
Wiktionary — gracioso

gracioso.notes: Classic false friend with English 'gracious': in modern Spanish gracioso means 'funny, amusing' (or 'cute'), whereas English 'gracious/courteous' is amable, cortés, or gentil.

grande.etymology: Grande continues Latin grandis ('large, full-grown, grand'), which largely replaced magnus across spoken Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grande

grande.notes: Shortens to gran before any singular noun—masculine or feminine (un gran día, una gran idea)—often shifting sense toward 'great'.

granito.etymology: Diminutive formed within Spanish from grano ('grain, seed; pimple, skin blemish', inherited from Latin grānum 'grain, kernel') + diminutive suffix -ito. (A separate homonym, granito 'granite rock', was borrowed from Italian granito 'grained stone', from the same Latin grānum root.)

history.meaning: grain / pimple > tiny spot, blemish, or grain

cognates.meaning: borrowed (< OFr grain) and native Germanic cognates (< PIE *ǵr̥h₂nóm)

rootFamily.gloss: grain; pimple; point (ir al grano 'to get to the point')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grano
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: granito

granito.notes: In everyday skin talk, un granito softens un grano ('pimple, spot'); it also appears in aportar su granito de arena ('to do one's little bit / chip in').

gratis.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin grātīs ('without reward, for nothing, free of charge'), contracted from grātiīs, ablative plural of grātia ('favor, thanks').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gratis
Wiktionary — gratis

grave.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin gravis ('heavy, weighty, low-pitched, serious, solemn').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grave
Wiktionary — grave

grieta.etymology: Evolved by initial voicing and metathesis from Old Spanish crieta ('crack, fissure'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *crepta, feminine past participle of Classical Latin crepāre ('to crack, burst').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grieta
Wiktionary — grieta

grifo.etymology: From Late Latin gryphus ('griffin'), from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grýps, 'hook-beaked griffin'); applied to water taps and faucets because medieval and Renaissance spouts were commonly cast in the shape of a griffin's head.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grifo
Wiktionary — grifo

gris.etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan or Old French gris ('grey'), which entered Gallo-Romance from West Germanic *grīs ('grey').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gris
Wiktionary — gris

gritar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quīrītāre, variant of Classical Latin quirītāre ('to raise a public outcry, shriek, appeal to the Quirītēs or Roman citizens for aid').

history.meaning: to cry out in public, scream

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gritar
Wiktionary — gritar

grito.etymology: Deverbal noun from gritar ('to shout, cry out'), descending from Latin quirītāre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grito
Wiktionary — grito

grueso.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin grossus ('thick, bulky, coarse'), with regular diphthongization of stressed short o to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grueso
Wiktionary — grueso

guantazo.etymology: Derived within Spanish from guante ('glove') + blow-denoting suffix -azo ('hard strike delivered with'). Guante entered Castilian via Catalan guant / Old Occitan gan from Frankish *want ('glove, mitten'). Historically a strike across the face with a glove to issue a duel, guantazo generalized to a hard open-handed slap.

history.meaning: blow with a glove > hard open-handed slap

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guantazo
Wiktionary — guantazo

guantazo.notes: Suffix -azo productively turns objects and body parts into blows in Spanish: guantazo ('slap'), puñetazo ('punch'), codazo ('elbow nudge'), portazo ('door slam').

guapo.etymology: Traced by the DLE (following Corominas) ultimately to Latin vappa ('flat, spoiled wine; figuratively a good-for-nothing rogue or swaggering ruffian', probably transmitted through French dialectal vape / northern Gallo-Romance with w- > gu-). In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Spanish picaresque slang, un guapo meant a bold, flashy tough guy or dandy, which then ameliorated to 'dashing, handsome, good-looking'.

history.meaning: swaggering ruffian, bold brawler, flashy dresser

cognates.meaning: Neapolitan swaggering tough guy (borrowed from Golden Age Spanish guapo!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guapo
Wiktionary — guapo

guapo.notes: In Spain, guapo/guapa is the universal everyday word for 'handsome/pretty' (and a friendly vocative from shopkeepers: ¡Dime, guapa!), and colloquially ¡Qué guapo! also means 'How cool!'. Interestingly, parts of the Caribbean and Southern Cone still preserve the older Golden Age sense 'bold, brave, or quarrelsome'.

guapísimo.etymology: Absolute superlative of guapo ('extremely handsome, gorgeous'), combining the stem guap- (ultimately < Latin vappa via Golden Age Spanish 'dashing gallant') with the learned superlative suffix -ísimo (< Latin -issĭmus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guapo
Wiktionary — guapísimo

guapísimo.notes: Note estar guapísima ('you look gorgeous right now/always in appearance') with estar rather than ser when giving a direct compliment.

guardado.etymology: Participial adjective of guardar ('kept, put away, guarded'), which was borrowed from Germanic (Gothic *wardōn, 'to watch over, guard, keep').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guardado
Wiktionary — guardado

guardar.etymology: Guardar entered Romance from Germanic *wardōn ('to watch over, keep safe, guard'), cognate with English ward and guard.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guardar

guardar.notes: Everyday Spanish uses guardar for putting something away safely in a drawer, pocket or storeroom as well as keeping a secret.

guardas.etymology: Second-person singular (tú) present indicative of guardar ('you keep, hold onto, put away'), borrowed in early Iberia from Germanic (Visigothic *wardōn 'to watch over, guard, protect', from Proto-Germanic *wardōną, cognate with English ward and Old French garder).

history.meaning: you keep / hold onto (also plural noun: guards, endpapers)

cognates.meaning: you look at, watch (shifted semantically in Italian)
borrowed (< OFr garder) and native (< OE weardian) Germanic doublets

rootFamily.gloss: to keep, save (a file), put away

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guardar
Wiktionary — guardas

guardas.notes: Present-tense questions like ¿Me lo guardas? ('Will you hold onto this for me?') are the polite, natural Peninsular way to make everyday requests.

guiar.etymology: Borrowed via Old Occitan or Catalan guiar from Germanic (Gothic *wīdan or Frankish *wītan, 'to direct, point out the way, guide').

history.meaning: to watch over, show the way

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guiar
Wiktionary — guiar

guion.etymology: Derived within Spanish from guía ('guide', deverbal from guiar 'to guide, lead', of Germanic origin < Gothic *wītan 'to watch over, direct') + suffix -ón. Originally denoting the royal or ecclesiastical banner carried ahead to guide a procession or army, guion came to mean a written outline, a typographical hyphen/dash, and in modern theatre, film, and television, a 'script' or 'screenplay'.

history.meaning: processional lead banner; written outline or index
screenplay, script; hyphen or dialogue dash

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guion
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: guion

guion.notes: Key 2010 RAE spelling rule: because Silent u in gui- is part of the digraph gu (/ɡ/) and i + o forms a rising diphthong, guion counts orthographically as a monosyllable and is written WITHOUT an accent mark (guion, never *guión, just like truhan and Sion).

guiones.etymology: Plural of guion ('scripts, screenplays; hyphens'), formed with -es on guion (derived from guía 'guide' + -ón, ultimately from Germanic *wītan 'to direct, show the way').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guion
Wiktionary — guiones

guiones.notes: Neither singular guion (orthographic monosyllable) nor plural guiones (paroxytonic word ending in -s: guio-nes) carries a written accent mark.

gustar.etymology: Gustar continues Latin gustāre ('to taste, take a sip of'), shifting in early modern Spanish from 'someone tastes X' to 'X tastes pleasing to someone'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gustar

gustar.notes: The thing liked is the grammatical subject: me gusta el té (singular) vs me gustan los bollos (plural).

gusto.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin gustus ('a tasting, sipping, flavor, liking'), related to the verb gustāre ('to taste').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gusto
Wiktionary — gusto

guárdamelo.etymology: Orthographic compound uniting the affirmative tú imperative guarda ('keep, put away', from Visigothic/Germanic *wardōn) with two enclitic pronouns: indirect-object me ('for me', < Latin mē) and direct-object lo ('it', < Latin illum), taking a mandatory written accent on the fourth-from-last syllable (sobresdrújula).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guardar

guárdamelo.notes: Whenever two object pronouns attach to an affirmative command, indirect always precedes direct (me lo, te la, se lo), and the resulting sobresdrújula word always requires a written accent mark on the verb stem (guárdamelo, dímelo, pásamelo).

guía.etymology: Deverbal noun from guiar ('person or book that guides; guiding lead'), ultimately of Germanic origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guía
Wiktionary — guía

haber.etymology: Haber descends from Latin habēre, which the DLE glosses as to have. Modern Spanish uses it especially as the helper in compound tenses and in impersonal expressions of existence.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: haber

haber.notes: Ha llamado and hemos ido use haber as an auxiliary, while impersonal hay ('there is / there are') fused medieval ha + locative y ('there', from Latin ibi). Ordinary possession is expressed with tener.

habilidad.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin habilitātem (nominative habilitās, 'aptitude, suitability, nimbleness'), abstract noun from habilis ('easily handled, manageable, adroit, skillful'), derived from habēre ('to hold, have, handle').

history.meaning: to hold > nimble, skillful > aptitude, skill

cognates.meaning: skill, capacity (via Old French ableté < habilitātem)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: habilidad
Wiktionary — habilidad

habilidad.notes: On Spanish acting CVs (videobooks and fichas), the section labeled Habilidades lists special performance skills such as singing, fencing (esgrima), horse riding, accents, or languages.

habitación.etymology: Habitación comes from Latin habitātio, habitātiōnis ('dwelling, living space', from habitāre, 'to dwell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: habitación

habitación.notes: Standard Peninsula Spanish word for a hotel room or bedroom (la habitación cuatro; plural las habitaciones).

hablar.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish fablar from Vulgar Latin fābulāre (Classical deponent fābulārī, 'to converse, chat, talk'), derived from fābula ('conversation, story', from fārī 'to speak').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hablar
Wiktionary — hablar

hablaran.etymology: Third-person plural -ra imperfect subjunctive of hablar ('if they spoke / could speak'), continuing the Latin pluperfect indicative fābulāverant (syncopated fābulārant), which shifted in medieval Castilian into a counterfactual subjunctive. Hablar descends from Late Latin fābulārī / *fābulāre ('to converse, chat, tell stories', from fābula 'story, talk'), showing regular Castilian aspiration and loss of initial f- (fablar > hablar) and consonant evolution -bl-.

history.meaning: if they spoke / could speak (imperfect subjunctive)

cognates.meaning: moral tale (learned loan from the same Latin fābula)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hablar
Wiktionary — hablaran

hablaran.notes: Appears in the classic Spanish wistful idiom ¡Ay, si las paredes / piedras hablaran! ('Oh, if these walls / stones could talk!'), with no written accent (contrast future hablarán, 'they will speak').

hacer.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish fazer from Latin facere ('to make, do, build, perform'), with regular Castilian change of initial f- to silent h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer
Wiktionary — hacer

hacia.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish faza / faz a ('facing toward'), a compound prepositional phrase formed from faz ('face', < Latin faciēs) + a ('to', < Latin ad).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacia
Wiktionary — hacia

hacían.etymology: Third-person plural imperfect indicative of hacer ('they used to make / were making'), inherited from Latin faciēbant (imperfect of facere 'to do, make'), evolving via Old Spanish fazién / fazían with regular loss of -b- in -ēbant > -ían and Castilian initial f- > h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer
Wiktionary — hacían

hacían.notes: In donde se hacían 'Los Borgia', passive se triggers plural verb agreement with a plural title.

hala.etymology: Traditional Peninsular Spanish interjection of expressive origin (also spelled ¡ala! in informal writing), documented since Golden Age Spanish to urge brisk movement, express amazement, or close an interaction ('Come on!', 'Alright then!', 'Whoa!'). While the DLE classifies it primarily as an expressive vocalization, philologists since Corominas note likely reinforcement from Andalusi Arabic invocation wa-llāh ('by God!', compare ¡ojalá!).

history.meaning: come on!, alright then!, wow!, go! (sports cheer)

rootFamily.gloss: hopefully, I wish (< Andalusi Arabic law šá lláh)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hala
Wiktionary — hala

hala.notes: Always spelled with silent h- in standard Spanish (¡Hala, nos vemos! 'Alright then, see you!'; ¡Hala Madrid! in football cheers; ¡Hala, qué dices! 'Whoa, no way!').

hambre.etymology: Hambre descends from Vulgar Latin *famĭne (from Classical Latin famēs, famis, 'hunger'), via Old Spanish fambre with regular f- > silent h- and -mn- > -mbr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hambre

hambre.notes: Feminine noun beginning with stressed /a/: singular takes el (el hambre), yet adjectives remain feminine (mucha hambre, never *mucho hambre!).

harto.etymology: Inherited from Latin fartus ('stuffed, crammed full, sated'), past participle of farcīre ('to stuff, fill full', whence English farce via French), showing regular Castilian evolution of initial f- > h- (Old Spanish farto > harto). From 'sated with food', it developed the figurative meaning 'fed up, sick and tired' (estar harto de) and, in older prose and Andean/Chilean Spanish, 'a lot, very'.

history.meaning: to stuff, cram > stuffed full, sated

cognates.meaning: full, abundant, fed up (estar farto de)
broad comedy, originally 'comic stuffing/interlude' (< French farce < farcīre)

rootFamily.gloss: to satiate; hartarse de 'to get fed up with / do tons of'

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: harto
Wiktionary — harto

harto.notes: Paired with estar + de: Estoy harta de que no me escuchéis ('I'm sick and tired of you all not listening to me'). Notice that a change of subject after estar harto de que triggers the subjunctive.

hará.etymology: Third-person singular synthetic future indicative of hacer ('he/she/it will do or make'), continuing Old Spanish fará, forged in Vulgar Latin from a syncopated stem of facere ('to do, make', *far-) fused with the third-person singular present of habēre (habet > ha), with Castilian f- > h-.

morphemes.meaning: do, make (< Old Spanish far- < Latin facer[e])

history.meaning: will do, will make (or epistemic 'probably ago/is')

rootFamily.gloss: would do/make (conditional built on the same har- stem)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer
Wiktionary — hará

hará.notes: Hacer uses the same shortened stem har- throughout both the future (haré, harás, hará...) and the conditional (haría, harías...).

haría.etymology: First- and third-person singular conditional of hacer ('I / he / she / it would do or make'), continuing Old Spanish faría, formed in Vulgar Latin by fusing syncopated *far- (< facere 'to do, make') with the reduced imperfect of habēre (*habēbat > *ēa > -ía), with Castilian initial f- > h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer
Wiktionary — haría

haría.notes: Very frequent in polite or hopeful Peninsular expressions such as Me haría mucha ilusión (colloquially shortened to me haría ilu, 'that would make me so happy / I'd love that').

hasta.etymology: Hasta comes through Hispanic Arabic ḥattá from Classical Arabic ḥattà. The DLE also records influence from the Latin expression ad ista, meaning up to that. Its main modern use marks an endpoint in space, time or quantity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hasta

hasta.notes: Hasta pronto is a farewell looking ahead to a future meeting.

haya.etymology: First- and third-person singular present subjunctive of haber (both as perfect auxiliary 'that I/he/she have' and as existential impersonal 'that there be'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *haja for Classical Latin habeam / habeat (present subjunctive of habēre 'to have, hold'), with palatalization of intervocalic -bj- to -y-.

history.meaning: that I / he, she, it have
that there be; that one have (+ participle)

cognates.meaning: that one have / that there be
that one have / that there be

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: haber
Wiktionary — haya

haya.notes: Standard subjunctive of existential hay (a no ser que haya alguna cuestión, 'unless there is some issue'); avoid the widespread nonstandard analogical variant *haiga. (A separate homonym, el/la haya, means 'beech tree' < Latin fāgea.)

hecha.etymology: Feminine singular of the irregular strong past participle hecho ('done, made, turned into'), inherited from Latin facta (feminine past participle of facere 'to do, make'), showing two hallmark Castilian sound changes: initial f- > h- and vocalization/palatalization of -ct- > *-jt- > -ch- (contrast Portuguese feita, French faite, Italian fatta).

cognates.meaning: learned (< Latin factum) and Old French (< fait) loans

rootFamily.gloss: calendar date (frozen from Old Spanish 'letter made on...')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hecho
Wiktionary — hecha

hecha.notes: Estar hecho/hecha + noun phrase expresses an intense state in idiomatic Spanish: estar hecha un lío ('all mixed up / in a mess'), estar hecha polvo ('exhausted / devastated'), estar hecha una furia ('furious').

hecho.etymology: Hecho continues Latin factus ('made, done', past participle of facĕre), showing two hallmark Castilian sound changes: initial f- > silent h- and medial -ct- > -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hecho
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer

hecho.notes: Functions as past participle of hacer, adjectival recién hecho ('freshly made/baked'), and noun un hecho ('a fact').

hedda.etymology: Scandinavian feminine given name famous internationally through Henrik Ibsen's 1890 tragedy Hedda Gabler; formed in Norwegian and Swedish as a geminated hypocoristic of Hedvig (< Old High German Haduwīg, composed of Proto-Germanic *haþuz 'battle' + *wīg 'fight, war', doubly signifying 'contender in battle').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Hedda

hedda.notes: One of modern theatre's benchmark dramatic roles; in Paquita Salas, Paquita confuses the title Hedda Gabler with the name of a young living adaptor.

helado.etymology: Helado continues Latin gelātus ('frozen, frosted', from gelāre, 'to freeze'), replacing initial Latin g- before e with silent h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: helado
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: helar

helado.notes: As an adjective it means freezing cold (agua helada); as a masculine noun (un helado) it means ice cream.

hello.etymology: Unadapted English greeting quoted in an English-language self-tape audition ('Hello, my name is...'); recorded in nineteenth-century English as an alteration of hallo / hollo (an older Germanic exclamation used to hail a ferryman or attract attention from afar), popularized worldwide from 1877 onward when Thomas Edison championed it as the standard greeting for answering the telephone.

history.meaning: shout to call attention from a distance
hello (spoken in an English audition introduction)

sources.title: Wiktionary — hello

hello.notes: Part of the classic English 'slate' (presentación / perfil en inglés) that Spanish actors record at the start of international casting tapes.

henrik.etymology: Scandinavian (Norwegian, Danish, Swedish) masculine given name—here referring to Norwegian dramatist Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906)—borrowed via Middle Low German Hinrik from Old High German Heimirīh / Heinrīh, composed of Proto-Germanic *haimaz ('home, house') + *rīks ('ruler, king').

rootFamily.gloss: Spanish form of the same Germanic name

sources.title: Wiktionary — Henrik

henrik.notes: Foreign author names are preserved unadapted in modern Spanish (una obra de Henrik Ibsen), though royal figures historically translate to Enrique.

hermana.etymology: Inherited from Latin (soror) germāna ('full biological sister born of the same parents'), feminine of germānus ('of the same stock or bud, genuine', derived from germen 'sprout, bud, seed'). In Hispania and Portugal, emphatic frāter/soror germāna ('true sibling') completely displaced Classical Latin frāter and soror (which survived in French frère/sœur and Italian fratello/sorella), with initial Latin g- before e palatalizing and eventually dropping while retaining mute orthographic h-.

cognates.meaning: closely related, relevant (from the same Latin germānus!)

rootFamily.gloss: germ, seed (learned loan from the base noun)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hermano
Wiktionary — hermana

hermana.notes: Note that Latin germānus 'full-blooded sibling' (whence hermano/hermana and English germane) is etymologically distinct from the Roman ethnonym Germānī ('Germans', Spanish germano).

hermanito.etymology: Affective diminutive formed within Spanish from hermano ('brother') + -ito; hermano descends from Latin germānus ('full brother or sister, born of the same parents').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hermano
Wiktionary — hermanito

hermano.etymology: Hermano descends from Latin germānus ('full brother, born of the same parents'), replacing Classical Latin frāter in Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hermano

history.meaning: own brother / sister (of the same parents)

hermano.notes: Feminine la hermana means sister; plural los hermanos covers brothers or brothers and sisters together.

herramienta.etymology: Inherited from Latin ferrāmenta ('iron implements, tools'), originally the neuter plural of ferrāmentum ('iron tool', from ferrum 'iron'), reinterpreted in Romance as a feminine singular noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: herramienta
Wiktionary — herramienta

hiba.etymology: Arabic feminine given name (Arabic هِبَة Hiba, 'gift, blessing, divine grant'), borne in Spanish cinema and television by Madrid-born actress Hiba Abouk (of Tunisian and Libyan heritage); derived as a verbal noun from the Classical Arabic root و-ه-ب (wahaba, 'to give freely, bestow').

sources.title: Wiktionary — هبة (hiba)

hiba.notes: In Spanish pronunciation, initial H- in Hiba is ordinarily silent (/ˈiba/), following standard Spanish orthography unless pronounced with a light aspirated /h/ in Arabic fashion.

hiciera.etymology: First- and third-person singular -ra imperfect subjunctive of hacer ('if I / he / she / it did or made'), continuing Old Spanish fiziera, inherited from the Latin strong pluperfect indicative fēceram / fēcerat (perfect stem fēc- of facere 'to do, make'), with vowel raising e > i in the strong preterite stem hic- and regular Castilian f- > h-.

morphemes.meaning: did, made (< Old Spanish fiz- < Latin fēc-)

cognates.meaning: pluperfect indicative / imperfect subjunctive of fazer

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer
Wiktionary — hiciera

hiciera.notes: Standard in hypothetical si-clauses: Si lo hiciera bien... ('If she did it well...').

hiedra.etymology: Hiedra descends directly from Latin hedĕra ('ivy'), showing diphthongization of short stressed ĕ > ie and syncope of the unstressed internal vowel (*hied(e)ra > hiedra).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hiedra

hiedra.notes: The RAE accepts both spellings hiedra and yedra, with hiedra preferred in standard prose.

hielo.etymology: Descends from Latin gelu / gelum ('frost, ice'), with regular Spanish diphthongization of short stressed ĕ > ie and palatal spelling hi-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hielo

hielo.notes: Related to the learned adjective glacial (< glaciēs) and verb helar (< gelāre).

hierba.etymology: Inherited from Latin herba ('grass, green plant, herb'), with regular diphthongization of stressed short e to ie (written hie- at the start of a word).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hierba
Wiktionary — hierba

hierbabuena.etymology: Univerbated Spanish botanical compound uniting hierba ('herb, grass', inherited from Latin herba with regular diphthongization of stressed short ĕ > ie) + buena ('good, wholesome', < Latin bona), literally 'good herb', naming culinary spearmint (Mentha spicata) for its pleasant aroma and digestive properties.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hierbabuena
Wiktionary — hierbabuena

hierbabuena.notes: In Spain, hierbabuena specifically denotes milder culinary spearmint (used in Andalusian puchero broth, fresh spring rolls, and mojitos), distinguished from sharper peppermint (menta piperita). Both hierbabuena and yerbabuena are accepted by the RAE.

hierro.etymology: Hierro continues Latin ferrum ('iron'), displaying two classic Castilian sound changes: initial f- > silent h- and stressed short ĕ > ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hierro

hierro.notes: Learned derivatives like férreo and ferrocarril ('railway') preserve Latin initial f-.

hija.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish fija from Latin fīlia ('daughter'), showing regular Castilian aspiration and loss of initial f- and palatalization of -li- before a vowel to -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hijo
Wiktionary — hija

hijo.etymology: Inherited from Latin fīlius ('son', from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- 'to suckle', originally 'suckling child'), exhibiting two defining Castilian phonological developments: aspiration and loss of initial Latin f- (fīlius > Old Spanish fijo > modern hijo) and palatalization/velarization of Latin -li- before a vowel (*-lj- > Old Spanish /ʒ/ > modern jota /x/).

cognates.meaning: befitting a son or daughter (learned loan < Latin fīliālis)

rootFamily.gloss: petty nobleman (< Old Spanish fijo d'algo, 'son of wealth/worth')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hijo
Wiktionary — hijo

hijo.notes: Colloquial Peninsular speech constantly uses ¡Hijo! / ¡Hija (mía)! as an affectionate or exasperated vocative among adults ('Honestly, my dear!').

hinchado.etymology: Participial adjective of hinchar ('swollen, puffed up, inflated'), which descends from Latin inflāre ('to blow into, puff up', from in- + flāre 'to blow'), with palatalization of medial -fl- to -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hinchado
Wiktionary — hinchado

historia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin historia ('narrative, account, history'), from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, 'inquiry, knowledge obtained by investigation, narrative'), from ἵστωρ (hístōr, 'witness, learned judge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: historia
Wiktionary — historia

histórico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin historicus ('of or belonging to history'), from Ancient Greek ἱστορικός (historikós, 'historical, precise in inquiry').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: histórico
Wiktionary — histórico

hogaza.etymology: Continues Late Latin focācia ('round flatbread baked in hot hearth ashes'), derived from Latin focus ('hearth'), with initial f- > h- and -ci- > -z-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hogaza

hogaza.notes: Exact etymological cognate of Italian focaccia and French fougasse.

hoja.etymology: Descends from Latin folia, originally the neuter plural of folium ('tree leaf, sheet'), reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a feminine singular noun, with initial f- > h- and -li- > -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hoja

hoja.notes: Means both a tree leaf (hoja de tilo), a sheet of paper, and a hinged casement.

hola.etymology: The DLE classifies hola as an expressive formation (attested in early modern Spanish as ola to hail someone or express surprise) and compares English hello and German hallo. It does not identify either foreign greeting as the single ancestor, so no definite borrowing chain or older root is asserted here.

history.meaning: expressive call to draw attention or show surprise

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hola
Wiktionary — hola#Spanish

hola.notes: Its familiar greeting use is established across the Spanish-speaking world. The initial h- was added orthographically (distinguishing hola from ola 'wave') and is completely silent.

hollywood.etymology: Proper name of the Los Angeles district that became the global capital of American cinema in the 1910s; coined in 1887 by real-estate developer Harvey Henderson Wilcox's wife Daeida Wilcox as an English compound of holly ('holly shrub', < Old English holegn) + wood ('forest, grove', < Old English wudu).

history.meaning: ranch and suburb northwest of downtown Los Angeles
metonym for the American motion-picture industry

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hollywoodiense
Wiktionary — Hollywood

hollywood.notes: In Spain, speakers usually pronounce Hollywood with an initial Spanish jota (/ˈxoliβuð/ or /ˈxoliɡuð/), and its standard Spanish relational adjective is hollywoodiense (or hollywoodense).

hombre.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish omne / ombre from Latin hominem (accusative of homō 'human being, man'), with syncope of the unstressed vowel (*hom'ne) and dissimilation of -mn- to -mbr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hombre
Wiktionary — hombre

hombro.etymology: Inherited from Latin umĕrus ('shoulder, upper arm'), syncopated to *um'ru, developing an epenthetic -b- between -m- and -r- and an unetymological initial h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hombro

hombro.notes: Learned anatomical derivatives such as húmero keep the Latin stem.

hondo.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish fondo from Latin fundus ('bottom, lowest part', used adjectivally in Vulgar Latin for 'deep' by back-formation from profundus), with change of initial f- to silent h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hondo
Wiktionary — hondo

hora.etymology: Hora continues Latin hōra ('hour, time of day'), borrowed from Ancient Greek hṓra ('season, hour').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hora

hora.notes: Silent h-; ¿Qué hora es? asks the clock time, while media hora means half an hour.

horario.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late/Medieval Latin hōrārius ('pertaining to the hours; schedule, timetable'), derived from Classical Latin hōra ('hour', < Ancient Greek ὥρα).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: horario
Wiktionary — horario

hornear.etymology: Formed within Spanish from horno ('oven', inherited via Old Spanish forno from Latin furnus) + the verbal suffix -ear ('to bake in an oven').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hornear
Wiktionary — hornear

horno.etymology: Horno continues Latin furnus ('oven, kiln'), showing the characteristic Castilian shift of initial Latin f- to silent h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: horno

horno.notes: Related verb hornear means 'to bake in the oven'.

horrible.etymology: Horrible comes from Latin horribĭlis ('dreadful, bristling', from horrēre, 'to bristle or shudder').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: horrible

horrible.notes: Same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns (un ruido horrible, una reseña horrible).

hostelería.etymology: Derived in Spanish from hostelero ('innkeeper, restaurateur') + -ería ('hospitality and restaurant trade'), built on Old Spanish hostal (< Medieval Latin hospitāle 'guesthouse, inn', from hospes 'host, guest').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hostelería
Wiktionary — hostelería

hotel.etymology: Borrowed from French hôtel ('mansion, hotel'), which evolved from Old French ostel (< Medieval Latin hospitāle 'guesthouse, lodging', derived from Classical Latin hospes, hospitis 'host, guest').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hotel
Wiktionary — hotel

house.etymology: Unadapted English noun ('dwelling, legislative chamber, dynasty') cited here inside the title of the political drama series House of Cards; inherited in English from Old English hūs ('house, shelter'), from Proto-Germanic *hūsą.

sources.title: Wiktionary — house

house.notes: Note the idiomatic difference behind the title: English 'house of cards' corresponds in idiomatic Spanish to un castillo de naipes ('castle of playing cards'). Also borrowed separately in Spanish as música house ('house music', named after Chicago's Warehouse club).

hoy.etymology: Inherited from Latin hodiē ('today', a Classical contraction of hōc diē 'on this day'), with regular palatalization of -di- before a vowel to -y.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hoy
Wiktionary — hoy

hubiéramos.etymology: First-person plural -ra imperfect subjunctive of the auxiliary verb haber ('[if] we had' / conditional alternative 'we would have'), continuing Old Spanish oviéramos, from the Latin strong pluperfect indicative habuerāmus (built on habu-, perfect stem of habēre 'to have'), with vowel raising o > u (hub-) and mandatory esdrújula accent.

morphemes.meaning: had (< Old Spanish ov- < Latin habu-)

history.meaning: (if) we had; we would have (+ past participle)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: haber
Wiktionary — hubiéramos

hubiéramos.notes: Because -ra descends from the Latin pluperfect indicative, hubiéramos llegado is fully grammatical in educated Spanish both in the si-clause ('if we had gone') and in the result clause ('we would have gone so far', alongside habríamos llegado)—whereas -se (hubiésemos) belongs mainly to the si-clause.

hubiésemos.etymology: First-person plural -se imperfect subjunctive of haber ('if we had'), descending via Old Spanish oviéssemos from the Latin pluperfect subjunctive habuissēmus (perfect stem habu- of habēre 'to have' + -issēmus), with raising of pretonic o > u.

morphemes.meaning: had (< Old Spanish ov- < Latin habu-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: haber
Wiktionary — hubiésemos

hubiésemos.notes: Look at how naturally Peninsular speech alternates the two subjunctive forms within a single counterfactual sentence: Si tú y yo lo hubiésemos hecho un poquito mejor, hubiéramos llegado tan lejos.

huele.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative (and tú imperative) of oler ('smells, gives off an odor'), inherited from Latin olet, third-person singular of olēre ('to emit a smell, be fragrant or rank', Archaic Latin olēre / odēre, related to odor and Ancient Greek ὄζω ózō). Stressed short Latin ŏ diphthongized regularly to ue, and Spanish orthography adds initial silent h- before syllable-initial ue- so medieval manuscripts would not misread uele as *vele.

morphemes.meaning: smell (< Latin ol-, unstressed stem ol-)

history.meaning: to emit a smell > it smells

cognates.meaning: relating to smell / scent (learned loans from the same root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oler
Wiktionary — huele

huele.notes: Classic Spanish spelling-and-stem pattern: unstressed forms have NO h- (oler, olía, olemos), while stressed diphthongized forms gain silent h- before ue- (huelo, hueles, huele, huelen)—just like hueso vs. óseo and huevo vs. oval.

huevo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ŏvum (Classical Latin ōvum, 'egg'), with diphthongization of open o to ue and addition of orthographic h- before initial ue-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: huevo
Wiktionary — huevo

hum.etymology: Expressive onomatopoeic interjection representing a closed-mouth nasal murmur of hesitation, reflection, skepticism, or reluctant realization ('hmm, um').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hum
Wiktionary — hum

hum.notes: Recorded in the DLE under hum to transcribe a pensive or doubtful 'hmm...' in dialogue.

humanidad.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin hūmānitātem (nominative hūmānitās, 'human nature, humankind, culture, kindness'), abstract noun derived from hūmānus ('human, humane, refined', related to homō 'human being' and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰem- 'earth', compare humus).

history.meaning: humanity, humankind; compassion; plural humanidades 'the humanities'

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: humanidad

humanidad.notes: Requires the definite article in Spanish when referring to humankind in general: toda la historia de la humanidad ('all of human history').

huésped.etymology: Huésped comes from Latin hospes, hospĭtis, which meant both 'host' and 'guest' in Roman hospitality.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: huésped

huésped.notes: In modern Spanish el huésped / la huésped means 'lodging guest', while el anfitrión means 'host'.

hyundai.etymology: Brand name of the South Korean industrial and automotive conglomerate founded by Chung Ju-yung in 1947; Revised/McCune-Reischauer romanization of Korean 현대 (Hyeondae), a Sino-Korean compound of 現代 meaning 'modernity, the present era' (現 hyeon 'appear, present, current' + 代 dae 'generation, age, era').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Hyundai

hyundai.notes: In Spain, speakers typically pronounce Hyundai along Spanish spelling lines as /ˈjundai/ or /iunˈdai/.

húmedo.etymology: Learned continuation of Latin humĭdus (also spelled umĭdus, 'moist, damp'), from humēre ('to be moist').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: húmedo

húmedo.notes: Unstressed initial h- was written by medieval association with humus ('earth, soil').

i.etymology: Unadapted English first-person singular subject pronoun ('I') spoken in an English-language self-tape audition ('and I am 25 years old'); descended in English from Middle English ich / I < Old English ic, from Proto-Germanic *ek, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂—the exact Indo-European ancestor of Latin ego and Spanish yo.

history.meaning: I (spoken in an English casting introduction)

cognates.meaning: I (< Vulgar Latin *eo < Classical Latin ego < PIE *éǵh₂)

sources.title: Wiktionary — I

i.notes: Two learner contrasts in that single audition sentence: unlike English I, Spanish yo is never capitalized mid-sentence and is normally omitted unless emphasized; and age uses tener ('tengo 25 años'), never ser ('*soy 25 años').

ibsen.etymology: Norwegian/Danish patronymic surname of dramatist Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906, 'father of modern realistic drama'); formed in Dano-Norwegian from the masculine personal name Ib (Danish and Low German pet form of Jakob, via Late Latin Iācōbus < Hebrew Yaʿăqōḇ) + Germanic patronymic suffix -sen ('son of Ib').

history.meaning: son of Ib (family surname of Henrik Ibsen)

cognates.meaning: Iberian names/patronymics from the Jacob/Iago family

rootFamily.gloss: Ibsenian, characteristic of Henrik Ibsen's theatre

sources.title: Wiktionary — Ibsen

ibsen.notes: Pronounced /ˈibsen/ in Spanish; Ibsen's Hedda Gabler and Casa de muñecos (A Doll's House, Casa de muñecas) are staples of the Spanish stage.

idea.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin idea ('archetype, concept, notion'), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, 'form, look, ideal prototype'), derived from ἰδεῖν (ideîn, 'to see').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: idea
Wiktionary — idea

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ideal
Wiktionary — ideal

idioma.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin idiōma from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, 'peculiarity, specific property, distinctive phrasing or tongue of a community'), derived from ἰδιόομαι ('to make one's own'), from ἴδιος (ídios, 'one's own, private, distinct').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: idioma
Wiktionary — idioma

idéntico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Scholastic Latin identicus ('the very same, identical'), derived from identitās, which was built on Classical Latin idem ('the same').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: idéntico
Wiktionary — idéntico

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: iglesia
Wiktionary — iglesia

igual.etymology: Inherited from Latin aequālis ('even, level, equal, like'), derived from aequus ('level, equal'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -qu- to -gu- and apocope of final -e.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: igual
Wiktionary — igual

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: igualmente
Wiktionary — igualmente

ilu.etymology: Colloquial Peninsular Spanish affective clipping (apocope) of ilusión ('excitement, joyful anticipation, fond hope'), preserving the first two syllables of ilusión (< Latin illūsiōnem).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ilusión

ilu.notes: Typical playful Peninsular trisyllabic/bisyllabic clipping alongside porfa (< por favor), peli (< película), compi (< compañero), and finde (< fin de semana): ¡Qué ilu! / Me haría mucha ilu ('I'd be so thrilled!').

ilusionado.etymology: Participial adjective of ilusionar(se) ('excited, full of hopeful anticipation'), formed within Spanish from ilusión (< Latin illūsiōnem 'mockery, illusion', from illūdere: in- + lūdere 'to play'). In modern Spanish—above all in Spain—ilusión underwent a remarkable positive semantic shift from 'deceptive mirage' to 'eager hope, joyful excitement about something ahead'.

cognates.meaning: deluded, deceived (retains the older negative sense!)

rootFamily.gloss: excitement, dream, hope (me hace mucha ilusión)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ilusionar

ilusionado.notes: Essential Peninsular vocabulary: where an English speaker says 'I'm so excited about the new project!', natural Spanish says Estoy muy ilusionado/a con el proyecto (never *excitado, which sounds sexual or agitated).

imagen.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Latin imāginem (nominative imāgō, 'likeness, portrait, statue, reflection, mental picture', related to imitārī 'to imitate' and aemulus 'rivaling').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: imagen

imaginar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin imāginārī ('to form a mental picture, fancy, imagine'), deponent verb derived from imāgō, imāginis ('image, likeness').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: imaginar

impecable.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin impeccābilis ('incapable of sinning, faultless, flawless'), formed from negative in- + peccāre ('to sin, err, stumble').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: impecable
Wiktionary — impecable

important.etymology: Unadapted English adjective ('significant, urgent') quoted in an English-language self-tape audition line ('But it's very important...'); borrowed into fifteenth-century English via Middle French important from Medieval Latin importantem (present participle of importāre 'to bring in, carry consequence', from in- + portāre 'to carry').

history.meaning: important (spoken in an English audition script)

sources.title: Wiktionary — important

importante.etymology: Borrowed (via Italian importante or Medieval Latin importāns, importantis) from importāre ('to bring in; in Medieval Latin, to be of consequence, matter').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: importante

importar.etymology: Importar comes from Latin importāre ('to bring in, carry weight, be of consequence'), developing both commercial ('import') and evaluative ('matter, mind') uses.

imprenta.etymology: Borrowed via Catalan empenta / imprenta (or Old French empreinte) from Late Latin imprenta, a remodeled feminine past participle of Classical Latin imprimere ('to press into, stamp, print').

Wiktionary — inclinar

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: incluido
Wiktionary — incluido

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: incluso
Wiktionary — incluso

incorporación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin incorporātiōnem (nominative incorporātiō, 'embodiment, union into one body'), action noun of incorporāre ('to unite into a body', from in- 'into' + corpus, corporis 'body').

joining, addition to a cast/staff/team; highway merge lane

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: industria

infantil.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin infantīlis ('of or belonging to infants or young children'), derived from īnfāns, īnfantis ('little child', literally 'unable to speak', from in- + fārī 'to speak').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: infantil
Wiktionary — infantil

inicial.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin initiālis ('of the beginning, initial; first letter of a word or name'), derived from initium ('entrance, beginning', from inīre 'to enter upon, begin').

Wiktionary — inspeccionar
