sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: inspector
Wiktionary — inspectora

instante.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin instāns, instantis ('present, pressing, immediate; brief moment of time'), substantivized present participle of instāre ('to stand upon, be close at hand').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: instante
Wiktionary — instante

instrumento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnstrūmentum ('implement, tool, apparatus, means'), formed with the instrumental suffix -mentum from īnstruere ('to build in, equip, furnish, prepare', from in- + struere 'to pile up, construct').

history.meaning: to equip > tool, implement, musical instrument

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: instrumento
Wiktionary — instrumento

instrumento.notes: Remember the verb collocation: in Spanish you 'touch' a musical instrument—tocar un instrumento musical (never *jugar un instrumento).

insuperable.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin insuperābilis ('that cannot be passed over or overcome, insurmountable, unsurpassed'), formed from negative in- + superābilis (from superāre 'to overcome, surpass').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: insuperable
Wiktionary — insuperable

intelectual.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin intellectuālis ('relating to the understanding or mind'), derived from Classical Latin intellectus ('perception, discernment, intellect'), action noun of intellegere ('to discern, comprehend', from inter- 'between' + legere 'to choose, gather, read').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: intelectual
Wiktionary — intelectual

intelectual.notes: Spelled with a single -l- in Spanish (intelectual, inteligente), unlike English and Italian double -ll-.

intentar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin intentāre ('to stretch out toward, aim at, endeavor, attempt'), the frequentative of intendere (in- + tendere 'to stretch').

history.meaning: to stretch toward, direct one's effort

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: intentar
Wiktionary — intentar

interior.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin interior, interiōris ('inner, farther inside'), comparative adjective formed from the root of inter / intrā ('within').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: interior
Wiktionary — interior

internacional.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English international—famously coined in 1780 by British philosopher Jeremy Bentham (originally for international jurisprudence, replacing 'law of nations')—combining Latinate prefix inter- ('between, among') + nacional ('national', from nación < Latin nātiōnem 'birth, people, nation').

history.meaning: existing or carried on between nations

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: internacional
Wiktionary — internacional

internacional.notes: Invariable for gender (proyección internacional, el mundo internacional), forming plural internacionales.

internet.etymology: Late-twentieth-century borrowing from English Internet, shortened in the 1970s (in DARPA / TCP/IP networking documents by Vint Cerf, Yogen Dalal, and Carl Sunshine) from internetwork, combining Latinate prefix inter- ('between, interconnecting') + English net ('network, mesh', < Old English nett).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: internet
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: internet

internet.notes: Ambiguous in grammatical gender (both el internet and la internet—the latter via la red—are valid), though in Peninsular Spanish it is most often used WITHOUT an article at all (buscar en internet, antes no había Internet).

interruptor.etymology: Learned formation from Latin interruptor ('one that breaks off'), agent noun from interrumpere ('to break between, interrupt'), adopted in physics and electrical engineering for a circuit switch.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: interruptor

intrusión.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intrūsiōnem (nominative intrūsiō, 'unlawful entry, forcing in'), built on Classical Latin intrūsus, past participle of intrūdere ('to thrust in, force in', from in- 'into' + trūdere 'to push, shove, thrust').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: intrusión
Wiktionary — intrusión

intrusión.notes: Perdón por la intrusión ('Sorry to intrude / barge in') is a polite formula when stepping unannounced into an office or conversation.

invierno.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish ivierno (with epenthetic nasal -n-) from Latin hībernum (tempus) ('wintry season, winter'), derived from hiems ('winter').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: invierno
Wiktionary — invierno

invitación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin invītātiōnem (nominative invītātiō, 'invitation, entertainment, challenge'), action noun from invītāre ('to invite as a guest, treat, summon').

rootFamily.gloss: to invite; to pick up the bill / treat (¡Te invito yo!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: invitación
Wiktionary — invitación

invitación.notes: Remember that in Spanish bars and restaurants, invitar (Te invito a un café) specifically means 'to pay for / treat someone', not merely to ask them along!

invitar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin invītāre ('to ask as a guest, entertain, summon, treat').

history.meaning: to invite, entertain as a guest

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: invitar
Wiktionary — invitar

invocar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin invocāre ('to call upon, appeal to, summon by name'), formed from in- ('upon, toward') + vocāre ('to call', derived from vōx, vōcis 'voice').

history.meaning: to call upon (a deity, witness, or law)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: invocar
Wiktionary — invocar

invocar.notes: Playfully used in everyday Spanish (¡La hemos invocado!, alongside Hablando del rey de Roma) when someone phones or appears the very moment you were talking about them. Orthographic c -> qu before -e (invoqué, invoque).

ir.etymology: The infinitive ir comes from Latin ire, meaning to go. Modern ir is highly irregular and also works with another verb to express motion, a future action or a gradually developing process.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ir

ir.notes: In hemos ido creciendo, ido is the past participle of ir. The expression describes gradual growth; it does not describe a journey.

is.etymology: Unadapted English third-person singular present copula ('is') spoken in an English-language self-tape audition ('Hello, my name is...'); inherited in English from Old English is < Proto-Germanic *isti < Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti ('is'), making it an exact Indo-European cognate of Latin est and Spanish es.

history.meaning: is (spoken in an English audition slate)

sources.title: Wiktionary — is

is.notes: While English introduces names with 'My name is...', natural Spanish usually prefers the reflexive verb llamarse (Me llamo Mariona) or Soy Mariona over the stiffer literal calque Mi nombre es....

isola.etymology: Italian topographic surname (Camilla Isola) identical to the Italian noun isola ('island'), inherited from Latin īnsula ('island', with Vulgar Latin loss of -n- before -s-: īsula > isola)—making it a direct Romance cognate of Spanish isla.

history.meaning: island; Italian place and family surname

cognates.meaning: island (< Vulgar Latin īsula, with syncope)
island (< OFr isle) / isolate (< Late Latin īnsulātus)

rootFamily.gloss: island (learned doublet famous from Sancho Panza's Ínsula Barataria)

sources.title: Wiktionary — isola

isola.notes: Italian Isola keeps the stressed antepenultimate syllable of Latin īnsula (Í-so-la), whereas Spanish syncopated the unstressed vowel to produce disyllabic isla.

it.etymology: Unadapted English third-person singular neuter pronoun ('it') quoted in an English-language audition line ('It is very important to give...'); inherited in English from Old English hit (with loss of initial h- in unstressed contexts), from Proto-Germanic *hit.

history.meaning: 3rd-person singular neuter pronoun and dummy subject

rootFamily.gloss: it (tonic Spanish neuter pronoun used mainly after prepositions: para ello)

sources.title: Wiktionary — it

it.notes: Crucial structural contrast: Spanish has NO dummy subject pronoun corresponding to English 'it'—sentences like 'It is very important' or 'It is raining' must start directly with the verb (Es muy importante, Llueve, never *Ello es muy importante).

it's.etymology: Unadapted English contraction of it is ('it's'), fusing neuter pronoun it (< Old English hit) + copula is (< Old English is), quoted in an English audition exchange ('It's easy').

cognates.meaning: is (complete Spanish equivalent without dummy pronoun)

sources.title: Wiktionary — it's

it's.notes: English 'It's easy' maps to two words in Spanish: Es fácil (or ¡Está chupado! colloquially in Spain).

izquierda.etymology: Izquierda was borrowed into medieval Castilian from Basque ezkerra ('the left hand, left-handed'), displacing inherited Latin sinister.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: izquierda
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: izquierdo

izquierda.notes: One of Spanish's most famous Basque loanwords; a la izquierda means 'on / to the left'.

izquierdo.etymology: Pre-Roman Paleohispanic borrowing closely shared with Basque ezker ('left, left-handed'), which displaced Classical Latin sinister across Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: izquierdo
Wiktionary — izquierdo

ja.etymology: Natural onomatopoeic interjection imitating the burst of breath in laughter (commonly repeated as ¡ja, ja!).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ja
Wiktionary — ja

jabón.etymology: Jabón descends from Late Latin sapo, sapōnis ('soap'), an early loanword into Latin from Germanic *saipō.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jabón

jabón.notes: Initial Latin s- palatalized in Old Spanish (xabón > modern jabón).

jaleo.etymology: Deverbal noun from jalear ('to cheer on dancers and singers with rhythmic claps and shouts, or rouse hunting hounds'), derived within southern/Peninsular Spanish from the expressive interjection ¡hala! (pronounced with aspirated /h/ > velar /x/, spelled j-). Originally naming lively nineteenth-century Andalusian song-and-dance cheering, jaleo broadened into 'commotion, ruckus, busy chaos, fuss'.

morphemes.meaning: shout of encouragement (< ¡hala! with aspirated j-)

history.meaning: come on! > to cheer on with shouts and claps

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jaleo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jalear

jaleo.notes: Quintessential Peninsular word for hectic hubbub or trouble: mucho jaleo en la oficina ('total chaos at the office'), armar/montar un jaleo ('make a huge fuss'), meterse en jaleos ('get into messy trouble').

jamás.etymology: Univerbation in Old Spanish (or via Old Occitan jamais) of ya (< Latin iam 'already, now') + más (< Latin magis 'more'), shifting from 'evermore' in negative contexts to 'never'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jamás
Wiktionary — jamás

jardín.etymology: Borrowed from French jardin ('garden'), from Old French jart, itself of Frankish origin (*gardo, 'enclosure, yard', cognate with English yard and garden).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jardín
Wiktionary: jardín#Spanish

jarra.etymology: Borrowed from Hispanic Arabic ǧárra, from Classical Arabic ǧarrah ('earthenware water vessel, pitcher, jar').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jarra
Wiktionary — jarra

jarrita.etymology: Diminutive formed within Spanish from jarra ('pitcher, jug', < Arabic ǧarrah) + -ita ('small pitcher, little jug').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jarra
Wiktionary — jarrita

jefa.etymology: Feminine form of jefe ('female boss, head, manager'), created in modern Spanish from jefe (< French chef < Latin caput 'head').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jefe
Wiktionary — jefa

jefe.etymology: Borrowed from French chef ('head, leader, commander'), which evolved from Latin caput ('head').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jefe
Wiktionary — jefe

jersey.etymology: Borrowed from English jersey ('knitted woolen sweater or pullover'), named after the Channel Island of Jersey, long celebrated for its knitted woolens.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jersey
Wiktionary — jersey

jet.etymology: Twentieth-century borrowing from English jet ('jet-propelled aircraft', also inside the compound jet lag and jet set), shortened in English from jet engine / jet stream; English jet ('spurt, stream') came from Middle French jeter ('to throw, hurl, spurt'), from Vulgar Latin *iectāre (frequentative of Classical Latin iacere 'to throw')—making English jet a hidden cognate of native Spanish echar!

history.meaning: jet aircraft; element of jet lag

cognates.meaning: jet (avião a jato) / to cast, lay

rootFamily.gloss: to throw, pour, cast (native Spanish cognate)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jet
Wiktionary — jet

jet.notes: Standard Spanish equivalent for 'jet plane' in formal registers is avión a reacción (or reactor), while jet privado and jet lag dominate everyday speech.

joder.etymology: Inherited from Latin futuere ('to have sexual intercourse with'), reshaped in Vulgar Latin as second/third conjugation *futere, yielding Old Spanish hoder (with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- > -d-) and—via dialectal retention/velarization of aspirated initial h- (< f-) to /x/—modern Spanish joder.

history.meaning: to copulate; figuratively to ruin, annoy
to screw up, bother; exclamation 'damn! / bloody hell!'

rootFamily.gloss: minced polite euphemisms starting with jo-

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: joder
Wiktionary — joder

joder.notes: Strong vulgar register, yet heard constantly in casual Peninsular Spanish as an interjection of frustration, shock, or even enthusiasm (¡Joder, qué bueno!); softened in family-friendly speech to ¡Jolín!, ¡Jolines!, ¡Jope!, or ¡Jo!.

jodido.etymology: Past participle and participial adjective of joder ('ruined, screwed up; tough, tricky, in a bad way'), built with -ido on joder (< Vulgar Latin *futere < Classical Latin futuere).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jodido
Wiktionary — jodido

jodido.notes: In compound tenses (me has jodido toda la prueba) it means 'you've ruined/wrecked the whole audition for me'; as an adjective with estar (está jodido) it colloquially means 'it's really tough/tricky' or 'he's in rough shape' (vulgar register).

jon.etymology: Basque masculine given name (borne in Spanish television by Basque actor Jon González), standardized in unified Basque (Euskara Batua) from traditional Basque Done Johane / Jon, adapted from Late Latin Iōhannēs < Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs) < Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, 'YHWH has been gracious').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Jon

jon.notes: Pronounced /jon/ (or /ʒon/ in parts of the Basque Country), never with the Spanish velar jota /x/ of Jorge or José!

jorge.etymology: Traditional Spanish masculine given name descending via Late Latin Georgius from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios), derived from γεωργός (geōrgós, 'farmer, husbandman, tiller of the soil'), a compound of γῆ (gê, 'earth, land') + ἔργον (érgon, 'work').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Jorge

jorge.notes: Both j and g before e represent the exact same velar fricative sound in Spanish: /ˈxorxe/. Referenced in the episode via veteran Spanish actor Jorge Roelas.

jornada.etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan jornada or Italian giornata ('a day's journey, a day's work, working day'), derived from Vulgar Latin diurnum ('day', from Classical Latin diurnus 'daily', built on diēs 'day').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jornada
Wiktionary — jornada

josé.etymology: Classic Spanish masculine given name (appearing here inside the surname San José, 'Saint Joseph', of actress Lidia San José), transmitted through Ecclesiastical Latin Iōsēph / Iōsēphus and Ancient Greek Ἰωσήφ (Iōsḗph) from Biblical Hebrew יוֹסֵף (Yōsēf, 'may He [God] add / increase [another child]', from yāsaf 'to add').

rootFamily.gloss: traditional hypocoristic of José (from older Josepe, reinforced by folk etymology P.P. = Pater Putativus)

sources.title: Wiktionary — José

josé.notes: Notice how older Spanish Josepe / Josef lost its final consonant to yield oxytonic José; in compound names (José Luis, María José), everyday speech often shortens it to Jose without final stress.

joven.etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis ('young, youthful; young person').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: joven
Wiktionary — joven

joya.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Spanish from Old French joie ('jewel, precious gift, joy'), descending from Late Latin gaudia (reanalyzed as feminine singular from the neuter plural of Classical Latin gaudium 'joy, delight', from gaudēre 'to rejoice'), with Gallo-Romance palatalization of initial g- before a (contrast native Castilian gozo < gaudium).

cognates.meaning: delight (< OFr joie) / gem (< OFr joel)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: joya
Wiktionary — joya

joya.notes: Figuratively, ser una joya (or una joyita) praises an undiscovered talent ('a hidden gem')—or, with heavy irony (¡Menuda joyita!), calls someone a real piece of work!

juanfran.etymology: Colloquial Peninsular compound hypocoristic fusing Juan + the clipped initial syllable of Francisco (Juan Francisco). Juan descends via Late Latin Iōhannēs and Greek Ἰωάννης from Hebrew Yōḥānān ('God has been gracious'); Francisco descends from Medieval Latin Franciscus ('Frenchman', nicknamed onto Giovanni di Pietro Bernardone—Saint Francis of Assisi—by his silk-merchant father).

sources.title: Wiktionary — Juanfran

juanfran.notes: Peninsular Spanish loves fusing two-part given names into punchy two-syllable blends stressed on the first element (JUÁN-fran, JUÁN-ma, MÍ-riam/MARI-carmen).

juegas.etymology: Second-person singular (tú) present indicative of jugar ('you play'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *iocās (Classical Latin deponent iocāris, 'you jest, joke', from iocus 'joke, pastime'), showing regular Castilian diphthongization of stressed short Latin ŏ > ue (juegas vs. unstressed jugamos).

cognates.meaning: jest (borrowed in the 17th c. from the same Latin iocus!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jugar
Wiktionary — juegas

juegas.notes: Jugar en primera división ('to play in the top flight / big leagues', borrowed from La Liga football) is a favorite Spanish metaphor for reaching top-tier professional success.

juego.etymology: Inherited from Latin iocum (nominative iocus, 'jest, joke, verbal play'), which in Spoken Latin across the Roman Empire displaced Classical Latin lūdus ('game, sport, play'), undergoing regular Castilian palatalization/velarization of initial i- before back vowel (i- > /ʒ/ > /x/, spelled j-) and diphthongization of stressed short ŏ > ue.

rootFamily.gloss: playful, recreational (learned adjective preserving Classical lūdus!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: juego
Wiktionary — juego

juego.notes: Besides 'game' (proponer un juego) and 'gambling' (el juego), un juego de... also means a 'matching set' (un juego de sábanas, un juego de llaves), and hacer juego con means 'to match (in clothing/decor)'.

juegue.etymology: First- and third-person singular present subjunctive of jugar ('that I / he / she play'), continuing Vulgar Latin *iocet (< Classical iocētur, from iocārī 'to jest, play'), showing stressed diphthongization ŏ > ue and orthographic gu before -e to preserve the voiced velar /ɡ/ sound.

morphemes.meaning: play (< Latin ioc-, spelled gu before e)

history.meaning: that I / he / she / usted play

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jugar
Wiktionary — juegue

juegue.notes: Triggered by concessive clauses such as por mucho que juegue en primera división ('no matter how much I/she may play in the first division'). Note the silent u in -gue- needed to prevent g + e from sounding like /x/.

jueves.etymology: Jueves descends from Late Latin Iovis [dies] ('day of Jupiter'), preserving the genitive Iovis of Latin Iuppiter.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jueves

jueves.notes: Because jueves already ends in unstressed -es, its plural is unchanged: el jueves / los jueves.

jugamos.etymology: First-person plural present and preterite indicative of jugar ('we play / we played'), descending from Vulgar Latin *iocāmus / *iocāvimus (< Classical Latin iocārī 'to jest, joke'), where unstressed pretonic o raised in medieval Castilian to u (jugamos vs. stressed juego).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jugar
Wiktionary — jugamos

jugamos.notes: Remember that jugar takes the preposition a before the name of a game or sport in Spanish: jugamos a las cartas, jugamos al fútbol, jugamos a un montón de cosas.

jugar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iocāre, active remodeling of Classical Latin deponent iocārī ('to jest, joke, banter', derived from iocus 'joke'), which supplanted Classical Latin lūdere ('to play'). Old Spanish jogar raised its unstressed root vowel o > u, making jugar the ONLY u -> ue stem-changing verb in modern Spanish!

history.meaning: to play (a game, sport, or match); to gamble

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: jugar
Wiktionary — jugar

jugar.notes: Three essential contrasts for English 'play': (1) jugar a = play a game/sport (jugar un partido, jugar al tenis); (2) tocar = play a musical instrument; (3) interpretar / hacer un papel = play an acting role!

junta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of juntar ('meeting, board, council; joint or seam between fitted pieces'), inherited from Latin iūncta, feminine past participle of iungere ('to join, yoke together').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: junta
Wiktionary — junta

junto.etymology: Junto continues Latin iunctus ('joined, linked together', past participle of iungĕre, 'to yoke or join').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: junto

junto.notes: Plural juntos/juntas means 'together' agreeing with the subjects, while invariable junto a + noun means 'next to / beside'.

justo.etymology: Justo descends from Latin iustus ('fair, exact, rightful', from ius, 'law, right').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: justo

justo.notes: Used adverbially before location or time phrases to mean 'right / exact' (justo al lado de la cama = right next to the bed).

kayak.etymology: Borrowed (via English and French kayak or Danish kajak) from Greenlandic / Inuktitut qajaq ('one-person skin-covered Arctic hunting canoe propelled with a double-bladed paddle', from Proto-Eskimo *qayar).

rootFamily.gloss: canoe/kayak (traditional everyday word in Spain < Taíno piragua)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: kayak
Wiktionary — kayak

kayak.notes: Masculine noun (ir en kayak, plural kayaks). One of Spanish's very few everyday palindromes!

kebab.etymology: Contemporary culinary loanword transmitted via Turkish kebap and English kebab from Arabic كَبَاب (kabāb, 'roasted or skewered meat'), an ancient Near Eastern culinary term cognate with Aramaic kabbābā and Akkadian kabābu ('to burn, char, roast').

history.meaning: döner kebab wrap/sandwich or kebab takeaway shop

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: kebab
Wiktionary — kebab

kebab.notes: In Spain, un kebab (plural kebabs, stressed on the final syllable: /keˈbab/) is the quintessential late-night comfort takeaway—either in pita bread or wrapped in flatbread (un dürüm).

kikirikí.etymology: Onomatopoeic formation (standardized in the DLE primarily as quiquiriquí, alongside variant kikirikí) imitating the four-beat high-pitched crowing of a rooster.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quiquiriquí
Wiktionary — quiquiriquí

kikirikí.notes: Both spellings (quiquiriquí and kikirikí) carry a written accent on the final stressed -í; in Paquita Salas, Paquita famously uses a loud rooster crow as her mobile phone ringtone!

kilo.etymology: Clipped form of kilogramo ('kilogram'), borrowed via French kilogramme, a metric compound combining Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, 'thousand') + γράμμα (grámma, 'small weight, gram').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: kilo
Wiktionary — kilo

kétchup.etymology: Hispanized orthographic adaptation of English ketchup (earlier catchup, catsup), which entered English in the late seventeenth century via maritime trade in Maritime Southeast Asia from Hokkien (Southern Min Chinese) kê-tsiap (鮭汁, 'brine of pickled fish or shellfish'), long before nineteenth-century Anglo-American recipes reinvented it as a spiced sweet tomato condiment.

cognates.meaning: soy sauce (from the same Hokkien source)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: kétchup
Wiktionary — kétchup

kétchup.notes: Takes a written accent on é in Spanish (el kétchup) because it is stressed on the first syllable (/ˈketʃup/) and ends in -p. Note regional variation: Spain uses kétchup, while Mexico commonly says salsa cátsup.

la.etymology: Both feminine singular article la ('the') and feminine direct-object pronoun la ('her, it') continue unstressed Latin illa / illam ('that').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: la
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

la.notes: In clock time, singular la una ('one o'clock') contrasts with plural las dos, las tres...

lado.etymology: Lado continues Latin latus ('flank, side'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to Castilian -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lado

lado.notes: Al lado de ('next to, beside') and al lado ('on the side / next door') are core spatial building blocks.

ladridos.etymology: Plural of ladrido ('bark, barking of a dog'), formed with the animal-sound nominal suffix -ido (< Latin -ītus, compare mugido, rugido, aullido) from ladrar ('to bark'), which descends regularly from Classical Latin lātrāre ('to bark, bay, rant'), showing lenition (voicing) of intervocalic -tr- > -dr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: misterioso
Wiktionary — misterioso

mitad.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish meitad from Latin medietās, medietātis ('middle, half'), derived from medius ('middle, half').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mitad
Wiktionary — mitad

miércoles.etymology: Descends from Latin [diēs] Mercŭriī (reshaped in Vulgar Latin as *Mercŏris, 'day of Mercury'), with short stressed ĕ diphthongizing to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: miércoles

miércoles.notes: Retains proparoxytonic stress and invariable plural los miércoles.

mochila.etymology: Derived within Golden Age Spanish from mochil ('farmhand, errand boy, young squire who carried soldiers' provisions on his back'), itself built on mocho ('cropped, shorn, hornless', referring to boys and servants whose hair was cropped short). By metonymy, the name of the young pack-carrier transferred to the leather or canvas knapsack strapped to his shoulders!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mochila
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mochil

mochila.notes: Universal pan-Hispanic word for 'backpack / rucksack' (also used figuratively in cargar con una mochila emocional, 'to carry emotional baggage').

moda.etymology: Borrowed in the late seventeenth century from French la mode ('fashion, prevailing style of dress or custom'), a feminine specialization of Latin modus ('measure, rhythm, manner, way'—which separately gave masculine el modo in Spanish).

rootFamily.gloss: way, manner, grammatical mood (masculine doublet < modus)
modern (related via Late Latin modernus < modo 'just now')
model (< Italian modello, diminutive of modus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: moda
Wiktionary — moda

moda.notes: Key idioms: estar de moda ('to be fashionable / trendy / in style'), ponerse de moda ('to come into style'), pasar de moda ('to go out of style').

modelo.etymology: Modelo was borrowed from Italian modello. The DLE takes that word back through reconstructed Vulgar Latin *modellus to Latin modŭlus, associated with measure or a measured rhythm. The asterisk identifies the reconstructed stage.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: modelo

history.meaning: a diminutive formation behind Italian modello

modelo.notes: Spanish uses modelo both for a pattern to copy and for a person who models. A person can be el modelo or la modelo.

moderno.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin modernus ('of the present time, modern', first attested in the 5th–6th centuries), derived from the Latin adverb modo ('just now, recently').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: moderno
Wiktionary — moderno

mojado.etymology: Participial adjective of mojar ('wet, damp, soaked'), descending from Vulgar Latin *molliāre ('to soften in water, wet').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mojado
Wiktionary — mojado

mojar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *molliāre ('to soften by steeping in water, wet, soak'), derived from Classical Latin mollis ('soft, pliant'), with regular palatalization of -lli- to Castilian -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mojar
Wiktionary — mojar

molestar.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin molestāre ('to trouble, annoy, disturb'), derived from molestus ('troublesome, irksome', related to mōlēs 'heavy mass, burden').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: molestar
Wiktionary — molestar

momento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mōmentum ('movement, impulse, brief interval of time'), contracted from *movimentum, from movēre ('to move').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: momento
Wiktionary — momento

moneda.etymology: Moneda continues Latin monēta, originally an epithet of Juno Moneta near whose Roman temple coins were minted.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: moneda

moneda.notes: Means an individual metal coin (unas monedas) as well as currency in general.

montante.etymology: Active participial noun from montar (reinforced by French montant, 'upright post of a frame, transom window over a door, total amount'), from Vulgar Latin *montāre ('to go up, mount', built on mōns, montis 'mountain').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: montante
Wiktionary — montante

montar.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Iberia via Old Occitan / Old French monter ('to go up, climb, mount a horse'), descending from Vulgar Latin *montāre, a denominal verb built on Classical Latin mōns, montis ('mountain, hill'). From 'mounting a horse or stage scaffolding', Spanish developed the transitive senses 'to assemble, set up, stage, or start up (a business, band, or scene)'.

morphemes.meaning: climb, mount, set up (< Latin montem)

history.meaning: to ride; to assemble, put together, start up; to edit (film)

cognates.meaning: to go up, assemble, edit (a film)
to climb onto, set up (via Old French monter)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: montar
Wiktionary — montar

montar.notes: Super productive in Peninsular Spanish: montar una banda / empresa ('start a band / business'), montar una obra ('stage a play'), montar un número / pollo ('make a scene'), nata montada ('whipped cream').

montaña.etymology: The DLE traces montaña to Vulgar Latin *montanĕa, from Latin montānus ('mountainous'), built on mons, montis ('mountain').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: montaña

montaña.notes: Used figuratively in una montaña de ('a huge pile of').

montera.etymology: Shortened from gorra montera, feminine of montero ('belonging to a huntsman or mountain hunting'), derived from monte ('mountain, wooded hunting ground', < Latin montem) + suffix -era (< -āria). Originally a peaked cloth cap worn by hunters in the hills, la montera came in the nineteenth century to designate the traditional black astrakhan/chenille cap worn by Spanish bullfighters.

history.meaning: bullfighter's black cap; glass skylight roof

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: montera
Wiktionary — montera

montera.notes: Immortalized in the classic Spanish idiom ponerse el mundo por montera ('to put the world on as one's cap' = 'to take on the world boldly without caring a whit about convention or gossip'), echoed in Rosalía's opening theme song for Paquita Salas ('Con el mundo por montera, maneja la ciudad')!

montón.etymology: Derived within Spanish from monte ('hill, mound, wooded elevation', < Latin montem, nominative mōns) + augmentative suffix -ón (< Latin -ōnem): literally 'a big mound or heap', grammaticalized colloquially in un montón de ('a ton of, loads of').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: montón
Wiktionary — montón

montón.notes: Watch two opposite idioms: un montón (te quiero un montón, un montón de cosas) means 'tons / loads', whereas ser del montón ('to be from the general heap') means 'to be run-of-the-mill, nothing special'!

morder.etymology: Inherited from Latin mordēre ('to bite, grip with the teeth, sting', from Proto-Indo-European *h₂merd- 'to bite, crush', cognate with English smart 'to sting painfully'), retaining second-conjugation -er with regular diphthongization of stressed short ŏ > ue (muerdo, muerde).

cognates.meaning: bite-sized piece (< OFr morsel) / biting of conscience (< remorsus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: morder
Wiktionary — morder

morder.notes: Just as in English ('Relax, I don't bite!'), Spanish uses ¡Tranquilas, que no muerdo! to put nervous newcomers at ease, and no morderse la lengua ('not to bite one's tongue') for speaking bluntly.

morir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin morīre, an active fourth-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latin deponent morī ('to die').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: morir
Wiktionary — morir

mostaza.etymology: Inherited/formed from Vulgar Latin *mustācea (feminine of Classical Latin mustāceus 'made with grape must'), derived from mustum ('unfermented new wine, grape must', whence Spanish mosto), because crushed mustard seeds were traditionally blended into tart grape must to prepare condiment paste.

history.meaning: new wine / grape must > mustard paste mixed with must

cognates.meaning: pungent seed condiment (via Old French moustarde < mustum)

rootFamily.gloss: unfermented grape juice / must (popular non-alcoholic bar drink in Spain!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostaza
Wiktionary — mostaza

mostaza.notes: Next time you order un mosto ('grape juice') in a Spanish tapas bar, you are drinking the exact Latin base (mustum) from which mostaza ('mustard') took its name!

mostrador.etymology: Mostrador derives from mostrar ('to show, display', from Latin monstrāre) + instrument/place suffix -dor: originally a shop counter where goods were laid out to show customers.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrador
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrar

mostrador.notes: Standard Spanish word for a hotel reception desk, café bar counter, or shop counter.

mostrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre ('to point out, show, indicate', derived from mōnstrum 'divine omen, portent', from monēre 'to warn, advise'), with early Spoken Latin reduction of the cluster -nstr- > -str- (mōstrāre > mostrar) and diphthongization in stressed syllables (muestro).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrar
Wiktionary — mostrar

mostrar.notes: In casual Peninsular speech, enseñar ('Show me your dress' = Enséñame el vestido) is often used where slightly more formal registers use mostrar (mostrar el producto).

motivo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late and Medieval Latin mōtīvus ('moving, impelling; cause or reason for action'), derived from mōtus, past participle of movēre ('to move').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: motivo
Wiktionary — motivo

moto.etymology: Feminine noun created by apocope (clipping) of motocicleta ('motorcycle'), adapted from French motocyclette, a late-nineteenth-century compound of moto- (< Latin mōtor 'mover', from movēre 'to move') + (bi)cyclette (diminutive built on Greek κύκλος kúklos 'wheel, circle').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: moto
Wiktionary — moto

moto.notes: Like la foto (< fotografía), la moto stays feminine despite ending in -o: una moto nueva. Bonus Peninsular idiom: vender la moto ('to sell someone a bill of goods / give a slick sales pitch')!

motor.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin mōtor, mōtōris ('mover, one that imparts motion'), an agent noun derived from movēre ('to move').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: motor
Wiktionary — motor

mover.etymology: Inherited from Latin movēre ('to move, set in motion'), with regular diphthongization of stressed short o to ue in stem-stressed forms (mueve).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mover
Wiktionary — mover

mucho.etymology: Inherited from Latin multus, multum ('much, many'), showing regular Castilian vocalization and palatalization of the cluster -ult- to -uch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho
Wiktionary — mucho

muchísimo.etymology: Muchísimo combines mucho (from Latin multus) with the learned superlative suffix -ísimo (from Latin -issĭmus) to express 'very much' or 'a great deal'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -ísimo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: mucho

muchísimo.notes: Muchísimo inflects as an adjective before nouns (muchísimas gracias) and stays invariable as an adverb after verbs.

morphemes.meaning: large amount or degree, from mucho

mudanza.etymology: Formed within Spanish from mudar ('to change, move house', < Latin mūtāre 'to change, alter, move') + the abstract suffix -anza (< Latin -antia).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mudanza
Wiktionary — mudanza

mudo.etymology: Mudo continues Latin mūtus ('mute, silent, unable to speak'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mudo

mudo.notes: Applied to silent letters (la hache muda) and to a piano key whose hammer fails to strike.

mueble.etymology: Continues Latin mōbilis ('movable', from movēre 'to move'): originally bienes muebles ('movable goods', as opposed to real estate), narrowed to household furniture.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mueble

muero.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of morir ('I die / I'm dying'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *moriō for Classical Latin deponent morior ('I die', from Proto-Indo-European *mer- 'to die'), with regular Castilian diphthongization of stressed short ŏ > ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: morir
Wiktionary — muero

muero.notes: In everyday Spanish, natural or hyperbolic dying is nearly always pronominal (morirse): un día me muero, me muero de hambre ('I'm starving'), me muero de vergüenza ('I'm mortified').

mugido.etymology: Masculine sound-noun derived with suffix -ido (< Latin -ītus, compare ladrido, rugido) or directly from Latin mūgītus ('lowing, bellowing of cattle, rumbling'), action noun of mūgīre ('to low, moo', an ancient Indo-European echoic verb built on *mū-, cognate with Ancient Greek μυκάομαι).

history.meaning: to low, bellow > lowing of cattle
moo, lowing of a cow or bull

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mugido
Wiktionary — mugido

mugido.notes: Appears regularly in Spanish closed-captioning stage directions—(Mugido)—for the sound of cows in countryside scenes; remember g before i sounds like Spanish jota (/muˈxido/).

mujer.etymology: Inherited from Latin mulier, mulierem ('woman, wife'), with Vulgar Latin shift of stress to the penultimate vowel and regular Castilian palatalization of -li- before a vowel to -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mujer
Wiktionary — mujer

mundillo.etymology: Lexicalized diminutive formed within Spanish from mundo ('world, society', < Latin mundus) + diminutive suffix -illo (< Latin -ellus); specialized figuratively as el mundillo ('the little insider world, professional scene, or clique' surrounding a trade such as cinema, fashion, publishing, or bullfighting).

history.meaning: small world; professional scene or coterie

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mundillo
Wiktionary — mundillo

mundillo.notes: Notice how suffix -illo often creates lexicalized new meanings in Spanish rather than simple smallness: bocadillo ('baguette sandwich'), bolsillo ('pocket'), pasillo ('hallway'), and este mundillo ('this industry scene').

mundo.etymology: Mundo continues Latin mundus. The DLE describes the world sense of that Latin word as a semantic calque of Greek kósmos: the meaning was modelled on the Greek expression rather than its sound being borrowed.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mundo

mundo.notes: Todo el mundo uses world collectively for everyone and takes a singular verb.

municipal.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mūnicipālis ('belonging to a mūnicipium or self-governing town'), derived from mūniceps ('citizen of a free town', from mūnia 'civic duties' + capere 'to take').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: municipal
Wiktionary — municipal

murió.etymology: Third-person singular preterite indicative of morir ('died'), continuing Vulgar Latin *morīvit (> *morió), where the palatal glide (yod) in the ending -ió raised the preceding mid root vowel o to high u (murió, murieron, muriendo vs. morimos).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: morir
Wiktionary — murió

murió.notes: Only two verb families in Spanish alternate o -> ue -> u across present and preterite: dormir (duermo / durmió) and morir (muero / murió)!

muro.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin mūrus ('stone wall, city wall').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: muro

muro.notes: Typically denotes a thick exterior or load-bearing stone wall, whereas la pared (< pariēs) is an interior wall.

musical.etymology: Learned derivative from Medieval Latin mūsicālis ('belonging to music'), built on Classical Latin mūsica < Ancient Greek μουσική (τέχνη) (mousikḗ [tékhnē], 'art of the Muses', from Μοῦσα Moûsa 'Muse'). Its modern use as a masculine noun (un musical, 'a stage or film musical') was reinforced in the twentieth century as a semantic loan from English musical (comedy).

morphemes.meaning: music, art of the Muses (< mūsica)

history.meaning: musical (adjective); stage or screen musical (masculine noun)

cognates.meaning: relating to music; musical theatre production

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: musical
Wiktionary — musical

musical.notes: Madrid's Gran Vía—often nicknamed 'el Broadway madrileño'—is the hub of Spanish-language teatro musical.

muy.etymology: Muy is a shortened form of older muito, which continues Latin multum. The DLE also identifies it as a reduced form of mucho; this older family therefore supplies both very and much in modern Spanish.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: muy
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho

muy.notes: In muy claro it raises the degree of clear. It does not change for the number or gender of the people involved.

muñoz.etymology: Historic Spanish patronymic surname ('son of Muño', borne here by actor and singer Miguel Ángel Muñoz), documented across Castile, Navarre, and León since the ninth century (Munioz); formed from the medieval Iberian given name Muño / Munio (a pre-Roman Paleohispanic / Vasco-Aquitanian name attested in Roman Hispania as Munius, widely linked to Basque muino 'hill, mound') + patronymic suffix -oz (variant of -ez).

rootFamily.gloss: sibling patronymic formed with -iz ('son of Muño')

sources.title: Wiktionary — Muñoz

muñoz.notes: Because Muñoz is oxytonic (stressed on the final syllable: mu-ÑOZ) ending in -z, it takes NO written accent—contrast paroxytonic González, López, and Pérez!

my.etymology: Unadapted English first-person singular possessive determiner ('my') spoken in an English self-tape audition slate ('Hello, my name is...'); developed in Middle English by loss of final -n before consonants from Old English mīn ('mine, my'), from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz < Proto-Indo-European *me-, making it an Indo-European cognate of Latin meus and Spanish mi / mío.

sources.title: Wiktionary — my

my.notes: Funny parallel in linguistic history: English shortened mine -> my before nouns just as Latin meus/mea shortened in unstressed pre-nominal Spanish to mi!

mágico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin magicus ('pertaining to magic'), from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós), derived from μάγος (mágos, 'Magian priest, magician', from Old Persian maguš).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mágico
Wiktionary — mágico

más.etymology: Más developed through the older form maes from Latin magis. The modern word expresses a greater quantity or degree and can also intensify a comparison.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: más

más.notes: Más de before a number sets a threshold: más de veinticinco means more than twenty-five.

máximo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin maximus ('greatest, largest, highest'), irregular superlative of magnus ('great, large', from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: máximo
Wiktionary — máximo

máximo.notes: Common expressions: como máximo ('at most'), al máximo ('to the fullest').

métete.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative of pronominal meterse ('get in, step further inside, get involved'), uniting mete + enclitic reflexive pronoun te (< Latin tē) with an esdrújula accent. Meter continues Latin mittere ('to send, let go, hurl'), which underwent a pan-Romance semantic shift in Late Latin from 'throwing/sending into' to 'putting, placing inside'.

history.meaning: get inside!, step into frame!, get involved!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: meter
Wiktionary — métete

métete.notes: High-frequency Peninsular idioms with meterse: ¡Métete más (en plano)! ('Step further into the camera frame!'), ¡Métete en tus asuntos! ('Mind your own business!'), meterse a actor ('go into acting'), meterse con alguien ('pick on / tease someone').

métrico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin metricus ('pertaining to meter or measurement'), from Ancient Greek μετρικός (metrikós), derived from μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: métrico
Wiktionary — métrico

mí.etymology: Mí continues Latin dative pronoun mihi ('to me'). In modern Spanish it survives as the stressed first-person singular pronoun used after prepositions (para mí, cerca de mí).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mí
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

mí.notes: The written accent distinguishes prepositional pronoun mí ('me') from unaccented possessive determiner mi ('my').

mío.etymology: Stressed possessive pronoun and postnominal determiner ('mine, my'), inherited from Latin meus, meum ('my, mine'), with closing of e in hiatus to í by analogy with feminine mía (< mea).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mío
Wiktionary — mío

míralo.etymology: Orthographic compound combining the affirmative tú imperative mira ('look at, check', from mirar < Vulgar Latin *mīrāre < Classical mīrārī 'to marvel at') + enclitic masculine/neuter direct-object pronoun lo ('it, him', < Latin illum), written with an esdrújula accent.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mirar

míralo.notes: Míralo en la agenda ('Check it in your planner!') shows mirar in its everyday sense of 'check / look up', alongside exclamatory ¡Míralo él! ('Just look at him!').

móvil.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mōbilis ('easy to move, movable, changeable', contracted from *movibilis, derived from movēre 'to move', with Spanish v reflecting etymological connection to mover). In late-twentieth-century Peninsular Spanish, teléfono móvil shortened by ellipsis to el móvil ('mobile phone').

history.meaning: movable; motive (of a crime); mobile phone (Spain)

cognates.meaning: movable; furniture (mobile phone in Portugal = telemóvel)

rootFamily.gloss: piece of furniture (inherited popular doublet < mōbilem!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: móvil
Wiktionary — móvil

móvil.notes: Signature Spain vs. Latin America vocabulary split: Spain says el móvil ('mobile phone'), whereas Latin America universally says el celular (or el celu). And notice the doublet: Latin mōbilis gave inherited el mueble ('piece of furniture', i.e. movable property vs. bienes inmuebles 'real estate') and learned el móvil!

música.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mūsica ('the art of music'), from Ancient Greek μουσική (τέχνη) (mousikḕ tékhnē, 'art of the Muses'), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, 'Muse').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: música
Wiktionary — música

nada.etymology: Inherited from the Vulgar Latin phrase (rēs) nāta ('(a thing) born, anything existing', feminine past participle of nāscī 'to be born'), which in negative constructions ('not a born thing') became the negative pronoun 'nothing'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nada
Wiktionary — nada

nadie.etymology: Nadie evolved from Old Spanish nadi, continuing the Latin plural phrase (homĭnēs) nātī ('people born', i.e. 'any living soul') used in negative clauses.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nadie

nadie.notes: Stands alone before the verb (Nadie dice que no) or pairs with no before the verb (No hay nadie).

name.etymology: Unadapted English noun ('personal appellation') spoken in an English self-tape audition ('Hello, my name is...'); inherited in English from Old English nama < Proto-Germanic *namô < Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ ('name'), making it an Indo-European cognate of Latin nōmen and Spanish nombre!

history.meaning: name (spoken in an English audition slate)

cognates.meaning: name (< Old Spanish nomne < Latin nōminem < PIE *h₁nómn̥)

sources.title: Wiktionary — name

name.notes: See how Latin nōminem became Spanish nombre via syncope and dissimilation/epenthesis (nōmine > nomne > nomre > nombre—the exact same path that turned hominem into hombre and fāminem into hambre!).

naranja.etymology: Borrowed from Hispanic Arabic naranǧa, from Classical Arabic nāranǧah ('bitter orange'), transmitted via Persian nārang from Sanskrit nāraṅga ('orange tree').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: naranja
Wiktionary — naranja

nariz.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nārīcae / Late Latin nārīcēs ('nostrils, nose'), an extended derivative of Classical Latin nāris, nārēs ('nostril, nose').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nariz
Wiktionary — nariz

natación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin natātiōnem (nominative natātiō, 'swimming, place for swimming'), action noun of natāre ('to swim', frequentative of nāre 'to float, swim').

rootFamily.gloss: to swim (inherited popular verb < natāre, with -t- > -d-!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: natación
Wiktionary — natación

natación.notes: In Spanish, the everyday verb shows voiced -d- (nadar), while the name of the sport or class keeps learned Latin -t- (tenemos natación, hacer natación).

natalie.etymology: French and English feminine given name (here referring to Academy Award–winning actress Natalie Portman), borrowed via French Nathalie from Late Latin Natālia, derived from (diēs) natālis ('birthday—specifically Christmas Day, natālis Domini', built on nātus, past participle of nāscī 'to be born').

history.meaning: Christian feminine name originally given to girls born at Christmas

cognates.meaning: Natalia (source through which French popularized Nathalie)

sources.title: Wiktionary — Natalie

natalie.notes: Both Natalie/Natalia and French Noël ('Christmas' < natālis) trace back to the same Latin Christmas phrase diēs natālis!

natural.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nātūrālis ('by birth, innate, according to nature, unforced'), derived from nātūra ('birth, innate character, nature'), built on nātus, past participle of nāscī ('to be born', Old Latin gnāscī < Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- 'to beget').

history.meaning: natural, unpretentious; room-temperature (agua natural); native of (natural de)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: natural
Wiktionary — natural

natural.notes: Handy Peninsular restaurant tip: pedir agua del tiempo or agua natural means unchilled 'room-temperature water' (not 'still water', which in Spain is agua sin gas!). Also ser natural de Navarrete means 'to be a native of Navarrete'.

navarrete.etymology: Historic municipality in La Rioja (famed for its pottery and Camino de Santiago heritage, and celebrated in Paquita Salas as Paquita's beloved hometown); founded and chartered in 1195 by Alfonso VIII of Castile as a fortified border settlement facing the Kingdom of Navarre, its name derives from Navarra (from pre-Roman/Basque naba 'high mountain-ringed valley plain' + -ar) + diminutive/toponymic suffix -ete.

history.meaning: fortified Camino de Santiago town near the Navarrese frontier
Riojan town (and widespread Spanish habitational surname)

sources.title: Wiktionary — Navarrete

navarrete.notes: Sits just west of Logroño in La Rioja, renowned for red Riojan wine, market-garden produce (alcachofas, pimientos, melocotones), and traditional red-clay pottery.

navarretense.etymology: Demonym (gentilicio) of Navarrete ('from or belonging to Navarrete'), formed from the toponym Navarrete + the learned Latinate demonym suffix -ense (< Latin -ēnsis, 'belonging to a place').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -ense

navarretense.notes: Demonyms in -ense are invariable for grammatical gender (un vecino navarretense / soy navarretense) and are never capitalized in Spanish.

navarreteña.etymology: Feminine of navarreteño, vernacular demonym (gentilicio) of Navarrete ('native or resident of Navarrete'), formed from Navarrete + the productive Spanish place-origin suffix -eña (< Latin -inea, the same suffix seen in madrileña, malagueña, and riojana/logroñesa).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -eño

navarreteña.notes: Many Spanish towns have two competing gentilicios—one popular (-eño/-ano) and one learned (-ense)—which Paquita playfully hedges between in Yo soy navarreteña de corazón o navarretense!

navidad.etymology: Inherited from Late Ecclesiastical Latin nātīvitātem (nominative nātīvitās, '[Christ's] Nativity, birth'), derived from Classical Latin nātīvus ('born, innate', from nātus, past participle of nāscī 'to be born'), undergoing syncope of the unstressed internal syllable and voicing/loss of dentals (nātīvitātem > Old Spanish nadvidad > navidad).

cognates.meaning: birth of Christ (via Old French nativité)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: navidad
Wiktionary — Navidad

navidad.notes: Capitalized as the name of the holiday (¡Feliz Navidad!, ¿Ya es Navidad?), and often used in the plural (las Navidades) for the entire Spanish holiday season stretching from December 24 (Nochebuena) through January 6 (el Día de Reyes).

ndel.etymology: Fictional surname of avant-garde theatre director 'Aakif Ndel' invented by the writers of Paquita Salas (Season 1, Episode 2) specifically for phonetic comedy: the unusual initial nasal-stop cluster Nd- (reminiscent of West/Central African or cosmopolitan Europeanized surnames) merges in rapid speech with 'Aakif' so that Paquita mishears Aakif Ndel as 'Aquí Fandel'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Ortografía — secuencias consonánticas iniciales

ndel.notes: Because native Spanish phonotactics never allow word-initial nd-, Spanish listeners instinctively resyllabify unfamiliar foreign clusters across word boundaries (Aakif Ndel -> 'Aquí Fandel').

necesitar.etymology: Learned or Medieval Latin formation (necessitāre, 'to compel, stand in need of'), built on Classical Latin necessitās ('need, necessity'), from necesse ('unavoidable, needful').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: necesitar
Wiktionary — necesitar

negra.etymology: Feminine singular of negro ('black, dark'), inherited from Latin nigra (masculine niger, accusative nigrum, 'glossy black, dark, gloomy'), showing regular Romance lowering of stressed short Latin ĭ > e and voicing of -gr-.

history.meaning: black (feminine); quarter note in music; bad luck (tener la negra)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: negro
Wiktionary — negra

negra.notes: Ponerse negra (la pantalla) means 'to go blank/black'; applied to a person in Peninsular slang, ¡Me pones negra! means 'You're driving me mad / infuriating me!', and tener la negra means 'to have a run of rotten luck'.

negritos.etymology: Masculine plural diminutive of negro ('black', < Latin nigrum) + suffix -ito + plural -s; quoted here inside Paquita's malapropism 'Cien negritos' for the traditional Spanish stage title Diez negritos (Agatha Christie's 1939 mystery novel and 1943 play now titled Y no quedó ninguno / And Then There Were None).

history.meaning: diminutive plural (traditionally in the play title Diez negritos)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: negro

negritos.notes: In modern Spanish editions, Agatha Christie's mystery was retitled Y no quedó ninguno (matching English And Then There Were None), though older Spanish stage revivals long billed it as Diez negritos—which Paquita inflates tenfold to 'Cien negritos' (blending it with 101 dálmatas!).

negro.etymology: Negro continues Latin niger, nigra, nigrum ('glossy black, dark'), with short Latin ĭ lowering regularly to Castilian e.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: negro

negro.notes: Té negro is black tea; for black espresso coffee in Spain, speakers normally say un café solo.

nena.etymology: Feminine of nene ('baby, toddler; colloquially kid, girl, sweetheart'), an expressive nursery formation (Lallwort) created from reduplicated child-speech syllables nen- (parallel to Catalan nen/nena 'boy/girl', Italian ninnolo/ninna, and Spanish niño).

history.meaning: little girl; colloquially 'young woman, kid, babe/darling'

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nene
Wiktionary — nena

nena.notes: Very common in warm, slightly maternal Peninsular speech (esta nena, ¡Hola, nena!), and even more frequent in Eastern Spain (Catalonia/Valencia, reinforced by Catalan nena) and Argentina.

nepotismo.etymology: Borrowed (via French népotisme or directly) from Italian nepotismo ('favoritism shown to relatives, originally the Renaissance papal practice of elevating a pope's nephews to cardinalates and lucrative offices'), built on Italian nepote ('nephew, grandson') < Latin nepōtem (nominative nepōs, 'grandson, descendant; in Late Latin, nephew').

rootFamily.gloss: grandson (inherited popular Castilian cousin < Vulgar Latin *neptus / nepōtem!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nepotismo
Wiktionary — nepotismo

nepotismo.notes: In everyday Peninsular Spanish, hiring relatives or friends through connections is colloquially called enchufismo (entrar por enchufe, 'to get in via connections').

nervio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Vulgar/Late Latin nervium for Classical Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, bowstring, muscle, vigor', from Proto-Indo-European *sneh₁wr̥, cognate with Ancient Greek νεῦρον neûron 'sinew, nerve').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nervio
Wiktionary — nervio

nervio.notes: In the plural, ¡Qué nervios! ('What nerves / I'm so nervous!') and ponerse de los nervios ('to get worked up / stressed out') are constant before auditions and exams.

nerviosa.etymology: Feminine singular of nervioso ('nervous, anxious, high-strung; relating to the nerves'), reshaped on nervio from Latin nervōsus—which in Classical Latin meant 'sinewy, muscular, vigorous, energetic' before modern medicine shifted its everyday meaning to 'excitable, anxious'!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nervioso
Wiktionary — nerviosa

nerviosa.notes: Watch ser vs. estar: estoy muy nerviosa means 'I'm feeling really nervous right now (before the casting)', whereas soy muy nerviosa means 'I'm a high-strung / anxious person by temperament'.

nerviosas.etymology: Feminine plural of nervioso ('nervous, jittery'), formed from nervio (< Latin nervium / nervus) + adjectival suffix -osas (< Latin -ōsās).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nervioso

nerviosas.notes: Pairs with vosotros/vosotras plural verb forms in Spain when addressing an all-female group: estáis muy nerviosas.

nervioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nervōsus ('sinewy, vigorous'; remodeled on nervio < Late Latin nervium / Classical nervus 'sinew, tendon, nerve'), shifting in modern usage to 'relating to the nerves, anxious, excitable'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nervioso
Wiktionary — nervioso

nevera.etymology: Nevera derives from nieve ('snow', from Latin nix, nivis) + place suffix -era: historically an icehouse packed with mountain snow to preserve food, now the household refrigerator.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nevera
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nieve

nevera.notes: La nevera (alongside el frigorífico) is the everyday Peninsula Spanish word for fridge.

ni.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish ni / nin from Latin nec ('and not, nor, neither').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ni
Wiktionary — ni

nieto.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *neptus ('grandson'), a masculine form remodeled on feminine nepta (for Classical Latin nepōs, nepōtis 'grandson, descendant').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nieto
Wiktionary — nieto

nieve.etymology: Continues Latin nix, nivis (accusative nivem, 'snow'), reshaped with diphthong ie by analogy with the verb nieva (< Vulgar Latin *nĕvat).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nieve

nieve.notes: Blanco como la nieve is a proverbial comparison for spotless white fabric.

ninguno.etymology: Inherited from Latin nec ūnus ('not even one, no one, none'), via Old Spanish neguno with voicing of -c- to -g- and anticipatory nasalization to ninguno.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ninguno
Wiktionary — ninguno

nivel.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Iberia from Old Occitan nivel ('plumb-line level, horizontal plane', compare Catalan nivell and Old French nivel > niveau), descending from Vulgar Latin *lībellus ('little balance, carpenter's level'), diminutive of Classical Latin lībra ('pair of scales, balance, level'), with consonant dissimilation of l...l > n...l.

cognates.meaning: horizontal plane, tier (via Old French livel < *lībellus, before French dissimilated to niveau!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nivel
Wiktionary — nivel

nivel.notes: Notice how Italian livello and English level kept the original initial l- of Latin *lībellus, while Occitan, French (niveau), Spanish (nivel), and Portuguese (nível) dissimilated it to n-! Common phrase: a nivel europeo / nacional ('at the European / national level').

niña.etymology: Feminine of niño ('child, girl'), a hallmark medieval Castilian expressive nursery word (Old Spanish ninno / ninna) formed by affective consonant gemination and palatalization (*ninno > niño, with Latin/proto-Romance -nn- palatalizing regularly in Castilian to -ñ-, just as annus > año).

history.meaning: girl, female child; pupil of the eye (la niña del ojo)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: niño
Wiktionary — niña

niña.notes: In Spain (especially southern Spain and affectionate showbusiness speech like Paquita's), la niña / mis niñas is warmly used for grown young women whom the speaker mentors or dotes on ('my girl' = está la niña nominada).

niñas.etymology: Feminine plural of niño ('girls, female children'), from Old Spanish ninnas (expressive nursery root *ninn- with Castilian palatalization -nn- > -ñ-).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: niño

niñas.notes: Las niñas refers specifically to an all-female group of girls, whereas mixed groups of boys and girls use masculine plural los niños.

niño.etymology: Inherited from Old Spanish ninno, an expressive nursery formation built on the palatal nasal reduplication *ninno ('child, little one').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: niño
Wiktionary — niño

niños.etymology: Masculine plural of niño ('boys; children'), descending from Old Spanish ninnos, an expressive Castilian nursery creation (*ninno) with regular palatalization of geminate -nn- > -ñ-.

cognates.meaning: Pacific climate oscillation (borrowed from Peruvian Spanish '[Christ] Child')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: niño
Wiktionary — niños

niños.notes: Don't forget 'personal a' when human beings are the direct object of a verb: Está entrenando a los niños ('He is coaching the kids').

no.etymology: No continues Latin nōn ('not'). In Spanish it serves both as the standalone negative answer ('no') and as the preverbal negator placed directly before the verb phrase.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: no

no.notes: When negative words like nadie or nada follow the verb, no still precedes the verb (No hay nadie en el patio).

noche.etymology: Noche descends regularly from Latin nox, noctis ('night'), showing palatalization of medial -ct- > -ch- (compare leche < *lacte, ocho < octo).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: noche

noche.notes: Esta noche means 'tonight', anoche means 'last night', and ¡Buenas noches! serves as both 'good evening' after dark and 'good night'.

nogal.etymology: Derived with the tree-collective suffix -al from Vulgar Latin *nucālis, built on Latin nux, nucis ('walnut, nut').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nogal

nombrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin nōmināre ('to call by name, name, appoint'), with regular syncope (*nōm'nāre) and dissimilation of -mn- to -mbr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nombrar
Wiktionary — nombrar

nombre.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish nomne from Latin nōmen, nōminis ('name, noun'), with syncope of the unstressed vowel (*nōm'ne) and regular Castilian evolution of -mn- to -mbr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nombre
Wiktionary — nombre

nominado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun of nominar ('nominated; nominee'), learned borrowing from Latin nōminātus, past participle of nōmināre ('to call by name, appoint or propose for office', derived from nōmen, nōminis 'name'). Its modern awards-season sense ('shortlisted for a prize', nominada al Goya) expanded in the late twentieth century under English influence.

history.meaning: to name, propose for office > named, nominated
nominated (for an award or reality-TV vote); nominee

cognates.meaning: put forward as a candidate for an award or office

rootFamily.gloss: to name, appoint (inherited popular doublet < nōmināre!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nominar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: nominar

nominado.notes: After decades of purist debate (preferring candidato/finalista), the RAE fully endorsed nominar and nominado for awards such as the Oscars and Goyas!

norma.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nōrma ('carpenter's square, rule, pattern, standard').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: norma
Wiktionary — norma

nos.etymology: Unstressed object and reflexive pronoun nos ('us, to us, ourselves') continues Latin accusative/dative nōs unchanged.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nos

nos.notes: Also marks reciprocal action: ¡Nos vemos! ('See you!', literally 'we see each other') and nos tuteamos ('we use tú with each other').

nosotros.etymology: Nosotros fused Old Spanish nos ('we', from Latin nōs) with otros ('others', from Latin altĕrōs), originally contrasting 'we ourselves (as opposed to others)' before becoming the standard subject pronoun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nosotros

nosotros.notes: Feminine nosotras is used when an all-female group speaks of itself.

nota.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin nota ('mark, sign, written character, musical note, memorandum').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nota
Wiktionary — nota

noticia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nōtitia ('celebrity, being known, acquaintance, knowledge, news'), derived from nōtus ('known', past participle of nōscere 'to come to know').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: noticia
Wiktionary — noticia

novata.etymology: Feminine form of novato ('beginner, novice, newcomer'), derived from Latin novātus / novus ('new') with the suffix -ato (used for young animals or beginners).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: novato
Wiktionary — novata

noveno.etymology: Ordinal numeral formed in Spanish from nueve ('nine', < Latin novem) + the suffix -eno (< Latin -ēnus), largely replacing inherited nono (< Latin nōnus 'ninth').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: noveno
Wiktionary — noveno

novia.etymology: Feminine of novio, continuing Vulgar/Hispano-Latin novia ('bride, newlywed wife'), built on Classical Latin novus ('new': originally nova nūpta, 'new bride' on her wedding day), broadening within Spanish to cover all three stages of romance: 'girlfriend', 'fiancée', and 'bride'.

rootFamily.gloss: new (< Latin novus, with diphthongization ŏ > ue)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: novio
Wiktionary — novia

novia.notes: Context decides which English word fits! At a wedding (¡No eres la novia!, ¡Viva la novia!), la novia means 'the bride'; in everyday life (mi novia), it means 'my girlfriend' (or 'fiancée', also mi prometida).

novio.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned from Hispano-Latin novius ('newlywed husband, bridegroom'), derived from Classical Latin novus ('new', preserving un-diphthongized o because of the following palatal glide yod in -ius, contrast nuevo < novum!). Extended in Spanish from 'groom' to 'fiancé' and 'boyfriend'.

history.meaning: groom; fiancé; boyfriend; plural los novios 'the bride and groom / couple'

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: novio
Wiktionary — novio

novio.notes: Phonological gem: why did Latin novum diphthongize to nuevo while novius stayed novio? In Castilian, the palatal glide (yod) in -io raised/checked short ŏ and blocked diphthongization (the exact same reason octō > ocho and noctem > noche didn't diphthongize!).

nuestro.etymology: Nuestro continues Vulgar Latin *noster, nostra, nostrum ('our, ours'), showing diphthongization of short stressed ŏ to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nuestro

nuestro.notes: Agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed (nuestro barrio, nuestra puerta, nuestros clientes).

nueve.etymology: Nueve descends from Latin novem ('nine'), with stressed short ŏ diphthongizing regularly to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nueve

nuevo.etymology: Nuevo continues Latin novus ('new, fresh, recent'), diphthongizing stressed short ŏ to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nuevo

nuevo.notes: De nuevo means 'again' (¡Buenos días de nuevo! = Good morning again!).

numerito.etymology: Diminutive formed within Spanish from número ('number; theatrical act; colloquial scene or fuss', < Latin numerus) + -ito.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: número
Wiktionary — numerito

nunca.etymology: Inherited from Latin numquam / nunquam ('never', formed from negative ne- + unquam 'ever').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nunca
Wiktionary — nunca

número.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin numerus ('number, count, measure, rhythm').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: número
Wiktionary — número

o.etymology: The conjunction o ('or') continues Latin aut ('or'), with Latin au monophthongizing regularly to Castilian o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: o

o.notes: Changes spelling and sound to u before words starting with /o/ (o- or ho-, e.g. siete u ocho).

objeto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obiectum ('something presented to the senses or mind, object, goal'), neuter past participle of Classical Latin obicere (ob- + iacere 'to throw before, present').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: objeto
Wiktionary — objeto

obra.etymology: Inherited from Latin opera ('work, effort, labor'), originally feminine singular collective alongside the neuter plural of opus, operis ('work, accomplishment'), undergoing regular Castilian syncope of the unstressed post-tonic vowel (-e-) and voicing of intervocalic -p- > -b- (opera > obra).

history.meaning: work, artistic creation, stage play (obra de teatro), construction site (obras)

cognates.meaning: Italian musical loan / learned Latin verb

rootFamily.gloss: musical opera (doublet borrowed from Italian opera!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: obra
Wiktionary — obra

obra.notes: Three core everyday meanings in Spain: una obra (de teatro) = 'a play'; una obra maestra = 'a masterpiece'; estar en obras = 'to be under construction / renovation'.

ochenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin octāginta (for Classical Latin octōgintā 'eighty', derived from octō 'eight'), with regular Castilian palatalization of -ct- to -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ochenta
Wiktionary — ochenta

ocho.etymology: Ocho descends regularly from Latin octō ('eight'), with medial -ct- palatalizing to Castilian -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ocho

ocho.notes: Las ocho en punto means 'eight o'clock sharp'.

octava.etymology: Learned feminine form of Latin octāvus ('eighth', from octo 'eight'), short for octāva consonántia ('eighth note of the diatonic scale').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: octava

octava.notes: The popular inherited outcome of octāvus is ochavo (a historic copper coin).

ocupado.etymology: Participial adjective of ocupar ('busy, occupied, taken'), from Latin occupātus, past participle of occupāre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ocupado
Wiktionary — ocupado

ocupar.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin occupāre ('to take possession of, fill a space, employ, keep busy'), formed from ob- + capere ('to take, seize').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ocupar
Wiktionary — ocupar

odiar.etymology: Learned or semi-learned verb from Late Latin odiāre ('to hate', built on Classical Latin odium 'hatred', replacing the defective Classical verb ōdisse).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: odiar
Wiktionary — odiar

of.etymology: Unadapted English preposition ('of') quoted inside the conversational phrase 'Of course' (and the series title House of Cards); inherited in English as the unstressed proclitic doublet of off, from Old English of ('away from, out of, of'), from Proto-Germanic *ab < Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó.

history.meaning: away from, out of, belonging to
preposition; in 'of course' = 'naturally, as a matter of course'

rootFamily.gloss: of course! (¡Claro! / Por supuesto = Spanish equivalents of 'Of course!')

sources.title: Wiktionary — of

of.notes: 'Of course!' is one of the stock English phrases Spanish characters proudly toss out to claim fluency before an international audition starts.

oficial.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin officiālis ('belonging to duty or office; magistrate's assistant, official'), derived from Classical Latin officium ('service, duty, office').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oficial
Wiktionary — oficial

oficina.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin officīna ('workshop, manufactory, office'), contracted from *opificīna, from opifex ('craftsman, worker', from opus 'work' + facere 'to make').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oficina
Wiktionary — oficina

oficio.etymology: Oficio continues Latin officium, duty, service or function. Spanish uses it for a skilled trade or craft learned through practice as well as an official duty or occupation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oficio

oficio.notes: Compare el oficio (a skilled craft or trade) with la oficina (an office room or workplace).

ofrecer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *offerēscere, an inchoative remodeling of Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, offer', from ob- + ferre 'to carry').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ofrecer
Wiktionary — ofrecer

oh.etymology: Natural expressive interjection continuing Latin ō / oh, voicing surprise, wonder, joy, or regret.

pepe.etymology: Traditional Spanish hypocoristic of the masculine name José ('Joseph', < Latin Iōsēphus < Ancient Greek Iōsḗph < Hebrew Yōsēf, 'may He add'). Romance philologists link Pepe to infant-speech labial reduplication on the stressed final syllable of medieval Jusepe / Josepe (exact parallel to Italian Giuseppe > Peppe / Beppe), while a celebrated Hispanic folk tradition derives it from the abbreviation P.P. for Latin Pater Putativus ('putative/earthly father [of Christ]'), written beside Saint Joseph's name in liturgical calendars.

piensa.notes: Used conversationally in Pues piensa que... ('Just bear in mind / think about the fact that...'), imperative piensa invites the listener to reframe a situation.
