pila.etymology: Inherited from Latin pīla ('pillar, pier, stacked column'), originally denoting a heap or stack; in 1800 Alessandro Volta built the first electric battery out of a vertical stack of alternating zinc and copper discs (Italian pila di Volta, French pile électrique), giving Spanish pila its modern sense 'small battery cell'. (A homonymous Spanish noun pila 'stone basin, sink, baptismal font' descends separately from Latin pila 'stone mortar'.)

cognates.meaning: heap, stack; early physics term 'voltaic pile'

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pila
Wiktionary — pila

pila.notes: Spanish distinguishes una pila (a small AA/AAA household battery) from una batería (a rechargeable phone or car battery). From the toy metaphor comes the ubiquitous idiom ponerse las pilas ('to put one's batteries in' = 'to get moving, buckle down, step up one's game').

pillar.etymology: Borrowed in the Renaissance via Italian pigliare (reinforced by Old French piller), descending from Vulgar Latin *pīliāre ('to plunder, seize, snatch'), an expanded form of Classical Latin pīlāre / compīlāre ('to pillage, rob'). In modern Peninsular Spanish it relaxed from 'plunder' into an indispensable everyday verb meaning 'to catch, grab, pick up, or understand'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pillar
Wiktionary — pillar

pillar.notes: One of Peninsular Spanish's most versatile colloquial verbs: pillar un resfriado ('catch a cold'), pillar un taxi ('grab a cab'), ¿Lo pillas? ('Do you get it?'), and ¡Ya te pillaré! ('I'll catch up with you / get you yet!').

pillaron.etymology: Third-person plural preterite indicative of pillar ('they caught [us]'), combining the borrowed Italianate stem pill- (< pigliare < Vulgar Latin *pīliāre 'to seize, catch') with the inherited preterite ending -aron (< Latin -ārunt < -āvērunt).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pillar
Wiktionary — pillaron

pillaron.notes: Nos pillaron (with unspecified plural 'they') is the idiomatic Spanish equivalent of passive 'We got caught / busted!'

pimiento.etymology: Inherited from Latin pigmentum ('coloring matter, pigment', derived from pingere 'to paint, color'), which in Late and Medieval Latin shifted to 'aromatic herb, pungent spice' and yielded Old Spanish pimienta ('black pepper'). When sixteenth-century Spaniards encountered New World Capsicum fruits, they coined the masculine counterpart pimiento for the pepper plant and its fleshy pods (such as the famous roasted pimientos of La Rioja and Navarre).

history.meaning: bell pepper, sweet or hot Capsicum pepper

cognates.meaning: bell pepper / chili or black pepper
pimento (borrowed from Spanish) and pigment (learned Latinate doublet)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pimiento
Wiktionary — pimiento

pimiento.notes: Gender marks a clean culinary distinction in Spain: la pimienta is ground peppercorn on the table, el pimiento is the fresh or roasted vegetable pepper, and el pimentón is paprika.

pinchado.etymology: Participial adjective of pinchar ('punctured, flat, pricked'), derived from Vulgar Latin *pūnctiāre (built on Classical Latin pūnctus, past participle of pungere 'to prick, pierce').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pinchado
Wiktionary — pinchado

pintado.etymology: Participial adjective of pintar ('painted, colored'), from Vulgar Latin *pīnctāre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pintado
Wiktionary — pintado

pintar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīnctāre ('to paint'), built on *pīnctus (nasalized variant of Classical Latin pictus, past participle of pingere 'to paint, embroider').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pintar
Wiktionary — pintar

pintura.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīnctūra for Classical Latin pictūra ('painting, picture, pigment'), derived from pingere ('to paint').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pintura
Wiktionary — pintura

pinza.etymology: Borrowed from Italian pinza or French pince ('pincer, clip, clothespin, tweezers'), deverbal noun from Old French pincier (< Vulgar Latin *pīnctiāre 'to pinch, nip').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pinza
Wiktionary — pinza

pisar.etymology: Inherited from Latin pīnsāre ('to pound in a mortar, stamp, tread upon'), frequentative of pīnsere ('to pound, crush'), with regular reduction of -ns- to -s-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pisar
Wiktionary — pisar

piso.etymology: Deverbal noun from pisar ('to tread, step on', < Latin pīnsāre), evolving semantically from 'trodden ground, floor surface' to 'story of a building' and 'apartment occupying a floor'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: piso
Wiktionary — piso

pistola.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century via French pistole and German Pistole, ultimately from Czech píšťala ('whistle, pipe; early Hussite hand-cannon', derived from the onomatopoeic Slavic verb píštěti 'to whistle, hiss'), coined during the fifteenth-century Bohemian Hussite Wars and adapted in Spanish with the feminine ending -a.

rootFamily.gloss: pistol shot; starting gun (pistoletazo de salida)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pistola
Wiktionary — pistola

pistola.notes: Along with robot and polca, pistola is one of the very few everyday Spanish words of Czech origin! Putting una pistola en la sien ('a gun to one's temple') is a common hyperbole for extreme pressure.

piti.etymology: Colloquial Peninsular Spanish personal nickname Piti, formed from the expressive diminutive stem piti- ('tiny, petite', compare pitiminí and French petit) or by hypocoristic clipping of names such as Esperanza / Pitita or Pilar; in the episode no full legal name is stated behind the nickname.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pitiminí

piti.notes: In Spain, short two-syllable nicknames ending in -i (Piti, Sofi, Paqui, Chuchi) are ubiquitous in casual and show-business circles; note that lowercase un piti is also Madrid slang for a cigarette.

pizarra.etymology: Pre-Roman Paleohispanic borrowing closely linked to Basque lapitz-arri ('slate stone', from lapitz 'slate' + harri 'stone'), applied first to dark roofing slate and later to writing blackboards.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pizarra
Wiktionary — pizarra

pizca.etymology: Deverbal noun from pizcar ('to pinch, nip off a tiny piece'), an expressive creation akin to pellizcar and Italian pizzicare, meaning 'a tiny pinch, speck, bit'.

history.meaning: to pinch off a tiny bit

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pizca
Wiktionary — pizca

pizza.etymology: Modern internationalism borrowed from Italian pizza (originally Southern Italian and Neapolitan seasoned flatbread, first attested in Medieval Latin at Gaeta in 997 CE); Italian etymologists debate whether pizza continues Byzantine Greek pítta (πίττα, 'flat cake, pie'), Lombardic bizzo ('mouthful, bite of bread'), or Vulgar Latin *pīnsāre ('to pound, flatten dough').

history.meaning: baked flatbread topped with tomato and cheese

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Italian (and Greek/Levantine pita if from the same Mediterranean root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pizza
Wiktionary — pizza

pizza.notes: Because double -zz- does not exist natively in Spanish orthography, the RAE writes pizza in italics as an unadapted Italianism; speakers in Spain pronounce it [ˈpit.sa], [ˈpid.sa], or [ˈpiθ.θa].

placa.etymology: Borrowed from French plaque ('flat metal or stone plate, badge, cooking hob'), which derives from Middle Dutch placke ('flat disk, coin, patch').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: placa
Wiktionary — placa

placita.etymology: Diminutive formed within Spanish from plaza ('public square, plaza') + -ita; plaza descends from Vulgar Latin *plattea for Classical Latin platēa ('broad street, courtyard') < Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, 'wide street').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plaza
Wiktionary — placita

plan.etymology: Borrowed from French plan ('ground plan, draft, project, scheme'), substantivized from the French adjective plan ('flat', < Latin plānus, influenced by Italian piano).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plan
Wiktionary — plan

plancha.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages via Old French planche ('plank, flat board, metal plate'), descending from Late Latin planca ('flat board, slab', feminine of Classical Latin plancus 'flat-footed', from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂n̥kós 'flat'). From 'heated flat metal plate', Spanish developed both 'clothes iron / grill griddle' and the Peninsular colloquial metaphor tener mucha plancha ('to have a mountain of ironing = to have tons of pending work').

history.meaning: metal plate; clothes iron; griddle; backlog of work (colloquial)

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old Norman French planke (< Late Latin planca)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plancha
Wiktionary — plancha

plancha.notes: Two essential Peninsular expressions use la plancha: culinary a la plancha ('seared on a hot flat griddle', e.g., gambas a la plancha) and office slang tener mucha plancha ('to be swamped with a huge pile of work, like a basket of unironed laundry').

planear.etymology: Conflates two derivations: 'to plan, devise a project' formed in Spanish from plan ('project') + -ear; and 'to glide on outstretched wings' borrowed from French planer (< Late Latin plānāre 'to make level').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: planear
Wiktionary — planear

plano.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin plānus ('flat, level, even, plane; drawn map or floorplan'), forming a doublet alongside inherited popular llano.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plano
Wiktionary — plano

planta.etymology: Planta continues Latin planta ('sprout, shoot; sole of the foot'), extending from a living plant and ground footprint to each storey or floor of a building.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: planta

planta.notes: In Spain la planta baja is the ground floor, la primera planta is one flight up, and la segunda planta is two flights up.

plantado.etymology: Participial adjective of plantar ('planted, standing firm; left waiting'), inherited from Latin plantātus, past participle of plantāre ('to set shoots in the ground, fix firmly', from planta).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plantado
Wiktionary — plantado

plateado.etymology: Participial adjective of platear ('silver-plated, silvery'), derived from plata ('silver', originally 'flat sheet or plate of metal', from Vulgar Latin *platta 'flat').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plateado
Wiktionary — plateado

plato.etymology: Substantivized masculine noun from Vulgar Latin *plattus ('flat, shallow dish'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platýs, 'broad, flat').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plato
Wiktionary — plato

plaza.etymology: Plaza descends from Vulgar Latin *plattea (Classical Latin platēa, 'broad street, courtyard', from Greek plateîa, 'wide way').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plaza

plaza.notes: Diminutive la placita names a small, intimate neighbourhood square.

plegable.etymology: Derived within Spanish from plegar ('to fold', < Latin plicāre) + the suffix -ble ('foldable, collapsible').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plegable
Wiktionary — plegable

plegar.etymology: Semi-learned reflex of Latin plicāre ('to fold, bend together'), preserving the initial cluster pl- alongside the inherited popular doublet llegar ('to arrive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plegar
Wiktionary — plegar

pleno.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin plēnus ('full, complete, entire'), forming a learned doublet alongside inherited popular lleno.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pleno
Wiktionary — pleno

pluma.etymology: Learned or semi-learned retention of Latin plūma ('soft down feather, plumage'), preserving the initial cluster pl- intact (unlike purely popular Spanish words where initial pl- palatalized to ll-, as in plovere > llover or plēnus > lleno). Extended in modern Spanish to a quill/fountain pen and, in Peninsular colloquial slang, to 'campiness, flamboyant or effeminate mannerisms' (from ostentatious decorative plumage).

rootFamily.gloss: feather duster; (ver el plumero) 'see someone's true motives'
to pluck; fleece someone of money

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pluma
Wiktionary — pluma

pluma.notes: In Spain's queer and theatrical vernacular, tener pluma (or subirse de pluma) refers to visible campiness or flamboyant gesture—frequently reclaimed with pride (¡Viva la pluma!).

pobre.etymology: Inherited from Latin pauper, pauperem ('poor, of scanty means'), showing monophthongization of au to o and regular voicing of -p- before -r- to -b-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pobre
Wiktionary — pobre

pobres.etymology: Plural of pobre ('poor; unfortunate; poor people'), inherited from Latin pauper, pauperem ('of small means, producing little', an ancient compound of paucus 'few, little' + -per from parere 'to produce, bring forth'), with regular monophthongization of au to o, syncope of the post-tonic vowel, and voicing of -p- to -b-.

cognates.meaning: poor (via Anglo-Norman povre) and pauper (learned Latin legal borrowing)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pobre
Wiktionary — pobre

pobres.notes: Word position changes meaning with pobre: after the noun (una familia pobre) it means 'financially poor', whereas before the noun (¡pobre mujer!) it expresses sympathy ('unfortunate, poor thing').

poco.etymology: Poco descends regularly from Latin paucus ('few, little'), with Latin au monophthongizing to Castilian o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poco

poco.notes: Un poco de ('a little bit of') stays masculine singular even before feminine uncountable nouns (un poco de leche, un poco de agua).

podemos.etymology: First-person plural present indicative of poder ('we can, we are able to'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *potēmus (infinitive *potēre, regularized from Classical Latin anomalous posse, itself a univerbation of potis 'able, powerful' + esse 'to be'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

cognates.meaning: learned/French borrowings from the same Latin pot- stem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poder
Wiktionary — podemos

podemos.notes: Because stress falls on the ending -emos rather than the root, podemos keeps unstressed o (unlike diphthongized yo puedo, tú puedes, él puede).

poder.etymology: Poder evolved from Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularizing Classical Latin posse ('to be able, have power').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poder

poder.notes: Followed directly by an infinitive without any preposition (¿Puede ayudarme?, no puedo abrirla).

policía.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin polītīa ('state organization, public administration'), from Ancient Greek politeía (πολιτεία, 'citizenship, civic order, commonwealth', derived from polítēs 'citizen' and pólis 'city-state'). Under eighteen- and nineteenth-century French influence (police), its meaning narrowed from 'good civic order and urban cleanliness' to the law-enforcement institution and, by metonymy, an individual police officer.

cognates.meaning: doublets via French from Late Latin polītīa

rootFamily.gloss: politics, policy (from the same Greek pólis family)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: policía
Wiktionary — policía

policía.notes: Watch the article gender: la policía (feminine) is the collective police force ('Call the police!'), whereas un policía / una policía is an individual male or female officer (as in the Austrian detective series Rex, un policía diferente).

polvo.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish polvos (with labial metathesis from *pūlvos) from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, a second-declension remodeling of Classical Latin pulvis, pulveris ('dust, powder').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: polvo
Wiktionary — polvo

pondría.etymology: First- or third-person singular conditional of poner ('I/he/she would put'), formed from the syncopated Old Spanish future/conditional stem ponr- (< poner + había, Latin pōnere habēbat) with an epenthetic consonant -d- inserted to ease the transition from alveolar nasal n to trilled r (pon- + -d- + -ría).

morphemes.meaning: transitional stop between n and r

cognates.meaning: would lay (eggs) — showing the exact same epenthetic -d-!

rootFamily.gloss: I will put (future with the same pondr- stem)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — pondría

pondría.notes: Notice the shared epenthetic -d- rule across Spanish irregular futures and conditionals: poner -> pondría, tener -> tendría, venir -> vendría, salir -> saldría, valer -> valdría.

ponemos.etymology: First-person plural present indicative of poner ('we put, write down, include'), descending from Latin pōnimus (1pl of third-conjugation pōnere 'to put, place', < archaic *posinere), regularized into the Spanish second conjugation (-er, -emos).

morphemes.meaning: put, place, write down (< Latin pōnere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — ponemos

ponemos.notes: When filling out a CV or form in Spain, poner often means 'to write down / list' (le ponemos que ha hecho un capitulito = 'we'll put down that she did a little episode').

poner.etymology: Poner continues Latin pōnĕre ('to place, put, set down'), shifting to the Spanish second conjugation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner

poner.notes: Irregular forms include pongo (1sg present), pon (tú command), puse/puso (preterite), and puesto (past participle).

ponga.etymology: First- or third-person singular present subjunctive (and usted imperative) of poner ('put, pour, serve'), built on the velarized stem pong- (as in 1sg indicative pongo), which arose in Iberian Romance by analogy with verbs whose Latin -eō / -iō endings evolved a velar -g- (such as tangō / *tengō > tengo, *vengō > vengo), ultimately from Latin pōnere ('to put, place').

rootFamily.gloss: I put (1sg indicative base of all pong- subjunctives)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — ponga

ponga.notes: In Spanish hospitality and bars, poner is the natural verb for serving food or drink: ¿Quieres que te ponga un café? ('Shall I pour/make you a coffee?').

ponme.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative pon of poner fused with the enclitic first-person singular indirect object pronoun me ('put on for me; serve/pour me'). Bare imperative pon resulted from regular Old Spanish apocope of final -e after single alveolar n in Latin pōne ('put!').

morphemes.meaning: for me, to me (1sg indirect object)

history.meaning: put on for me / get me (a drink, episode, song)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — ponme

ponme.notes: One of the handiest everyday chunks in Spain: Ponme otro capítulo ('Put on another episode for me') at home, and Ponme una caña / un gin-tonic ('Get me a draft beer / gin and tonic') at a bar—never harsh, perfectly natural.

ponte.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative pon of poner (< Latin pōne, 'place!, put!') fused with the enclitic reflexive pronoun te (< Latin tē, 'yourself'). Used both for putting on clothing and for positioning oneself or adopting a pose.

history.meaning: stand/pose like this; put on (clothing); get to work (ponte a...)

rootFamily.gloss: to put on; become; move into position

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — ponte

ponte.notes: During photo shoots or auditions, ¡Ponte así! means 'Stand like this / strike this pose!'; on the phone in Spain, ¡Ponte! means 'Come to the phone / take the receiver!'

poquillo.etymology: Affective diminutive of poco ('little, a bit') formed with -illo (< Latin -icellus / -iculus) and orthographic change c -> qu before i to preserve the velar stop [k]. Base word poco descends from Latin paucus ('few, scarce, small'), with regular monophthongization of au to o.

history.meaning: a little -> a tiny bit, slightly

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poco
Wiktionary — poquillo

poquillo.notes: In Peninsular Spanish, un poquillo (se agobió un poquillo) is a warm, understated hedge that downplays awkwardness or stress ('just a teeny bit').

por.etymology: Por merges Latin pro ('on behalf of, in exchange for, because of') and per ('through, along, by means of') into a single versatile Spanish preposition.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: por

por.notes: Marks parts of the day (por la mañana, por la tarde), movement through space (por el puente, por la escalera), and cause or motive (por favor).

porcelana.etymology: The DLE identifies porcelana as a borrowing from Italian porcellana, originally the glossy white cowrie shell and later applied to translucent Chinese ceramic ware whose glaze recalled the shell.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: porcelana

porcelana.notes: Besides teacups, classic electrical fuse carriers were traditionally made of white insulating porcelana.

porque.etymology: Causal conjunction formed in Old Spanish by univerbating the preposition por (< Latin pro / per) and the conjunction que (< Latin quid / quod, 'for the reason that, because').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: porque
Wiktionary — porque

portero.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin portārius ('gatekeeper, doorkeeper'), derived from Classical Latin porta ('city gate, door', cognate with portus 'harbor') plus the occupational suffix -ārius (> Spanish -ero).

morphemes.meaning: door, gate (< Latin porta; compare puerta)

cognates.meaning: gatekeeper (via Anglo-Norman portier; luggage 'porter' comes separately from portare 'to carry')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: portero
Wiktionary — portero

portero.notes: In Madrid apartment blocks, el portero (or el conserje) staffs the ground-floor lobby and accepts deliveries; el portero automático is the entryway intercom buzzer, and in soccer el portero is the goalkeeper.

portman.etymology: English surname Portman (here referring to Academy Award–winning actress Natalie Portman, who adopted her maternal grandmother's maiden name as her screen surname), from Middle English portman ('townsman, burgess of a market town or port; town gatekeeper'), a compound of Old English port ('harbor, market town, gate', itself early-borrowed from Latin portus and porta) + mann ('person, man').

morphemes.meaning: port, market town, gate (< Old English port < Latin portus/porta)
citizen or keeper (< Old English mann)

history.meaning: citizen of a port or market town; occupational surname
American-Israeli film actress cited in casting dialogue

sources.title: Wiktionary — portman

portman.notes: Curiously, English Portman and Spanish portero share the exact same ultimate Latin root (porta / portus)!

portón.etymology: Augmentative formed within Spanish on the non-diphthongized stem port- of puerta ('door, gate', < Latin porta) + -ón ('large entrance gate, heavy outer door').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: portón
Wiktionary — portón

posada.etymology: Posada derives from posar ('to lodge, rest, set down one's load', from Late Latin pausāre, 'to pause, halt for rest').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posada
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posar

posada.notes: Historically a traditional Spanish coaching inn where travellers paused for lodging and meals.

posible.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin possibilis ('capable of happening or being done'), derived with the potential suffix -bilis from the stem of posse ('to be able', Classical contraction of potis esse).

history.meaning: that may exist or be done

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French from Late Latin possibilis

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posible
Wiktionary — posible

posible.notes: Written with a single -s- in Spanish (posible, posibilidad), unlike English and French 'possible'. Notice also the high-frequency idiom a lo mejor / es posible que (+ subjunctive).

posición.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin positiō, positiōnem ('act of placing, situation, posture, standing'), derived from positus, the past participle of pōnere ('to put, place, set').

history.meaning: position, posture, social or financial standing

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French from Latin positiōnem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posición
Wiktionary — posición

posición.notes: While posición means 'social standing, stance, or physical posture' (su dinero, su posición), an open 'job position' at a company is usually un puesto de trabajo rather than una posición.

postal.etymology: Borrowed from French postal (derived from poste 'mail service' < Italian posta < Latin posita 'fixed relay station for couriers'), used both as an adjective ('postal') and a feminine noun ('postcard', short for tarjeta postal).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: postal
Wiktionary — postal

praga.etymology: Spanish exonym for Prague, capital of the Czech Republic, borrowed via Medieval Latin Praga from Old Czech Praha (before Czech underwent the 12th–13th-century sound shift g > h). Slavic toponymists connect Old Czech *Praga either to práh (< Proto-Slavic *porgъ, 'threshold; river ford or rocky rapid' across the Vltava) or to a derivative of pražiti ('to parch, dry, clear forest by fire').

history.meaning: ford/threshold rapid or sun-baked ridge on the Vltava

cognates.meaning: borrowed via French from Medieval Latin Praga

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: praguense
Wiktionary — Praga

praga.notes: Because Latin scribes recorded Praga centuries before Czech g shifted to h (Praha), Western European languages preserve the older [g] stop.

precio.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin pretium ('worth, value, price, reward').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: precio
Wiktionary — precio

preciosidad.etymology: Formed from precioso ('lovely, gorgeous, precious', < Latin pretiōsus 'valuable, costly', from pretium 'price, worth') + abstract quality suffix -idad (< Latin -itātem, cf. Late Latin pretiōsitās). In modern Spanish it shifted from 'monetary costliness' to 'something breathtakingly lovely or a gem'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preciosidad
Wiktionary — preciosidad

preciosidad.notes: In Peninsular Spanish, esta preciosidad de papel means 'this absolute gem of a role', and ¡Qué preciosidad! is an enthusiastic compliment for a baby, pet, outfit, or view.

precioso.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin pretiōsus ('of great value, costly, precious, lovely'), derived from pretium ('value, price').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: precioso
Wiktionary — precioso

preguntar.etymology: Inherited by metathesis and voicing (Old Spanish pescudar / preguntar) from Vulgar Latin *praecontāre for Classical Latin percontārī ('to inquire closely, interrogate, ask').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preguntar
Wiktionary — preguntar

prensa.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages via Old Catalan or Old Occitan premsa ('winepress, clamp'), which evolved with nasal epenthesis from Late Latin pressa ('pressing device'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin premere ('to press, squeeze'). Extended from the movable-type printing press to newspapers, journalists, and news media collectively.

history.meaning: mechanical press; print media, journalism, the press

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French presse from Late Latin pressa

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prensa
Wiktionary — prensa

prensa.notes: In Spanish celebrity culture, la prensa del corazón (or la prensa rosa) is the gossip/celebrity tabloid press that scrutinizes actors' private lives.

preocupado.etymology: Participial adjective of preocupar ('worried, anxious'), a learned borrowing from Latin praeoccupāre ('to seize beforehand, take possession of the mind in advance'), composed of prae- ('before') + occupāre ('to seize, occupy', itself ob- + capere 'to take').

morphemes.meaning: seize, occupy the mind (< Latin occupāre)

cognates.meaning: semi-false friend: English means 'distracted in thought', whereas Spanish preocupado directly means 'worried'!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preocupado
Wiktionary — preocupado

preocupado.notes: False-friend nuance: Estoy preocupada means 'I'm worried', not merely 'my mind is elsewhere' (which is estoy distraída or estoy en otra cosa).

preocupar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praeoccupāre ('to seize beforehand; occupy the mind beforehand, cause anxiety'), formed from prae- ('before') + occupāre ('to seize, occupy').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preocupar
Wiktionary — preocupar

preparado.etymology: Participial adjective of preparar ('prepared, ready, trained'), borrowed from Latin praeparātus, past participle of praeparāre (prae- + parāre 'to make ready beforehand').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preparado
Wiktionary — preparado

preparando.etymology: Gerund of preparar ('preparing, getting ready'), formed with -ando on learned/semi-learned preparar, from Latin praeparāre ('to make ready beforehand': prae- 'before' + parāre 'to arrange, make ready').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preparar
Wiktionary — preparando

preparando.notes: In acting and exam contexts, estar preparando un papel / unas oposiciones means actively studying, rehearsing, and working up a role or exam.

preparar.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin praeparāre ('to make ready in advance, equip'), composed of prae- ('before, in front') + parāre ('to arrange, furnish, make ready').

history.meaning: to prepare, cook, rehearse; (prepararse) to get ready

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Middle French préparer from Latin praeparāre

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: preparar
Wiktionary — preparar

preparar.notes: Because bare Latin parāre shifted in Spanish to parar ('to stop'), Spanish relies on prefixed preparar whenever 'prepare' is meant.

presentar.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin praesentāre ('to place before, exhibit, show immediately'), derived from praesēns, praesentis ('present, at hand', old participle of praeesse 'to be in front of').

morphemes.meaning: at hand, before one's eyes (< Latin praesentem)

history.meaning: at hand -> to set before, show
to introduce (people); host (a TV show); submit

cognates.meaning: verb borrowed via Old French présenter

rootFamily.gloss: to show up; audition / sit an exam (presentarse a un casting)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: presentar
Wiktionary — presentar

presentar.notes: Crucial false-friend trap: 'to introduce someone' is ALWAYS presentar (Os presento a mi novia = 'Let me introduce my girlfriend to you all'), never introducir (which means 'to insert'!).

presión.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pressiō, pressiōnis ('a pressing down, crowding, pressure'), derived from pressus, past participle of premere ('to press').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: presión
Wiktionary — presión

presupuesto.etymology: Substantivized irregular past participle of presuponer ('budget, cost estimate; prior assumption'), formed from pre- (< Latin prae-) + supuesto (< Latin suppositus 'placed under, assumed').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: presupuesto
Wiktionary — presupuesto

prima.etymology: Elliptical substantivization of Latin prīma ('first', feminine of prīmus, superlative of *pri- 'before'), shortened from Late/Medieval Latin consobrīna prīma > Old Spanish cormana prima ('first cousin', as opposed to second or third cousins). Eventually the adjective prima/primo stood alone for 'cousin'.

rootFamily.gloss: male cousin; gullible sucker (hacer el primo)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: primo
Wiktionary — prima

prima.notes: Because prima/primo lost its original 'first' sense once it came to mean any cousin, Spanish now says prima hermana ('sister-cousin') when specifying a 'first cousin'!

primavera.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra ('first spring'), reshaped from Classical Latin prīmō vēre ('at the beginning of spring'), combining prīmus ('first') and vēr ('spring').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: primavera

primero.etymology: Inherited from Latin prīmārius ('of the first rank, chief, first'), derived from prīmus ('first'), with regular development of -ārius to Castilian -ero.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: primero
Wiktionary — primero

primo.etymology: Inherited from Latin prīmus ('first'); as a kinship noun ('cousin'), shortened from Late Latin (cōnsobrīnus) prīmus ('first cousin').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: primo
Wiktionary — primo

principal.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin principālis ('first in rank or importance, chief, main'), derived from princeps, principis ('first, chief').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: principal
Wiktionary — principal

principio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin principium ('beginning, origin, fundamental rule or principle'), derived from princeps (prīmus 'first' + capere 'to take').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: principio
Wiktionary — principio

prisa.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish priessa ('crowd, pressure, urgency, haste'), inherited from Late Latin pressa, substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin premere ('to press, urge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prisa
Wiktionary — prisa

privado.etymology: Borrowed or inherited from Latin prīvātus ('set apart from the state, personal, private'), past participle of prīvāre ('to set apart, deprive', from prīvus 'individual, one's own').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: privado
Wiktionary — privado

probador.etymology: Derived within Spanish from probar ('to try on, test', < Latin probāre) + the locative/agent suffix -dor ('fitting room, dressing room; tester').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: probador
Wiktionary — probador

probar.etymology: Inherited from Latin probāre ('to test, examine, try out, prove'), derived from probus ('good, genuine, upright'), with regular diphthongization of stressed short o to ue (prueba).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: probar
Wiktionary — probar

problema.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin problēma ('question proposed for solution'), from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, 'anything thrown forward, obstacle, task'), from προβάλλειν ('to put forward').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: problema
Wiktionary — problema

problemas.etymology: Plural of problema ('problem, trouble'), a learned borrowing via Latin problēma from Ancient Greek próblēma (πρόβλημα, 'something thrown or jutting forward: barrier, riddle, question proposed for debate'), derived from probállō (pro- 'forward' + bállō 'to throw').

morphemes.meaning: result noun (< Greek -ma, masculine in Spanish)

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French and Latin from Greek próblēma

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: problema
Wiktionary — problema

problemas.notes: Classic Greek -ma gender rule: like el tema, el sistema, el drama, and el idioma, Greek neuter nouns in -ma entered Spanish as MASCULINE (estos problemas, muchos problemas).

prodigio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōdigium ('prophetic sign, omen, marvel, wondrous event'), composed of archaic prevocalic prefix prōd- ('forth, beforehand') + an element connected either to agere ('to drive') or archaic *agiō ('I say, foretell', cf. aiō and adāgium).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prodigio
Wiktionary — prodigio

prodigio.notes: Used in apposition without a preposition for gifted youngsters: un niño prodigio / una niña prodigio ('a child prodigy').

producciones.etymology: Plural of producción ('production'), a learned borrowing from Latin prōductiō, prōductiōnem ('lengthening, bringing forth'), derived from prōdūcere (prō- 'forward' + dūcere 'to lead'); in the twentieth century extended under English and French influence to film, television, and theatrical productions.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: producción
Wiktionary — producciones

producciones.notes: Orthographic rule: Spanish -cción keeps double cc (producción, producciones) whenever a kindred word in the family has -ct- (producto, productor).

producir.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin prōdūcere ('to lead forth, bring out, bring into being'), composed of prō- ('forth, forward') + dūcere ('to lead, draw'). Adapted into the Spanish -ir conjugation on the pattern of conducir, reducir, and traducir.

history.meaning: to lead forth, bring out, generate
to produce, yield; finance/oversee a film or show

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: producir
Wiktionary — producir

producir.notes: All Spanish -ducir verbs keep Latin's sigmatic perfect (prōdūxī -> produje, produjo, produjeron, never *producí!) and take -zc- in 1sg present (produzco) and present subjunctive (produzca).

producto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōductum ('something brought forth'), neuter singular of prōductus, the past participle of prōdūcere (prō- 'forth' + dūcere 'to lead, draw out').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: producto
Wiktionary — producto

producto.notes: In TV advertising shoots, mostrar el producto refers to keeping the sponsor's item clearly visible to the camera.

productor.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōductor, prōductōrem ('one who brings forth or leads out'), agent noun from prōdūcere; adopted in twentieth-century cinema, theater, and music as a semantic calque of English film/record producer.

rootFamily.gloss: female producer; production studio (una productora de cine)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: productor
Wiktionary — productor

productor.notes: In Spanish media jargon, feminine la productora on its own usually means 'the production company/studio' (trabaja para una productora), as well as a female producer.

profesional.etymology: Derived from profesión ('profession, occupation', < Latin professiō, -ōnis, from profitērī 'to declare publicly') + the relational suffix -al.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: profesional
Wiktionary — profesional

profesión.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin professiō, professiōnem ('public declaration, open avowal of one's calling or occupation'), derived from professus, past participle of profitērī ('to declare openly, avow', from pro- 'forth, publicly' + fatērī 'to acknowledge, confess').

history.meaning: to declare publicly -> avowed occupation, profession

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French from Latin professiōnem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: profesión
Wiktionary — profesión

profesión.notes: Among Spanish actors, la profesión (used simply with the definite article: compañeros de la profesión) affectionately denotes the acting/theater trade itself.

profesora.etymology: Feminine form of profesor, learned borrowing from Latin professor, professōris ('public teacher, one who professes an art or branch of knowledge'), derived from profitērī ('to declare openly').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: profesor
Wiktionary — profesora

progreso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōgressus ('a going forward, advance, progress'), action noun from prōgredī (prō- 'forward' + gradī 'to step, walk').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: progreso
Wiktionary — progreso

prometer.etymology: Inherited from Latin prōmittere ('to send forth, let go; to foretell, promise'), compounded from prō- ('forth, forward') and mittere ('to send').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prometer
Wiktionary — prometer

pronto.etymology: Pronto continues Latin promptus. The Spanish word can refer to readiness or speed and also functions as an adverb for an early or near-future time.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pronto

pronto.notes: Hasta pronto means see you soon; pronto does not describe the person’s character in this farewell.

propiedad.etymology: Inherited from Latin proprietātem (nominative proprietās, 'peculiarity, ownership, property'), derived from proprius ('one's own').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propiedad
Wiktionary — propiedad

propietario.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin proprietārius ('owner of property'), derived from Classical Latin proprietās ('ownership').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propietario
Wiktionary — propietario

propio.etymology: Semi-learned reflex of Latin proprius ('one's own, special, particular'), with dissimilatory loss of the second r (Old Spanish proprio > propio).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propio
Wiktionary — propio

proponer.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned from Latin prōpōnere ('to set forth, display, put forward an idea'), composed of prō- ('forward, before') + pōnere ('to put, place'), conjugating identically to base verb poner across all tenses.

history.meaning: to set before, put forward, intend
to propose, suggest; (proponerse) to set one's mind on

rootFamily.gloss: purpose, resolution (a propósito = by the way / on purpose)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: proponer
Wiktionary — proponer

proponer.notes: False-friend tip: proponer means 'to suggest an idea or plan' (te voy a proponer un juego); for 'to propose marriage', Spanish says pedir matrimonio or pedir la mano.

proporción.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōportiōnem (nominative prōportiō, 'comparative relation, symmetry'), univerbated from prō portiōne ('according to each part').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: proporción
Wiktionary — proporción

propuesta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of proponer (< Vulgar Latin *prōposita, Classical Latin prōposita 'things set forth', with diphthongization of short stressed ŏ to ue before syncope: *propŏs'ta > propuesta).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propuesta
Wiktionary — propuesta

propuesta.notes: In Spanish casting rooms, llevar una propuesta ('bringing a take/interpretation') is essential actor jargon: directors expect an auditioning actor to arrive with a clear creative choice rather than reading lines flatly.

protagonista.etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek prōtagōnistḗs (πρωταγωνιστής, 'actor who plays the chief role in a Greek tragedy or comedy'), a compound of prō̂tos (πρῶτος, 'first') + agōnistḗs (ἀγωνιστής, 'combatant, stage actor', from agṓn 'dramatic contest, struggle').

history.meaning: first actor in a dramatic competition
lead character, lead actor/actress, central figure

rootFamily.gloss: to star in, play the lead

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: protagonista
Wiktionary — protagonista

protagonista.notes: Common-gender noun (el protagonista / la protagonista), and unlike English (where 'protagonist' sounds literary), Spanish uses protagonista constantly for 'the lead actor/star' of any show—often clipped to el/la prota.

protagonizar.etymology: Formed in modern Spanish from protagonista ('lead actor, central figure', < Ancient Greek prōtagōnistḗs 'chief actor') + verbalizing suffix -izar (< Late Latin -izāre < Greek -ízein).

morphemes.meaning: lead role, first actor (< Greek prōtagōnistḗs)
to act as / perform (< Late Latin -izāre)

history.meaning: lead actor -> to star in, headline, be at the center of

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: protagonizar
Wiktionary — protagonizar

protagonizar.notes: Protagonizar is the natural Spanish transitive verb for English 'to star in' (protagonizar una serie = 'to star in a series'), since Spanish estrellar means 'to crash/smash'!

protegido.etymology: Participial adjective of proteger ('to protect, shelter'), from Latin prōtegere (prō- 'in front' + tegere 'to cover, roof').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: protegido
Wiktionary — protegido

prueba.etymology: Deverbal noun from probar ('to test, prove, try'), continuing Late Latin proba (from Classical Latin probāre 'to test, approve', from probus 'good, upright'), with regular diphthongization of tonic short o > ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prueba
Wiktionary — prueba

príncipe.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin prīnceps, prīncipem ('first citizen, leader, sovereign, prince'), an ancient compound of prīmus ('first') + -ceps (agent stem of capere 'to take' — literally 'one who takes the first place').

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French prince from Latin prīncipem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: príncipe
Wiktionary — príncipe

príncipe.notes: In the episode's line protagonista de El Príncipe, El Príncipe refers to the hit 2014–2016 Telecinco crime drama set in the Príncipe Alfonso neighborhood of Ceuta (starring Álex González and Hiba Abouk).

prórroga.etymology: Postverbal noun derived from learned prorrogar ('to extend a deadline or term'), borrowed from Latin prōrogāre ('to ask the assembly to prolong an official's command, defer, extend'), composed of prō- ('forward, onward') + rogāre ('to ask, propose a motion').

history.meaning: to prolong a magistrate's term, extend a deadline
to extend -> deadline extension; extra time / overtime (sports)

cognates.meaning: to suspend/extend a parliamentary session (< Latin prōrogāre)

rootFamily.gloss: to extend (a contract, run, or deadline)
to beg, request (inherited reflex of rogāre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prórroga
Wiktionary — prórroga

prórroga.notes: In Spanish soccer (continuation of the partido amistoso joke!), la prórroga means 'extra time / overtime' when a match is tied after 90 minutes.

próxima.etymology: Feminine singular of próximo ('nearest, next, upcoming'), a learned borrowing from Latin proximus ('nearest, next', irregular superlative of the adverb/preposition prope 'near').

rootFamily.gloss: fellow human being, neighbor (older semi-inherited doublet!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: próximo
Wiktionary — próxima

próxima.notes: In the farewell ¡Hasta la próxima!, feminine la próxima leaves implicit la próxima vez ('until next time!').

próximo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin proximus ('nearest, next'), irregular superlative related to the adverb/preposition prope ('near').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: próximo
Wiktionary — próximo

ps.etymology: Initialism PS standing for Paquita Salas in the agency name PS Management, combining the protagonist's given-name hypocoristic Paquita (< Francisca) and Castilian topographic surname Salas (< plural of sala 'hall, manor').

history.meaning: talent agency founded by Paquita Salas

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Ortografía: siglas y acrónimos

ps.notes: Pronounced letter by letter in Spanish as pe ese [pe ˈese]; pairing her traditional Spanish initials with English 'Management' captures Paquita's endearing attempt to sound sleek and international.

publi.etymology: Colloquial Peninsular Spanish apocopated clipping (acortamiento) of publicidad ('advertising, TV commercials'), retaining its base noun's feminine gender (la publi) and ultimately tracing back via French publicité to Latin pūblicus ('of the people, public').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: publi
Wiktionary — publi

publi.notes: Officially included in the RAE dictionary: hacer publi means acting in TV/print commercials, while watching TV, están en la publi means 'it's on a commercial break'.

publicidad.etymology: Borrowed from French publicité (initially 'state of being public knowledge', and from the nineteenth century 'commercial advertising'), derived from public (< Latin pūblicus 'belonging to the people or state', altered from Old Latin poplicus < populus 'people' under the influence of pūbēs 'adult population').

cognates.meaning: semi-false friend: English 'publicity' is media coverage/PR, whereas Spanish publicidad primarily means paid 'advertising'!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: publicidad
Wiktionary — publicidad

publicidad.notes: False-friend alert: in Spanish, la publicidad normally means paid commercial 'advertising' (anuncios de publicidad), whereas PR/press buzz is promoción or prensa.

pueblo.etymology: Inherited from Latin populum (accusative of populus, 'a people, nation, community'), via syncopated Late Latin *poplu, with voicing of -p- to -b- and regular Castilian diphthongization of short stressed ŏ to ue (Old Spanish poblo > pueblo). Uniquely in Spanish, the word expanded from 'inhabitants of a settlement' to the physical 'village or small country town' itself.

history.meaning: village, small town; a people, nation

cognates.meaning: people (via Anglo-Norman poeple) and pueblo (borrowed from Spanish)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pueblo
Wiktionary — pueblo

pueblo.notes: Cultural touchstone in Spain: almost every urban Spaniard speaks fondly of mi pueblo ('my family's ancestral village', like Paquita's Navarrete), where people return for summer fiestas and weddings.

puente.etymology: Puente continues Latin pons, pontis ('bridge'), diphthongizing stressed short ŏ to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puente

puente.notes: Masculine in modern standard Spanish: el puente de piedra, cruzar el puente.

puerta.etymology: Puerta descends regularly from Latin porta ('city gate, doorway, door'), with stressed short ŏ diphthongizing to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puerta

puerta.notes: Covers both a room's door and the main street entrance or gate of a building.

pues.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *postius, comparative reshaping of Classical Latin post ('after, behind'), with diphthongization of short o > ue and apocope.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pues
Wiktionary — pues

puesto.etymology: Irregular past participle of poner ('put, placed') and noun ('stall, post, position'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *positus (Classical positus, participle of pōnere) via syncope (*postu) and diphthongization o > ue.

history.meaning: placed, wearing; market stall, job post

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puesto
Wiktionary — puesto

pulsar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pulsāre ('to beat, strike, push, throb'), frequentative verb formed from pellere ('to drive, strike').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pulsar
Wiktionary — pulsar

pulso.etymology: Borrowed from Latin pulsus ('push, beat, arterial pulse'), action noun from pellere ('to beat, drive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pulso
Wiktionary — pulso

pum.etymology: Expressive onomatopoeia imitating the sound of a heavy impact, bang, thud, or knock.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pum
Wiktionary — pum

punto.etymology: Punto continues Latin punctum ('prick, dot, exact point in space or time', from pungĕre, 'to pierce').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: punto

punto.notes: En punto after a clock hour means 'on the dot / sharp' (a las ocho en punto); estar a punto de + infinitive means 'to be about to'.

puntualidad.etymology: Derived from puntual ('punctual, exact', from punto < Latin punctum 'point') + abstract noun suffix -idad.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puntualidad
Wiktionary — puntualidad

puro.etymology: Inherited from Latin pūrus ('clean, unmixed, pure, plain').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puro
Wiktionary — puro

pusimos.etymology: First-person plural preterite indicative of poner ('we put, we placed'), continuing the strong Latin u-stem perfect posuimus (infinitive pōnere), where the semivowel w in -ui- raised the preceding root vowel o to u by metaphony (*poswimus > pusimos).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — pusimos

pusimos.notes: In colloquial Peninsular storytelling, cogimos y pusimos... ('we up and put...') uses coger y + verb as a vivid narrative launcher ('went ahead and...').

puso.etymology: Third-person singular preterite indicative of poner ('put, placed; [reflexive se puso] became, reacted'), inherited from the strong Latin perfect posuit (< pōnere), with raising of the root vowel o to u induced by the following labiovelar glide w (posuit > *poswo > puso) and unstressed final -o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner
Wiktionary — puso

puso.notes: Strong preterites like puso, tuvo, estuvo, pudo, and supo are stressed on the root (PÚ-so), never on the final -o. Idiomatic ¡Cómo se puso la prensa! means 'How worked up / wild the press got!'

puta.etymology: Pan-Romance vulgarism (compare Italian putta 'wench [archaic]', French pute, Portuguese puta), traced by Joan Corominas and the RAE to Vulgar Latin *pūtta ('girl, lass', expressive geminate variant of Classical Latin pūta, feminine of pūtus 'boy, lad'), which underwent pejorative narrowing from 'young woman, wench' to 'prostitute'; some scholars note secondary reinforcement from Latin pūtida ('stinking, rotten').

rootFamily.gloss: to screw over, give someone a hard time (vulgar)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puto
Wiktionary — puta

puta.notes: Register note: strongly vulgar, yet pervasive in everyday Peninsular speech as a prenominal intensifier (esta puta frase = 'this goddamn line', ni puta idea = 'not the faintest fucking clue') and paradoxically positive in ¡De puta madre! ('awesome, fantastic!').

página.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina ('sheet of papyrus, written page, column'), related to pangere ('to fasten, fix together').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: página
Wiktionary — página

pájaro.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin passaru (Classical Latin passer, 'sparrow'), which broadened in Ibero-Romance to mean any small bird.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pájaro
Wiktionary — pájaro

párrafo.etymology: Semi-learned adaptation of Late Latin paragraphus, from Ancient Greek parágraphos (pará 'beside' + gráphein 'to write', originally a marginal stroke marking a section break).

history.meaning: marginal mark indicating a text division

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: párrafo
Wiktionary — párrafo

público.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pūblicus ('belonging to the people, public, common'), derived from Old Latin poplicus (from populus 'people').

history.meaning: of the state or people, public

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: público
Wiktionary — público

que.etymology: Unaccented que continues unstressed Latin quid and quem, merging relative pronoun ('who, which, that') and subordinating conjunction ('that, than') into one high-frequency connector.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: que

que.notes: Unaccented que connects clauses (creo que sí, más que ayer), whereas accented qué asks direct or indirect questions (¿Qué hora es?).

quedar.etymology: Quedar continues Latin quiētāre ('to rest, become still', from quiētus), shifting in Spanish to 'stay, remain, be left, or arrange to meet'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quedar

quedar.notes: Reflexive quedarse means 'to stay' (me quedo toda la semana), non-reflexive quedar means 'to be left' or 'to meet up' (quedar al mediodía).

quede.etymology: First- or third-person singular present subjunctive (and usted imperative) of quedar ('to remain, end up, be left'), inherited from Late/Vulgar Latin quiētāre ('to rest, keep still', derived from Classical Latin quiētus > Vulgar Latin quētus > Spanish quedo 'still, quiet'), with voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

morphemes.meaning: remain, end up (< Late Latin quiētāre 'to rest')

history.meaning: at rest -> to come to rest, remain

cognates.meaning: to leave (divergent semantic path from Medieval Latin quietāre 'discharge a debt, release'!)
remarkable semantic opposites from the exact same Latin root quiētus!

rootFamily.gloss: still, motionless (learned doublet of archaic quedo)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quedar
Wiktionary — quede

quede.notes: Resultative quedar + past participle (que esta prueba quede enviada hoy) means 'that this audition tape gets/ends up sent today'. Also marvel at how Latin quiētāre split into opposite meanings: Spanish quedar ('to stay') vs. French quitter / English quit ('to leave')!

quedó.etymology: Third-person singular preterite indicative of quedar ('stayed, remained, was left'), formed on quedar (< Late Latin quiētāre 'to rest, stay still', from quiētus) with the stressed preterite ending -ó (< Vulgar Latin -aut < Classical -āvit).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quedar
Wiktionary — quedó

quedó.notes: Idiomatic la cara que se les quedó ('the look left frozen on their faces') vividly pictures shock or speechlessness.

quejar.etymology: Inherited (almost always reflexive quejarse, 'to complain, groan') from Old Spanish quexar ('to press hard, afflict, distress'), descending from Vulgar Latin *quassiāre ('to strike repeatedly, shatter, bruise'), frequentative built on quassus, past participle of Classical Latin quatere ('to shake, beat'). Reflexive quexarse originally meant 'to lament being crushed or afflicted', whence modern 'to complain'.

history.meaning: to press, distress / to groan, lament

cognates.meaning: to crush, annul (via Old French quasser < quassāre)

rootFamily.gloss: to afflict (preserving Old Spanish's transitive meaning!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quejar
Wiktionary — quejar

quejar.notes: No me puedo quejar ('I can't complain') is a classic upbeat Spanish response to ¿Qué tal estás? Notice that the clitic me can climb before poder (no me puedo quejar = no puedo quejarme).

quemador.etymology: Derived within Spanish from quemar ('to burn') + agent/instrument suffix -dor.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quemador
Wiktionary — quemador

quemar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caimāre / *cremāre, usually explained as Classical Latin cremāre ('to burn') crossed with Late Latin cauma (< Ancient Greek kaûma, 'burning heat').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quemar
Wiktionary — quemar

querer.etymology: Querer continues Latin quaerĕre, which the DLE glosses as seeking or asking. Modern Spanish uses querer both for wanting something and for feeling affection toward a person.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: querer

querer.notes: With a person introduced by a (querer a alguien), querer expresses love or affection; before a noun or infinitive (quiero un café, queremos descansar), it expresses a wish.

querido.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from querer ('to love, want'), inherited from Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for, desire').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: querido
Wiktionary — querido

queso.etymology: Inherited from Latin cāseus ('cheese') via Vulgar Latin *cāseum > *caisu > queso, preserving the original Latin noun rather than the Late Latin innovation fōrmāticum (French fromage, Italian formaggio).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: queso
Wiktionary — queso

quico.etymology: Lexicalized Peninsular Spanish common noun (spelled quico or kiko, usually plural quicos / kikos) for crunchy salted roasted giant corn kernels, generalized from the mid-twentieth-century Spanish commercial trademark Kikos (marketed in Valencia by Churruca S.A.), itself named after the popular Spanish nickname Kiko / Quico (hypocoristic of Francisco or Federico).

history.meaning: nickname for Francisco/Federico -> brand of toasted corn nuts

rootFamily.gloss: alternative RAE headword spelling for roasted corn nut

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: kiko
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quico

quico.notes: A quintessential Spanish bar and kiosk snack (maíz frito/tostado): when a tavern is out of hot tapas like torreznos, offering a bowl of quicos with a drink is peak everyday Spain.

quien.etymology: Inherited from Latin quem, the accusative singular of the relative/interrogative pronoun quī / quis ('who, whom'), with diphthongization of tonic short e > ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quien
Wiktionary — quien

quieren.etymology: Third-person plural present indicative of querer ('they want; they love'), inherited from Latin quaerunt (infinitive quaerere, 'to seek, ask for, try to obtain'), with regular monophthongization of Latin ae to open ĕ and Castilian diphthongization of stressed ĕ to ie.

rootFamily.gloss: affection, darling (often linked to the car-/quer- sphere)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: querer
Wiktionary — quieren

quieren.notes: With a personal direct object introduced by a (Todos te quieren), querer means warm, genuine 'love' (for family, friends, or partners), whereas querer + noun/infinitive means 'to want'.

quieto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin quiētus ('at rest, calm, still', past participle of quiēscere), forming a doublet with popular inherited quedo.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quieto
Wiktionary — quieto

quince.etymology: Inherited from Latin quīndecim ('fifteen', compounded from quīnque 'five' + decem 'ten').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quince
Wiktionary — quince

quitar.etymology: Inherited from Old Spanish quitar ('to release from debt, free, remove'), via Gallo-Romance from Late/Medieval Latin quiētāre ('to quiet, discharge a claim', from quiētus).

history.meaning: to remove, take away, take off

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quitar
Wiktionary — quitar

quizá.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish quiçab / quiçabe, a phonetic reduction of the romance clause quién sabe (Latin quis sapit, 'who knows?').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quizá
Wiktionary — quizá

quizás.etymology: Variant of quizá ('perhaps, maybe', from Old Spanish quiçab < quién sabe 'who knows?') enlarged with analogical adverbial -s (compare jamás, además).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quizás
Wiktionary — quizás

quién.etymology: Interrogative and exclamatory pronoun ('who?, whom?') inherited from Latin quem (accusative singular of quis), spelled with an orthographic tilde to distinguish it from relative quien.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quién
Wiktionary — quién

qué.etymology: Interrogative and exclamative qué continues stressed Latin quid ('what?'), written with an acute accent to distinguish it from unstressed conjunction/relative que.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: qué

qué.notes: Used in questions (¿Qué hora es?, ¿Qué pasa?) and exclamations before nouns or adjectives/adverbs (¡Qué alivio!, ¡Qué bien!).

quédate.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative queda of quedarse ('stay!, remain!') fused with the enclitic reflexive pronoun te; adding the unstressed enclitic pushes stress onto the antepenultimate syllable, requiring the written accent (quédate). Ultimately from Late Latin quiētāre ('to rest, remain still', from quiētus).

rootFamily.gloss: to stay, remain; keep (quedarse con algo)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quedar
Wiktionary — quédate

quédate.notes: Notice the difference between non-reflexive quedar ('to arrange to meet up': ¿Quedamos mañana?) and reflexive quedarse ('to stay put': Quédate ahí tranquila).

radiador.etymology: Derived from radiar ('to emit heat or rays', from Latin radiāre, from radius 'ray, spoke') + instrument suffix -dor.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: radiador
Wiktionary — radiador

rama.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin rama, originally the collective plural of Classical Latin rāmus ('branch, bough').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rama
Wiktionary — rama

rapidez.etymology: Derived within Spanish from rápido ('fast, swift', from Latin rapidus) + abstract noun suffix -ez.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rapidez
Wiktionary — rapidez

raro.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin rārus ('thinly spaced, scarce, uncommon, extraordinary').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: raro
Wiktionary — raro

rato.etymology: Inherited from Latin raptus ('sudden snatching, carrying off, burst of movement', verbal noun of rapere 'to snatch, seize'), with assimilation of the consonant cluster -pt- to -t-. In Iberian Romance the sense shifted from 'a sudden gust or impulse' (Old Spanish a ratos 'in bursts') to 'a short span or while of time'.

cognates.meaning: short while (colloquial borrowing alongside native estona)
learned/French borrowings from the same Latin raptus!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rato
Wiktionary — rato

rato.notes: False-friend alert: el rato has NOTHING to do with rodents ('rat' is la rata, 'mouse' is el ratón)! Essential time chunks: un rato ('a while'), pasar un buen rato ('have a good time'), and todo el rato ('all the time / constantly').

ratón.etymology: Derived from rato / rata ('rat', from Romance/Late Latin rattus of uncertain expressive or Germanic origin) + suffix -ón (functioning here as a diminutive/specifying suffix for the smaller 'mouse').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ratón
Wiktionary — ratón

razón.etymology: Razón continues Latin ratio, ratiōnis ('reckoning, calculation, reason, rightness').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: razón

razón.notes: Feminine noun (la razón, las razones); tener razón means 'to be right' (literally 'to have reason').

re.etymology: Musical solfège syllable for the second degree of the diatonic scale (pitch D), extracted by Guido d'Arezzo from the word resonāre in the medieval Latin hymn Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: to resound (second line of Ut queant laxis)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: re
Wiktionary — re

real.etymology: Convergence of two Latin adjectives: (1) inherited from Latin rēgālis ('royal, kingly', from rēx 'king') with loss of intervocalic -g-, and (2) learned borrowing from Late Latin reālis ('actual, real', from rēs 'thing, matter').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: real
Wiktionary — real

realidad.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitātem (nominative reālitās, 'actual existence'), derived from Late Latin reālis (< Classical Latin rēs, 'thing, fact').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: realidad
Wiktionary — realidad

reapertura.etymology: Formed within Spanish from iterative prefix re- ('again') + apertura ('opening', learned borrowing from Latin apertūra, from aperīre 'to open').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reapertura
Wiktionary — reapertura

rebajar.etymology: Formed within Spanish from prefix re- ('down, back, further') + bajar ('to lower, bring down'), itself derived from bajo ('low, short' < Late Latin bassus 'thickset, low in stature').

history.meaning: low -> to lower -> to reduce, thin down, discount

rootFamily.gloss: price reduction; (pl. las rebajas) seasonal store sales

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rebajar
Wiktionary — rebajar

rebajar.notes: From rebajar comes Spain's favorite shopping word: las rebajas ('the winter/summer clearance sales').

rebanada.etymology: Participial noun from rebanar ('to slice bread or other food into flat portions'), of uncertain Hispano-Romance origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rebanada
Wiktionary — rebanada

rec.etymology: International audiovisual abbreviation REC clipped from English record ('to capture sound or video'), displayed on camera viewfinders and recording buttons. English record itself was borrowed via Old French recorder from Latin recordārī ('to call back to mind, remember', built from re- 'again' + cor, cordis 'heart', the ancient seat of memory).

history.meaning: to remember, set down in memory
to capture audio/video -> camera recording indicator

rootFamily.gloss: to remember, remind (Spanish's inherited cognate of English record!)
sports/world record (older borrowing from the same English word)

sources.title: Wiktionary — rec
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recordar

rec.notes: In Spain, darle al rec ('hitting REC') is both everyday self-tape/camcorder talk (inspiring Paquita's confusion with photography!) and famous as the title of the 2007 Spanish found-footage horror classic [REC].

recado.etymology: Postverbal noun from Old Spanish recabdar ('to collect, secure, accomplish carefully', modern recaudar), descending from Vulgar Latin *recapitāre ('to gather up under a head, settle'), formed from re- + caput, capitis ('head'). Its meaning evolved from 'careful provision or commission entrusted to someone' to 'errand' and 'message left for an absent person'.

rootFamily.gloss: to collect (taxes/funds), gross at the box office

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recado
Wiktionary — recado

recado.notes: Two high-frequency everyday uses in Spain: dejar un recado ('leave a phone/desk message for someone') and hacer recados ('run errands around town').

recepcionista.etymology: Recepcionista combines recepción (from Latin receptio, 'welcoming, receiving') with agent suffix -ista (from Greek -istēs via Latin -ista).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recepcionista
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recepción

recepcionista.notes: Like all -ista person nouns, recepcionista keeps the same spelling for both genders: el recepcionista / la recepcionista.

recepción.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin receptiōnem (nominative receptiō, 'act of receiving, shelter, welcome'), derived from recipere ('to receive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recepción
Wiktionary — recepción

recibir.etymology: Inherited from Latin recipere ('to take back, accept, welcome, receive'), compounded from re- ('back') and capere ('to take').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recibir
Wiktionary — recibir

recibo.etymology: Deverbal noun from recibir ('to receive'), originating in the first-person present formula recibo ('I receive...') written at the head of payment acknowledgments.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recibo
Wiktionary — recibo

reciente.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin recēns, recentem ('fresh, newly arisen, young, recent'), adapting the stressed short e to Castilian diphthong ie while preserving the learned -ci- spelling.

rootFamily.gloss: newly, just (apocopated adverb before participles: recién llegado)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reciente
Wiktionary — reciente

reciente.notes: Before a past participle, reciente always shortens to recién: recién hecho ('freshly made'), recién casados ('newlyweds').

recién.etymology: Recién is the apocopated adverbial form of reciente ('recent, fresh', from Latin recens, recentis), used directly before past participles.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recién
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reciente

recién.notes: In Spain recién pairs chiefly with past participles: bollos recién hechos ('freshly baked buns'), café recién hecho ('freshly brewed coffee').

recoger.etymology: Inherited from Latin recolligere ('to gather back up, collect again'), composed of re- ('back, up') + colligere ('to gather together', itself com- + legere 'to pick, gather; read'), evolving regularly in Castilian identically to coger (colligere > coger).

history.meaning: to pick up (objects or people); tidy up; harvest

cognates.meaning: learned Latinate borrowing ('gather back into memory')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recoger
Wiktionary — recoger

recoger.notes: Unlike bare coger (which is taboo in several Latin American countries), prefixed recoger ('to pick up off the floor / pick someone up / tidy a room') is completely polite everywhere in the Spanish-speaking world!

reconocer.etymology: Inherited from Latin recognōscere ('to know again, recall, inspect, acknowledge'), from re- ('again') + cognōscere ('to come to know').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reconocer
Wiktionary — reconocer

recordar.etymology: Inherited from Latin recordārī ('to call back to mind, remember'), formed from re- ('again, back') + cor, cordis ('heart', regarded in Roman antiquity as the seat of memory).

history.meaning: to bring back to heart/mind, remember

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recordar
Wiktionary — recordar

recto.etymology: Recto comes as a learned borrowing from Latin rectus ('straight, upright, direct', past participle of regĕre, 'to guide straight').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recto

recto.notes: Todo recto ('straight ahead') is the standard Peninsula Spanish phrase when giving walking directions.

recuerdo.etymology: Deverbal noun from recordar ('to remember', from Latin recordārī), exhibiting regular diphthongization of stressed short o > ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recuerdo
Wiktionary — recuerdo

recuperar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin recuperāre ('to get back, regain, restore'), doublet of inherited recobrar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recuperar
Wiktionary — recuperar

red.etymology: English color word Red inside the proper agency name Red Carpet ('red carpet', Spanish alfombra roja), descending from Old English rēad ('red'), from Proto-Germanic *raudaz and Proto-Indo-European *h₁roudhós ('red', the same Indo-European root behind Latin ruber / russus and Spanish rojo).

history.meaning: red (ceremonial red carpet of film premieres)
rival talent agency opened by Fernando Canelón

cognates.meaning: red (< Latin russus, distant Indo-European cognate)

sources.title: Wiktionary — red

red.notes: Here Red is the English word inside Fernando's flashy rival agency Red Carpet (contrasting with Paquita's homely PS Management). Don't confuse it with native Spanish feminine noun la red ('net, network, the Web', inherited from Latin rēte)!

redondo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin retundus (disimilated from Classical Latin rotundus, 'wheel-shaped, circular, round', derived from rota 'wheel').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: redondo
Wiktionary — redondo

reencuentro.etymology: Formed within Spanish from iterative prefix re- ('again') + encuentro ('meeting, encounter', deverbal from encontrar < Late Latin incontrāre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reencuentro
Wiktionary — reencuentro

refranero.etymology: Formed within Spanish from refrán ('proverb, traditional saying') + collective/repository suffix -ero (< Latin -ārium, 'collection or book of'). Base noun refrán was borrowed from Old Occitan refranh ('birdsong burden, poetic refrain, oft-repeated saying'), derived from Vulgar Latin *refrangere (< Classical Latin refringere 'to break back, echo', from re- + frangere 'to break').

history.meaning: proverb -> proverb collection, folk wisdom corpus

cognates.meaning: musical chorus (false friend for Spanish refrán = 'proverb', while song 'chorus' is el estribillo!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: refranero
Wiktionary — refranero

refranero.notes: False-friend gem: Spanish un refrán means 'a proverb/folk saying' (celebrated since Don Quixote's Sancho Panza as el refranero español), whereas the 'refrain/chorus' of a song is el estribillo!

regalo.etymology: Postverbal noun from regalar ('to give as a gift; originally to feast, pamper, entertain lavishly'), borrowed in the sixteenth century from Middle French régaler (or via Italian regalare), derived from Old French gale ('pleasure, festivity, merrymaking'; compare English gala and regale), often secondarily associated by speakers with Latin rēgālis ('fit for a king').

history.meaning: festivity, delight -> to entertain lavishly, treat

cognates.meaning: to entertain lavishly with food or stories (< French régaler)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: regalo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: regalar

regalo.notes: False-friend reminder: el regalo is the everyday Spanish word for 'gift / present' (while el presente means 'the present time', except in formal idioms like hacer presente).

regaló.etymology: Third-person singular preterite indicative of regalar ('he/she gave as a gift'), combining regalar (< Middle French régaler 'to treat, present') with the stressed -ar preterite ending -ó (< Latin -āvit).

history.meaning: to give as a present -> he/she gifted

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: regalar
Wiktionary — regaló

regaló.notes: Watch the minimal stress pair: el regalo [reˈɣalo] ('the gift') vs. me la regaló [reɣaˈlo] ('he gave it to me as a gift').

registrar.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin registrāre ('to copy into a register, record, inspect'), derived from registrum ('register').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: registrar
Wiktionary — registrar
