registro.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin registrum, altered from Late Latin regesta ('things recorded, list, archive'), neuter plural participle of regerere ('to carry back, transcribe').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: registro
Wiktionary — registro

regla.etymology: Continues Latin regŭla ('straight wooden strip, ruler, guiding standard'), derived from regĕre ('to guide straight, rule').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: regla

regla.notes: Unites both concrete 'measuring ruler' and abstract 'rule / kitchen regulation' in a single word.

reina.etymology: Inherited from Latin rēgīna ('queen', archaic feminine derivative formed with *-īna on rēx, rēgis 'king', from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs), showing regular loss of intervocalic -g- before front vowel ī (rēgīna > Old Spanish reína > diphthongized reina).

cognates.meaning: Latinate royal terms from rēgīna / rēx

rootFamily.gloss: king (los reyes = the king and queen)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reina
Wiktionary — reina

reina.notes: In Spain, tener a alguien como una reina ('treating someone like a queen / waiting on her hand and foot') and affectionate vocative ¡Hola, reina! ('Hey, gorgeous/queen!') are everyday warm expressions.

reja.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *regula ('bar, rod', Classical Latin rēgula 'straight bar, rule'), denoting a wrought-iron window grating or grille.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reja
Wiktionary — reja

rejilla.etymology: Diminutive of reja ('iron bar, grating') formed with the suffix -illa, denoting a small grate, mesh screen, vent grille, or woven cane panel.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rejilla
Wiktionary — rejilla

relación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin relātiō, relātiōnem ('carrying back, official report, connection, reference'), derived from relātus, the suppletive past participle of referre ('to bring back, relate', from re- + ferre 'to carry').

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French from Latin relātiōnem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: relación
Wiktionary — relación

relación.notes: Single una relación covers both English 'a connection/relation' and 'a romantic relationship' (cuando una relación termina).

relajar.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin relaxāre ('to loosen again, slacken, unbend, ease'), composed of re- ('back, again') + laxāre ('to loosen, widen', from laxus 'loose, slack'), showing evolution of intervocalic -x- ([ks]) through medieval palatal [ʃ] to modern velar j [x].

history.meaning: to loosen, relax; (relajarse) to chill out, unwind

cognates.meaning: doublets from Latin relaxāre (direct vs. via Old French)

rootFamily.gloss: relaxation, chill time (modern Anglicism from the same root)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: relajar
Wiktionary — relajar

relajar.notes: Usually reflexive relajarse ('¡Relájate!'), though in casual Peninsular speech bare imperative ¡Relaja un poco! ('Ease up / chill out a bit!') is also lively and idiomatic.

relax.etymology: Twentieth-century borrowing from English relax, re-imported into Spanish as a masculine noun ('relaxation, calm, chill time'); English relax was itself borrowed in the late Middle Ages from Latin relaxāre ('to loosen, ease', re- + laxāre), making Spanish relax and native verb relajar etymological twins.

cognates.meaning: relaxation (likewise borrowed from English as a noun!)

rootFamily.gloss: to relax (native Spanish verb from the same Latin source)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: relax
Wiktionary — relax

relax.notes: Notice the part-of-speech twist! In English 'relax' is a verb, whereas in Spanish (and Italian) el relax is a NOUN meaning 'relaxation / chill time' (de relax, un poquito de relax), fully accepted in the RAE dictionary.

rellano.etymology: Formed within Spanish from prefix re- + llano ('flat, level ground', inherited from Latin plānus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rellano
Wiktionary — rellano

rellenar.etymology: Formed within Spanish from intensive prefix re- ('completely, again') + llenar ('to fill'), itself derived from lleno ('full'), inherited from Latin plēnus ('full') with regular Castilian palatalization of initial cluster pl- to ll-.

history.meaning: full -> to fill -> to fill out (a form), refill, stuff

cognates.meaning: via Old French replenir from the same Latin plēnus root

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rellenar
Wiktionary — rellenar

rellenar.notes: Peninsular vs. Latin American usage: in Spain, 'to fill out a form' is rellenar un formulario / una ficha, whereas Latin America usually says llenar un formulario.

reloj.etymology: Reloj entered Old Spanish via Old Catalan relotge from Latin horologium ('time-teller, sundial, clock', from Ancient Greek hōrológion).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reloj

reloj.notes: Covers both a wall/church clock and a wristwatch; plural adds -es: los relojes.

relojero.etymology: Derived from reloj ('clock, watch', via Old Catalan relotge from Latin hōrologium < Ancient Greek hōrológion 'hour-teller') + occupational suffix -ero.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: relojero
Wiktionary — relojero

relámpago.etymology: Inherited from Old Spanish relámpago, derived from archaic relampar ('to flash', from Vulgar Latin *relampāre, related to Latin lampas < Greek lampás 'torch, flash') + unstressed suffix -ago.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: relámpago
Wiktionary — relámpago

remover.etymology: Inherited from Latin removēre ('to move back, withdraw, stir'), from re- ('back, again') + movēre ('to move').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: remover
Wiktionary — remover

renacimiento.etymology: Derived within Spanish from renacer ('to be born again, revive', < Late Latin renāscī, composed of re- 'again' + nāscī 'to be born') + action-noun suffix -miento (< Latin -mentum), reinforced in cultural usage as a calque of Italian rinascimento and French renaissance.

history.meaning: to be born anew, spring up again
to be reborn -> rebirth, career comeback; the Renaissance

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: renacimiento
Wiktionary — renacimiento

renacimiento.notes: Capitalized el Renacimiento denotes the European historical period; lowercase un renacimiento means a personal or artistic 'rebirth / career renaissance'.

renfe.etymology: Acronym RENFE (also styled Renfe), coined in 1941 from the initials of Red Nacional de los Ferrocarriles Españoles ('National Network of Spanish Railways') upon the state consolidation of Spain's broad-gauge rail companies; today officially Renfe Operadora.

history.form: Red Nacional de los Ferrocarriles Españoles -> RENFE
history.meaning: Spain's state passenger and freight rail operator

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Ortografía: siglas y acrónimos (Renfe)
Wiktionary — Renfe

renfe.notes: In everyday Peninsular speech, la Renfe (feminine because la red is feminine!) often refers metonymically to the local train station or commuter rail line itself: Sale ahora para la RENFE ('He's heading out for the train station right now').

reparación.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin reparātiōnem (nominative reparātiō, 'restoration, renewal'), from reparāre ('to repair, restore').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reparación
Wiktionary — reparación

reparar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin reparāre ('to restore, make ready again, mend'), compounded from re- ('again') and parāre ('to prepare, furnish').

history.meaning: to repair, fix; to notice (reparar en)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reparar
Wiktionary — reparar

repartidor.etymology: Agent noun formed within Spanish from repartir ('to distribute, deliver') + agent suffix -dor.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: repartidor
Wiktionary — repartidor

repartir.etymology: Formed from prefix re- + partir ('to divide, split, share', inherited from Latin partīre / partīrī, from pars 'part').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: repartir
Wiktionary — repartir

reparto.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from repartir ('to distribute, deliver, assign roles').

history.meaning: delivery, distribution; cast (of a play or film)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reparto
Wiktionary — reparto

repetir.etymology: Semi-learned adaptation of Latin repetere ('to seek again, go back over, repeat'), from re- ('again') + petere ('to go toward, seek').

history.meaning: to strike or seek again, repeat
to repeat, have a second helping

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: repetir
Wiktionary — repetir

repre.etymology: Colloquial Peninsular Spanish apocopated clipping (acortamiento) of representante ('talent agent, manager; representative'), preserving common gender (el repre / la repre) and ultimately deriving from Latin repraesentāns, repraesentantis.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representante

repre.notes: Signature Madrid actor and music-industry slang alongside la publi ('commercials'), la peli ('movie'), and el prota ('the lead'): ¿Tú tienes repre ahora? ('Do you have an agent right now?').

representante.etymology: Representante is formed from representar and the ending -nte. The base verb continues Latin repraesentāre, and the ending historically comes from Latin active present participles. A representative is someone who performs the action of representing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representante
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -nte

representante.notes: For a talent agent, the DLE specifies managing artists’ contracts and professional affairs. The person noun can take el or la without changing representante.

representar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin repraesentāre ('to make present again, bring vividly before the eyes, depict, act on behalf of'), composed of re- ('again') + praesentāre ('to set before, show', from praesēns 'present').

morphemes.meaning: again, in place of (< Latin re-)

history.meaning: to bring before the eyes, portray, stand in for

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French from Latin repraesentāre

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representar
Wiktionary — representar

representar.notes: Notice the double theatrical life of representar: an actor representa una obra ('performs a play'), while an agent like Paquita representa a una actriz ('represents an actress').

represento.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of representar ('I represent [you as an agent]'), combining learned Latinate representar (< repraesentāre) with the 1sg indicative ending -o.

history.meaning: I bring before the eyes, stand in for

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representar
Wiktionary — represento

represento.notes: Present-tense yo te represento ('you come to Madrid and I'll be your agent') uses the vivid Spanish present for an immediate career promise.

repuesto.etymology: Irregular past participle of reponer ('replaced, restored') and noun ('spare part, backup supply'), from Latin repositus (past participle of repōnere 'to put back, store up').

history.meaning: put back, stored away in reserve

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: repuesto
Wiktionary — repuesto

resbalar.etymology: Spanish verb meaning 'to slip, slide', formed with prefix res- (< Latin re- + ex-) on an expressive Hispano-Romance stem (linked by Corominas to Old Spanish esvarar 'to slip').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: resbalar
Wiktionary — resbalar

reserva.etymology: Reserva is the deverbal noun of reservar, from Latin reservāre ('to keep back, save for someone', from re- + servāre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reserva
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reservar

reserva.notes: Tengo una reserva a nombre de... ('I have a reservation under the name of...') is the key hotel check-in phrase.

reservado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from reservar ('reserved, discreet, booked; private section'), from Latin reservātus.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reservado
Wiktionary — reservado

reservar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin reservāre ('to keep back, save up, preserve'), from re- ('back') + servāre ('to keep, guard').

history.meaning: to keep back, save for later

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reservar
Wiktionary — reservar

reseña.etymology: Reseña derives from reseñar ('to record identifying marks, review'), continuing Latin resignāre / *risignāre (built on signum, 'mark, sign').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reseña
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reseñar

history.meaning: note down marks -> review; brief report

reseña.notes: Today una reseña covers book reviews as well as online guest reviews of hotels and cafés.

resfriar.etymology: Formed within Iberian Romance from intensive prefix res- (< Vulgar Latin *re-ex-) + friar / frío ('cold', inherited from Vulgar Latin *frīgdus < Classical Latin frīgidus 'cold, chill'). Literally 'to chill thoroughly', whence reflexive resfriarse ('to catch a chill / catch a cold').

history.meaning: to cool down -> to catch a cold

cognates.meaning: to catch a cold, cool off

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: resfriar
Wiktionary — resfriar

resfriar.notes: Conjugates with a hiatus accent on -í- in boot forms (me resfrío, te resfrías), though in the periphrastic future te vas a resfriar the infinitive carries no accent. Classic Spanish grandmother/mother warning whenever someone goes out underdressed!

resguardar.etymology: Formed within Spanish from intensive prefix res- + guardar ('to guard, keep, protect', borrowed from Germanic *wardōn 'to watch over').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: resguardar
Wiktionary — resguardar

respetar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin respectāre ('to look back at, regard with consideration'), frequentative of respicere (re- 'back' + specere 'to look').

history.meaning: to look back upon, show regard for

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: respetar
Wiktionary — respetar

respirar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin respīrāre ('to breathe out and in, catch one's breath'), from re- ('back, again') + spīrāre ('to breathe, blow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: respirar
Wiktionary — respirar

resultar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin resultāre ('to spring back, echo; in Medieval Latin, to follow as an outcome'), frequentative of resilīre ('to leap back').

history.meaning: to rebound; to arise as a consequence
to turn out, result, prove to be

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: resultar
Wiktionary — resultar

retar.etymology: Inherited through Old Spanish rieptar / reptar ('to accuse formally of treason before the king and challenge to judicial combat'), descending from Latin reputāre ('to count over, reckon, impute a fault to someone', from re- + putāre 'to reckon, judge'). Syncope of unstressed -u- (*rep'tāre > reptar) followed by assimilation of -pt- to -t- yielded modern retar ('to challenge, dare').

morphemes.meaning: challenge, dare (< Old Spanish reptar < Latin reputāre)

history.meaning: to impeach a noble, challenge to a judicial duel
to challenge, dare; (Southern Cone/Andes) to scold

cognates.meaning: learned doublet from the exact same Latin reputāre!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: retar
Wiktionary — retar

retar.notes: Fascinating doublet: medieval chivalric retar ('to challenge/dare': ¿Tú a mí me estás retando?) and learned reputar ('to deem') come from the exact same Latin verb! Note also regional variation: in Argentina, Chile, and Peru, retar means 'to scold a child'.

retirar.etymology: Formed from prefix re- ('back') + tirar ('to pull, draw').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: retirar
Wiktionary — retirar

retrasada.etymology: Feminine participial adjective of retrasar ('to delay, set back, slow down'), formed within Spanish from prefix re- + atrás / tras ('behind, back', inherited from Latin trāns 'across, beyond').

rootFamily.gloss: to delay, postpone; (retrasarse) to run late

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: retrasado
Wiktionary — retrasada

retrasada.notes: Register alert: for flights, trains, or clocks, retrasado/a is completely neutral ('delayed, running late'); when applied to a person (Vamos, que soy retrasada), it replicates an older clinical label turned harsh self-deprecating or offensive slang (exact register equivalent of English 'retarded'), so learners should recognize it in dialogue without using it toward others.

reunir.etymology: Formed (likely reinforced by French réunir) from prefix re- ('together again') + unir ('to unite, join'), descending from Late Latin ūnīre ('to make one, join into a unity', derived from Classical Latin ūnus 'one').

history.meaning: to gather together; (reunirse) to meet up, hold a meeting

cognates.meaning: built from the same Latin elements

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reunir
Wiktionary — reunir

reunir.notes: Pronominal reunirse (nos reunimos = 'we get together / meet') covers both business meetings and regular gatherings of friends—much broader than English 'reunite'.

reunión.etymology: Derived from reunir ('to gather, meet') + action-noun suffix -ión (< Latin -iōnem), modeled on French réunion (ultimately from Latin re- + ūnus 'one').

cognates.meaning: semi-false friend: English 'reunion' is a nostalgic regathering after years apart, whereas Spanish reunión is the ordinary everyday word for any 'meeting'!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reunión
Wiktionary — reunión

reunión.notes: Key false friend: Tengo una reunión simply means 'I have a (work) meeting', whereas an English 'class/family reunion' is un reencuentro (or reunión de antiguos alumnos).

revisar.etymology: Borrowed via French réviser from Late Latin revīsāre ('to look over again, inspect'), frequentative of Classical Latin revīdere ('to see again').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: revisar
Wiktionary — revisar

revuelto.etymology: Irregular past participle of revolver ('stirred up, scrambled, messy, unsettled'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *revolutus (Classical revolūtus, participle of revolvere 'to roll back, turn over').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: revuelto
Wiktionary — revuelto

rex.etymology: Classic European dog name Rex (here the German Shepherd hero of the Austrian crime series Kommissar Rex, broadcast in Spain as Rex, un policía diferente), taken directly from Classical Latin rēx ('king', from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs, whose inherited Spanish descendant is rey).

history.meaning: traditional name for German Shepherds and guard dogs

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rey
Wiktionary — Rex

rex.notes: Kommissar Rex (aired endlessly on Spanish daytime TV as Rex, un policía diferente) is a nostalgic 1990s–2000s pop-culture touchstone in Spain.

reír.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rīdīre, a fourth-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latin rīdēre ('to laugh, smile'). Loss of intervocalic -d- yielded Old Spanish reír (via dissimilation of *riír > reír), requiring a written hiatus accent on the -í- even in the infinitive.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reír
Wiktionary — reír

reír.notes: Reír, sonreír, and freír are the only three common Spanish verbs whose infinitive carries a written accent (-ír), marking the two-syllable hiatus [reˈiɾ]. Note that 'laugh at' takes preposition de: reírse de algo.

rico.etymology: Early Germanic loanword from Gothic reiks ('powerful, noble, ruler'), cognate with English rich and German reich.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rico
Wiktionary — rico

rincón.etymology: Inherited through Hispanic Arabic rukún (from Classical Arabic rukn, 'corner, pillar, support'), with nasal insertion yielding medieval rencón and modern rincón.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rincón

riquísimo.etymology: Synthetic absolute superlative of rico ('rich; delicious'), formed with the suffix -ísimo (< Latin -issimus) and orthographic c > qu before i.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: riquísimo
Wiktionary — riquísimo

ritmo.etymology: Borrowed via Latin rhythmus from Greek rhythmós ('measured motion, recurring proportion, beat'), related to rheîn ('to flow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ritmo

robar.etymology: Entered early Western Romance via Vulgar Latin *raubāre from West Germanic *raubōn ('to plunder, strip of spoils, rob', from Proto-Germanic *raubōną, cognate with Old English rēafian > bereave and Old French rober > English rob).

cognates.meaning: both borrowed via Old French from the same Germanic root!

rootFamily.gloss: clothing (originally 'captured loot/garments' from the same Germanic root!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: robar
Wiktionary — robar

robar.notes: Polite conversational softener: No te quiero robar mucho tiempo ('I don't want to take up much of your time'). And amazingly, Spanish ropa ('clothes') originally meant 'plundered garments' from the same root as robar!

roble.etymology: Inherited from Latin rōbur, rōboris ('hard oakwood, strength') via Vulgar Latin *rōbore > Old Spanish robre > roble (with dissimilation of r...r to r...l).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: roble
Wiktionary — roble

rodaje.etymology: Derived from rodar ('to roll; to shoot a film', < Latin rotāre 'to turn like a wheel', from rota 'wheel') + action-noun suffix -aje (< French -age < Latin -āticum), modeled in twentieth-century cinema on French tournage for the shooting of a motion picture (from rolling reels of celluloid through the camera).

history.meaning: to shoot film -> film shoot, principal photography

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rodaje
Wiktionary — rodaje

rodaje.notes: Core Spanish film-set vocabulary: estar de rodaje / en un rodaje means 'to be on set / on a film shoot'.

rodar.etymology: Inherited from Latin rotāre ('to turn like a wheel, roll, revolve'), denominal verb from rota ('wheel'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d- and diphthongization in boot forms (ruedo, ruedas). Extended in the early cinema era to 'shooting a film' because camera operators cranked revolving reels of film.

history.meaning: to whirl, roll like a wheel
to roll; to shoot/film (a movie or scene)

cognates.meaning: to roll, spin; shoot a film
to break in (an engine) / to roll

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rodar
Wiktionary — rodar

rodar.notes: In Spain, directors say ¡Rodando! ('Rolling!') right before ¡Acción!, and rodar una película is the idiomatic verb for 'to shoot a movie' (where Latin America also uses filmar or grabar).

rodará.etymology: Third-person singular future indicative of rodar ('will be filmed / will roll'), formed from the infinitive rodar (< Latin rotāre 'to roll') + the stressed future ending -á (< Vulgar Latin *habēt 'has [to]').

history.meaning: will roll; (se rodará) will be shot on location

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rodar
Wiktionary — rodará

rodará.notes: Passive-se se rodará en Praga ('it will be filmed in Prague') is far more idiomatic in Spanish than true passive será rodada.

rodeado.etymology: Participial adjective of rodear ('surrounded, encircled'), formed within Spanish from rueda / rodar (< Latin rota 'wheel, circle') + iterative suffix -ear ('to go around in a circle, surround').

rootFamily.gloss: detour, beating around the bush (sin rodeos); cattle roundup

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rodear
Wiktionary — rodeado

rodeado.notes: Note preposition choice: Spanish says rodeado DE ('surrounded BY': siempre está rodeado de niñas), and the noun el rodeo (borrowed into English!) literally means 'going in a circle'—as in hablar sin rodeos ('speaking without beating around the bush').

rodear.etymology: Derived within Spanish from rueda / roda ('wheel, circle', from Latin rota) + verbal suffix -ear.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rodear
Wiktionary — rodear

rodilla.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin rotella ('little wheel, kneecap'), diminutive of Classical Latin rota ('wheel'), which replaced Old Spanish hinojo (< Latin genuculum) as the standard word for 'knee'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rodilla
Wiktionary — rodilla

morphemes.meaning: small disc, heraldic roundel (< Late Latin rotella)

cognates.meaning: rowel of a spur (< Old French roele < rotella)

rootFamily.gloss: knee (inherited Castilian reflex of the same Latin rotella 'kneecap'!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: roela

roelas.notes: Jorge Roelas (beloved across Spain as Marcial in the 1990s hit series Médico de familia) makes a cameo in Paquita Salas's nostalgic world of 1990s Spanish television.

rogar.etymology: Inherited from Latin rogāre ('to ask, request, question, entreat'), preserving voiced intervocalic -g- and developing regular Castilian diphthongization of stressed short ŏ to ue in boot forms (ruego, ruegas, ruega).

serio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin sērius ('grave, earnest, weighty, no-nonsense', from Proto-Indo-European *swer- 'heavy', cognate with German schwer 'heavy, serious').

sesenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sexanta (contracted from Classical Latin sexāgintā, 'sixty', built from sex 'six' + the decimal element -āgintā 'tens'), with regular evolution of intervocalic -x- through palatal [ʃ] in Old Spanish sessaenta / sesenta to modern alveolar s.

sevilla.etymology: Andalusian capital and Spanish surname Sevilla (here referring to iconic Spanish film star, singer, and television presenter Carmen Sevilla, stage name of María del Carmen García Galisteo, 1930–2023). The city's name evolved through Andalusi Arabic Ishbīliya (إشبيلية) from Roman Hispalis (itself of Tartessian or Phoenician pre-Roman substrate origin), showing regular Arabic substitution of b for Latin p (which Arabic lacks) and subsequent Castilian evolution of -bīliya to Sevilla.

cognates.meaning: via French Séville from Spanish Sevilla

sevilla.notes: Notice how Seville's ancient Roman name Hispalis still survives in Spanish journalism and soccer (el conjunto hispalense), while Sevilla preserves the centuries of Arabic pronunciation!

seña.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin signa, originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin signum ('mark, sign, token, signal'), reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: seña

señalar.etymology: Derived within Spanish from señal ('sign, mark, signal', from Late Latin signāle < signum) + verbal suffix -ar.

señor.notes: Takes definite article el when speaking about someone (el señor Gómez), and no article when addressing someone directly (¡Buenos días, señor!).

señora.etymology: Señora was formed in medieval Spanish by adding feminine -a to señor (from Latin seniōrem) as the respectful title 'madam, Mrs, lady'.

si.etymology: Conditional conjunction ('if, whether') inherited from Latin sī ('if'); also the seventh musical solfège note si (pitch B), formed from the initials of Sancte Ioannes in Guido d'Arezzo's hymn Ut queant laxis.

sido.etymology: Past participle of ser ('been'), inherited from Old Spanish seído / sido, the regular weak past participle built on Old Spanish seer ('to sit, remain, be' < Latin sedēre 'to sit'). Because Classical Latin esse ('to be') lacked a past participle altogether, Spanish supplied sido from sedēre (whereas French été and Italian stato drew theirs from stāre 'to stand').

morphemes.meaning: be (< Old Spanish seer < Latin sedēre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ser

sido.notes: Used exclusively as an invariable masculine-form participle after auxiliary haber: ha sido, había sido, habría sido ('has been, had been, would have been').

siempre.etymology: Siempre descends regularly from Latin semper ('always, at all times'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie and final -er metathesizing to -re.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: siempre

siempre.notes: Siempre que + subjunctive means 'whenever / provided that'.

sien.etymology: Remarkably among Romance languages, Spanish sien ('temple of the head') does NOT come from Latin tempora (> French tempe, Italian tempia, English temple); instead, as shown by Joan Corominas and the RAE, it evolved from Old Spanish sen ('mind, judgment, sense'), borrowed via Old Occitan/French sen from West Germanic *sinn- ('sense, mind', compare German Sinn, Catalan seny, Italian senno). Diphthongization from sen to sien arose by analogy with sentir / siento, and its meaning shifted metonymically from 'seat of reason' to the side of the forehead.

history.meaning: seat of judgment -> temple of the head

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: sien

sien.notes: Feminine noun (la sien, las sienes). Watch out for the dual false friend: anatomical 'temple' is la sien, religious 'temple' is el templo, and don't confuse sien with cien ('one hundred', pronounced identically in seseo dialects)!

siento.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of sentir ('I feel; [lo siento] I'm sorry'), inherited from Latin sentiō (infinitive sentīre, 'to perceive through the senses, feel, think'), with regular Castilian diphthongization of short stressed ĕ to ie.

history.meaning: I feel; I regret (lo siento = 'I feel it' -> 'I'm sorry')

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Latin derivatives of sentīre

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: sentir

siento.notes: Notice TWO verbs share the exact form yo siento: sentir ('I feel / Lo siento = I'm sorry') and sentar ('I seat' / me siento = 'I sit down')!

siete.etymology: Siete continues Latin septem ('seven'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie and medial -pt- simplifying to -t-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: siete

siete.notes: Combines in plural setent- (setenta = 70) and ordinal séptimo ('seventh').

significar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin significāre ('to show by signs, indicate, mean'), compounded from signum ('sign') + -ficāre (< facere 'to make').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: significar

siguiente.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish siguiente from Latin sequentem (nominative sequēns, present participle of sequī 'to follow'), remodeled after the stem vowel of seguir.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: siguiente

silla.etymology: Silla descends regularly from Latin sella ('seat, chair, saddle', related to sedēre), with stressed short ĕ before palatalized -ll- raising to Castilian -i-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: silla

silla.notes: Contrast la silla (individual chair with a backrest) with el sillón (armchair).

silvia.etymology: Feminine given name Silvia, a Renaissance and modern revival of Classical Latin Silvia (famous in Roman legend through Rhea Silvia, mother of Romulus and Remus), feminine of Silvius ('belonging to the woods, forest-born'), derived from Latin silva ('forest, woodland', whose inherited Spanish noun is selva).

history.meaning: woodland -> 'of the forest' (Roman clan and personal name)

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin silva root

cognates.meaning: learned Greek twin of the same name

sources.title: Wiktionary — Sonia

sonido.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin sonitus (Classical sonitus, -ūs, 'noise, sound'), derived from sonāre ('to sound').

history.meaning: balance scale; large sum of silver

cognates.meaning: shared biblical semantic shift via Old French and Latin

teníamos.etymology: First-person plural imperfect indicative of tener ('we had'), inherited from Latin tenēbāmus (1pl imperfect of tenēre 'to hold, keep'), showing regular loss of intervocalic -b- in Spanish -er and -ir imperfects (-ēbāmus > -íamos) and semantic expansion of tener from 'hold' to 'have, possess'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tener
Wiktionary — teníamos

teníamos.notes: In Spanish agencies, nosotros teníamos un chiquito... means 'we used to represent / have a young actor on our roster...'.

tercero.etymology: Tercero derives from Latin tertiārius ('containing a third, third in order', built on tertius, 'third').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tercero

tercero.notes: Shortens to tercer before a masculine singular noun (el tercer día), while staying full in feminine la tercera planta.

terminando.etymology: Gerund of terminar ('finishing, wrapping up'), formed with -ando on learned/semi-learned terminar, from Latin termināre ('to mark off boundaries, limit, bring to a close'), denominal from terminus ('boundary stone, limit, end').

cognates.meaning: formal/harsh false tone: Spanish terminar simply means everyday 'finish'!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: terminar
Wiktionary — terminando

terminando.notes: Quedarse + gerund (tú te quedas terminando la prueba) is a super-natural Spanish construction meaning 'you stay behind finishing up the audition tape'.

terminar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin termināre ('to set bounds to, limit, finish, conclude'), derived from terminus ('boundary stone, limit, end').

history.meaning: to bound, bring to an end

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: terminar
Wiktionary — terminar

terror.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin terror, terrōrem ('great fear, dread, panic'), built with the state-noun suffix -or on terrēre ('to frighten, make tremble', causative from Proto-Indo-European *ters- 'to tremble').

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French from Latin terrōrem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: terror
Wiktionary — terror

terror.notes: Genre false-friend tip: an English 'horror movie' is ALWAYS una película de terror (or cine de terror, or colloquially una peli de miedo) in Spanish—never *película de horror!

terés.etymology: Catalan and Aragonese toponymic surname Terés (here of real-life Barcelona actress Mariona Terés, playing a fictionalized version of herself in Paquita Salas), historical orthographic and phonetic variant of the Catalan village name Tarés (in Les Garrigues, province of Lleida), documented across Catalonia and eastern Aragon since sixteenth-century census rolls.

history.meaning: toponym in Lleida (Les Garrigues) -> hereditary surname

sources.title: Institut d'Estadística de Catalunya — Cognoms de la població: Terés

terés.notes: Oxytone surname stressed on the final syllable [teˈɾes], reflected in its written acute accent.

tesón.etymology: Popular inherited Castilian descendant of Latin tēnsiō, tēnsiōnem ('stretching, tautness, sustained effort'), verbal noun of tendere ('to stretch, strain toward a goal'). Regular Vulgar Latin loss of n before s (tēnsiōnem > *tesione > tesón) separated inherited tesón ('unyielding grit, tenacity, perseverance') from its later learned Latinate doublet tensión ('physical or emotional tension').

cognates.meaning: tension, blood pressure (learned doublet from the exact same Latin word!)
stiffness; intense excitement/arousal (divergent slang shift in Portuguese!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tesón
Wiktionary — tesón

tesón.notes: Featured in the iconic flamenco-pop opening theme song of Paquita Salas (sung by Rosalía in Season 1: 'Pasión, tesón, que andando se hace camino...'): con mucho tesón praises admiring, tireless perseverance!

tetera.etymology: Derived within Spanish from té ('tea', ultimately from Hokkien Chinese tê) + vessel-forming suffix -tera / -era.

history.meaning: vessel for brewing and pouring tea

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tetera
Wiktionary — tetera

the.etymology: English definite article the (appearing here inside Mariona Terés's comedic broken-English audition scene), evolved from Middle English þe and late Old English þē, which replaced Classical Old English masculine nominative sē by leveling the initial dental fricative þ- across the demonstrative paradigm (< Proto-Germanic *sa / *þat, from Proto-Indo-European demonstrative *só, *séh₂, *tód).

sources.title: Wiktionary — the

the.notes: Appears inside an English-language Hollywood self-tape scene in Paquita Salas, where Spanish actors who barely speak English memorize lines phonetically (contrasting English invariable 'the' with Spanish four-way el, la, los, las).

this.etymology: English proximal demonstrative pronoun and determiner this (uttered inside Mariona's English-language casting self-tape), inherited from Old English þis (neuter nominative/accusative singular of þēs 'this'), built from the Proto-Germanic demonstrative stem *þa- plus a proximal reinforcing particle *-si.

sources.title: Wiktionary — this

this.notes: Part of the show's running comedy about Spanish actors bluffing 'high-level English' on their CVs ('But it's very important give this'). Spanish equivalents split by gender into este, esta, and neuter esto.

thriller.etymology: Unadapted English film and literary genre loanword thriller (masculine in Spanish: un thriller), formed in late-nineteenth-century English with agentive -er from thrill ('to send a shiver of excitement through'), which evolved by metathesis from Middle English thrillen < Old English þyrlian ('to pierce, perforate', from þyrel 'hole', related to through).

history.meaning: to pierce -> to excite -> suspense story

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: thriller
Wiktionary — thriller

thriller.notes: In Peninsular Spanish, speakers naturally adapt English initial th- to castilian interdental [ˈθɾileɾ] (or [ˈtɾileɾ]); native Spanish equivalents recommended by style guides are película de suspense (Spain) or de suspenso (Latin America).

ti.etymology: Inherited from Latin tibi ('to thee, for you', dative singular of tū), with regular loss of intervocalic -b- (*tii > ti).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ti
Wiktionary — ti

tiempo.etymology: Inherited from Latin tempus ('time, period, season, weather condition'), with regular diphthongization of tonic short e > ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tiempo
Wiktionary — tiempo

tiempos.etymology: Plural of tiempo ('time, era, weather'), inherited from Latin tempus ('time, period, season'), where the neuter singular form ending in -us was reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a masculine second-declension noun (*tempus > *tempo) with regular Castilian diphthongization of short stressed ĕ to ie.

cognates.meaning: learned borrowings from Latin tempus, temporis

rootFamily.gloss: season (of the year or of a TV series!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tiempo
Wiktionary — tiempos

tiempos.notes: Singular el tiempo is uncountable 'time' (no tengo tiempo) or 'weather' (¿qué tiempo hace?), while plural los tiempos means historical 'times / eras' (Los tiempos cambian = 'Times change'—the central theme of Paquita Salas!).

tienda.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin tenda ('tent, market stall covered by an awning'), derived from Classical Latin tendere ('to stretch out cloth'), with diphthongization of short e > ie.

history.meaning: stretched canvas tent or market booth

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tienda
Wiktionary — tienda

tierno.etymology: Inherited from Latin tenerum (nominative tener, 'soft, delicate, young'), with diphthongization of tonic short e > ie and metathesis of -nr- > -rn- (*tienero > *tienro > tierno).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tierno
Wiktionary — tierno

tigretón.etymology: Iconic Spanish snack-cake trademark Tigretón (marketed in Spain since the early 1970s by Bimbo alongside Pantera Rosa and Bony), formed playfully from tigre ('tiger', < Latin tigris < Ancient Greek tígris, of Old Iranian origin) + diminutive/stem -et- + augmentative suffix -ón ('big little tiger', matching the cartoon tiger cub on the wrapper).

morphemes.meaning: big snack roll / playful mascot name

history.meaning: chocolate-coated rolled sponge cake filled with apricot jam and cream

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tigre

tigretón.notes: Major cultural touchstone in Spain (and Paquita's ultimate comfort food when heartbroken!): every Spaniard who grew up from the 1970s onward knows the rivalry between Tigretón and Pantera Rosa snack cakes.

tilo.etymology: Derived from Latin tilia ('linden tree, lime tree'), reshaped into a masculine tree noun tilo (while feminine tila denotes the calming herbal infusion made from its blossoms).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tilo
Wiktionary — tilo

timbre.etymology: Timbre came into Spanish via Old French timbre ('small bell struck with a hammer'), from Latin tympănum ('drum, tambourine', from Greek týmpanon).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: timbre

timbre.notes: Names a doorbell, a hotel reception desk bell (tocar el timbre), an ink seal, or vocal tone.

tinta.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin tincta ('dyed water, colored ink'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin tingere ('to wet, dip, dye').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tinta
Wiktionary — tinta

tipo.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin typus from Ancient Greek týpos (τύπος, 'blow, die-stamp impression on a coin, carved relief, model, pattern'), derived from týptō (τύπτω, 'to strike, stamp'). In colloquial Spanish across Spain and the Americas, un tipo ('a character/specimen') developed the everyday slang sense 'a guy, fellow, dude'.

cognates.meaning: type; guy, fellow (exact same colloquial sense!)
borrowed via French/Latin from Greek týpos

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tipo
Wiktionary — tipo

tipo.notes: Notice how three Romance languages share this exact slang shift: Spanish un tipo, French un type, and Italian un tipo all mean 'a guy / some dude' (hay un tipo por ahí = 'there's some guy hanging around out there').

tirar.etymology: Pan-Romance verb (attested in Medieval Latin tirāre) of uncertain ultimate origin (variously connected to Germanic *tīran 'to pull, tear' or Vulgar Latin), meaning 'to pull, draw' and 'to throw, cast'.

history.meaning: to pull (tirar de); to throw, toss, knock over

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tirar
Wiktionary — tirar

tirón.etymology: Derived within Spanish from tirar ('to pull') + sudden-action/augmentative suffix -ón.

history.meaning: tug, yank, pull (de un tirón 'in one go')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tirón
Wiktionary — tirón

titular.etymology: Denominal verb formed from título ('title, inscription, heading', semi-learned borrowing from Latin titulus 'label, placard, title of honor') + first-conjugation suffix -ar.

morphemes.meaning: first-conjugation verb ending (also relational adj. suffix -āris)

history.meaning: to give a title to; (titularse) to be titled; graduate with a degree

rootFamily.gloss: accent mark / tilde (popular inherited doublet of título!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: titular
Wiktionary — titular

titular.notes: For books, films, and songs, reflexive titularse is super natural: un libro que se titula... ('a book titled...'). Noun homograph el titular means 'newspaper headline' or 'starting player' on a team!

tiza.etymology: The DLE records tiza as a borrowing from Nahuatl tizatl ('white chalky earth, gypsum'), adopted into Spanish from Mexico and generalized in Spain for blackboard chalk.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tiza

tiza.notes: Cartel de tiza or escrito con tiza describes a chalk-written market sign.

to.etymology: English directional/recipient preposition and infinitive marker to (uttered inside Mariona's broken-English audition line 'give this envelope to the...'), inherited from Old English tō ('to, toward, at'), from West Germanic *tō (cognate with German zu).

sources.title: Wiktionary — to

to.notes: Part of the English audition script read aloud in Paquita Salas, corresponding functionally to Spanish preposition a ('entregar este sobre a...').

toalla.etymology: Borrowed via Old Spanish toaja / Gallo-Romance from Frankish/Germanic *þwahljō ('cloth for drying hands after washing', derived from *þwahan 'to wash').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: toalla
Wiktionary — toalla

tobillo.etymology: Inherited via Old Spanish toviello from a diminutive of Latin tūber ('swelling, bump, bony protuberance'), referring to the rounded prominence of the anklebone.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tobillo
Wiktionary — tobillo

tocar.etymology: Pan-Romance verb from Vulgar Latin *toccāre, of expressive/onomatopoeic origin imitating the dry tap toc of striking a bell or knocking on wood.

history.meaning: to touch; to play (an instrument); to knock/ring; to be one's turn

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tocar
Wiktionary — tocar

todavía.etymology: Todavía fused toda + vía (from Latin tōta via, 'all the way, continually'), shifting from 'always' in medieval Spanish to 'still' (affirmative) and 'yet' (with no).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: todavía

todavía.notes: Todavía está caliente means 'it is still warm', while ¿Todavía no? means 'Not yet?'.

todo.etymology: Todo comes from Latin totus, meaning whole or entire. Spanish uses this inherited word both for a complete whole and for all the members of a group.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: todo

todo.notes: In todo el mundo the complete world stands for everyone. Todo follows the singular masculine mundo even though many people are meant.

toma.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative (and 3sg present indicative) of tomar ('here, take this!; have [a drink/bite]'), a characteristically Iberian Romance verb (Spanish and Portuguese tomar) that largely displaced Latin capere / accipere. Its ultimate origin is uncertain: the RAE marks tomar as of uncertain origin, while Corominas favors an expressive/onomatopoeic creation (*tumb- / *tom- imitating the sound of dropping or clapping hands onto an object) over older philological proposals linking it to Latin autumāre ('to affirm, claim ownership').

history.meaning: here you go!, take this! (imperative); film take (noun: toma uno)

rootFamily.gloss: to take; have food or drink
drink up / have yourself (tómate el café)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tomar
Wiktionary — toma

toma.notes: When handing someone anything in Spain (a mug of tea, keys, change), speakers say ¡Toma! (informal tú) or ¡Tome! (formal usted) where English says 'Here you go!' Also on a film set, feminine noun una toma means a camera 'take' (¡Toma dos!).

tomar.etymology: The DLE marks tomar ('to take; to have food or drink') as of uncertain Hispanic origin (variously linked to Latin autumāre or an expressive root).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tomar

tomar.notes: Most natural Spanish verb for ordering or having a drink or snack: ¿Qué va a tomar?, tomo un té con miel.

tomate.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Nahuatl tomatl ('plump fruit, tomatillo'), extended in New Spain from xitomatl to the red tomato and spread worldwide through Spanish.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tomate

tomate.notes: Alongside chocolate, aguacate, and cacahuete, one of the great Nahuatl food words transmitted to European languages via Spanish.

tono.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin tonus ('tension of a cord, pitch, tone'), from Ancient Greek tónos ('stretching, string, musical pitch', from teínein 'to stretch').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tono
Wiktionary — tono

tonterías.etymology: Plural of tontería ('silliness, foolish remark, nonsense'), formed with the quality/behavior suffix -ería on tonto ('silly, foolish, dumb'). Following Corominas and the RAE, tonto is an expressive Romance creation (sound-symbolic of dullness or stupor, compare tontorrón and Italian tonto), perhaps influenced by Latin attonitus ('thunderstruck, dazed, stupefied').

history.meaning: piece of nonsense -> silly remarks, nonsense

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tontería
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tonto

tonterías.notes: Unlike English uncountable 'nonsense', Spanish uses countable plural tonterías: ¡Anda, qué tonterías! ('Oh come on, what nonsense!') and dejarse de tonterías ('cut the nonsense').

toque.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from tocar ('to touch, tap, ring, play'), with orthographic c > qu before e.

history.meaning: act of touching, tapping, or ringing

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: toque
Wiktionary — toque

torcer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torquēre (Classical Latin torquēre, 'to twist, wind, bend, sprain'), with regular diphthongization in stressed forms (tuerce).

history.meaning: to twist, bend, sprain, turn (a corner)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: torcer
Wiktionary — torcer

tormenta.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin tormenta (originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin tormentum, 'hurling engine, violent twisting, upheaval', from torquēre 'to twist'), reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun meaning 'storm'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tormenta
Wiktionary — tormenta

tornillo.etymology: Diminutive of torno ('lathe, turning spindle', from Latin tornus < Ancient Greek tórnos 'lathe, circular chisel'), formed with the suffix -illo.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tornillo
Wiktionary — tornillo

torre.etymology: Inherited from Latin turrem (accusative of turris, 'tower, fortified turret', itself an ancient Mediterranean loanword parallel to Ancient Greek týrsis, τύρσις), with regular Romance lowering of short stressed ŭ to o.

history.meaning: tower; chess rook; Tarot card The Tower

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French tor / tourete from Latin turrem

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: torre
Wiktionary — torre

torre.notes: Feminine noun (la torre). In tarot readings (a favorite pastime in Paquita Salas!), la carta de la torre ('The Tower') portends a sudden shake-up, and in chess la torre is the 'rook / castle'.

torreznos.etymology: Plural of torrezno ('thick strip of marinated pork belly fried until the rind puffs into a golden crackle', famed specialty of Soria and Castile), derived from torrar ('to toast, roast') < Classical Latin torrēre ('to parch, roast, scorch with heat'). Documented in Nebrija and Covarrubias alongside Old Spanish torrendo (< Latin gerundive torrendus 'piece meant to be roasted'), whose consonant cluster -nd- evolved in rural Castilian into the characteristic suffixal sequence -zn- (compare rodezno, lobezno).

morphemes.meaning: traditional Castilian nominal suffix (from Old Spanish torrendo)

history.meaning: roasted strip of salt pork or bacon

cognates.meaning: learned/French borrowings from Latin torrēre and its participle tostus

rootFamily.gloss: to toast (from Latin frequentative tostāre < torrēre!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: torrezno
Wiktionary — torrezno

torreznos.notes: Paquita Salas single-handedly sparked a nationwide revival of ordering un gin-tonic y unos torreznos (especially Torreznos de Soria, thick pork belly with an airy, blistered crunchy skin)!

tose.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative of toser ('coughs', here a subtitle caption cue [FINA TOSE]), inherited from Vulgar Latin *tusset (infinitive *tussēre, shifted into the second conjugation from Classical Latin fourth-conjugation tussīre 'to cough', denominal from tussis 'cough'), with regular lowering of short stressed ŭ to o.

cognates.meaning: medical borrowing ('whooping cough') from Latin tussis

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: toser
Wiktionary — tose

tose.notes: Watch conjugation class: unlike French tousser (-er = 1st conj.) and Italian tossire (-ire = 3rd conj.), Spanish toser is an -er verb (yo toso, tú toses, ella tose).

tostada.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of tostar ('to toast, roast'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *tostāre, derived from Classical Latin tōstus (past participle of torrēre 'to parch, roast').

history.meaning: piece of toast, toasted bread slice

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tostada
Wiktionary — tostada

totalmente.etymology: Adverb formed from invariant singular adjective total ('total, whole', learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tōtālis, derived from Classical Latin tōtus 'all, whole, entire') + adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

rootFamily.gloss: total; 'anyway / long story short' (Peninsular discourse filler!)
all, everything (inherited reflex of Latin tōtus)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: totalmente
Wiktionary — totalmente

totalmente.notes: Used standalone as enthusiastic agreement in Spain: ¡Totalmente! (or clipped to ¡Total!, 'Totally! / 100%!').

trabaja.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative (and tú imperative) of trabajar ('works; work!'), inherited via Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre ('to torture on the tripālium; suffer torment, toil hard'), denominal verb built on Late Latin tripālium (attested in 582 CE at the Council of Auxerre: a three-staked wooden restraint or torture frame, compounded from tri- 'three' + pālus 'stake').

history.meaning: three-staked frame -> to torment, strain, labor

cognates.meaning: both borrowed from Old French travailler (< *tripāliāre)!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajar
Wiktionary — trabaja

trabaja.notes: Unforgettable etymology: Spanish trabajar, French travailler, and English travel all trace back to Late Latin tripālium ('three-stake torture instrument')—a reminder of how grueling both medieval labor and medieval journeys felt!

trabajador.etymology: Agentive adjective and noun formed from trabajar ('to work', < Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre, from Late Latin tripālium 'three-staked frame') + agent suffix -dor (< Latin -tōrem).

morphemes.meaning: one who works / inclined to work (< -tōrem)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajador
Wiktionary — trabajador

trabajador.notes: Notice how single Spanish trabajador/a translates TWO English patterns: as a noun un trabajador ('a worker') and as an adjective Es muy trabajadora ('She is very hard-working').

trabajar.etymology: The DLE traces trabajar to reconstructed Vulgar Latin *tripaliāre, associated with torture, and ultimately to Late Latin tripalium, a three-timber instrument of torture. The asterisk marks an inferred historical form rather than an attested spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajar

trabajar.notes: Modern trabajar covers physical or intellectual activity, paid employment and practising a profession. Those present-day meanings should be learned in their own contexts.

trabajazo.etymology: Expressive Peninsular Spanish augmentative formed from trabajo ('work, performance', postverbal noun of trabajar < Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre) + appreciative augmentative suffix -azo (< Latin -āceus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -azo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajo

trabajazo.notes: Spaniards love appreciative -azo nouns for enthusiastic praise: un trabajazo ('a phenomenal job / tour-de-force performance'), un papelazo ('an incredible role'), un peliculón / exitazo ('a smash hit')!

trabajo.etymology: Deverbal noun from trabajar ('to work, labor'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre ('to torment, put to hard labor'), derived from Late Latin tripālium ('three-staked frame of restraint', from trēs 'three' + pālus 'stake').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajo

traer.etymology: Inherited from Latin trahere ('to draw, drag, pull along, bring'), with regular loss of intervocalic -h-/-g-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: traer
Wiktionary — traer

traigo.etymology: First-person singular present indicative of traer ('I bring'), evolved from Old Spanish trayo (< Vulgar Latin *trahiō, remodeled from Classical Latin trahō, infinitive trahere 'to pull, drag, draw'), acquiring an epenthetic velar -g- in late medieval Castilian on the model of caigo, oigo, and digo.

rootFamily.gloss: bring (present subjunctive / usted command built on traig-)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: traer
Wiktionary — traigo

traigo.notes: Deictic direction rule: Spanish strictly separates traer ('bring here toward the speaker': Que traigo un paquete) from llevar ('take away over there').

traje.etymology: Masculine noun el traje ('suit, outfit, traditional costume'), borrowed in the fifteenth–sixteenth centuries from Portuguese traje (older trajo), a postverbal noun from Portuguese trazer ('to bring, carry, wear garments', cognate with Spanish traer < Latin trahere). Literally 'what one carries or wears on one's body'—an exact semantic parallel to English outfit/wear, Latin habitus (< habēre 'to hold'), and German Tracht (< tragen 'to carry').

history.meaning: business suit; costume/outfit (traje de baño, traje de luces)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: traje

traje.notes: Fun double life of the spelling traje: noun el traje ('the suit / outfit', borrowed from Portuguese) vs. verb yo traje ('I brought', 1sg preterite of traer < Latin trāxī)—both ultimately from Latin trahere! Idiomatically in Spain, hacerle un traje a alguien means 'to gossip mercilessly / tear someone to shreds behind their back'.

trama.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned from Latin trāma ('weft or woof—the crosswise threads drawn by the shuttle through the vertical warp on a loom', from archaic *trāgma, derived from trahere 'to draw across'). Metaphorically extended to a 'woven plot, intrigue, or dramatic storyline'.

history.meaning: weft threads woven across a loom
fabric weft; dramatic plot, storyline; conspiracy

rootFamily.gloss: to plot, hatch a scheme (¿Qué estás tramando?)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trama
Wiktionary — trama

trama.notes: In Spanish TV writers' rooms, la trama is the character's storyline or arc across episodes (el personaje tenía una trama increíble).

trampa.etymology: Noun of expressive or Germanic origin (related to Late Latin trappa < Frankish *trappa, 'snare, pitfall, trapdoor', with nasal insertion).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trampa

tranquila.etymology: Feminine singular of tranquilo ('calm, relaxed, quiet, unworried'), a learned borrowing from Classical Latin tranquillus ('calm, still, hushed', originally of calm seas and weather, likely built from trāns- + a stem related to quiēs 'rest').

cognates.meaning: poetic/formal in English, whereas Spanish tranquilo/a is super everyday!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tranquilo
Wiktionary — tranquila

tranquila.notes: One of the most reassuring single words in Spanish: telling a female friend ¡Tú tranquila! (or to a man ¡Tranquilo!) means 'Relax / Don't worry at all, I've got this!'

tranquilizar.etymology: Derived from tranquilo ('calm, serene', learned borrowing from Latin tranquillus) + causative verbal suffix -izar (< Late Latin -izāre < Greek -ízein), compare Late Latin tranquillizāre and French tranquilliser.

cognates.meaning: semi-false friend: English usually implies sedating with drugs, whereas Spanish tranquilizar simply means 'to reassure / calm down'!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tranquilizar

tranquilizar.notes: False-friend caution: ¡Tranquilízate! simply means 'Calm down / take a breath!' (never medical 'sedate yourself'!), and Eso me tranquiliza means 'That puts my mind at ease'.

tranquilo.etymology: Tranquilo comes as a learned borrowing from Latin tranquillus ('calm, still, peaceful').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tranquilo

tranquilo.notes: Used both to describe quiet places (un patio tranquilo) and to reassure people ('don't worry / take it easy': ¡Tranquilo!).

traído.etymology: Past participle of traer ('brought'), formed on the Spanish stem tra- (< Old Spanish traer < Latin trahere 'to pull, draw', with loss of intervocalic -h-) + the -er/-ir weak participial ending -ído (< -ītum), displacing Classical Latin strong participle tractus (which survives in learned tracto and popular trecho).

triunfo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin triumphus ('ceremonial victory procession granted to a victorious Roman general'), which entered Old Latin via Etruscan from Ancient Greek thríambos (θρίαμβος, 'processional hymn to Dionysus'), with regular Spanish assimilation of -mph- to -nf-.

history.meaning: Dionysian processional hymn > Roman victory celebration

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: triunfo

tronca.etymology: Feminine colloquial Peninsular vocative of tronco ('mate, bro, dude; [f.] girl, sis'), metaphorically extended in late-twentieth-century Madrid cheli and youth slang from tronco ('tree trunk, sturdy stem'), inherited from Latin truncus ('lopped tree trunk; maimed, cut off').

tumbar.etymology: Built on the pan-Romance onomatopoeic root *tumb- (evoking the sound of falling heavily or hitting the ground; compare French tomber, Old Occitan tombar, and English tumble). sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: táper

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tutear

tuviéramos.etymology: First-person plural -ra imperfect subjunctive of tener ('we had'), continuing Old Spanish toviéramos, built on the analogical strong preterite stem tuv- (remodeled from Latin tenēre under the phonetic influence of Old Spanish ove > hube < Latin habuī 'I had').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tener

tuya.etymology: Stressed (tonic) second-person singular (informal tú) feminine possessive adjective and pronoun ('yours, of yours'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *tuia, reshaped from Classical Latin tua ('your, yours') by analogy with interrogative cūia ('whose') alongside mía and suya.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tuyo

tv.etymology: International initialism TV for televisión ('television'), coined in mid-twentieth-century English from the Greco-Latin hybrid television (Greek tēle- 'far' + Latin vīsiō 'sight') and used universally in Spanish schedules, remote controls, and closed-caption speaker tags.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tú

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: uno

valladolid.etymology: Historic Castilian capital Valladolid (seat of the royal court in the sixteenth–seventeenth centuries and home of the Seminci film festival), documented in eleventh-century medieval charters as Valladolide / Valle de Olid. Its pre-Castilian origin is classically debated: modern Hispanic toponymists (following Menéndez Pidal, Corominas, and Nieto Ballester) favor a Celtic-Latin hybrid Vallis Tolitī ('Valley of the Confluence of Waters', referring to the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers), whereas older traditions proposed either Arabic Balad al-Walīd ('Town of al-Walīd') or folk-etymological Latin Vallis Olīvētum ('Valley of Olive Groves', which inspired the city's learned gentilic vallisoletano despite Castile's frosty non-olive climate).

history.meaning: settlement at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva

vaya.notes: Before a noun without an article, exclamative ¡vaya + noun! means 'what a...!' (¡Vaya leche! = 'What a smack / nasty blow!', ¡Vaya día! = 'What a day!'). Don't confuse spelling vaya ('go / wow') with la valla ('fence / billboard') or la baya ('berry')!

vecinal.etymology: Derived from vecino ('neighbor', < Latin vīcīnus) + relational suffix -al.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vecinal
Wiktionary — vecinal

vecino.etymology: Inherited from Latin vīcīnus ('neighboring; neighbor'), derived from vīcus ('row of houses, street, quarter, village').

history.meaning: living in the same quarter, neighbor

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vecino
Wiktionary — vecino

veinte.etymology: Veinte descends from Latin vīgintī ('twenty') via Vulgar Latin *vīnti, with loss of voiced -g- and raising/diphthongization into Castilian veinte.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinte

veinte.notes: Base of fused compounds veintiuno (21) through veintinueve (29).

veinticinco.etymology: Veinticinco fuses veinte (from Latin vīgintī, 'twenty') + y ('and') + cinco (through Vulgar Latin *cinque from Latin quīnque, 'five') into a single compound numeral.

veinticuatro.etymology: Univerbated compound numeral from veinte y cuatro (Latin vīgintī 'twenty' + et 'and' + quattuor 'four').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinticuatro

veintinueve.etymology: Univerbated compound numeral from veinte y nueve (Latin vīgintī 'twenty' + et 'and' + novem 'nine').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veintinueve
Wiktionary — veintinueve

veintiocho.etymology: Univerbated compound numeral from veinte y ocho (Latin vīgintī 'twenty' + et 'and' + octō 'eight').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veintiocho
Wiktionary — veintiocho

veintiséis.etymology: Single-word compound cardinal numeral ('twenty-six') formed by univerbation of Old Spanish veinte y seis: veinte ('twenty' < Latin vīgintī) + coordinating conjunction y ('and' < Latin et) + seis ('six' < Latin sex).

morphemes.meaning: six (< Latin sex, accented in oxytone compound)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veintiséis
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: cardinales

veintiséis.notes: Accent puzzle solved: standalone seis ('six') is a monosyllable and NEVER takes an accent, whereas fused veintiséis has three syllables ending in stressed -s [bejntiˈsejs], so Spanish accent rules require a written acute on é!

velvet.etymology: Title of the hit 2014–2016 Spanish period television drama Velvet (set in a late-1950s Madrid haute-couture department store named Galerías Velvet), using the English noun velvet ('terciopelo'). English velvet itself came via Anglo-Norman and Old Occitan veluet from Vulgar Latin *villūtus ('shaggy, plush-napped'), derived from Classical Latin villus ('tuft of soft hair, nap of cloth'—the exact same root as Spanish vello and the -pelo/-vello element of terciopelo!).

cognates.meaning: velvet (< Old Occitan velos < Latin villōsus)

sources.title: Wiktionary — velvet
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: terciopelo

velvet.notes: Along with El puente viejo and Vis a vis, landing a role on Velvet is the dream gig for mid-2010s Spanish TV actors in Paquita Salas.

vender.etymology: Inherited from Latin vendere ('to sell'), itself contracted in early Latin from vēnum dare ('to put up for sale').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vender
Wiktionary — vender

venga.etymology: Grammaticalized Peninsular Spanish discourse marker and interjection ('come on!, alright!, let's go!; okay, bye!'), originating as the third-person singular present subjunctive / usted imperative of venir ('come'). Form venga continues Latin veniam, veniat (< venīre 'to come'), having developed a velar -g- in Iberian Romance (parallel to teneam > tenga, pōnam > ponga).

history.meaning: come (subj.); come on!, alright!, sounds good!

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: venga
Wiktionary — venga

venga.notes: Arguably THE #1 signature word of Peninsular Spain! Spaniards use ¡Venga! to rally people (Venga, vamos al coche = 'Come on, let's get to the car'), to agree (Venga, vale = 'Alright, deal'), to express disbelief (¡Venga ya! = 'Oh come off it!'), and to hang up the phone (¡Venga, hasta luego!).

venir.etymology: Venir continues Latin venīre ('to come') with unchanged infinitive spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: venir

venir.notes: Shares many stem patterns with tener: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen; la semana que viene means 'next week'.

venta.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vendita ('sale, things sold'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin vendere ('to sell'), via syncope (*vend'ta > venta).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: venta
Wiktionary — venta

ventana.etymology: Ventana derives from Vulgar Latin *(fenestra) ventāna ('wind-opening', built on Latin ventus, 'wind'), uniquely replacing fenestra in Castilian and Portuguese.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ventana
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viento

history.meaning: opening for wind and air -> window

ventana.notes: Notice how English 'window' ('wind-eye', from Old Norse vindauga) was coined from the exact same image of wind!

ventilador.etymology: Borrowed from Latin ventilātor ('winnower, fan-maker') or derived from ventilar ('to air, fan', < Latin ventilāre, from ventus 'wind') + suffix -dor.

history.meaning: to fan, set air in motion

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ventilador
Wiktionary — ventilador

ver.etymology: Ver evolved from Old Spanish veer, continuing Latin vidēre ('to see') after regular loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver

ver.notes: Retains the fuller stem ve- in veo ('I see'), veía (imperfect), and past participle visto; ¡A ver! means 'Let's see!'.

verano.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(tempus) verānum ('springtime season', from Classical Latin vēr 'spring'); in medieval Spanish it denoted late spring/early summer while estío meant high summer, before verano shifted to 'summer' and primavera took over 'spring'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verano
Wiktionary — verano

verdad.etymology: Verdad continues Latin verĭtas, veritātis ('truth', from vērus, 'true'), with syncope of unstressed -i- and voicing of -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verdad

verdad.notes: ¿Verdad? at the end of a statement asks 'right? / isn't it?', and ¿De verdad? asks 'Really?'.

verde.etymology: Verde continues Vulgar Latin *virde, syncopated from Classical Latin virĭdis ('green, fresh, flourishing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verde

verde.notes: Two-form adjective: singular verde for both genders (el árbol verde, la farmacia verde), plural verdes.

verdura.etymology: Derived from verde ('green', inherited from Latin viridis) + abstract/collective suffix -ura.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verdura
Wiktionary — verdura

vergüenza.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin verēcundia ('modesty, bashfulness, sense of shame', derived from verērī 'to feel awe, respect, or fear'), with regular Hispano-Romance syncope of the pretonic vowel (*vercundia), voicing of -c- after r (-g-), diphthongisation of short u before yod (üe), and assibilation of -ndj- to -nz-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vergüenza
Wiktionary — vergüenza#Spanish

vergüenza.notes: The diaeresis (ü) shows that the u in -güe- is pronounced ([beɾˈɣwenθa] / [beɾˈɣwensa]); tener vergüenza or dar vergüenza regularly translates 'to feel shy or embarrassed'.

verja.etymology: Borrowed from Old French verge or Catalan verja (from Latin virga, 'green shoot, rod, metal bar'), denoting an iron grating, railing, or fence.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verja
Wiktionary — verja

verso.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin versus ('furrow turned by the plow at the end of a field; hence a line of writing or line of poetry'), derived from versus, past participle of vertere ('to turn').

history.meaning: to turn -> plow-turn, line of verse
line of poetry; verse (as opposed to prosa 'prose')

rootFamily.gloss: stanza (what English casually calls a 'verse' of a song!)
prose (< Latin prōrsa ōrātiō 'straight-ahead speech' without turning!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verso
Wiktionary — verso

verso.notes: Precision tip: in Spanish, un verso is a SINGLE line of poetry (or classical Golden Age verse theater: recitar en verso), whereas a multi-line stanza or song 'verse' is una estrofa!

verte.etymology: Infinitive ver ('to see') fused with the enclitic second-person singular (tú) direct object pronoun te ('to see you, seeing you'). Infinitive ver contracted in the late Middle Ages from Old Spanish veer (< Classical Latin vidēre 'to see', from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- 'to see, know'), after loss of intervocalic -d-.

morphemes.meaning: to see (< Old Spanish veer < Latin vidēre)

rootFamily.gloss: to look (a certain way); meet up

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver

verte.notes: Warm greeting/parting staple: Me alegro de verte ('Great to see you / Glad to see you!'). Notice Spanish uses the infinitive after prepositions (de verte) where English uses '-ing' ('of seeing you').

vertical.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin verticālis ('directly overhead, upright'), derived from Classical Latin vertex, verticis ('highest point, zenith, crown').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vertical
Wiktionary — vertical

very.etymology: English degree intensifier very (spoken inside Mariona's broken-English audition tape: 'But it's very important give this'), borrowed in Middle English as verray ('true, genuine') from Old French verai (modern vrai), descending from Vulgar Latin *vērācus (< Classical Latin vērax / vērus 'true'—making English very a direct Romance cousin of Spanish verdadero and veraz!).

cognates.meaning: truthful / truth (from the same Latin vērus family!)

sources.title: Wiktionary — very

very.notes: Delightful hidden link: English 'very' (used in Mariona's English audition line) isn't Germanic at all—it shares the same Latin root vērus ('true') as Spanish de verdad!

verás.etymology: Second-person singular (tú) future indicative of ver ('you will see'), formed from infinitive ver (< Old Spanish veer < Latin vidēre 'to see') + stressed future ending -ás (< Vulgar Latin *habēs 'you have [to]').

history.meaning: you have to see -> you will see

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver
Wiktionary — verás

verás.notes: Two classic conversational chunks: reassuring ¡Ya verás! ('You'll see—it'll go great!') and story-opener Verás... ('Look / Let me explain...').

ves.etymology: Second-person singular (tú) present indicative of ver ('you see'), contracted from Old Spanish vees (< Classical Latin vidēs, 2sg of vidēre 'to see') following regular loss of intervocalic -d-. (Also serves as a widespread non-standard colloquial Peninsular variant of imperative ve 'go!', though standard RAE prescribes ve.)

rootFamily.gloss: I see (preserving Old Spanish's two-syllable stem ve-!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver
Wiktionary — ves

ves.notes: Homophone alert in seseo dialects (Latin America, Andalusia, Canary Islands): tú ves ('you see', with -s) sounds identical to la vez ('the time/occasion', with -z), while Castilian Peninsular distinguishes [bes] from [beθ].

vestido.etymology: Inherited from Latin vestītus ('clothed, dressed; attire, garment'), past participle and noun from vestīre ('to clothe', from vestis 'garment').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vestido
Wiktionary — vestido

vestir.etymology: Inherited from Latin vestīre ('to clothe, dress, adorn'), denominal verb from vestis ('garment, clothing', from Proto-Indo-European *wes- 'to clothe', cognate with English wear and vest), showing regular Spanish vowel raising e -> i in boot and third-person preterite/gerund forms (visto, vistes, vistió, vistiendo).

history.meaning: to wear, dress someone; (vestirse) to get dressed

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vestir
Wiktionary — vestir

vestir.notes: Watch the ser/estar + vestido pattern: estar vestida así means 'being dressed like this', while vestirse de... means 'to dress up as...'.

vestíbulo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vestibulum ('forecourt, entrance court of a house, foyer').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vestíbulo

veta.etymology: Inherited from Latin vitta ('headband, fillet, ribbon, stripe'), which shifted in Spanish to denote a colored streak in wood grain, marble, or rock.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veta

veía.etymology: First- or third-person singular imperfect indicative of ver ('I/he/she/anyone used to see or watch'), inherited from Old Spanish veía (< Latin vidēbam / vidēbat, from vidēre 'to see'). Because Old Spanish had the two-syllable infinitive veer, its imperfect stem ve- + -ía stayed three-syllable veía even after veer contracted to ver!

morphemes.meaning: see, watch (< Old Spanish veer < vidēre)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver

veía.notes: Now you know why ver is one of ONLY THREE irregular imperfects in all of Spanish (alongside era and iba): veía isn't capricious—it simply preserves medieval veer's e!

viajar.etymology: Derived from viaje ('journey, trip') + verbal suffix -ar.

rootFamily.gloss: to defeat, overcome; expire (< Latin vincere)
