victoria.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin victōria ('victory'), derived from victor ('conqueror', from vincere 'to win, conquer').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: victoria
Wiktionary — victoria

vida.etymology: Inherited from Latin vīta ('life, way of living', related to vīvus 'alive' and vīvere 'to live'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- > -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vida
Wiktionary — vida

videobook.etymology: Spanish acting- and casting-industry pseudo-Anglicism videobook ('actor's video showreel / demo reel'), coined in Spain by combining vídeo (< English video < Latin videō 'I see') with book (earlier borrowed into European modeling and acting agencies as el book for a printed portfolio of headshots, from Old English bōc 'book').

history.meaning: edited video reel of an actor's best scenes

rootFamily.gloss: video (stressed VÍ-de-o in Spain, vi-DE-o in Latin America)

videobook.notes: Classic Spanish 'false Anglicism' (like footing for 'jogging' or parking for 'parking lot'!): native English casting directors call this a 'showreel' or 'demo reel', whereas in Madrid every actor and repre calls it el videobook!

viejo.etymology: Viejo descends from Vulgar Latin *veclus, syncopated from Classical Latin vetŭlus (diminutive of vetus, 'old'), with medial -cl- palatalizing to Old Spanish -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viejo

viejo.notes: Placed before a noun (viejos amigos), viejo means 'long-standing' rather than elderly.

viendo.etymology: Gerund of ver ('seeing, watching'), inherited from Old Spanish veyendo (< Classical Latin videndō, ablative gerund of vidēre 'to see'), where loss of intervocalic -d- and absorption of the stem vowel into the palatal/diphthongal ending -iendo yielded modern viendo.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver
Wiktionary — viendo

viendo.notes: Used with estar for watching a film, series, or video right now: lo estés viendo ('you're watching it').

vienes.etymology: Second-person singular (tú) present indicative of venir ('you come'), inherited from Latin venīs (infinitive venīre, 'to come', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- 'to step, come', cognate with English come!), with regular Castilian diphthongization of short stressed ĕ to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: venir
Wiktionary — vienes

vienes.notes: Deictic rule: unlike English (where a guest says 'I'm coming to your house!'), Spanish venir strictly moves TOWARD the speaker's current location (tú nunca vienes de visita = 'you never come here to visit me'; going to someone else's place is ir!).

viento.etymology: Inherited from Latin ventus ('wind'), with regular diphthongization of tonic short e > ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viento
Wiktionary — viento

viernes.etymology: Viernes continues Latin (diēs) Venĕris ('day of Venus'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie, metathesis of -nr- > -rn-, and analogical weekday -s.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viernes

viernes.notes: Invariable in the plural: el viernes ('on Friday'), los viernes ('on Fridays').

viga.etymology: Inherited from Latin bīga ('two-horse chariot, chariot pole', contracted from bi- + iugum 'yoke'), whose sense shifted in Ibero-Romance to a heavy timber beam or girder.

history.meaning: pair of yoked horses, chariot pole

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viga
Wiktionary — viga

vigilar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vigilāre ('to stay awake, keep watch'), derived from vigil ('awake, alert').

history.meaning: to watch over, guard, keep an eye on

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vigilar
Wiktionary — vigilar

vinagre.etymology: Borrowed via Catalan or Old Occitan vinagre, a compound of vin ('wine', < Latin vīnum) + agre ('sour, sharp', < Latin ācrem).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vinagre

vinagre.notes: In native Castilian, Latin ācrem separately yielded agrio ('sour').

vino.etymology: Homophonous convergence of two distinct Latin words in Spanish: (1) masculine noun el vino ('wine', as in dos botellas de vino), inherited from Classical Latin vīnum ('wine'); and (2) third-person singular preterite verb vino ('he/she came', as in Macarena vino a verme), inherited from Classical Latin vēnit (3sg perfect of venīre 'to come'), with root raising ē -> i leveled from 1sg vēnī (> vine).

cognates.meaning: early Germanic/French borrowings from Latin vīnum / vīnea

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vino

vino.notes: Classic Spanish pun/wordplay pair: Vino a traer el vino ('She came to bring the wine')—syntax makes instantly clear whether vino is the noun 'wine' or the preterite 'came'!

vis.etymology: Element of the Spanish expression and hit 2015–2019 prison-drama title Vis a vis ('face to face; private/conjugal prison visit'), adapted from French vis-à-vis ('face to face, opposite'), built from Old French vis ('face, countenance'), inherited from Latin vīsus ('sight, look, appearance', verbal noun of vidēre 'to see'; compare English visage).

history.form: vis a vis -> Vis a vis
history.meaning: private prison visit -> hit Spanish thriller series

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vis
Wiktionary — vis a vis

vis.notes: In Spain's penitentiary vocabulary, un vis a vis specifically denotes an inmate's private family or conjugal visit—hence the clever title of the women's-prison thriller Vis a vis!

visillo.etymology: Derived within Spanish from viso ('sight, sheer under-slip through which light shows', < Latin vīsus) + diminutive suffix -illo.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: visillo
Wiktionary — visillo

visita.etymology: Deverbal noun from visitar ('to go to see, visit'), borrowed from Latin vīsitāre (frequentative of vidēre 'to see').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: visita
Wiktionary — visita

vista.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vīsta ('sight, view, vision'), formed on the participle of Classical Latin vidēre ('to see').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vista
Wiktionary — vista

vistazo.etymology: Derived within Spanish from vista ('sight, look') + suffix -azo (indicating a quick, single action).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vistazo
Wiktionary — vistazo

vitorea.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative of vitorear ('cheers, acclaims aloud', here subtitle stage direction [CLARA VITOREA]), formed in Spanish with iterative -ear from the celebratory cry ¡vítor! ('hurrah!, hail the victor!'), itself a semi-learned borrowing from Classical Latin victor ('conqueror, winner', agent noun of vincere 'to conquer', famous from the red VÍTOR monograms painted on Spanish university walls for new doctors).

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin victor, victōria

RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vítor

vitorea.notes: Because Spanish lacks a single everyday verb cognate with English 'to cheer', subtitles and prose constantly use vitorear (CLARA VITOREA = '[CLARA CHEERS]')!

vivir.etymology: Vivir continues Latin vīvēre ('to live, be alive, dwell'), shifting to the Spanish -ir conjugation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vivir

vivo.etymology: Inherited from Latin vīvus ('alive, living, lively').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vivo
Wiktionary — vivo

volar.etymology: Inherited from Latin volāre ('to fly, move swiftly through the air'), with regular diphthongization in stressed forms (vuela).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: volar
Wiktionary — volar

volvemos.etymology: First-person plural present indicative of volver ('we return, come back; we are back together'), inherited from Latin volvimus (infinitive volvere, 'to roll, turn round, wind', from Proto-Indo-European *welH- 'to turn, roll'), with semantic shift in Iberian Romance from 'turn back around' to 'come/go back, return'.

to give back, return an item

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: volver

volvemos.notes: Unstressed root o in volvemos (vs. diphthongized vuelvo, vuelves, vuelve). In relationships or partnerships, Que volvemos announces 'We're getting back together / we're back in business!'

volver.etymology: Volver continues Latin volvĕre ('to roll, turn around'), developing in Spanish into the primary verb for 'to return, come back'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: volver

volver.notes: Stem-changing o -> ue (vuelvo, vuelve) with past participle vuelto; volver a + infinitive is the idiomatic Spanish way to say 'do something again'.

vosotros.etymology: Vosotros fused Old Spanish vos ('you', from Latin vōs) + otros ('others', from Latin altĕrōs) in late medieval Castilian to mark plural informal 'you all' distinctly from singular respectful vos.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vosotros

vosotros.notes: Everyday plural of tú across Peninsula Spain (feminine vosotras), paired with -áis / -éis / -ís verb endings and imperative -ad / -ed / -id (mirad, subid).

voz.etymology: Inherited from Latin vōcem (nominative vōx, 'voice, sound, call, word').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: voz
Wiktionary — voz

vuelta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volvita / *volta ('turn, return, revolution'), feminine participial noun of Classical Latin volvere ('to roll, turn'), with diphthongization of short o > ue.

history.meaning: turn, return, lap, stroll (dar una vuelta), change

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vuelta
Wiktionary — vuelta

vuestro.etymology: Second-person plural (vosotros) possessive determiner and pronoun ('your, yours'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *voster, *vostrum, which reshaped Classical Latin vester ('your [plural]') by vocalic analogy with first-person plural noster ('our'), followed by regular Castilian diphthongization of short stressed ŏ to ue.

cognates.meaning: your (< archaic Old Latin voster / analogy with nosso)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vuestro
Wiktionary — vuestro

vuestro.notes: Hallmark of Peninsular Spanish whenever addressing a group of friends, students, or coworkers (luchad por vuestros sueños = 'fight for your dreams!', where Latin America uses luchen por sus sueños).

válvula.etymology: Learned borrowing from Modern/Late Latin valvula ('little folding door, anatomical or mechanical valve'), diminutive of Classical Latin valva ('leaf of a folding door').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: válvula
Wiktionary — válvula

véndelo.etymology: Affirmative second-person singular (tú) imperative vende of vender ('sell!') fused with the enclitic masculine/neuter direct object pronoun lo ('sell it!'). Verb vender descends from Latin vēndere ('to sell'), an ancient contraction of vēnum dare ('to put up for sale', with vēnum cognate with English vend and Greek ōnḗ 'price').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vender
Wiktionary — véndelo

véndelo.notes: In auditions and pitching, ¡Véndelo! means 'Sell it!'—deliver the performance or pitch with total conviction.

vía.etymology: Semi-learned retention of Classical Latin via ('road, highway, path, channel, method', from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰyeh₂ 'way, wagon-track', from *weǵʰ- 'to convey in a vehicle', cognate with English way). In modern Spanish it functions both as a feminine noun ('railway track, thoroughfare, channel') and—reinforced by Latin ablative viā ('by way of') and international usage—as a preposition ('via, through': vía link).

history.meaning: track, lane, route (noun); via, by way of (preposition)

cognates.meaning: via (Latin borrowing) and way (Germanic Indo-European cognate!)

rootFamily.gloss: trip, journey (< Provençal/Catalan viatge < Latin viāticum)
to send (< Late Latin inviāre 'put on the road')

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vía
Wiktionary — vía

vía.notes: Unlike English unaccented 'via', Spanish vía ALWAYS keeps its written hiatus accent [ˈbi.a] even in prepositional phrases like vía correo, vía WhatsApp, or vía link.

washington.etymology: English habitational surname Washington (here of British-born Spanish television host and actress Belinda Washington, who stars as herself in Episode 1 of Paquita Salas), originating from the town of Washington in Tyne and Wear, northeastern England, recorded in Old English as Hwæsingatūn ('estate or enclosure [tūn] of the people [-inga-] of a leader named Hwæsa').

history.meaning: homestead of Hwæsa's kinsfolk (County Durham / Tyne and Wear)
beloved 1990s–present Spanish TV presenter and actress

sources.title: Wiktionary — Washington

washington.notes: Belinda Washington (co-host of the legendary 1990s Telecinco gossip show ¡Qué me dices!) is a household name across Spain, making her self-parodying role in Paquita Salas an instant crowd favorite.

web.etymology: Late-twentieth-century borrowing from English (World Wide) Web (invented in 1989–1990 by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN), using English web ('spiderweb, interwoven network'), inherited from Old English webb ('woven fabric, tapestry'), from Proto-Germanic *wabją ('something woven', derived from the root of weave).

history.meaning: website (short for página web / sitio web); the Web

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: web
Wiktionary — web

web.notes: Gender tip: in Spain, la web (feminine, elliptic for la página web) is the everyday word for an individual 'website' (quítala de la web = 'take her off the website!'), not just the entire Internet.

whatsapp.etymology: Global messaging trademark WhatsApp (launched in 2009 by Jan Koum and Brian Acton), coined in English as a punning blend of the casual greeting What's up? ('What's going on?') + app (clipping of software application).

history.meaning: WhatsApp platform; an individual WhatsApp message

rootFamily.gloss: RAE Hispanicized common noun for a WhatsApp message

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: wasap
Wiktionary — WhatsApp

whatsapp.notes: Spain is overwhelmingly a WhatsApp country (far more than SMS): mandar un WhatsApp (pronounced [ɡwaˈsap] or [waˈsap], also spelled un wasap by the RAE) means 'to send a text message on WhatsApp'.

wikipedia.etymology: Proper name of the collaborative online encyclopedia Wikipedia (launched in January 2001 by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger), blending wiki (borrowed by programmer Ward Cunningham in 1995 from Hawaiian wikiwiki 'quick, fast' for user-editable web pages) + -(encyclo)pedia (< Neo-Latin encyclopaedia < Hellenistic Greek enkyklopaideía 'well-rounded general education').

sources.title: Wiktionary — Wikipedia

wikipedia.notes: Often used in Spanish either without an article (Míralo en Wikipedia) or with feminine article la Wikipedia (matching la enciclopedia).

xviii.etymology: Roman numeral XVIII ('18 / eighteenth'), composed of additive symbols X ('ten') + V ('five') + III ('three'), continuing standard ancient Roman epigraphic notation; in Spanish historical and artistic style expressions (muy XVIII, el siglo XVIII), it represents el siglo dieciocho ('the eighteenth century').

rootFamily.gloss: eighteen (spoken form of XVIII for centuries and kings)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Ortografía: números romanos

xviii.notes: Two golden Spanish rules for centuries: (1) ALWAYS write centuries in uppercase Roman numerals (siglo XVIII, never *siglo 18); and (2) from XI (11) onward, ALWAYS read them aloud as cardinal numbers, not ordinals—so muy XVIII is pronounced [muj ðjeθiˈotʃo]!

y.etymology: The conjunction y continues Latin et ('and'), which diphthongized in Old Spanish and reduced in unstressed position to a palatal vowel spelled y.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: y

y.notes: Before words beginning with an /i/ sound spelled i- or hi- (such as invierno or hijo), y changes to e to avoid repeating the same vowel sound.

ya.etymology: Ya descends regularly from Latin iam ('already, by now, right away'), with initial Latin i- palatalizing before a vowel into Castilian y-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ya

ya.notes: Depending on tense and tone, ya means 'already' (ya son las doce), 'now' (ya eres del equipo), or 'coming right away!' (¡Ya voy!).

years.etymology: Plural of English noun year (spoken inside Mariona Terés's English self-tape introduction 'and I am 25 years old'), inherited from Old English ġēar ('year'), from Proto-Germanic *jērą ('year, harvest season') and Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁r- ('year, spring').

history.meaning: quoted English self-tape formula ('25 years old')

sources.title: Wiktionary — year

years.notes: Appears in the standard English actor-slate formula ('My name is..., and I am 25 years old'), contrasting English 'I AM 25 years old' with Spanish 'TENGO veinticinco años' ('I HAVE 25 years').

yo.etymology: Yo comes through Vulgar Latin eo from Latin ego. The DLE groups it with the related case forms me and mí; modern Spanish uses yo when the speaker is the subject.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo

yo.notes: Yo can be omitted when the verb already identifies the speaker, or retained for contrast and emphasis.

yudoca.etymology: Hispanicized borrowing (also spelled judoca; common gender el yudoca / la yudoca) from Japanese 柔道家 (jūdōka, 'practitioner of judo'), compounded from Sino-Japanese 柔道 (jūdō, coined in 1882 by Kanō Jigorō from 柔 jū 'gentle, yielding' + 道 dō 'way, martial path') plus the specialist agent suffix 家 (-ka, 'expert, practitioner').

rootFamily.gloss: karate practitioner (sharing the same Japanese -ka suffix!)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yudoca
Wiktionary — yudoca

yudoca.notes: Common-gender noun despite ending in -a: un yudoca (male) / una yudoca (female), just like karateca. The RAE accepts both phonetic yudoca and etymological judoca.

zanahoria.etymology: The DLE derives zanahoria from Hispanic Arabic safunnárya (via North African Arabic), ultimately borrowed from Greek staphylînē agría ('wild carrot / parsnip').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: zanahoria

zanahoria.notes: Shared uniquely across Iberian Romance alongside Portuguese cenoura and Catalan safanòria.

zapato.etymology: Word of uncertain medieval origin (attested in Early Medieval Hispanic Latin as sapatum / zabatum, connected with Arabic sabbāṭ and Turkic/Mediterranean footwear terms).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: zapato
Wiktionary — zapato

zoom.etymology: Twentieth-century optical and photographic borrowing from English zoom (short for zoom lens, introduced in 1930s cinematography from aviation slang to zoom 'to climb or swoop rapidly with a humming roar'), an English onomatopoeia imitating rapid motion.

history.meaning: camera or smartphone screen zoom (hacer zoom)

rootFamily.gloss: RAE Hispanicized spelling of optical zoom

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: zum
Wiktionary — zoom

zoom.notes: In Spain, speakers pronounce zoom either [θum] or [sum] and form the verb phrase with hacer: ¡Es que yo no sé hacer zoom! ('I don't know how to zoom in!').

zumo.etymology: Borrowed from Andalusi Arabic zúm (Classical Arabic zūm, 'juice, sap'), itself from Ancient Greek zōmós ('broth, sauce, juice').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: zumo
Wiktionary — zumo

ángel.etymology: Masculine personal name Ángel (here in the compound given name of Madrid actor and singer Miguel Ángel Muñoz) and common noun ángel ('angel'), semi-learned borrowing from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ángelos (ἄγγελος, 'messenger, envoy', translated in the Septuagint for Hebrew mal'ākh 'messenger of God').

history.meaning: angel; effortless charm (tener ángel); masculine given name

cognates.meaning: via Old French and Ecclesiastical Latin from Greek ángelos

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ángel
Wiktionary — ángel

ángel.notes: In Spanish showbiz and flamenco, tener ángel ('having angel') is a wonderful idiom meaning 'to have natural charisma, warmth, and stage magic'!

ángeles.etymology: Plural of ángel ('angels'), here in the Californian metropolis Los Ángeles—founded by Spanish settlers in 1781 as El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles ('The Town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels'). Ultimately from Late Latin angelus < Ancient Greek ángelos ('messenger').

history.form: (El Pueblo de la Reina de) los Ángeles -> Los Ángeles

rootFamily.gloss: native or resident of Los Angeles

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: Los Ángeles
Wiktionary — Los Ángeles

ángeles.notes: Because Los Ángeles is originally a Spanish name, Spanish keeps the written acute accent on Án-ge-les [los ˈaŋxeles] (never unaccented English *Los Angeles)!

árbol.etymology: Inherited from Latin arborem (nominative arbor, 'tree'), with dissimilation of the final -r to -l (Old Spanish árbor > árbol) and a shift from Latin feminine to Romance masculine gender.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: árbol
Wiktionary — árbol

ático.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin Atticus (< Ancient Greek Attikós, 'Athenian, of Attica'); in classical architecture it designated a low decorative story above the main entablature, and hence a top-floor apartment or penthouse.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ático
Wiktionary — ático

él.etymology: Third-person masculine singular tonic pronoun ('he, him') inherited from Latin ille ('that one, he'), written with a diacritical accent to distinguish it from the unstressed article el.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: él
Wiktionary — él

época.etymology: Learned borrowing via Modern/Late Latin epocha from Ancient Greek epokhḗ (ἐποχή, 'check, pause, fixed astronomical point, starting point of a historical era'), derived from epékhō (epi- 'upon' + ékhō 'to hold, stop'). Broadened in modern Romance from a 'fixed chronological reference point' to an entire 'historical era, period, or age'.

history.meaning: era, historical period, time of life

cognates.meaning: grand/geological in English, whereas Spanish época is very everyday!

rootFamily.gloss: period piece, costume drama (serie de época, vestuario de época)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: época
Wiktionary — época

época.notes: Essential TV/film phrase: una serie de época / una película de época (or Paquita's cozy una cosita de época) is the exact Spanish term for a 'period drama / costume drama'!

éxito.etymology: Éxito comes as a learned borrowing from Latin exĭtus, meaning an going out, outcome or result. In modern Spanish the word narrowed specifically to a favourable outcome or success.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: éxito

éxito.notes: Watch out for the false friend with English 'exit': éxito means success, whereas a physical exit or departure is la salida.

íntimo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin intimus ('inmost, deepest, most secret; closest friend'), an irregular superlative built with *-tmmos on the prepositional/adverbial root in / intrā ('in, within', opposite of extimus 'outermost').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Late Latin intimātus / intimus

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: íntimo
Wiktionary — íntimo

íntimo.notes: False-tone note: whereas English 'intimate friends' can sound formal or romantic, Spanish somos íntimas amigas is the completely normal, everyday way to say 'we're super close / best friends'!

óptica.etymology: Learned borrowing via Medieval Latin optica from Ancient Greek optikḗ [tékhnē] (ὀπτική, 'the science of sight and light'), feminine adjective built on the Indo-European visual root *h₃ekʷ- ('eye, to see'; compare Greek ópsis 'sight, view' and ophthalmos 'eye').

history.meaning: optics (physics); optician's shop; figurative viewpoint or angle

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: óptica
Wiktionary — óptica

óptica.notes: Three useful meanings in Spain: (1) physics 'optics'; (2) a high-street glasses/contact-lens store (ir a la óptica = 'go to the optician's'); and (3) figuratively 'perspective, horizon' (abrir un poco la óptica = 'broaden one's outlook / field of view').

óscar.etymology: Hispanicized accented spelling Óscar of Hollywood's Academy Award statuette (dubbed Oscar in the 1930s by Academy librarian Margaret Herrick, reportedly because the golden figure resembled her Uncle Oscar), from the English masculine given name Oscar—itself drawing on two converging traditions: Old Irish Oscar ('deer-friend': os 'deer' + cara 'friend', popularized across Romantic Europe by James Macpherson's Ossian poems) and Old English Ōsgār / Old Norse Ásgeirr ('god-spear').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: óscar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: Óscar

óscar.notes: Two neat RAE grammar rules: (1) because paroxytone Ós-car ends in -r (not -n, -s, or a vowel), it MUST carry a written acute accent on Ó-; and (2) when naming the awards ceremony in the plural, the RAE recommends invariable los Óscar (la gala de los Óscar, rather than *los Óscars)!

último.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ultimus ('farthest, most distant, last'), superlative formed from the Indo-European distal root *ul- (compare ultrā 'beyond').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: último
Wiktionary — último

único.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin ūnicus ('one and only, sole, unmatched of its kind'), derived with -icus from ūnus ('one', < Old Latin oinos < Proto-Indo-European *óynos).

history.meaning: only (before noun / con lo); unique, one-of-a-kind (after noun)

cognates.meaning: borrowed via French from Latin ūnicus

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: único
Wiktionary — único

único.notes: Word-order superpower: BEFORE a noun or with neuter lo, único means 'THE ONLY' (el único problema = 'the only problem', Lo único que quiero es descansar = 'The only thing I want is to rest'); AFTER a noun, it means 'UNIQUE / one-of-a-kind' (una oportunidad única)!
